Reviews: The house tour is excellent and the estate walk is worth the extra; photography rules are strict. Pair with House on the Rock for whiplash.

Uniqueness: Sixty five acres of azaleas, camellias and roses on the Fowl River, with a 1930s mansion and a river cruise.
Reviews: The spring azaleas are the show, and the house tour is a bonus. Hot in summer, so go early.

Adventure: Dexter Avenue King Memorial Baptist Church
Uniqueness: The church where Martin Luther King Jr. pastored during the Montgomery bus boycott, with the pulpit, the stained glass and a basement exhibit.
Reviews: The sanctuary is still in use and the guides tell the boycott story from the pews. Dress respectfully.

Uniqueness: A 600 foot deep canyon on Lookout Mountain with a rim drive, waterfalls and trails, one of the deepest canyons east of the Mississippi.
Reviews: The rim drive has the overlooks and the canyon floor has the waterfalls. Go after rain for the flow.

Uniqueness: A Mississippian mound complex with 29 mounds, a plaza and a museum of engraved pottery and copper, on the Black Warrior River.
Reviews: The scale is impressive and the museum explains the culture well. Climb the big mound for the view.

Uniqueness: A campus with life size village sites for each Alaska Native culture, from Iñupiat sod houses to a Tlingit clan house, with artists working and dancers performing.
Reviews: The village sites and the dance performances are the reasons to come; it is the best introduction to Alaska's Native cultures before you travel anywhere else in the state.

Uniqueness: A boat into Favorite Channel or Stephens Passage where humpbacks feed in summer, with a naturalist and a hydrophone to hear them.
Reviews: The bubble net feeding is the thing people hope for and the hydrophone is the surprise; the boats are small and the water can be rough.

Uniqueness: A curved white building holding a 36,000 year old mummified bison, Alaska Native art and a sound room where you can hear the aurora translated into audio.
Reviews: The blue bison and the art galleries are the highlights and the architecture is the photograph; the aurora room is the surprise.

Uniqueness: A working musk ox farm where you meet animals that look like walking carpets, learn how their qiviut wool is harvested and usually get within a few feet of the herd.
Reviews: The tour is funny and informative and the animals are absurdly photogenic; the gift shop sells qiviut yarn at prices that will shock you.

Uniqueness: The best collection of Native American art in the country, with a room of katsina dolls, contemporary Indigenous painting and a courtyard of pueblo jewelry makers.
Reviews: The katsina gallery and the board of trustees' collection are the highlights; the museum is frank about the boarding schools and the jewelry market is real.

Uniqueness: The white desert mission on the Tohono O'odham reservation, with painted interior walls, carved doors and a restoration that has lasted decades.
Reviews: The interior is the surprise and the fry bread stand outside is the local lunch; it is an active church, so visitors should respect services.

Uniqueness: Two districts of saguaro forest around Tucson, with a scenic loop drive, petroglyphs and trails through cactus that can live 150 years.
Reviews: The west district at sunset is the photograph and the east district has the loop drive; go early or late, the midday heat is dangerous.

Uniqueness: A living cave with guided tours through cathedral sized rooms, flowstone and a underground stream, run by the Forest Service.
Reviews: The living cave is the real thing, not a commercial show cave. Book the longer tour.

Uniqueness: A presidential library on the Arkansas River with the Oval Office, the campaign memorabilia and a park and bridge on the riverfront.
Reviews: The exhibits are well done and the river park is free. Allow two hours.

Uniqueness: A Victorian mountain town of steep streets, stone walls, springs and a loop of shops and inns, built around healing water.
Reviews: The town is hilly and charming, with a famous passion play and a haunted hotel. Park and walk.

Uniqueness: The highest point in Arkansas, with a lodge on the rim, hang gliding, trails and a view over the Arkansas River valley.
Reviews: The drive up is the adventure and the overlooks are the payoff. The lodge is a good base.

Uniqueness: A one room museum of scent in a Berkeley cottage, with antique perfume organs, ambergris, civet and hundreds of raw materials you can smell, assembled by a perfumer over decades.
Reviews: It is small, strange and fascinating, and the self guided visit takes an hour; the owner's books are for sale and the collection is the real thing. Open Saturdays only.

Uniqueness: A perfumer's studio where you smell raw materials and blend your own fragrance in a small workshop, then take home a bottle of something nobody else owns.
Reviews: It is intimate and intensely sensory and the instructor explains the chemistry without jargon; a genuinely unusual gift.

Uniqueness: An island in the bay with an immigration station known as the Ellis Island of the west, Civil War barracks and a five mile loop with views of the city and Marin.
Reviews: The immigration museum is the emotional stop and the bike loop is the fun; the ferry books out and the island has no cars.

Uniqueness: The largest collection of restored locomotives in the country, in a 100,000 square foot building on the old Central Pacific shops, with a cab forward and a dining car you can walk through.
Reviews: The roundhouse and the sleeper car are the highlights and the weekend excursion train is the add on; children can climb on several cars.

Uniqueness: A desert polo field turned into a fashion show and a festival, with giant art installations, a Ferris wheel and headliners under the stars.
Reviews: The production is unmatched and the heat, walking and prices are brutal; the campgrounds are their own scene.

Typical Customer: History families, school groups, gold rush fans
Uniqueness: A gold rush town preserved as a living park, with a working stagecoach, a candy store in a brick 1850s building and shopkeepers in period dress.
Reviews: The stagecoach ride and the panning are the family draws; the town is small and the summer heat is serious.

Uniqueness: Ten acres of underground rooms, courtyards and fruit trees dug by one Sicilian immigrant with hand tools over 40 years to escape the valley heat.
Reviews: Visitors are astonished it exists; the tour is the only way in and the temperature stays in the 70s while Fresno bakes outside.

Uniqueness: Old growth coast redwoods within 30 minutes of the Golden Gate Bridge, with a boardwalk loop through trees that were standing before Columbus.
Reviews: Parking requires a reservation and the main loop is crowded by ten; the Dipsea and Bootjack trails are the escape and the fog keeps it cool.

Uniqueness: A painted adobe mountain covered in Bible verses and flowers, built by one man over thirty years in the desert near Slab City.
Reviews: It is sincere, free and deeply strange; respect the artist's rules and bring water. Combine with Bombay Beach.

Uniqueness: A baking and cooking school near the beach with classes in sourdough, croissants, pasta and seasonal cooking, taught in a bright open kitchen.
Reviews: The pastry classes are the strongest and the small groups mean real attention; book the bread series if you want a skill.

Uniqueness: Five peaks above a preserved gold rush main street, with above treeline bowls, a high speed gondola and a town you can walk at the base.
Reviews: The high alpine terrain is the draw and the altitude is real; the town is lively and the lift lines on peak weekends are the complaint.

Uniqueness: A ski mountain above a preserved Victorian mining town, with extreme terrain and a July wildflower bloom that draws botanists from other countries.
Reviews: Skiers come for the steeps and the town is the reason to stay; the wildflower festival in July books a year out.

Uniqueness: Daniel Libeskind's angular steel building and a collection of Native American, Latin American and western art, including the finest collection of Indigenous art in the country.
Reviews: The Indigenous arts galleries are the reason curators visit and the architecture is the family puzzle; the building is confusing and the map helps.

Uniqueness: The world's largest mineral hot springs pool, a block long and fed by a Yampah spring at 122 degrees, with the Colorado River running past the wall.
Reviews: The pool is the family side and the smaller therapy pool is quieter; it is busiest in ski season and the water is body temperature.

Typical Customer: Stephen King fans, couples, ghost hunters
Uniqueness: The grand hotel that inspired The Shining, with a nightly ghost tour through the concert hall, the tunnels and room 217, plus a hedge maze and mountain views.
Reviews: The tour is more history than scare and that is why it works; the hotel itself is worth a drink even if you do not stay.

Uniqueness: A forge in the Connecticut woods where you make a knife or a small blade in a day, with coal forges, anvils and instructors who teach the hammer rhythm first.
Reviews: The day is physical and satisfying and the shop smells like coal and hot steel; classes fill months ahead.

Uniqueness: A 1.5 mile road course in the Berkshire foothills where spectators can walk the paddock, sit on the hill at the uphill and watch vintage cars race without a grandstand ticket.
Reviews: The Labor Day vintage festival is the weekend to go; the track is small, the access is unmatched and the loudest cars are the point.

Uniqueness: The oldest college art museum in the western hemisphere, with a Van Gogh, a Trumbull revolution cycle and a room of African art, all free.
Reviews: The Trumbull paintings and the modern galleries are the route; it is free and rarely crowded on weekday afternoons.

Uniqueness: The du Pont gunpowder works on the Brandywine, with water powered mills you walk through, a powder yard demonstration that shakes the valley and the family mansion.
Reviews: The explosion demonstration is the reason children agree to the museum; the walk along the raceway is beautiful and mostly shaded.

Uniqueness: The flag that inspired the anthem, Julia Child's kitchen, the Greensboro lunch counter and Dorothy's ruby slippers in one free building on the Mall.
Reviews: The Star Spangled Banner room is the quiet moment and the transportation hall is for children; the building is easier to enter than the newer museums.

Uniqueness: The first museum of modern art in the country, in a Dupont Circle house with Renoirs, Rothkos and a Rothko room designed for quiet looking.
Reviews: The Rothko room is the reason people return and the house scale makes it intimate; it is small and the admission is modest.

Uniqueness: A seven mile barrier island of white sand, a wooden pier, a village of cottages and a free trolley that runs the length of it.
Reviews: The trolley makes it easy without a car, and the beach is wide and calm. Sunsets at the pier are the ritual.

Uniqueness: The oldest masonry fort in the continental United States, built from coquina shell stone that absorbed cannonballs, on the oldest continuously occupied European street grid in the country.
Reviews: Rangers fire cannons on weekends; the walls are fun to climb and the history is brutal and well told. Combine with the old town at dusk.

Uniqueness: A 1,200 acre former ranch turned wetland preserve with a boardwalk, oak hammocks and alligators everywhere, one of the best wildlife walks in central Florida.
Reviews: The alligators are close and the birds are abundant. Go early and stay on the path.

Uniqueness: The 2.5 mile superspeedway where NASCAR's biggest race runs, with a track tour, a museum and the banked turns you can walk on.
Reviews: The track tour is the way to feel the banks, and the 500 is the bucket list event. Book tours ahead.

Uniqueness: A flat-bottomed fan boat skims a sawgrass river at 40mph, stopping for alligators, herons and the strange silence of the actual swamp.
Reviews: Coopertown is the oldest operator and gets praise for real guides; the souvenir-photo upsell is universal. Bring ear protection for kids.

Uniqueness: Eighty three acres of tropical plants, with a rainforest, a butterfly conservatory, a palm collection and a tram tour.
Reviews: The butterfly house and the tram are the easy wins, and the collection is world class. Hot in summer, so go early.

Uniqueness: A free museum with a butterfly rainforest, fossil skeletons, Florida's native cultures and a giant shark jaw, on the UF campus.
Reviews: The butterfly rainforest is the kid hit and the fossils are serious. Free, with a small fee for the butterfly house.

Uniqueness: A state park with dunes, a coastal dune lake, a beach of white sand and campsites under scrub oak, on Scenic 30A.
Reviews: The beach is quieter than the towns and the dune lake is unusual. Book camping early.

Uniqueness: A sea island cotton plantation with the planter's house and the tabby slave cabins still standing, on a marsh island in the Timucuan preserve.
Reviews: The slave cabins are the powerful part, and the ranger talks are excellent. Free.

Uniqueness: A Cuban neighborhood centered on Calle Ocho, with cigar rollers, ventanitas, domino players at Maximo Gomez Park and croquetas on every block.
Reviews: Go hungry and walk Calle Ocho, then sit in the domino park. The cigar shops are happy to show you how it is done.

Uniqueness: A sea turtle hospital with tanks of recovering turtles, a surgical suite and nesting beach programs, free to visit.
Reviews: The turtles are close and the staff explain the injuries and the nesting season. Free, with a donation suggested.

Uniqueness: A 140,000 acre refuge beside the space center, with a wildlife drive, manatees, alligators and some of the best birding in the state.
Reviews: The Black Point drive is the easy win, especially in winter for waterfowl. Bring binoculars and bug spray.

Uniqueness: One of the oldest and largest state parks, with a canopy walkway, a river boat tour, alligators and a grassy prairie.
Reviews: The canopy walk and the boat tour are the two things to do, and the gators are everywhere. Go early.

Uniqueness: A 21,000 acre prairie with wild horses, bison, alligators and a boardwalk, plus a sinkhole that once drained a lake.
Reviews: The bison and horses are a surprise in Florida, and the observation tower is the view. Bring bug spray.

Uniqueness: A first magnitude spring with glass bottom boat tours, kayak rentals and monkeys in the trees, one of Florida's oldest attractions.
Reviews: The glass bottom boat is the classic and the spring water is impossibly clear. Kayaking is the better way to see it.

Uniqueness: A park on the pass between the Gulf and St. Andrews Bay, with a snorkeling jetty, a shell island ferry and a beach that stays calm.
Reviews: The jetty snorkeling is the draw, with fish and clear water. Good for kids.

Uniqueness: Twin waterfalls dropping 150 feet side by side, reached by a paved half mile trail through hemlock and rhododendron in the Chattahoochee forest.
Reviews: The trail is steep in spots but paved, and the falls are loud after rain. Go early to beat the Helen crowds.

Uniqueness: A bare granite monadnock with solution pits, rare plants and red pools, twenty minutes from downtown Atlanta and unlike anything else in the metro.
Reviews: The loop is easy and the rock is otherworldly. Wear grippy shoes, bring water, and go early because there is no shade.

Uniqueness: A campus with the 1928 Swan House, a Civil War exhibit, a reconstructed farm and gardens, telling Atlanta's story from the Creek land to the civil rights era.
Reviews: The Swan House and the farm are the two poles and both are good. The Cyclorama is the older attraction, now restored.

Uniqueness: The highest state park in Georgia, with a summit overlook at 3,640 feet, a waterfall trail and campsites in a hardwood forest.
Reviews: The overlook is the best sunset in the state, and the trail to Ada-Hi Falls is short and steep. Bring a jacket, even in summer.

Uniqueness: A Victorian cemetery on a bluff over the Wilmington River, with live oaks, Spanish moss and the graves that made Midnight in the Garden of Good and Evil famous.
Reviews: People come for the book and stay for the sculpture. Go early, keep your voice down, and skip it during a funeral.

Uniqueness: A puppetry museum with Jim Henson's original Muppets, a global collection of marionettes and a working theater that stages shows for kids and adults.
Reviews: The Henson gallery is the reason adults come without kids. The puppet shows cost extra and are worth it, especially the adult nights.

Adventure: Chief Vann House State Historic Site
Typical Customer: History travellers, architecture people, Cherokee history readers
Uniqueness: A brick federal style mansion built by a Cherokee planter in 1804, with a floating staircase and hand carved mantels, preserved as the finest surviving building of the Cherokee Nation before removal.
Reviews: The house is beautiful and the story of how the Vanns lost it is the part that lands. Guided tours explain the spiral staircase and the removal.

Uniqueness: Three thousand acres of pine forest with motocross tracks, peewee tracks, ATV trails and rental cabins, so a family with mixed skill levels can ride in the same day.
Reviews: The pee wee track makes it a real family destination; the main motocross track is serious. Rentals and gear are available on site.

Uniqueness: Six earthen mounds built by the Mississippian culture a thousand years ago, with a plaza, a village site and a museum of copper and shell art.
Reviews: The scale of the mounds is the surprise, and the museum explains the chiefdom well. Climb the largest mound for the view.

Adventure: Georgia Museum of Agriculture and Historic Village
Typical Customer: Families, school groups, farm history people
Uniqueness: A recreated 1870s south Georgia town with a working steam train, a turpentine still, a grist mill and a farm, built as the state's agricultural museum and run by the college next door.
Reviews: The train ride and the turpentine operation get the most talk. It is big enough to fill an afternoon and rarely crowded on weekdays.

Season / Dates: First and last weekends of each month, reservations required
Uniqueness: Eight thousand protected acres on Lookout Mountain with a blue-green lake below a waterfall, opened to the public only on the first and last weekends of the month, with a trail network that connects to the Chattanooga trail system.
Reviews: The waterfall and lake are the payoff and the limited weekends keep it quiet. Reservations go fast in spring, so book when the window opens.

Typical Customer: History travellers, Cherokee history readers, school groups
Uniqueness: The capital of the Cherokee Nation before removal, reconstructed with the council house, the supreme court building and the print shop where the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper was set in Sequoyah's syllabary.
Reviews: The print shop is the part people do not expect, a bilingual newspaper printed here in the 1820s. The site is quiet and the story is heavy.

Uniqueness: Guided canoe and kayak trips into the Okefenokee from the Suwannee Canal, through cypress tunnels where alligators and herons are routine.
Reviews: The guided canoe trip is the way to see the swamp quietly. Book ahead in spring and bring water.

Uniqueness: A state park inside the Okefenokee wilderness, reached by a long dirt road, with canoe rentals, guided boat trips and dark skies for stargazing.
Reviews: Remote in the best way, with cypress tunnels and almost no light pollution. Book canoe trips ahead and bring food.

Uniqueness: A park with the ruins of the New Manchester textile mill on the creek, burned by Sherman's troops, reached by a trail through pine and floodplain.
Reviews: The mill ruins are the photo and the story, and the red trail is a real hike with a rocky descent. Go early for parking.

Uniqueness: A science museum with a real T. rex, a mineral gallery, a planetarium and a fossil dig, plus a collection of vintage cars and aircraft.
Reviews: The dinosaur and the gem room are the hits, and the planetarium shows are included. Allow three hours.

Uniqueness: One of the largest museums of African American art and history in the South, with a gallery of Black artists and an exhibit on the Middle Georgia civil rights movement.
Reviews: The art collection is stronger than visitors expect and the local history is told plainly. Allow two hours.

Uniqueness: The only royal palace on American soil, with a throne room, a koa wood staircase and the quilt the queen made in prison, restored to the 1890s.
Reviews: The audio tour is the way to see it and the basement galleries add the overthrow story; book ahead and wear the booties they give you.

Uniqueness: A 212 foot waterfall on the Snake River, taller than Niagara, dropping into a canyon in the middle of the desert.
Reviews: The flow is diverted for irrigation and is strongest in spring; the overlook is a short walk and the park has a swimming area below.

Uniqueness: Twelve acres of pond, stream and strolling garden designed by a Japanese master gardener, with a tea house and a waterfall.
Reviews: Gardeners call it the best Japanese garden in the midwest and the koi are the family draw; the spring and fall are the peak seasons.

Uniqueness: A 1.25 mile promenade along the Chicago River with bars, kayak rentals, architecture tours and the bridges overhead.
Reviews: The river level view of the architecture is the reason, and the bars are a good stop. Best at sunset.

Uniqueness: A river town of brick storefronts, steep streets and 19th century houses, once a lead mining boomtown and now a weekend getaway.
Reviews: The main street is polished and the houses are beautiful. Busy in fall.

Uniqueness: A free zoo in the middle of the city with lions, apes, penguins and a farm, open every day of the year.
Reviews: Free and genuinely good, which is rare for a city zoo. The penguin house is the kid favorite.

Uniqueness: The largest state park in Indiana, with ridge trails, a fire tower, a lodge and some of the best fall color in the Midwest.
Reviews: The fire tower view is the payoff and the trails are rolling. October is packed.

Uniqueness: A living history park with an 1836 village, a Lenape camp, a working farm and a balloon ride.
Reviews: The interpreters are good and kids can try chores and crafts. Allow half a day.

Uniqueness: A museum of the 500 with winning cars, trophies and the bricks, plus a track tour on the speedway.
Reviews: The winning cars and the track tour are the reasons. Book the tour with the museum.

Uniqueness: An art museum and 152 acre campus with gardens, a lake, a greenhouse and a sculpture park.
Reviews: The gardens and the art are both strong, and the campus is a good walk. Free on some days.

Uniqueness: Two hundred prehistoric mounds shaped like bears, birds and lines on bluffs above the Mississippi, with trails through the woods.
Reviews: The bear mounds are subtle but the setting is beautiful. The bluff trail is a real hike.

Uniqueness: A 500 acre open air museum with an 1700s Ioway village, an 1850 farm, a 1900 farm and a small town, with interpreters in period dress.
Reviews: The breadth of the three farms is the strength, and kids can help with chores. Allow three hours.

Uniqueness: The Eisenhower boyhood home, museum and library, with his boyhood home furnished as it was and a gallery on the war and the interstate highways.
Reviews: The boyhood home and the Oval Office replica are the stops; the museum is honest about the decisions and the grounds are free.

Uniqueness: The last large expanse of tallgrass prairie in North America, with bison, prairie chickens and a horizon that does not stop.
Reviews: People call it the most underrated landscape in the Midwest; spring wildflowers are extraordinary. Watch for ticks.

Uniqueness: A 247 acre zoo with elephants, gorillas, a farm, a train and a children's petting area, one of the best in the Plains.
Reviews: Big enough for a full day and shady in stretches. The train is the kid favorite.

Uniqueness: A tour 650 feet underground in a working salt mine, with tunnels, mining equipment and a underground vault.
Reviews: The descent and the scale of the mine are the experience. Bring a jacket, it is cool down there.

Uniqueness: One of the only places in the world where a lunar rainbow forms regularly in the mist of a waterfall, visible a few nights a month, by reservation at the overlook.
Reviews: Seeing it is luck and patience; the falls are spectacular regardless. Night programs are well run by park staff.

Uniqueness: A 170,000 acre national recreation area between two lakes, with a bison and elk prairie, a planetarium and trails.
Reviews: The elk and bison range is the kid draw, and the lakes are good for boating. Allow a full day.

Uniqueness: A 60 foot natural sandstone arch on a ridge above Red River Gorge, with a skylift, a lodge and trails.
Reviews: The arch is an easy walk and the skylift saves the climb. Busy in fall.

Uniqueness: A small distillery in a stone building with copper stills, rickhouses and a tasting, on the Kentucky Bourbon Trail.
Reviews: The tour is polished and the setting is beautiful. Book ahead on weekends.

Uniqueness: Inmates ride bulls and compete in poker-on-horseback inside a maximum-security prison, with a craft fair of prison-made goods and a crowd of thousands.
Reviews: People call it the most complicated day of their trip, spectacle, exploitation and genuine skill all at once. Tickets sell out.

Uniqueness: The oldest cemetery in the city, with above ground tombs, the grave of Marie Laveau and a maze of family vaults.
Reviews: You can only enter with a guide now, and the history of the burial customs is the point. Book ahead.

Uniqueness: A living history village of Acadian, Creole and Native American houses on the bayou, with music, cooking and craft demonstrations.
Reviews: The music and food demos are the best part, and the village is shady and walkable. Good for kids.

Company / Access: Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands
Uniqueness: A ridge of granite hills above Camden harbor, with trails to Mount Battie and a view of Penobscot Bay and the islands.
Reviews: The Mount Battie road is the easy view and the ridge trail is the real hike; the park is popular in October.

Company / Access: Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association
Uniqueness: A state fair rebuilt around draft horses, oxen, heirloom seeds and woodlot skills, fried dough exists, but so does a working cider press and a sheepdog trial.
Reviews: People describe it as the anti-state-fair: earnest, enormous, and genuinely useful. Parking and the Saturday crowd are the recurring gripes.

Typical Customer: Groups, families with teens, adventure seekers
Uniqueness: Class IV and V whitewater on a dam controlled river, with a 12 foot drop at Magic Falls and a calmer float below for the second half.
Reviews: Outfitters say the autumn release weekends are the biggest water; the river is cold and the trip runs rain or shine.

Uniqueness: A shipyard museum on the Kennebec where a 19th century shipbuilding yard is preserved, with a working wooden boat shop and cruises on the river.
Reviews: The boat shop and the yard are the real thing and the river cruise is the add on; children like the lobstering exhibit.

Uniqueness: A flat two mile path along the granite cliffs of Acadia from Sand Beach to Otter Point, passing Thunder Hole and the pink granite ledges.
Reviews: Thunder Hole is the crowded stop and Otter Cliff is the photograph; the path is easy and the waves at high tide are the show.

Uniqueness: The largest ski area in the east by vertical, with above treeline terrain, a snowfields bowl and a drive that ends in the middle of nowhere.
Reviews: Skiers come for the steeps and the lack of crowds midweek; the access road is long and the wind holds lifts.

Uniqueness: The bloodiest single day in American history, preserved as farmland and lanes; the Cornfield and Burnside Bridge are within a short walk of the road.
Reviews: Rangers and the driving tour are highly rated; the visitor center film sets up the geography well. Quiet and sobering.

Adventure: Harriet Tubman Underground Railroad Visitor Center
Company / Access: National Park Service and Maryland State Parks
Typical Customer: History people, students, civil rights pilgrims
Uniqueness: A visitor center in the marsh landscape Tubman grew up in, telling her story through the places she worked and fled, with a driving tour to the sites.
Reviews: The building and the landscape carry the story and rangers lead walks; the driving tour takes a half day and the roads are flat and empty.

Uniqueness: A gorge walk past Muddy Creek Falls, the tallest in the state, under hemlocks that are among the oldest east of the Mississippi.
Reviews: The loop is a mile and the falls are the reward; the hemlock canopy keeps it cool in summer and icy in winter.

Uniqueness: The yard where every American naval officer is trained, with a chapel crypt holding John Paul Jones, a 1906 chapel dome and a museum of ship models.
Reviews: The guided tour is free and walks you past the midshipmen, who are still in formation; visitors need a government ID and the museum is separate.

Uniqueness: Colored clay cliffs on the western tip of Martha's Vineyard, tribal land above a beach of red and white sand, with a lighthouse and a view to the Elizabeth Islands.
Reviews: The cliffs are protected and you cannot climb them; the beach walk at low tide is the way and the sunset from the overlook is the photo.

Uniqueness: A red brick line through 16 Revolutionary sites in 2.5 miles, from a graveyard where Paul Revere is buried to the deck of the USS Constitution.
Reviews: Everyone says do it yourself with the free map and duck into the North End for cannoli. Guided tours get mixed reviews for crowd control.

Uniqueness: The Blaschka glass flowers, 4,300 models made of glass in the 1880s so accurate that botanists still use them, plus a whale skeleton ceiling and a mineral gallery.
Reviews: People come for the glass flowers and are surprised by the zoology galleries; the whole museum takes two hours and is good in any weather.

Uniqueness: The world's largest whaling museum, with half scale whale skeletons hanging over a full scale whaling ship, a scrimshaw collection and the logbooks of the voyages that made the city rich.
Reviews: The skeleton room is the one people describe; the museum does not soften the industry and the harbor walk outside completes it.

Uniqueness: Two hundred acres of a New England town rebuilt around a common, with a working farm, a tin shop, a printing office and interpreters who stay in character.
Reviews: Allow four hours and check the daily schedule for the blacksmith and the farm; children like the animals and the stagecoach.

Uniqueness: The pond where Thoreau built his cabin, with a replica of the house, a trail around the shore and a beach where people still swim in water clear enough to see the bottom.
Reviews: Go early in summer or the lot closes; the cabin site is a half mile walk and the far shore is quiet even on hot days.

Uniqueness: A Saarinen designed campus with a science museum, an art academy and a house by Eliel Saarinen, plus a Japanese garden and a fountain by Carl Milles.
Reviews: The art museum and the house are the stops and the gardens are a separate hour; it is a campus rather than a single museum.

Uniqueness: A 50-foot curtain of amber water tinted by cedar tannins, with a lower falls you can row to and a brewpub at the park entrance.
Reviews: The upper falls are the photo; the lower falls are the swim. Black flies in June are legendary.

Adventure: Grand Marais and the Gunflint Trail
Uniqueness: A harbor town at the edge of the Boundary Waters with a 57 mile road into the lakes, a donut shop and a coastline of basalt and birch.
Reviews: The Gunflint Trail and the harbor are the two reasons to come and the fall color is the season; the town is small and the wilderness starts immediately.

Uniqueness: The headwaters of the Mississippi, where you can wade across the river, plus old growth pine and a lodge.
Reviews: Walking across the Mississippi is the photo and the park is beautiful. The lodge is a good base.

Uniqueness: A 53 foot waterfall in a city park, with trails down to the creek and a seafood shack at the top.
Reviews: The falls are easy to reach and the park is lovely. The Sea Salt eatery is the local lunch.

Uniqueness: One thousand two hundred acres of display gardens, prairie and woods with a three mile drive, a sculpture garden and a bog walk.
Reviews: The azalea and hosta collections are the summer draws and the winter lights are the local tradition; the drive loop is the easy way to see it.

Uniqueness: A contemporary art center with a sculpture garden across the street, including the Spoonbridge and Cherry.
Reviews: The sculpture garden is free and the Spoonbridge is the photo. The museum is for contemporary tastes.

Uniqueness: The largest octagonal house in the country, unfinished since the Civil War, with its original crates and tools still inside.
Reviews: The unfinished interior is the fascinating part, and the tour explains why construction stopped. Book ahead in pilgrimage season.

Uniqueness: A Greek Revival mansion in the Natchez National Historical Park, with original furniture and the story of the enslaved people who ran the estate.
Reviews: The ranger tours are excellent and the slave quarters exhibit is part of the visit. Less flashy than the private houses and more honest.

Uniqueness: William Faulkner's home, preserved with his books, his outline of A Fable on the wall and the grounds he walked.
Reviews: Pilgrimage for readers, and the self guided tour lets you linger. The cedar grove is quiet.

Uniqueness: Sixteen miles of preserved siege lines, 1,300 monuments and the ironclad USS Cairo, pulled from the Yazoo River a century after it sank.
Reviews: The driving loop is excellent and the Cairo is the highlight; the terrain explains the campaign better than any book. Quiet and sobering.

Uniqueness: Cargo from a steamboat that sank in 1856, recovered intact from a cornfield, with tools, dishes, clothing and food still preserved.
Reviews: The everyday objects are the fascinating part, and the recovery story is improbable. Good for kids.

Uniqueness: A Romanesque cathedral with the largest mosaic collection in the world, 41 million pieces covering the ceiling in gold and color.
Reviews: The mosaics are astonishing and it is free. Go on a weekday for quiet.

Uniqueness: A stone castle ruin on a bluff above the Lake of the Ozarks, with a spring, a natural bridge and a waterfall in a dolomite canyon.
Reviews: The castle ruin is eerier and more beautiful than expected; the spring trail is a steep stair climb. Sunset is the time.

Uniqueness: A fossil bed where a volcanic ash fall killed a herd of rhinos, horses and camels 12 million years ago, now exposed in a working quarry.
Reviews: The skeletons are still in the ground where they died, which is the fascinating part. Seasonal, so check dates.

Uniqueness: A stretch of the Platte where half a million sandhill cranes stop each March, one of the largest bird migrations in the world.
Reviews: The dawn blinds are the way to see them close and the season is short; book months ahead and bring warm clothes.

Uniqueness: A free museum in a Art Deco building with European and American art, Native American works and a sculpture garden.
Reviews: Free and strong, with a beautiful building and a good cafe. The Western art collection is the local specialty.

Uniqueness: Three floors of race cars, engines and speed records, including land speed streamliners and a collection of pedal cars, in a building behind a parts warehouse.
Reviews: Car people call it a hidden gem; the engine cutaway displays are beautiful. Allow three hours.

Uniqueness: A spring fed river through the Sandhills with waterfalls, pine bluffs and a gentle current, one of the best floats in the Plains.
Reviews: The water is clear and the trip is easy. Rent a tube or a canoe and go in summer.

Adventure: Stuhr Museum of the Prairie Pioneer
Uniqueness: A 200 acre campus of relocated railroad town buildings around a lake, with a Pawnee earth lodge and a main building by Edward Durell Stone.
Reviews: The living history town and the Pawnee lodge are the reasons to give it three hours; the main building is a architectural landmark of its own.

Uniqueness: A museum in the Art Deco Union Station, with trains, a soda fountain, a street of old storefronts and the history of the Union Pacific.
Reviews: The station itself is gorgeous and the trains are the kid draw. Allow two hours.

Uniqueness: A glacier carved canyon in the Ruby Mountains with 12 miles of road, waterfalls and trailheads into alpine lakes, called the Switzerland of Nevada.
Reviews: The drive to the road end and the hike to Lamoille Lake are the standard; the canyon is snowed in from November to June.

Typical Customer: Poetry people, ranchers, folk music fans
Uniqueness: A week of cowboy poetry, music and storytelling in a Nevada cow town, with workshops, dances and performers who still work cattle.
Reviews: People arrive from ranches across the west and the late night sessions in the bars are the real festival; book lodging months ahead.

Uniqueness: A 7.6 mile road climbing 4,618 feet to the summit of the highest peak in the northeast, where the weather is measured in hurricane force and the view runs to Canada.
Reviews: The drive is narrow with no guardrails and the summit is 30 degrees colder; check the summit forecast, they close the road for wind.

Uniqueness: The sculptor's home and studio with the original plaster of the Shaw memorial, a colonnade he built for his casts and a garden that looks across the Connecticut River.
Reviews: Sculpture people call it a pilgrimage and the outdoor casts are the reason; the summer concert series on the lawn is the local event.

Uniqueness: The most decorated battleship in American history, with a 16 inch gun turret you can climb inside, a guided engine room tour and the captain's cabin.
Reviews: The turret climb is the thing people remember; the engine room tour costs extra and is worth it, and the deck view of Philadelphia is free.

Uniqueness: The oldest weekly professional rodeo in the country, running Saturday nights in a South Jersey field with bull riding, barrel racing and a calf scramble for children.
Reviews: Locals bring blankets to the bleachers and first timers are surprised by how fast the night goes; the funnel cake stand is the tradition.

Season / Dates: Year round, closed Mon–Tue in winter
Uniqueness: Forty-two acres of sculpture gardens built on a former state fairground, with life-size figures staged in unnervingly real tableaux.
Reviews: People are surprised by how much there is; the peacocks wander freely and the restaurant is genuinely good.

Typical Customer: History families, hikers, rev war people
Uniqueness: The winter encampment where the Continental Army survived 1779, with Washington's Ford Mansion, reconstructed log huts and 27 miles of trails through Jockey Hollow.
Reviews: The huts and the Wick House are the walk and the mansion tour is separate; the park is the first national historical park in the country.

Uniqueness: A university museum with a broad collection from ancient to modern, including Chinese bronzes and American painting, free to the public.
Reviews: The collection is better than most small city museums and it is free; the building is on the edge of the campus and easy to walk to.

Uniqueness: Edison's three story laboratory complex with 400,000 artifacts, a machine shop that could build anything and a recording studio where the first sound was captured.
Reviews: The chemistry lab and the machine shop are the best preserved; the ranger tour of the main building is worth timing your visit for.

Uniqueness: The largest collection of O'Keeffe's work in the world, from the Lake George flowers to the Ghost Ranch bones, in a adobe block a few steps from the plaza.
Reviews: The paintings and her studio objects together explain how she saw the landscape; the museum is small and the timed ticket keeps it calm.

Uniqueness: The red and yellow cliffs where Georgia O'Keeffe painted for decades, now a retreat and education center with trails, a museum and guided tours to her house.
Reviews: The landscape is the attraction and the tour to O'Keeffe's house needs booking; the trails are open and the light changes all afternoon.

Uniqueness: The longest aerial tram in the Americas: 2.7 miles up a sandstone cliff to a 10,378-foot summit with a restaurant and trails in the spruce forest.
Reviews: The ride is smooth and the view is enormous; sunset is the best slot. The restaurant is convenient, not a destination.

Uniqueness: A maze of rooms built from bottles and cement, filled with thousands of carved wooden figures and animated miniature scenes, on the road up to Sandia Crest.
Reviews: People describe it as a fever dream in the best way; the mechanical scenes are charming. Small and unforgettable.

Uniqueness: A campus museum on Blue Mountain Lake with a guideboat hall, a 19th century great camp, a logging exhibit you walk through and a working blacksmith.
Reviews: The guideboat collection is the surprise and the camp buildings are the reason to give it three hours; the lake view from the porch is the rest.

Uniqueness: A six story granite and limestone castle on an island in the St. Lawrence, abandoned mid construction in 1904 when the builder's wife died, now reached only by boat.
Reviews: The boat ride through the islands is half the trip; the upper floors were never finished and the story carries the tour.

Typical Customer: Hikers, trail runners, city day trippers
Uniqueness: A rock scramble straight up the Hudson Highlands from a train station platform, three false summits and a ridge walk with the river 900 feet below.
Reviews: It is the most crowded hike in the region for a reason; go before eight, wear real shoes, and skip it when the rocks are wet.

Uniqueness: A 1905 neoclassical gallery joined to a new SANAA building of glass bridges, holding one of the best modern collections in the country and a mirrored indoor bridge over a reflecting pool.
Reviews: The new building is the draw but the Clyfford Still and Rothko rooms are what artists come for; the free first Friday is when Buffalo goes.

Uniqueness: A wooden walkway rebuilt every spring that takes you to within 20 feet of Bridal Veil Falls, where the wind is 70 mph and the rain is going up.
Reviews: The Hurricane Deck is the whole point and the poncho is useless; go early or late to avoid the tour bus hours.

Typical Customer: Photographers, film people, house tour fans
Uniqueness: The Kodak founder's 1905 mansion turned photography museum, with a working film preservation lab, a Technicolor camera and the world's oldest photography collection.
Reviews: The house and the technology galleries are separate pleasures; the dryden theatre screenings are the local film school.

Uniqueness: Vanderbilt's 27 building Adirondack camp of log and twig work on a private lake, with a bowling alley and a guideboat fleet, reachable only by a long dirt road.
Reviews: The guided tour is the only way in and people describe the scale as a national park lodge; stay overnight if you can, the rooms are original.

Typical Customer: First time flyers, aviation people, gift buyers
Uniqueness: A sailplane ride off the ridge that hosted the first national soaring contest in 1930, where the engine is a tow plane and the silence after release is the attraction.
Reviews: Riders say the 20 minute flight feels longer and the thermal over the Chemung valley is the ride; book a week out and expect weather cancellations.

Uniqueness: Three floors of plaques, gloves, jerseys and the actual record of the game, in a village that invented the Cooperstown origin myth and then built a museum around it.
Reviews: Even casual fans are moved by the plaque room; induction weekend in July is a zoo but electric.

Uniqueness: A museum where you build a personal comedy profile at the door and the exhibits adapt to it, with Carlin's notebooks, a comedy club stage and a hologram room.
Reviews: People expect a small town museum and get two hours of interactive exhibits; the adult only late nights are the local favorite.

Uniqueness: A 250 acre Olmsted plan around the Haupt conservatory, with a patch of old growth forest that was never cut and a holiday train show that runs model trains past New York landmarks built out of bark.
Reviews: Regulars insist on the conservatory plus the forest trail; the orchid show in spring is the busiest week of the year and needs a timed ticket.

Uniqueness: Sixty countries of cooking at stall prices in Flushing Meadows Corona Park under the Unisphere, with a cap that keeps most plates at six dollars or less.
Reviews: Arrive at five before the lines form; the Trinidadian doubles and Colombian arepas are repeat picks, and half the stalls still want cash.

Adventure: Sporting Clays — Golf with a Shotgun
Uniqueness: A 14-station course through Hudson Valley woods and fields where you shoot clay targets along a walking route, scored like golf, the closest thing to a round of golf with a shotgun.
Reviews: Instructors are excellent with first timers and the setting is beautiful; bring a group and make it a morning. Reservations required.

Uniqueness: A natural history museum of the Adirondacks with an elevated walkway through the treetops, otters, and a bog you can walk into without getting wet.
Reviews: The Wild Walk canopy is the reason people drive three hours; the otter tank and the forest music installation are the sleepers.

Uniqueness: A ruined 1889 railroad bridge rebuilt as a 1.28 mile pedestrian deck 212 feet above the Hudson, with a glass elevator down to the river trail.
Reviews: Sunset is the time, the wind is constant, and the elevator on the Poughkeepsie side saves the stairs; it is fully accessible.

Company / Access: New York State Olympic Regional Development Authority
Uniqueness: An eight mile road that climbs to a parking lot at 4,500 feet, where a tunnel and elevator take you the last 300 feet to a summit view of the Adirondacks and Vermont.
Reviews: The elevator through the mountain is the quirk; bring a jacket, since it is 20 degrees colder up top even in July.

Uniqueness: The Connemara farm where the poet and biographer lived, with his study, his wife's goat herd and trails up the hill.
Reviews: The house tour is intimate and the goats are the kid draw. The grounds are free.

Uniqueness: The club where Nirvana, the Replacements and Superchunk played early shows, still booking indie and alternative acts in a room with no barrier between band and crowd.
Reviews: The sound is loud and the history is real. Check the calendar, because the good shows sell out.

Uniqueness: A 1.5 mile quad oval with 24 degree banks, host of the Coca-Cola 600, with a dirt track and a zMAX dragway on the same campus.
Reviews: The night race is the spectacle, and the infield is a party. The track tour runs on non race days.

Company / Access: Chimney Rock at Chimney Rock State Park
Uniqueness: A 315-foot granite monolith with an elevator cut through the mountain to the top, and a 404-foot waterfall, Hickory Nut Falls, a short trail away.
Reviews: The elevator saves the climb and the view over Lake Lure is the payoff; the stairs at the top are steep. Go early for the parking deck.

Uniqueness: A high heath bald on the Blue Ridge Parkway, covered in rhododendron and blueberries, with a short trail to a 360 degree view.
Reviews: The June rhododendron bloom is spectacular and the drive is half the experience. Bring a jacket and check the parkway closures.

Uniqueness: A quartzite ridge 25 minutes from Charlotte with a stair-and-scramble summit, 100-foot cliffs for top rope climbing and a view clear to the city skyline.
Reviews: Locals use it as a training hike; the backside trail is quieter and the cliffs draw Charlotte climbers after work. Parking fills by 9am on weekends.

Uniqueness: A brick ballpark in downtown Durham where the Bulls play under the Bull Durham legacy, with a snorting bull sign that lights up on home runs.
Reviews: Cheap seats, good food and a mascot that interacts with the crowd. The bull sign is the photo.

Uniqueness: A brick coastal fort built in the 1820s and fought over in the Civil War, with a moat, casemates and a beach on both sides.
Reviews: The fort is free and fun to explore, and the beach access makes it a two part day. Parking fills in summer.

Uniqueness: Class II and III whitewater on one of the oldest rivers in the world, with a hot spring town at the takeout and the Appalachian Trail crossing the bridge.
Reviews: Big enough for a thrill and safe enough for beginners. The hot tubs in town are the recovery plan.

Uniqueness: A Tuesday night contra dance with a live string band, a caller who walks beginners through every figure and a hall full of people of all ages swapping partners.
Reviews: No partner or experience needed, and the regulars are genuinely welcoming. The band alone is worth the cover.

Uniqueness: A 19th century cotton mill dye house turned music hall on the Haw River, with a general store and a pizza farm next door in a town of 1,600.
Reviews: The sound and setting are exceptional; shows sell out and the floor is general admission. Eat at the general store before the set.

Uniqueness: A 3,800 acre old growth forest with tulip poplars over 20 feet around, preserved as a memorial to the poet, reached by a two mile loop trail.
Reviews: The trees are genuinely enormous and the trail is easy. Go in spring for wildflowers and autumn for color.

Uniqueness: A clear mountain lake at the foot of the Blue Ridge, with a sandy swim beach, paddle rentals, and campsites on a peninsula.
Reviews: The water is clean and the beach is shallow, good for kids. Book campsites early in summer.

Uniqueness: A walk up window on a side street selling fried chicken, gizzards and sweet tea in paper boxes, with a line of nurses and construction crews by 11am.
Reviews: Charlotte natives treat it as scripture; the chicken is greasy, cheap and perfect. Cash only, no seats, no fuss.

Uniqueness: Fifty five acres of designed gardens in a Duke campus ravine, with a terraced rose garden, a Japanese garden and a native plant collection.
Reviews: Free, though parking costs on weekdays. The terraces in spring are the postcard.

Uniqueness: Eighteen thousand acres of rugged escarpment with the 80 foot High Shoals Falls, a staircase trail and trout streams, at the edge of the Blue Ridge.
Reviews: The waterfall loop is steep but short, and the park is less crowded than the big name gorge parks.

Uniqueness: A former hosiery mill turned glass studio and ceramics center in a small town, with classes, artist residencies and a cafe that locals treat as the town square.
Reviews: The scale is surprising for a town of 800 and the classes are small; book ahead for glassblowing weekends.

Uniqueness: A 600 foot granite dome with a loop trail, a waterfall, a historic mountain farm and trout streams, on the Blue Ridge escarpment.
Reviews: The summit loop is steep and worth it, with a view that feels much higher than it is. Go early for parking.

Uniqueness: Eleven ziplines and a sky bridge over a 1,100-acre gorge, with the longest line running a half mile above the Green River.
Reviews: Guides are funny and safety-focused; the hike between lines is real. Book the earliest slot for the best light and least heat.

Uniqueness: A 1,200-acre equestrian resort that hosts international show jumping, with Saturday Night Lights, a brewery and free general admission on many days.
Reviews: Even non-horse people enjoy the scene; parking is easy and the grounds are immaculate. Check the calendar for a big jumper night.

Uniqueness: A WWII battleship you can climb through from the engine rooms to the gun turrets, moored across the river from downtown, with a crew of veterans who volunteer on board.
Reviews: Plan on two hours and wear shoes you can climb ladders in; the depth of the ship surprises people. Veterans are often aboard to talk.

Uniqueness: A museum of rare American motorcycles, with boards of speed records, dirt track racers and military bikes, most of them in running condition.
Reviews: The curator starts engines, which makes it more alive than a normal museum. Even non riders enjoy it.

Uniqueness: The actual sand hill where the first powered flight left the ground, with a granite marker for each of the four flights and a replica camp building.
Reviews: Rangers give short talks that make the engineering drama vivid; the wind is constant. Combine with Jockey's Ridge sand dunes.

Company / Access: State Historical Society of North Dakota
Uniqueness: The state museum with a full size Triceratops, a reconstructed homestead shack and galleries on the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara nations, free on the capitol grounds.
Reviews: The adaptation gallery and the Native exhibits are the reasons to come and it is free; allow two hours and check the dome tour.

Uniqueness: Two warehouses of neon, bulb and painted signs from the last century, with a Main Street of storefronts and a workshop where restorers bring dead signs back to light.
Reviews: The neon room is a photographer's dream and the history of sign making is unexpectedly interesting; allow ninety minutes.

Uniqueness: The second oldest zoo in the country, with hippos, gorillas, a train and the Fiona the hippo story.
Reviews: Well laid out and shady, with the hippo exhibit as the draw. Allow half a day.

Uniqueness: A glasshouse with biomes from rainforest to desert, plus a butterfly garden and a collection of Chihuly glass.
Reviews: The Chihuly glass among the plants is the draw, and the butterfly house is a kid favorite.

Adventure: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
Company / Access: Rock and Roll Hall of Fame
Uniqueness: I.M. Pei's glass pyramid on the lake, holding Prince's guitar, Janis Joplin's Porsche and a hall of signatures that reads like a century of American noise.
Reviews: The films and artifacts are stronger than the interactives; allow four hours. The lakefront setting is best at sunset.

Uniqueness: A free art museum with a strong glass collection, Old Masters and a sculpture garden, in a Greek Revival building.
Reviews: The glass collection is the local specialty and the museum is free. A surprise for a mid sized city.

Uniqueness: A 1924 dance hall where Bob Wills and the Texas Playboys broadcast, still booking rock, country and indie acts under the original sign.
Reviews: The room is legendary and the sound is good. Check the calendar and buy ahead.

Uniqueness: A $465-million private park on the Arkansas River with a suspension bridge, a land bridge, giant slides and a boathouse, free, and better than most municipal parks in America.
Reviews: Parents call it the best free family day in the region; the playground is enormous and the beer garden is a nice touch.

Uniqueness: Frank Lloyd Wright's only built skyscraper, a 19 story copper and concrete tower with tours and a small hotel.
Reviews: For architecture people it is a pilgrimage, and the tour explains the design. The top floor view is a bonus.

Uniqueness: A 187,000 acre wetland in the high desert where 320 bird species have been recorded and sandhill cranes stage by the thousands in spring.
Reviews: The spring crane migration is the event and the auto tour route is the way to see it; the refuge is remote and the nearest town is 30 miles.

Uniqueness: A marble cave system with a tour through passages and a 1930s lodge at the entrance, reached by a winding road through the Siskiyous.
Reviews: The cave tour is ranger led and needs a ticket and the marble formations are the highlight; the road is narrow and the cave is 42 degrees.

Uniqueness: A formal garden on a sandstone bluff above a surf beach, built as the estate of a lumber baron, with a Japanese garden and a rose garden.
Reviews: The garden above the surf is the photograph and the winter storm waves are the local spectacle; the garden peaks in summer.

Uniqueness: The steepest four passenger gondola in North America, climbing 3,700 feet to the top of Mount Howard for a view of the Wallowa Mountains and Hells Canyon.
Reviews: The view from the top is the reason to ride and the trail along the summit is easy; the tram is weather dependent and the tickets are not cheap.

Uniqueness: The river cuts through the Kittatinny Ridge at a notch you can climb above on the Appalachian Trail, with a beach, a canoe launch and a view of New Jersey from the top.
Reviews: The Mount Tammany red dot trail is steep and crowded and the reward is the gap from above; the river beach is the easy alternative.

Company / Access: Society for the Preservation of the Duquesne Heights Incline
Uniqueness: A wooden 1877 funicular up Mount Washington, still run by hand by a operator in the upper station, ending at the three rivers view that defines the city.
Reviews: Ride up at dusk and walk down the steps or take it back; the upper station has a small museum of the machinery and the fare is cash friendly.

Uniqueness: The ridge where the modern raptor count began, with a lookout over the Kittatinny where hundreds of hawks and eagles pass on a good September day.
Reviews: Volunteers with clickers will teach you to identify a bird on the wing; the North Lookout is a short steep walk and the trail system continues for miles.

Uniqueness: A chocolate company's employee picnic ground turned 121 acre park with 15 coasters, a water park and a zoo, ringed by the smell of cocoa from the factory.
Reviews: Candymonium and Skyrush are the coaster draws; buy tickets online, arrive at opening and use the preview night if you are staying over.

Uniqueness: A 301 foot tall railroad viaduct that a tornado tore down in 2003, now a glass floored observation deck at the edge of the wreckage with the twisted towers still standing in the valley.
Reviews: The glass floor is the thrill and the fallen towers are the photo; the walk out is 600 feet and the valley is best in fall.

Typical Customer: Tool people, history fans, architecture students
Uniqueness: A concrete castle built to hold one man's collection of pre-industrial American tools, with a whaleboat hanging from the ceiling and a walkway that spirals up through six floors.
Reviews: The building is the exhibit and people describe it as a cathedral of hand tools; allow two hours because every case has something strange.

Typical Customer: Medical people, teens, the morbidly curious
Uniqueness: A Victorian cabinet of medical oddities: the Hyrtl skull collection, wax casts of disease, Einstein's brain slices and a giant colon named after its owner.
Reviews: People either find it fascinating or leave early; reviewers praise the respectful framing of human remains. Not for young kids.

Company / Access: Pennsylvania Department of Conservation and Natural Resources
Uniqueness: A seven mile sand spit curving into Lake Erie with eleven beaches, a flat multi use trail and a lagoon where migrating birds pile up in spring.
Reviews: Sunsets over the bay side are the local ritual; the peninsula trail is flat and the beaches get crowded only in July.

Uniqueness: The Bethlehem Steel plant turned arts campus, where the blast furnaces stand lit at night above a lawn that hosts free summer concerts and a film series.
Reviews: The furnaces at night are the photograph everyone takes; the free Levitt Pavilion shows are the local summer ritual.

Uniqueness: A craft campus in the Laurel Highlands with blacksmithing, glass, ceramics and wood workshops, plus lodging in cabins on the grounds.
Reviews: The classes are affordable and the setting is woodsy; it is close to Ohiopyle and Fallingwater for a combined trip.

Uniqueness: The winter camp where Washington's army survived 1777 with a reconstructed log city, earthworks you can walk and a 3,500 acre park with a bike trail through it.
Reviews: The ranger talks and the Muhlenberg Brigade huts are the best part; the loop road is flat and the park is free, which surprises people.

Uniqueness: Mohegan Bluffs drop 200 feet to a boulder beach, with a 19th century granite lighthouse offshore and 25 miles of empty road to bike.
Reviews: The ferry is the bottleneck; book bikes on the island and skip bringing a car. Mansion Beach and the bluffs are the two musts.

Uniqueness: A design school museum with a 12th century French chapel, a Mesopotamian lion, Gorham silver and a room of student work, all in a block of College Hill.
Reviews: The decorative arts and the costume galleries are quietly excellent; the museum is free on Sundays and students use it as a study hall.

Uniqueness: One of the largest undeveloped estuaries on the Atlantic coast, where the Ashepoo, Combahee and Edisto rivers braid through marsh and cypress, and dolphins and eagles are routine.
Reviews: Launch at Bennett's Point or Edisto and follow the marked paddling trail. There is no visitor center at the heart of it, which is why it stays quiet.

Uniqueness: A working thoroughbred training track where you can watch young horses gallop at dawn from the rail, on a track that has prepared winners for decades.
Reviews: Go before eight and stay quiet; trainers are working, not performing. Photographers love the fog and the light, and there is no admission.

Uniqueness: America's first public sculpture garden, with 2,000 works among live oaks and a Lowcountry zoo of native animals on a former rice plantation.
Reviews: The sculpture is world class and the zoo is a nice surprise for kids; summer heat is punishing. Go in March or November.

Uniqueness: A granite cliff at 3,200 feet looking over the Blue Ridge escarpment, with the Raven Cliff Falls suspension bridge hike and hawks migrating along the ridge in September.
Reviews: The view from the overlook is enormous and the fall hawk watch is a genuine spectacle. The falls trail is long and steep.

Uniqueness: The only large tea plantation in the United States, with a factory tour, a trolley through the fields and free samples of tea grown, picked and oxidized on the island.
Reviews: The trolley guide makes the history interesting even for non tea drinkers; the gift shop is dangerously good. A genuine oddity.

Uniqueness: The largest remaining old growth bottomland hardwood forest in the country, with a raised boardwalk over a cypress swamp and fireflies that sync in June.
Reviews: The firefly synchronization is a genuine phenomenon; mosquitoes are the price of admission. Rent a canoe for the Cedar Creek run.

Uniqueness: A beach park with maritime forest trails, a boneyard beach of fallen trees and a campground under live oaks, plus an environmental learning center.
Reviews: The beach is quieter than the resort islands and the forest trail is a real hike. Loggerhead turtles nest in summer, and the rangers run night walks.

Uniqueness: A brewery and restaurant in a converted warehouse with a wall of rare beer, a raw bar and a menu built for sharing, on the upper peninsula.
Reviews: The beer list is the draw and the food is better than brewery food. No reservations for the bar side, so go early.

Uniqueness: A 250 meter outdoor velodrome where you can watch track races for free on a Tuesday night, then take a beginner class on a fixed gear bike with no brakes.
Reviews: Locals call it the best free spectacle in York County; the beginner classes fill fast and the banked turns are terrifying in the best way.

Uniqueness: A working 1845 water powered mill that still grinds corn and grits, with a folklife festival on the third Saturday where potters, blacksmiths and shape note singers take over the grounds.
Reviews: The third Saturday festival is the day to go and the cornmeal is worth buying; the mill demonstration is genuinely interesting.

Uniqueness: Two thousand acres of longleaf pine and sand roads in the middle of Aiken, where horses still have the right of way and you can walk for hours without seeing a car.
Reviews: Locals guard it like a secret; the sand roads are soft and the horse traffic is real. Free and dog friendly.

Uniqueness: A mountain gorge where the Middle Saluda runs over granite slabs, with a 100-foot waterfall reached by a root-and-rock trail through hardwood forest.
Reviews: The falls hike is short but steep and slippery; the park limits parking, so reserve a pass online. Go after rain.

Uniqueness: The battlefield where backcountry militia stopped a British column in 1780, with a loop trail, earthworks, monuments and a museum.
Reviews: The trail is paved and the story is well told. It is one of the most important battlefields most people have never visited.

Uniqueness: The best preserved canal locks in the country sit beside a rocky ford on the Catawba River, and in late May the world's largest stand of rocky shoals spider lilies blooms in the current.
Reviews: The spider lily bloom is a genuine spectacle and the canal trail is easy; go in May and bring a camera. Quiet the rest of the year.

Typical Customer: Ghost hunters, families with teens, history buffs
Uniqueness: A jail that held pirates, Confederate prisoners and civil rights protesters, toured after dark with stories of executions, fires and the people who never left.
Reviews: The history is real and uncomfortable, which makes the ghost stories land harder. Guides are performers and researchers at once.

Uniqueness: The aircraft carrier Yorktown, a destroyer, a submarine and a Medal of Honor museum, all moored in Charleston Harbor and open to climb through.
Reviews: The carrier is enormous and the flight deck view is worth the ticket; it is a lot of stairs and ladders.

Uniqueness: A zoo built into the Saluda River bluffs with a 70-acre botanical garden across a footbridge, plus a skyfari over the elephants and gorillas.
Reviews: Consistently ranked among the best mid-size zoos in the country; the garden side is quiet and beautiful. Parking is easy and cheap.

Uniqueness: A downtown performing arts campus with a concert hall, a theater and an outdoor amphitheater, booking Broadway tours, symphony, jazz and big name concerts on the Reedy.
Reviews: The hall sounds excellent and the outdoor shows are a summer ritual. Check the schedule before a weekend trip.

Uniqueness: A 14 mile road through granite spires and two tunnels blasted through the rock, including a one lane eye of the needle passage.
Reviews: The tunnels and the Cathedral Spires are the photographs and the road is narrow; drive it early to avoid the tour buses.

Uniqueness: A 22 mile limestone canyon with three waterfalls, a scenic byway and trails to Bridal Veil Falls, 15 minutes from Spearfish.
Reviews: The drive is the attraction and the falls are short walks; it is the setting for Dances with Wolves and the canyon is busy in fall.

Uniqueness: A half mile concrete oval with 28 degree banks and 160,000 seats, known for the night race and the coliseum feel.
Reviews: The night race is the bucket list event, and the infield is a city. The track tour runs on non race days.

Uniqueness: A 1826 plantation house that became a field hospital after the Battle of Franklin, with bloodstains on the floor and a Confederate cemetery on the grounds.
Reviews: The house and the story of the McGavock family are powerful, and the cemetery is sobering. Pair it with Carter House.

Uniqueness: A 1830 house that became the center of the 1864 Battle of Franklin, with bullet holes in the brick and a tour that follows the family through the fight.
Reviews: The house and the battle story are told together, and the bullet scars are real. One of the best small house museums in the state.

Uniqueness: A ridge road along the edge of the Smokies with overlooks of the Tennessee Valley and the peaks, less crowded than the main park road.
Reviews: The views are as good as Cades Cove without the traffic. Go at sunrise or sunset.

Uniqueness: A Art Deco post office turned art museum, with touring exhibitions, a family gallery and a restored lobby of marble and brass.
Reviews: The building is half the visit and the shows are strong. Free for kids and sometimes for locals.

Uniqueness: A 315 acre nature center on the Tennessee River with quarry cliffs, trails, a boardwalk and kayak rentals, ten minutes from downtown.
Reviews: The quarry lake and the river boardwalk are the easy wins, and the trails have real climbs. Rent a kayak in summer.

Uniqueness: A town that made storytelling a profession, with nightly tellers in a small theater and a festival that fills the streets with people talking to rooms of strangers.
Reviews: The craft is astonishing and the audiences are warm; the museum is small but the live shows are the reason.

Uniqueness: The oldest registered distillery in the country, in a dry county, where whiskey is made with iron-free cave water and mellowed through sugar maple charcoal.
Reviews: The tasting tour is excellent and the dry-county irony is a running joke; book ahead. The angels' share smells like the whole town.

Typical Customer: Young adults, bachelorette parties, music fans
Uniqueness: A strip of bars where unknown bands play for tips from 10am to 3am, and the next star might be three feet away with a guitar and a day job.
Reviews: Go on a weekday afternoon for the best players and the least chaos; Saturday night is a different animal.

Uniqueness: The studio where Elvis, Dolly and the Everly Brothers recorded, with the original piano and tape machines still in place and a guide who plays the tapes.
Reviews: The tour is led by musicians and the stories are specific; it pairs with the Country Music Hall of Fame. Book the combo.

Uniqueness: One of the largest urban parks in the country, with 4,500 acres of lakes, trails, a buffalo herd, a zip line and a playground.
Reviews: The trails are flat and the lake is pretty, and the buffalo are a genuine surprise. Rent a bike at the boathouse.

Uniqueness: The largest urban bat colony in North America, 1.5 million Mexican free-tailed bats pour out from under a downtown bridge at dusk in a spiral that lasts twenty minutes.
Reviews: It is free and genuinely spectacular; the bat observation center is small but the bridge lawn is the spot. Bring a blanket.

Uniqueness: A granite maze of boulders and tinajas with hundreds of prehistoric pictographs, and some of the best bouldering in the country.
Reviews: The rock art tours are ranger led and limited and the climbing is world class; the park caps visitors and the desert heat is serious.

Uniqueness: Sixty miles of undeveloped barrier island with four wheel drive access, sea turtle releases in summer and the wreck of a Spanish ship in the dunes.
Reviews: The drive down the beach is the adventure and the further you go the emptier it gets; check tide tables and do not take a car that cannot handle sand.

Uniqueness: Two thousand acres of subtropical thorn forest on the Rio Grande where green jays, chachalacas and a dozen species found nowhere else in the country live.
Reviews: Birders come from around the world in winter and the hawk tower is the lookout; the tram is seasonal and the trails are flat and hot.

Uniqueness: A water park built into the Comal River, with spring fed chutes, uphill water coasters and a wave river that uses the actual current.
Reviews: The original park is still the best; reviews warn about crowds and tube rental logistics. Bring water shoes and a waterproof bag.

Uniqueness: The largest no kill animal sanctuary in the country, in Angel Canyon, with tours of the dog, cat and horse areas and volunteer shifts you can book.
Reviews: Visitors say the tour is moving and the canyon setting is beautiful; you cannot adopt on a whim but you can walk dogs for a morning.

Uniqueness: A natural amphitheater at 10,000 feet with hoodoos in pink and orange limestone, less visited than Bryce and just as strange.
Reviews: The rim trail at sunset is the photograph and the altitude is real; the road closes with snow from November to May.

Uniqueness: A promontory 2,000 feet above a gooseneck of the Colorado with a view into Canyonlands, where cowboys once corralled wild horses on a neck of land.
Reviews: Sunrise from the point is the classic and the mountain bike trail along the rim is a classic ride; the park is quieter than the national parks.

Uniqueness: A copper clad building above the valley with a dinosaur wall of 60 skeletons, a Great Salt Lake exhibit and a gallery on the Fremont and Ancestral Puebloan cultures.
Reviews: The dinosaur hall and the native voices gallery are the two reasons to come; the building's design and the terrace view of the Wasatch are the bonus.

Uniqueness: A steep resort at the top of Little Cottonwood Canyon with a tram to 11,000 feet, 500 inches of snow in a good year and a summer ride to a ridge walk.
Reviews: Skiers say the terrain is as serious as anywhere in the country and the canyon closes for avalanches; the tram runs year round.

Uniqueness: A 17 mile dirt road through red monoliths and mesas that look like Monument Valley without the fees or the crowds.
Reviews: The drive is the attraction and the camping is free; the road is graded but rough after rain and there are no services.

Uniqueness: A recreation of Shakespeare's indoor Blackfriars theater, lit by chandeliers with the house lights on, where actors can see and talk to the audience.
Reviews: The staging is energetic and the tickets are cheap for the quality; the town of Staunton is a good base.

Uniqueness: An Iowa class battleship docked at Nauticus, with turrets, crew quarters and a deck you can walk, plus a science center next door.
Reviews: The ship is enormous and the tour is self guided, so you can go at your pace. Good for kids.

Uniqueness: Saltwater cowboys herd wild ponies across the channel at slack tide, then auction the foals to keep the herd small, a 100-year old ritual on a barrier island.
Reviews: It is genuinely crowded and hot, and people still call it unforgettable. Watch from the water or a boat, not the packed shore.

Uniqueness: The mountain pass that opened the westward trail through the Appalachians, with earthworks, a visitor center and a ridge trail across three states.
Reviews: The view from the pinnacle is worth the climb, and the history is foundational. Free.

Uniqueness: A living history museum with replicas of the Susan Constant, a Powhatan village and a fort, telling the 1607 story.
Reviews: Kids can climb the ships and try on armor, and the museum covers the hard history of the colony. Good for a family day.

Uniqueness: Fifty acres of themed gardens with a conservatory, a children's garden, a rose garden and a lake, plus a holiday lights show.
Reviews: The conservatory is the winter win and the children's garden is genuinely good. Holiday lights sell out.

Uniqueness: A 100-acre Gilded Age estate with a Romanesque mansion, Japanese and Italian gardens, and a Virginia wildlife exhibit with otters, bobcats and black bears.
Reviews: Free grounds and a small mansion fee; the gardens are gorgeous in spring and the wildlife exhibits are better than expected for kids.

Uniqueness: A 850 foot natural tunnel carved by a creek through a mountain, with a chairlift, a train line through it and trails above.
Reviews: The tunnel is genuinely dramatic and the chairlift saves the climb. Go when the train passes through.

Uniqueness: Jefferson's rotunda and the lawn of pavilions and student rooms, a UNESCO World Heritage site and a working university.
Reviews: The lawn is the walk and the rotunda tour explains Jefferson's design. Free and central.

Uniqueness: The battlefield where Cornwallis surrendered in 1781, with earthworks, a siege line and a driving tour through the woods.
Reviews: The ranger talks make the siege make sense, and the earthworks are well preserved. Pair it with the American Revolution Museum.

Uniqueness: The tour of the Everett factory, the largest building by volume in the world, where 747s, 777s and 787s are assembled on catwalks above the floor.
Reviews: The factory floor is the thing people cannot get over and the tour needs booking; the gallery has a 787 dreamliner you can walk through.

Uniqueness: A glasshouse and garden of Dale Chihuly's work at the foot of the Space Needle, with a ceiling of glass flowers and towers that light up at night.
Reviews: The glasshouse and the garden at dusk are the two visits; the combo ticket with the Space Needle saves money and the exhibits are indoors on rainy days.

Uniqueness: A bridge 180 feet above a churning tidal channel between two islands, with cliffs, old growth forest and sea lions below.
Reviews: The bridge walk is free and thrilling; the currents are dangerous for swimming. Sunset from the bridge is the shot.

Uniqueness: A working water powered grist mill with a red roof over a mossy creek, surrounded by rhododendron and the New River Gorge, the most photographed mill in the state.
Reviews: Photographers queue at dawn for the mill and the creek; the park cabins are a quiet base for gorge hiking. Autumn is the peak.

Uniqueness: Ride a mantrip cart into a real worked coal seam with a former miner as your guide, then walk a recreated company town of shacks, church and school.
Reviews: The miner guides are the whole experience, funny, blunt and full of detail. The tour is cool underground even in August.

Uniqueness: Shay geared steam locomotives haul you up a logging railroad to Bald Knob, the third-highest point in the state, through a company town frozen in 1900.
Reviews: Rail fans love the sound of the Shays; the ride is long and slow, which is the point. Bring a jacket, the summit is cold.

Uniqueness: The only community owned team in major American sports, with a stadium tour that includes the tunnel, the frozen tundra and a hall of fame.
Reviews: The tour is excellent even for nonfans; game day tickets require a season ticket waiting list or luck.

Uniqueness: Sixteen acres of gardens with a Thai pavilion, a rose garden, a prairie and a conservatory.
Reviews: The Thai pavilion is the photo and the outdoor gardens are free. Quiet and pretty.

Uniqueness: A 3,700 acre park on Green Bay with a lighthouse, a beach, bike trails and a view of the Door County islands.
Reviews: The Eagle Bluff lighthouse and the bike loop are the highlights. Book camping early in summer.

Uniqueness: Eleven stages on the Lake Michigan shore for eleven days, with a giant American flag, fried cheese and a lineup that runs from hip hop to polka.
Reviews: It is cheap for a major festival and the lake breeze saves it; headliners cost extra. Bring a blanket and pace yourself.

Uniqueness: A late Frank Lloyd Wright house with a four winged plan around a central great hall, built for the Johnson wax family.
Reviews: For Wright fans it is a major house, and the great hall is the showpiece. Tours by reservation.

Uniqueness: The observatory that housed the largest refracting telescope in the world, with a terra cotta ornamented building and a 40 inch lens.
Reviews: The telescope and the building are the tour and the restoration is ongoing; tours are limited and book out in summer.

Uniqueness: A canyon 1,000 feet deep where the Bighorn River runs between Wyoming and Montana, with wild horses on the uplands and a lake for fishing and boating.
Reviews: The drive along the rim and the boat up the canyon are the two ways to see it; the park is quiet and the wild horses are a bonus.
