Typical Customer: History families, trail people, school groups
Uniqueness: The fur trading post and army fort that anchored the Oregon Trail, with 20 original buildings, Officers' Row and the treaty grounds where the 1851 council was held.
Reviews: The ranger tours and the restored barracks are the visit; it is free and the scale is bigger than people expect on the high plains.

Uniqueness: A free state bathhouse with water at 104 degrees, a travertine terrace above the Bighorn River and a buffalo herd in the park.
Reviews: The free bathhouse is the local institution and the state park is free; the commercial pools next door have slides and quieter hours.

Uniqueness: A WWII battleship you can climb through from engine room to gun turret, plus a submarine and a hangar of aircraft, all on Mobile Bay.
Reviews: Kids love the ladders and tight passages; veterans are often aboard telling stories. It is hot below deck in summer.

Uniqueness: A limestone hotel built as a cancer cure, later a college and a scam, now a haunted hotel with a ghost tour that climbs to the fifth floor and the morgue in the basement.
Reviews: The tour guides are performers and the building has real stories; the town of Eureka Springs is worth the weekend on its own.

Uniqueness: A state park dedicated to Ozark mountain culture, with working craft shops, herb gardens and nightly acoustic music in a 1,000-seat theater.
Reviews: The craft demonstrations are excellent and the evening shows are warm and unpretentious. Mountain View itself has pickin' on the square.

Uniqueness: A working taxidermy studio that teaches small classes in mouse and bird taxidermy, with a focus on craft and natural history rather than shock.
Reviews: Classes are small and expensive because they are real instruction, not a novelty. Check the calendar for beginner sessions before booking.

Uniqueness: A 19th century coastal village with a working shipyard, a whaleship you can board, and demonstration trades from coopering to sailmaking.
Reviews: Families rate it a full day; the wooden boat restoration yard is the sleeper hit. Some exhibits feel dated, which regulars find charming.

Uniqueness: Henry du Pont's 175-room mansion holding the world's premier collection of American decorative arts, set in 60 acres of naturalistic garden.
Reviews: The period rooms are jaw-dropping; the garden tram is the sleeper hit. Some find the guided only format slow.

Uniqueness: Giant pandas when the loan agreement allows, a free zoo in Rock Creek Park, and the compact Asia Trail that puts you feet from a sloth bear.
Reviews: Free entry makes it a DC staple; the pandas drive the crowds and the hill is steeper than it looks. Go at opening.

Uniqueness: A hovercraft glides over sawgrass, mud and shallow water where no boat can go, into mangrove tunnels and abandoned clam camps at the edge of the Ten Thousand Islands.
Reviews: The ride is smoother and louder than an airboat; reviews say the small-group trips beat the big-tour buses. Bring sunscreen and earplugs.

Uniqueness: A castle built from scrap aluminum and salvaged stained glass by an artist who lived in it, filled with wooden machines, painted ceilings and a 60 foot replica of a Spanish galleon.
Reviews: It is gloriously eccentric and the tour is funny; the boat tour and the restaurant are extras. Worth the drive inland.

Uniqueness: A DIY venue in a strip of businesses that has been the center of Atlanta's underground for decades, with a low stage, a cramped bar and bands that go on late.
Reviews: If a touring punk band plays Atlanta, they probably play here. Cash bar, earplugs recommended, no pretension.

Uniqueness: The Tudor house where the Allman Brothers lived, jammed and wrote their best records, now packed with instruments, posters and the original kitchen table.
Reviews: Fans call it a pilgrimage; the rooms are preserved rather than curated, which makes it feel lived in. Small and warm.

Uniqueness: A private road course in the north Georgia hills with elevation change, a kart track and a skid pad, open to members and to track day groups.
Reviews: The elevation makes it feel like a European circuit; instructors are good and the kart track is a cheap way to sample the property.

Uniqueness: A four hour round trip along the Toccoa River in open air cars, with a stop in a twin river town for barbecue and a walk across the state line.
Reviews: The open air car is the one to book; fall color trips sell out. It is relaxed and scenic rather than thrilling.

Uniqueness: A seven level Italianate mansion with a cantilevered spiral staircase, hand painted ceilings and the first indoor plumbing of its kind in the state.
Reviews: The guided tour is the only way in and the guides know the family scandals. The behind the scenes tour on select Saturdays is worth the upgrade.

Uniqueness: Georgia's Little Grand Canyon: 150-foot gullies of pink, orange and white sediment carved by poor farming in the 1800s, now a maze of hoodoos and narrow trenches.
Reviews: The colors are unreal in photos and real in person; the backcountry trail is muddy and the canyon floor is closed after rain.

Uniqueness: A 3,000 acre regenerative farm that slaughters on site and tours you through cattle, poultry and a solar powered abattoir, then feeds you at the farm store.
Reviews: The transparency is the experience and the farm store is excellent; book the tour rather than wandering. Kids like the animals.

Uniqueness: Eighteen sandstone canyons with waterfalls and a lodge on a bluff above the Illinois River, an hour and a half from Chicago.
Reviews: The canyons are beautiful and busy; go at 8am and take Trail 2. Bald eagles winter below the dam.

Uniqueness: A quarter mile avenue of 300-year old live oaks leading to a Greek Revival mansion, with the slave quarters and sugar operation interpreted alongside the beauty.
Reviews: The grounds are stunning and the slavery exhibits are more honest than most; the mint julep is a nice touch. Go early for photos.

Uniqueness: A working lobsterman pulls traps, bands a keeper, and explains the fishery in the same breath, then you eat a lobster on the dock that was in the water that morning.
Reviews: The good operators are loved for blunt humor and genuine knowledge; the bad ones are floating gift shops. Ask whether the boat is actually hauling gear before you book.

Uniqueness: The oldest active ballpark in the majors, with a hand-operated scoreboard, the Green Monster and a press box that still smells like 1912.
Reviews: Guides are old school funny and generous with stories; even nonfans rate it. Book early for the warning-track and Monster seats.

Uniqueness: An open entry art competition that takes over an entire city, venues in bars, churches, parks and museums, with the public voting for the winner.
Reviews: The scale is the point; some work is amateur and some is museum grade. Download the map and pick three venues.

Uniqueness: A triple waterfall on the Gooseberry River dropping into Lake Superior, with a trail along the gorge and pink granite shorelines nearby.
Reviews: Easy access and big payoff; it is crowded in summer. The Lake Superior shoreline at Split Rock is the bonus stop.

Uniqueness: A 630-foot stainless steel catenary arch with a tram that squeezes you into a pod and lifts you to a window the size of a shoebox over the Mississippi.
Reviews: The tram is claustrophobic and the view is worth it; the museum underneath is excellent and free. Book timed tickets.

Uniqueness: A Missouri institution: a raft, a cooler and a slow river through Ozark hills, with gravel bars for stopping and no schedule at all.
Reviews: The Huzzah and Current rivers are the classics; weekends get rowdy and the water is cold. Book the shuttle and bring a dry bag.

Uniqueness: A tiny classroom that runs cheap one off classes on everything from pickling to lock picking to the history of the subway, taught by anyone with something to teach.
Reviews: The range is the appeal and the prices are low; classes are small and sell out fast.

Uniqueness: A glassblowing studio in Gowanus where beginners make drinking glasses and vases in a two hour session, then pick them up after annealing.
Reviews: The instructors are working artists and the classes are small; it is a popular date night, so book early.

Uniqueness: A 1927 wooden coaster that still feels genuinely violent, beside a boardwalk of hot dogs, sideshows and Atlantic surf in the city's outer borough.
Reviews: Coaster purists insist on a back-seat ride; the rest of Coney is scruffy and that's the appeal. The Mermaid Parade in June is the day to go.

Uniqueness: A warehouse in Bushwick putting on circus, burlesque, immersive theater and themed parties with aerialists over the crowd and a strict no phones policy.
Reviews: The productions are wildly creative and the crowd dresses for it; shows sell out and the space gets packed. Check the dress code before you go.

Uniqueness: The prairie house Wright built for a Buffalo businessman, restored down to the art glass, with a pergola and conservatory that run the length of the block.
Reviews: Guides say the two hour tour is worth it over the one hour; the restoration is the story as much as the design.

Uniqueness: A rehabilitation center with hawks, owls and eagles on display and a flight show where a red tailed hawk passes inches over the crowd.
Reviews: The flight show is the reason to time your visit; staff are genuine experts and the injured birds have stories. Small and worthwhile.

Uniqueness: A drive through exotic animal park where zebras, giraffes and emus walk up to the car for feed, plus a wagon ride that gets you closer than a zoo allows.
Reviews: Buy the feed buckets and keep the windows up between handfuls; the wagon ride is better than driving yourself. Kids lose their minds.

Uniqueness: A 60 acre former steam locomotive shop with a working turntable, a roundhouse full of engines and train rides on the weekends, all in a preserved Southern Railway yard.
Reviews: Kids love the train ride and the turntable demo; rail fans say the collection punches above its size. Cheap and uncrowded.

Uniqueness: A 60-foot natural granite waterslide ending in an eight-foot plunge pool, with lifeguards and a queue of kids in innertubes.
Reviews: Everyone screams, everyone does it twice. Water is 55 degrees year round; go on a weekday morning and bring water shoes.

Uniqueness: A stone fire tower at 5,342 feet with a 360-degree view over four states, reached by a paved road and a short walk on the Appalachian Trail.
Reviews: The view is enormous and the drive is the adventure; the road is narrow and closes in winter. Sunset is the payoff.

Uniqueness: A two mile loop along the top of a 700 foot granite cliff, with cable rails on the exposed sections and peregrine falcons riding the updraft below you.
Reviews: The cliff edge is genuinely airy and the view over the valley is huge; go early for parking and avoid ice.

Uniqueness: A live oak estimated at 400 to 500 years old, with limbs the size of trees and a canopy that covers 17,000 square feet.
Reviews: People arrive for ten minutes and stay an hour; it is free and quietly awe inspiring. Go early to avoid tour vans.

Uniqueness: Two thousand acres of protected forest, dairy barn and lake minutes from Fort Mill, with 40 miles of trail and a kayak launch that feels a hundred miles from the interstate.
Reviews: The greenway is the reason people move to Fort Mill; trails are well kept and the barn events are charming. Bugs in summer, but that's the Carolinas.

Uniqueness: A cypress swamp garden dug by hand in the 1930s, with a flat bottom boat that poles you through trees draped in Spanish moss and water black as ink.
Reviews: The boat ride is short but memorable, and the butterfly house is a hit with kids. Go early for still water and fewer people.

Uniqueness: A rock crawling park in a hardwood gulch with ledges, waterfalls and trails rated from stock friendly to buggy only, and a crowd that will spot you through anything.
Reviews: The community is the point: strangers guide you up a ledge and cheer when you make it. Body damage is possible and expected.

Uniqueness: A lighthouse standing in the surf offshore, abandoned to erosion and stabilized by a seawall, visible from the beach and reachable only by boat.
Reviews: The view from Folly Beach at sunset is the shot and the story of the preservation fight is good; boat tours are seasonal.

Adventure: Oconee Station and Station Cove Falls
Uniqueness: A 1792 stone blockhouse that guarded the frontier beside a trading post, with a trail through cove forest to a 60 foot waterfall.
Reviews: The walk to the falls is easy and the blockhouse is a genuine relic; it is free and rarely crowded. Wear shoes for the roots.

Uniqueness: A 1,600-foot railroad tunnel abandoned half-finished before the Civil War, now a cool 50-degree cave you can walk into, with a 200-foot waterfall a short trail away.
Reviews: The tunnel is genuinely eerie and the falls are a five minute walk; it is free and easy for kids. Bring a jacket and a flashlight.

Season / Dates: Year round, Wed and Sat nights
Uniqueness: A food hall in a 1920s textile mill that clears the floor for line dancing twice a week, with instructors, a bar and a crowd that ranges from college students to grandmothers.
Reviews: The mill setting and the mixed crowd make it feel like a small town hall rather than a club. Go early for the lesson, stay for the band.

Uniqueness: The steepest passenger railway in the world at 72.7 percent grade, climbing Lookout Mountain in a wooden car that creaks the whole way.
Reviews: Sit on the right going up for the view; the ride is short and the wait can be long. Combine with Rock City at the top.

Uniqueness: Big Tex, Fletcher's corn dogs, a 55-foot Ferris wheel and an annual fried-food arms race that produced fried butter and fried beer.
Reviews: The food is the point and the rides are secondary; go on a weekday and split everything. Parking is a hike.

Uniqueness: The original chili cookoff in a ghost town at the edge of Big Bend, where serious competitors, campsite parties and a cemetery of chili legends collide.
Reviews: It is as much a camping festival as a cookoff; the chili is variable and the atmosphere is unmatched. Book lodging a year out.

Uniqueness: A island in the Great Salt Lake with a free roaming bison herd, bighorn sheep and water so salty you float without trying.
Reviews: The bison are everywhere and the lake views are strange and beautiful; bring bug spray in spring. Few crowds.

Uniqueness: Eighty-eight original and reconstructed buildings on the actual 18th century capital, with tradespeople who blacksmith, bind books and argue politics in character.
Reviews: The ticket price draws complaints, but the trades and the evening programs are rated excellent. Go in spring or fall; summer heat is brutal in wool.

Uniqueness: The largest scrap metal sculpture in the world, a 300 ton time machine built from industrial salvage by a former junkyard artist, surrounded by giant birds and a teapot orchestra.
Reviews: It is free, enormous and completely unexpected; photographers love it at sunset. A ten minute detour off the interstate.

Uniqueness: A free museum with a strong collection of American and European art, African masks, Asian ceramics and a sculpture garden.
Reviews: Free and better than expected, with a good cafe. The African collection is the surprise.

Uniqueness: A 126-foot-wide cave mouth billed as the largest in the world, with a 45-foot stalagmite called Goliath and a walkable, paved route through enormous chambers.
Reviews: Guides are funny and the scale is genuinely impressive; it is less commercial than Luray. Watch for bats.

Uniqueness: The bridge where marchers were beaten on Bloody Sunday in 1965, now a National Historic Landmark with a view of the Alabama River.
Reviews: Walking across is the experience, and the interpretive center nearby explains the march. Quiet and heavy.

Uniqueness: A day on Cook Inlet or Kachemak Bay pulling halibut that can weigh 100 pounds, with the catch processed and shipped home.
Reviews: The fishing is the reason people plan a whole trip and the water can be rough; book early, the good captains fill a year out.

Uniqueness: A mountain pass above treeline with a road to 3,000 feet, trails to alpine lakes and the ruins of a gold mine, an hour from Anchorage.
Reviews: The drive to the pass and the April ski season are the local secrets; the road is rough and the weather turns quickly.

Uniqueness: An island refuge with 3,500 Kodiak brown bears, salmon streams and a visitor center with mounted bears and a education gallery.
Reviews: The flight to a salmon stream to watch bears is the splurge and the visitor center is free; book through a licensed operator and keep your distance.

Uniqueness: A drive through wildlife park with black bears, wolves and bison roaming large forest enclosures, plus a walk through section with otters and jaguars.
Reviews: The drive through is the draw and the bears come close to the car; the walk through is smaller. A good stop on the way to the Grand Canyon.

Uniqueness: Fifty thousand desert plants from around the world on 140 acres in Papago Park, with a butterfly pavilion and a trail through a sonoran desert that looks planted but is wild.
Reviews: The cactus and succulent collection is the reason gardeners come and the butterfly exhibit runs in spring; summer heat limits the visit to early morning.

Uniqueness: A copper mining town built on a 30 degree slope above the Verde Valley, once called the wickedest town in the west, now galleries, wine bars and a state park.
Reviews: The sliding jail and the state park are the history and the view from the upper streets is the photograph; parking is on a steep hill and the town is busy on weekends.

Uniqueness: A drive through the Painted Desert and fields of petrified wood, with a 225 million year old log jam, petroglyphs and a 1930s inn built of stone.
Reviews: The Blue Mesa trail is the walk and the Painted Desert at sunset is the photograph; removing petrified wood is illegal and the park is 50 miles from anywhere.

Uniqueness: One of the largest aircraft collections in the country, with 400 planes across 80 acres, including a SR-71 and a B-29, plus a tram tour of the bone yard.
Reviews: The outdoor storage rows are the reason enthusiasts come and the tram saves walking; the hangars are hot in summer.

Uniqueness: A lava flow and cinder cone beside a 900 year old pueblo of red sandstone with a ball court and a blowhole, on the same loop road.
Reviews: The contrast between the black lava and the red pueblo is the photograph; the Wupatki ruins are quiet and the loop drive is 35 miles.

Uniqueness: A rebuilt art museum with a strong collection of American and Southern art, a sculpture garden and a restaurant.
Reviews: The renovation is impressive and the collection is free on some days. Good rainy day stop.

Uniqueness: A frontier fort and federal courthouse with the gallows, the jail and the story of the Trail of Tears passing through.
Reviews: The courtroom and the gallows are the sobering highlights, and the rangers tell the story well.

Uniqueness: Eight ornate bathhouses from the Gilded Age spa era, with one still operating a traditional whirlpool-and-needle-shower bath and others preserved as museums.
Reviews: The Buckstaff is the authentic experience, communal tubs, no frills, cheap; the modern spas are nicer and pricier.

Uniqueness: A contemporary art satellite of Crystal Bridges in a former cheese factory, with exhibitions, a rooftop bar and live music.
Reviews: The industrial space and the programming are both good, and the bar makes it a evening stop.

Uniqueness: A 3,849 foot peak where you can see more of the state than from any other summit, with a stone visitor center and fire lookout from the 1930s.
Reviews: Cyclists climb it as a rite of passage and the view from the summit on a clear day reaches the Sierra; the road is narrow and the heat is real in summer.

Uniqueness: A 1936 ocean liner turned hotel, with engine rooms, a first class dining room and haunted ship tours that go into the bow and the pool, where guests report voices.
Reviews: The ship is magnificent and the ghost tour is theatrical but rooted in real accidents; the hotel rooms are uneven.

Uniqueness: A 1907 seaside boardwalk with the Giant Dipper wooden coaster and a 1911 carousel, both national landmarks, right on the sand.
Reviews: The Giant Dipper still delivers; the boardwalk is free to walk and the food is fairground grade. Skip summer weekends.

Uniqueness: A castle being built by one family from hand gathered stone, with a fire breathing dragon, a glass ceiling and a stairway that climbs into the air.
Reviews: It is free, slightly dangerous and completely sincere; the builder's signs about government are part of the experience.

Adventure: Cook Street School of Culinary Arts
Uniqueness: A professional culinary school with a public recreation program, where you cook a three course menu in a real kitchen and drink wine while you do it.
Reviews: The classes are hands on and the instructors are working chefs; the pasta and knife skills sessions are the favorites.

Adventure: Submarine Force Museum and USS Nautilus
Uniqueness: Walk the cramped interior of the world's first nuclear submarine, then stand beside a control room that looks like a 1950s vision of the future.
Reviews: Free, uncrowded and genuinely fascinating; the audio tour is worth it. Visitors warn the submarine is tight for tall people.

Uniqueness: The oldest public art museum in the country, with a castle facade, a Hudson River School collection, the first Picasso bought by an American museum and a baroque cabinet of curiosities.
Reviews: The Morgan and the Hudson River rooms are the local favorites; the museum is quiet on weekday mornings and the café is in the old sculpture court.

Uniqueness: Louis Kahn's last building, a four story box of oak, linen and concrete holding the largest collection of British art outside Britain, including Constable and Turner.
Reviews: The building is as good as the paintings and the long gallery on the top floor is the place to sit; admission is free.

Uniqueness: A moat ringed Civil War fortress on an island in the Delaware River, reached by ferry, with prison barracks, tunnels and a living history garrison.
Reviews: The ferry and the moat make it an adventure; the prison history is grim and well told. Bring lunch, there is nothing on the island.

Uniqueness: The working theater where Lincoln was shot, with the presidential box preserved and a museum in the basement, still staging plays at night.
Reviews: The ranger talk in the box is worth waiting for and the Petersen House across the street is included; timed tickets go fast in spring.

Adventure: National Museum of the American Indian
Uniqueness: A curvilinear limestone building on the Mall with a collection organized by tribe rather than chronology, and a cafeteria of Native dishes from across the hemisphere.
Reviews: The cafeteria is a destination on its own and the galleries reward slow reading; the building's form and the landscape design are part of the exhibit.

Uniqueness: Portraits of every president and the people who changed the country, including the Lansdowne portrait of Washington, in a former patent office building.
Reviews: The presidential gallery and the modern portraits are the route and the courtyard is the quiet break; it is free and connected to the American Art Museum.

Uniqueness: Four hundred and forty six acres inside the city with the National Bonsai and Penjing Museum, a grove of state trees and the columns of the old Capitol standing in a meadow.
Reviews: The bonsai museum is the surprise and free; the Capitol columns are the photograph and the azalea collection peaks in late April.

Uniqueness: A state park on a barrier island with a wide beach, dunes, a salt marsh and campsites under oaks, minutes from the old city.
Reviews: The beach is quieter than the city beaches and the camping is shaded. Good for a combination history and beach day.

Uniqueness: A limestone shoreline where waves blast water through rock holes at high tide, the largest Anastasia limestone outcrop on the Atlantic coast.
Reviews: Go at high tide with a northeast wind for the blowholes, and wear shoes on the rock.

Uniqueness: A spring fed river with clear water, cypress and mangrove tunnels, manatees in winter and a campground at the launch.
Reviews: The paddle is easy and the spring runs are beautiful. Rent a kayak at the campground and go early.

Adventure: Cummer Museum of Art and Gardens
Uniqueness: A riverfront museum with European and American painting, porcelain and formal gardens on the St. Johns, with free admission on some days.
Reviews: The gardens on the river are as good as the collection, and the free days make it a bargain.

Uniqueness: The winter estates of Thomas Edison and Henry Ford, with their houses, laboratories, a 1929 botanical garden and Edison's rubber research.
Reviews: The labs are the interesting part and the banyan tree is enormous. Allow two hours.

Uniqueness: The Spanish colonial house where Hemingway wrote in the 1930s, with his furniture, his typewriter and dozens of polydactyl cats descended from his own.
Reviews: The cats are the fun and the writing studio is the history. Tours run continuously and are worth the ticket.

Uniqueness: A nightly street festival that exists only to watch the sun go down: buskers, sword swallowers, cats on tightropes and a crowd that applauds the horizon.
Reviews: It is touristy and completely charming; locals avoid it and visitors remember it. Get there an hour before sunset for a seat on the pier.

Uniqueness: A reconstructed 17th century Spanish mission and Apalachee village, with a council house, a friary and living history demonstrations.
Reviews: The reconstruction is convincing and the staff explain the collision of Spanish and Apalachee life. Good for kids.

Uniqueness: A museum on the beach where the frogmen trained, with boats, dive gear, a bin Laden raid exhibit and the history of naval special warfare.
Reviews: The artifacts are real and the stories are intense. Good for teenagers and adults.

Uniqueness: The first national wildlife refuge in the country, set aside by Theodore Roosevelt to protect pelicans, with a boardwalk and a bird's eye view of the lagoon.
Reviews: The history is the story and the birding is excellent in winter. Quiet and free.

Uniqueness: The tallest lighthouse in Florida, with 203 steps, a keeper's quarters museum and a view of the inlet and the ocean.
Reviews: The climb is hot but the view is worth it, and the museum explains the lighthouse keepers.

Uniqueness: A 3,500 acre wetland preserve with a 1.2 mile boardwalk through cypress, ferns and orchids, with otters, herons and alligators.
Reviews: The boardwalk is easy and cool, and the wildlife is close. A good break from the beach.

Uniqueness: A 26 acre pier district with a modern pier head, a beach, restaurants, a playground and a tram, on Tampa Bay.
Reviews: The design is the attraction and the sunset is the show. Free to walk, with paid parking.

Uniqueness: Women in mermaid tails perform underwater ballet in a natural spring theater, breathing through hoses, since 1947, the last of a vanished genre of roadside attraction.
Reviews: It is gloriously retro and the performers are genuinely athletic; the park's river cruise is a nice add. Kids are mesmerized.

Typical Customer: Young adults, food people, history people
Uniqueness: A historic cigar district of brick factories, mutual aid halls and rooster-filled streets, now bars, cigar shops and Cuban restaurants.
Reviews: Walk 7th Avenue, watch a cigar roller and eat a Cuban sandwich. Busy and loud on weekend nights.

Uniqueness: A 1.54 mile quad oval south of the city with NASCAR weekends, a dirt track next door and a Wednesday night short track series.
Reviews: The spring race is the big one and the infield is a scene. The short track nights are cheaper and closer to the action.

Uniqueness: A 27,000 acre campus with a Gothic stone chapel, a working farm, deer and trails, often called the largest campus in the world.
Reviews: The chapel and the oak allee are the photo stops, and the trails are open to the public. Drive the loop at dusk for deer.

Uniqueness: A 2.5 mile urban whitewater course on the Chattahoochee running through downtown, with Class III rapids, a zipline over the river and a blue heron rookery.
Reviews: The rafting is short and splashy and the zipline is the sleeper hit; the riverwalk is lovely at sunset.

Uniqueness: A museum inside the CDC campus tracing disease outbreaks, the smallpox campaign and the epidemiologists who chase them, with a real iron lung and a global map room.
Reviews: Surprisingly gripping for a government museum, and free. Bring photo ID for security, and check the open days.

Uniqueness: The best preserved earthwork fort on the Georgia coast, with the original bombproof shelters and a massive earthen wall that held out ironclads for years, sitting on a salt marsh at the mouth of the Ogeechee.
Reviews: The earthworks are intact enough to walk through and the marsh boardwalk is full of birds. Camping under the oaks is the local secret.

Uniqueness: A cypress mill pond with a covered bridge over the dam, a 1970s grist mill standing in the water, and a canoe trail that threads between white-barked cypress trunks hung with Spanish moss.
Reviews: The cypress pond in early morning is the photograph everyone wants, and the mill and covered bridge sit at the same landing. Cabins book out months ahead in spring.

Season / Dates: Year round, daylight, some areas closed in season
Uniqueness: A former army airfield and before that a Black owned settlement, now a refuge of salt marsh and old oaks where wood storks nest in numbers and the taxiways make a flat bike loop.
Reviews: The wood stork rookery in spring is the spectacle, hundreds of birds in the trees over the water. The old runway is a strange and good place to ride.

Typical Customer: History travellers, school groups, people who grew up with him
Uniqueness: Three sites in one small town, the depot that served as his campaign headquarters, the high school where the visitor center sits, and the farm without running water where he grew up, all preserved as they were.
Reviews: Since his death the farm and depot draw steady crowds. The boyhood farm is the one people say made the man legible.

Uniqueness: The oldest and largest Woodland mound complex in the southeast, with Georgia's oldest great temple mound, two burial mounds and a museum built partly inside an excavated mound.
Reviews: The scale of the temple mound surprises people who expect a small site. The museum is under federal review for its burial displays, so check what is open before driving.

Uniqueness: An Emory museum with Egyptian mummies, Greek pottery and South American gold, in a Michael Graves building with a quiet courtyard.
Reviews: The mummy gallery is the draw and the collection is deeper than expected for a university museum. Free on some days.

Uniqueness: Atlanta's oldest cemetery, with Victorian monuments, the graves of Gone with the Wind author Margaret Mitchell and golf great Bobby Jones, and a view of the skyline over the trees.
Reviews: The guided tour is worth the small fee and the self guided map is free. Go in the morning for light and quiet.

Uniqueness: The Greek Revival mansion where Georgia's governors lived before Atlanta, restored to its 1850s appearance, with the slave quarters and the story of the household included.
Reviews: The guided tour is excellent and honest about the enslaved staff. The staircase and the dome are the showpieces.

Uniqueness: A granite monadnock preserved as a national natural landmark, with ranger led hikes to the summit and a boardwalk around the base.
Reviews: The summit is only open on ranger tours, which is why it stays pristine. Book the tour and bring water.

Uniqueness: A quail hunting plantation with a 1930s main house, a carriage museum, dog cemeteries and sporting art, in the red hills of south Georgia.
Reviews: The house tour and the grounds are both good, and the sporting art is unusual. Check the season before driving out.

Season / Dates: Selected weekends and holidays, March to December
Typical Customer: Families with kids, retired couples, train people
Uniqueness: Georgia's official rolling state park runs vintage coaches out of the 1888 Cordele depot across Lake Blackshear to Plains and Americus, with the car windows open and nobody in a hurry.
Reviews: Riders talk about the lake crossing and the layover in Plains more than the seats. Book the dome car early for the summer runs.

Uniqueness: An island of live oak canopies, a working lighthouse, a village pier and the ruins of Fort Frederica, with shrimp boats and a beach at the south end.
Reviews: Park once and walk or bike. The lighthouse climb is worth it, and the crab shack near the pier is the local lunch.

Uniqueness: A 313 acre garden with a conservatory, a formal rose garden, woodland trails and a children's garden, run by the university and free most days.
Reviews: The conservatory is the rainy day win and the trails are shaded. Parking is free but the lot fills on spring weekends.

Uniqueness: A 270 foot swinging bridge over the Toccoa River on the Benton MacKaye Trail, with swimming holes and trout water below.
Reviews: The bridge sway is part of the fun and the river is cold and clear. Parking is limited, so go early.

Uniqueness: A ballpark with a surrounding block of restaurants, bars and a plaza that stays busy even when the team is away, plus a battery of pre game music.
Reviews: Buy the cheap seats and walk the concourse. The Battery is the pre game and post game plan, and the food is better than ballpark default.

Typical Customer: Rail fans, Civil War readers, families
Uniqueness: The first major railroad tunnel in the South and the first bored through the Appalachian range, 1,477 feet long, with the original drill marks still in the rock and the spot where the Great Locomotive Chase passed in 1862.
Reviews: Guided tours walk you into the bore with a flashlight and the guide tells the chase properly. Rail people call it the best railroad history stop in north Georgia.

Uniqueness: A 140,000 square foot indoor market run by an international staff, with produce from four continents, a bakery, a butcher and a fish counter that locals treat as a weekly ritual.
Reviews: Go hungry. The cheese and olive bars are the cheap thrill, and the prepared food counter is the lunch move. Parking is a contact sport on Saturdays.

Uniqueness: The state museum of Hawaii with a three story Hawaiian hall of feather cloaks and a sperm whale skeleton, plus a planetarium and a science center.
Reviews: The Hawaiian hall is the reason to come and the planetarium is good with children; it is the best single introduction to the islands.

Uniqueness: A crescent bay backed by mountains and a pier, with a river mouth, a reef and a view of the Na Pali coast from the water.
Reviews: The bay is the postcard of Kauai and the winter surf is for experts; parking is tight and the north shore gets rain.

Uniqueness: A 1,700 foot cliff trail with 26 switchbacks down to the leprosy settlement where Father Damien served, now a national historical park.
Reviews: The trail is steep and the settlement is still home to patients, so visits are guided and respectful; book through a licensed operator.

Typical Customer: History people, students, civil rights pilgrims
Uniqueness: The remains of a World War II camp where 13,000 Japanese Americans were incarcerated, with a reconstructed barrack, a guard tower and the original root cellar.
Reviews: The site is sparse and the stories are the exhibit; rangers lead walks and the isolation is part of the lesson.

Uniqueness: Weird sandstone hoodoos, camel shaped formations and a slot canyon in the Shawnee Hills, with a trail that threads between the rocks.
Reviews: People call it a mini-Utah in southern Illinois; it is free and rarely crowded. Combine with the wine trail.

Uniqueness: A downtown park with Cloud Gate, the Pritzker Pavilion, a fountain and a garden, on the old rail yards.
Reviews: The Bean is the photo and the park is a good walk. Free and central.

Uniqueness: A planned industrial town built by the Pullman company, with the factory, the row houses and the story of the 1894 strike.
Reviews: The architecture and the labor history together are the point. Free, with a visitor center.

Uniqueness: A cooking school and shop where you make a full menu in a small group, from knife skills to braising, then sit down and eat it with the class.
Reviews: The teaching is practical and the groups are friendly; date night classes book out.

Uniqueness: A zoo designed for children with a train, a carousel, a farm animal area and African lions, built into a wooded park.
Reviews: Parents call it one of the best children's zoos in the country and the train is the ritual; it is big enough for three hours.

Uniqueness: A national park of 15 miles of Lake Michigan beach, 200-foot dunes and black oak savanna, an hour from Chicago.
Reviews: The 3 Dune Challenge is a real workout with a great view; the beach is the cleanest near Chicago. Summer parking fills by 9am.

Uniqueness: A county with 31 covered bridges and a festival that fills them with craft fairs, food and traffic.
Reviews: Pick a few bridges and drive the back roads, and go early to beat the crowds. The festival is the busiest week.

Uniqueness: A campus with the Golden Dome, the basilica, the grotto and the football stadium, all walkable around two lakes.
Reviews: The basilica and the grotto are the quiet highlights, and game weekends are a scene. Free to walk.

Uniqueness: Seven villages settled by German Pietists, with communal kitchens, woolen mills, furniture shops and family style restaurants.
Reviews: The colonies are a good half day, with crafts and heavy German food. The woolen mill is the best stop.

Uniqueness: Six miles of trails connecting caves you can actually enter, including one with a 17-foot ceiling and a natural bridge, in the middle of Iowa farmland.
Reviews: Bring a headlamp and clothes you don't mind ruining; the caves are unpaved and genuinely dark. Mud is part of the deal.

Uniqueness: A 4.4 acre downtown park with 30 large outdoor sculptures, free and open at all hours, next to the art center.
Reviews: The scale is surprising for Des Moines and the park is easy to walk. Free.

Uniqueness: The largest museum of Norwegian American history in the country, with a reconstructed stave church, rosemaling and a boat hall of fjord craft.
Reviews: The stave church and the woodcarving collection are the reasons to come; the town also has a brewery and a bike trail along the Upper Iowa.

Uniqueness: A 44 foot steel sculpture of a Native American figure at the confluence of two rivers, with a fire ring lit at dusk and a bridge over the water.
Reviews: The sculpture is striking and the sunset fire is the moment. Free and quick.

Uniqueness: A working horse farm and museum with draft horses, retired racehorses and a show barn, plus the International Museum of the Horse.
Reviews: The draft horse demonstration is the crowd pleaser; the museum is thorough. Allow four hours and wear walking shoes.

Uniqueness: A 65,000 acre lake with 1,200 miles of shoreline, houseboat rentals and a reputation for striped bass.
Reviews: The lake is huge and the coves are quiet. Rent a houseboat for a weekend if you can.

Uniqueness: A 17 mile underground cavern with zip lines, a ropes course, mountain bike trails and a tram tour, in a former limestone mine.
Reviews: The underground zip line is the novelty and the bike trails are real. Book ahead.

Uniqueness: You walk the actual factory floor where bats are turned from billets, then hold the bat Babe Ruth used, all under a 120-foot steel bat.
Reviews: The factory tour is short and genuinely interesting; kids get a mini bat. The museum is a nice extra, not the main event.

Uniqueness: The pepper sauce aged in white oak barrels on a salt dome, with a museum, a jungle garden of camellias and a walk where you can see the barrels sweating.
Reviews: Cheap, quirky and genuinely interesting; the gardens are a surprise. The tasting room lets you try the family's reserve sauce.

Uniqueness: A 450 acre museum of Louisiana rural life with a plantation complex, slave cabins, a country store and farm equipment.
Reviews: The slave cabins and the working farm are the powerful parts. The grounds are shady and quiet.

Uniqueness: A Greek Revival mansion on Bayou Lafourche, still family owned and open for tours and overnight stays.
Reviews: The house is stunning and the family story is personal. Book ahead for a tour or a night.

Uniqueness: The oldest settlement in Louisiana, with a brick main street, a river walk, a fort site and 18th century houses.
Reviews: The river street is the photo and the meat pies are the local food. Christmas lights are a big draw.

Uniqueness: A World War II destroyer docked on the Mississippi, restored and open for self guided tours through the decks and turrets.
Reviews: The ship is tight and real, and the museum explains the Pacific war. Good for kids who like machines.

Uniqueness: A college museum with the Alex Katz collection, a Whistler room and a wing by Frederick Fisher, free and better than most city museums of its size.
Reviews: Art people make the drive from Portland for the Katz and the American galleries; the museum is free and the campus is walkable.

Company / Access: Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands
Uniqueness: A bold coast of volcanic headlands and spruce forest where the trail runs along the cliff edge to coves you can only reach on foot.
Reviews: The bold coast loop is the best coastal hike in the state and the fog is part of it; the trail is rough and the parking is a small lot on a dirt road.

Uniqueness: The largest lake in Maine, 40 miles long, ringed by unbroken forest where moose come down to the road at dusk and the steamboat Katahdin still runs.
Reviews: The drive along the eastern shore at dusk is the moose route; fly fishing for brook trout and the float plane rides are the local specialties.

Uniqueness: Washington's first lighthouse, on a headland above the entrance to Portland harbor, with the keeper's house and a park of gun emplacements around it.
Reviews: The park is free and the view of the lighthouse from the beach below is the photograph; the museum in the keeper's house is small.

Uniqueness: Eight connected peaks with a lift system that spreads crowds, wide groomers and a resort base that makes a week easy without a car.
Reviews: Families like the variety and the snowmaking; experts prefer Sugarloaf and the base area is a long walk from some lodging.

Uniqueness: The largest drive in screen in the country at 120 feet, with a strict no talking, no headlights rule and a snack bar that still makes real food.
Reviews: The rules are enforced and that is why the picture is good; arrive early for a good spot and tune the radio. A time machine.

Uniqueness: A waterfront campus of skipjacks, a lighthouse moved from the bay, a working boatyard and the Hooper Strait screw pile light, with crabbing demonstrations.
Reviews: The lighthouse and the skipjack are the highlights and the boatyard is where the work happens; children like the tonging and crab picking.

Uniqueness: A steam locomotive climb from Cumberland to Frostburg over the Allegheny divide, through a horseshoe curve and the 914 foot Brush Tunnel.
Reviews: The dome car and the open air car are the seats to book; the Frostburg stop is 90 minutes and the return is the same route.

Uniqueness: Two presidential birthplaces and the mansion where four generations of Adamses lived, toured by trolley with a ranger who knows the family letters.
Reviews: The trolley between the houses is part of the ticket and the library is the quiet highlight; the tour is ranger led and sells out in summer.

Uniqueness: The most decorated American battleship of the Second World War, the USS Massachusetts, plus a destroyer and a submarine you can walk through, all tied up together.
Reviews: Children can sleep on board with scout groups; the submarine is tight and the battleship guns are the photo.

Uniqueness: Four miles of barrier beach backed by dunes and a salt marsh, with a greenhead-free ocean side and a trail through the marsh to Ipswich Bay.
Reviews: The parking fee is steep and the beach is worth it; the marsh trail at low tide is the quiet alternative when the lot fills.

Uniqueness: A round stone barn and 20 Shaker buildings where a utopian community lived and worked, with gardens, a working farm and demonstrations of the furniture that shaped modern design.
Reviews: The round barn is the architectural highlight and the craft demos are the reason to check the daily schedule; the village is bigger than it looks.

Uniqueness: A candle factory turned museum with a 46 foot sperm whale skeleton on the roof, a restored 1840s whaleship hold and the story of the island that lit America.
Reviews: The roof walk with the skeleton and harbor view is the highlight; the museum is the best rainy day on the island.

Uniqueness: A reconstructed 1627 English village and a Wampanoag homesite where interpreters speak in period voice and answer questions about survival, diplomacy and food.
Reviews: The Wampanoag site gets the strongest praise for honest, contemporary framing. Families say it needs four hours and good shoes.

Uniqueness: A 40-foot deep spring so clear you can see the bottom from a self propelled raft, with ancient tree trunks and trout suspended in turquoise water.
Reviews: It is a 30-minute stop that people remember for years; the raft is free with park entry. Go early to avoid tour buses.

Uniqueness: A thousand acres of forested dunes with a trail to a wild Lake Michigan beach, where the sand hills are 200 feet high.
Reviews: The hike in keeps the crowd down and the beach is one of the least developed on the lake; the trail is sandy and the climb back is real.

Uniqueness: A lakefront district with a lift bridge, a maritime museum, a beach and a pier where ore boats pass through.
Reviews: The lift bridge and the ships are the draw, and the lake walk is windy and beautiful.

Uniqueness: A free zoo and conservatory with polar bears, gorillas, a Japanese garden and a carousel.
Reviews: Free and genuinely good for families, with the conservatory as the winter escape.

Typical Customer: House tour people, history fans, families
Uniqueness: A 39 room Jacobean mansion on Lake Superior with original furnishings and a carriage house, and the story of a 1977 murder that still draws visitors.
Reviews: The house and the lake setting are the tour and the crime story is the hook; the full mansion tour is worth the upgrade.

Uniqueness: The oldest state park in the country, with basalt cliffs above the St. Croix, glacial potholes and a boat tour through the Dalles.
Reviews: The pothole trail and the cliff overlooks are the walks and the river boat is the family option; the cliffs are popular with climbers.

Uniqueness: A science museum with a dinosaur hall, a Mississippi River exhibit, a omnitheater and a cell lab.
Reviews: The river exhibit and the dinosaurs are the highlights. Good for a rainy day.

Uniqueness: North Shore cliffs and waterfalls on the Baptism River, with a sea cave, a suspension bridge and trails to a high overlook of Lake Superior.
Reviews: TheShovel Point trail and the High Falls are the two walks; the park is busy in fall and the lake is cold year round.

Uniqueness: A museum in a 1942 USO building telling the stories of Black soldiers from the Revolution to today, with uniforms, medals and oral histories.
Reviews: Personal and well curated, and free. The local soldiers' stories are the strongest part.

Uniqueness: A museum of recorded music with instruments, stage clothes and interactive mixing stations, focused on Mississippi's outsize role in American music.
Reviews: The interactive studios are fun for kids and the artifacts are serious. A surprise for a small Delta town.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square of bookshops, bars, boutiques and restaurants, with the university a few blocks away and game day crowds that fill it.
Reviews: The square is the town's living room, busy on weekends and game days. The independent bookstore is the local anchor.

Uniqueness: A barbecue joint built from salvaged shacks and junk, with picnic tables under the trees, a stage for live blues and ribs that win competitions.
Reviews: The atmosphere is half the meal and the ribs are legitimately good; live music on weekends. A Gulf Coast institution.

Uniqueness: A brewery family's mansion where several members died by suicide, now a restaurant and inn with ghost tours, dinner theater and overnight rooms that guests leave early.
Reviews: The dinner mystery is campy and the history is genuinely tragic; overnight guests report doors and footsteps. Book the tour before you commit to a room.

Typical Customer: Western art people, history fans, families
Uniqueness: The largest collection of Charles Russell's paintings and sculpture, plus his log studio and the cabin where he worked, in his hometown.
Reviews: The studio and the watercolors are the reason art people come; the museum explains how a cowboy became the west's painter.

Uniqueness: The largest natural freshwater lake west of the Mississippi, 28 miles long with orchards along the east shore and islands you can camp on.
Reviews: The cherries in July and the water in August are the two seasons; the lake is deep and cold and the wind comes up in the afternoon.

Typical Customer: History families, ranch people, school groups
Uniqueness: A working cattle ranch that was the center of the open range era, with the original bunkhouse, blacksmith shop and a herd of cattle and horses.
Reviews: The rangers run the ranch with horses and the bunkhouse tour is the reason to come; it is free and the scale is bigger than a museum.

Uniqueness: One of the largest free flowing waterfalls in the northwest, where the Kootenai drops through a gorge, with a swinging bridge over the river to the far side.
Reviews: The swinging bridge is the thrill and the falls are the photograph; the trail is steep in places and the river is not for swimming.

Uniqueness: A glacial lake below Rising Wolf Mountain with a 1913 chalet, a boat shuttle and trails to twin waterfalls and a pass into the backcountry.
Reviews: The boat across the lake and the hike to Upper Two Medicine is the quiet alternative to the Going-to-the-Sun crowds; the water is cold and the wind is real.

Uniqueness: The farm of the first homesteader under the 1862 act, with a tallgrass prairie restoration, a heritage center and the original claim cabin.
Reviews: The prairie and the heritage center explain why the act changed the country; it is free and the trails are flat.

Uniqueness: A 100 acre botanical garden with a conservatory, a model train garden, a rose garden and a woodland trail.
Reviews: The model trains are the kid hit and the conservatory is the winter escape. Good in every season.

Uniqueness: A 400 foot tower with a Nebraska life mural, a unicameral chamber and an observation deck with a view of the plains.
Reviews: The building is one of the best state capitols, and the dome tour is worth it. Free.

Uniqueness: A bluff that guided Oregon Trail wagons, with a summit road, trails and a museum of the westward migration.
Reviews: The summit drive has the view and the trail is short. The Oregon Trail ruts are nearby.

Uniqueness: Badlands of mushroom shaped sandstone hoodoos and fossil beds, with a one mile loop through a landscape that looks like another planet.
Reviews: It is remote, quiet and stunning at sunset; the dirt road is impassable when wet. Bring water.

Uniqueness: Soft bentonite clay eroded into cathedral spires and slot canyons, with trails through the spires and a campground at the edge.
Reviews: The slot canyon trail is the walk and the spires glow at sunset; the clay is slippery when wet and the park is remote.

Uniqueness: A free balloon festival where 100 balloons launch at dawn from a park inside the city, with a glow show before sunrise and a teddy bear drop for children.
Reviews: The 5am glow is the photograph and the dawn patrol is worth the alarm; traffic is heavy and the parking shuttle is the way in.

Uniqueness: A bank, a school and a bottle house abandoned in the desert, plus an open air sculpture park of ghostly figures that makes the ruin feel haunted.
Reviews: The sculpture park is the surprise; go at golden hour and watch for heat and rattlesnakes. Combine with Death Valley.

Uniqueness: Twenty five original Shaker buildings on a hilltop, with a meetinghouse, a laundry, gardens and demonstrations of the inventions the community patented.
Reviews: The guides are excellent and the village is quiet; the Shaker furniture and the round barn are the highlights.

Typical Customer: House tour people, hikers, leaf peepers
Uniqueness: A 1914 Arts and Crafts mansion on a mountain above Lake Winnipesaukee, with a working farm, carriage roads and a waterfall trail on 5,000 acres.
Reviews: The view from the terrace is the reason to come and the trails are the surprise; the house tour is timed and the drive up is steep.

Uniqueness: Thirty-four miles of switchbacks, covered bridges and river pullouts through the White Mountains at peak color, one of the few drives that earns the detour.
Reviews: Locals warn that Columbus Day weekend is a parking lot; midweek dawn is the move. The Lincoln Woods trailhead is the best leg-stretch.

Uniqueness: A bare granite summit above the treeline with a 100 mile view, reached by a 1.8 mile trail that is one of the most climbed mountains in the world.
Reviews: The White Dot trail is steep and exposed and the summit is windy; start early, the parking lot fills by nine on weekends.

Uniqueness: Victorian painted-lady streets on one side, bottlenose dolphins and humpbacks off the point on the other, a beach town that never modernized.
Reviews: Dolphin sightings are near-guaranteed; the whale part is luck. The town's B&Bs and Cape May Point birding get equal praise.

Uniqueness: The highest point in the state with a 220 foot obelisk monument and a view of three states, plus a lake beach and ridge trails.
Reviews: The monument climb and the view are the payoff and the lake is the family swim; the ridge trail is the longer hike and the park is quiet in fall.

Uniqueness: Ten miles of undeveloped barrier beach with dunes, a maritime forest and no boardwalk, between the ocean and Barnegat Bay.
Reviews: The park closes when the lot fills, usually by nine in summer; the bay side is calm for children and the trails are empty in September.

Uniqueness: The shore bar where Springsteen built his reputation; still a working rock club with a summer stage, sticky floors and no pretension.
Reviews: Sound is hit or miss depending on the bill, but the history and the crowd carry it. Summer outdoor shows are the ones to catch.

Uniqueness: A lava field with ice caves, a sandstone arch and a 17 mile lava tube, on a high plateau where the flows are up to 100,000 years old.
Reviews: The lava tube needs a permit and a headlamp and the ice cave is a short walk; the landscape is black and strange and the trails are unmarked in places.

Uniqueness: A national monument of jagged granite peaks above the Rio Grande valley, with trails into the Organ Mountains and a desert of lava and petroglyphs.
Reviews: The Dripping Springs trail is the local hike and the peaks glow at sunset; the desert sections are exposed and the heat is serious in summer.

Uniqueness: A steep European style mountain with hike to terrain and chutes, in a high desert valley where the snow is dry and the sun is usually out.
Reviews: Experts rate the steeps with anything in Colorado and the base area is small; the drive from Taos is 20 minutes and the altitude is 9,200 feet.

Uniqueness: A 13 mile wide volcanic caldera with grassy valleys and forested rims, where elk herds graze and the Jemez River rises from springs.
Reviews: The elk in the valley at dusk are the reason to come and the preserve is quiet; the dirt roads close with snow and the backcountry needs a permit.

Uniqueness: Sixty five thousand acres of Allegheny plateau with two lakes, a stone casino built by the CCC and trails that run to the Pennsylvania line.
Reviews: The Red House and Quaker areas are the two bases; the CCC casino is the rainy day building and the fall color is the peak season.

Uniqueness: A sandstone gorge cut by the Ausable River with a mile of wooden walkways on the rim, a raft float through the inner chasm and a tube run down the side.
Reviews: The raft through the gorge is the thing to book; the rim walk alone is fine but the water is the point and it is cold in June.

Uniqueness: A tiny museum of New York ephemera: subway tokens, terrazzo samples, a shrine to the 1964 World's Fair and a drawer of artifacts from demolished buildings.
Reviews: It is the opposite of a blockbuster museum and that is the point; the rotating displays are made by neighbors.

Uniqueness: The research lab behind eBird and the Macaulay Library, with a viewing tower over Sapsucker Woods and a wall of screens playing recordings from every continent.
Reviews: Birders call the sound lab the best free attraction in the state; the trails are flat and the tower is open year round.

Uniqueness: A museum on the shore of Otsego Lake with a strong collection of American folk art, Native American art and the Eugene and Clare Thaw collection.
Reviews: The Thaw collection of Native art is the reason curators visit and the folk art galleries are the surprise; the lake setting is the rest.

Uniqueness: A car free barrier island of boardwalk villages, a sunken forest of holly and sassafras behind the dunes, and a lighthouse at the west end.
Reviews: Kismet and Ocean Beach are the busy villages, Watch Hill is the quiet one, and the deer will take your lunch if you leave it out.

Typical Customer: Rev war people, families, history teachers
Uniqueness: The stone fort at the narrows between Lake George and Lake Champlain, taken by Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys and later by Burgoyne, with a garden and boat tours on the lake.
Reviews: The fife and drum and the cannon demonstration run on a schedule; the hours between events are best spent on the walls and in the museum.

Uniqueness: Forty seven thousand acres of lakes and ridge line where Seven Lakes Drive winds past swimming beaches, a stone tower and the remains of colonial iron works.
Reviews: Lake Sebago is the swim, Anthony Wayne is the easy hike, and locals guard the quieter lakes; the park is bigger than the map suggests.

Uniqueness: Springwood, the Hudson river house where Roosevelt was born and ran a presidency, with his desk, his ship models and the grave where he and Eleanor are buried in the rose garden.
Reviews: The house tour and the library are separate tickets; the grounds and the Valkill cottage next door are the quiet part most people miss.

Typical Customer: Design people, mid century fans, gardeners
Uniqueness: Industrial designer Russel Wright's house built into a quarry and a woodland garden he planted by hand, with a moss floor and a pool that reflects the hemlocks.
Reviews: The house tour is the only way in and it is limited; designers leave talking about the window that frames a single tree.

Uniqueness: A Romanesque revival school building in Long Island City where the raw third floor rooms and the summer courtyard music series take more risks than most Manhattan museums.
Reviews: The sound installations and courtyard parties are the draw; check what is installed before going, since an empty floor is still a big walk.

Uniqueness: The oldest lighthouse in the state, commissioned by Washington, at the end of a 120 mile island, with 137 steps up and a view back along the whole south shore.
Reviews: The climb is tighter than people expect and the wind at the point is real; pair it with the bluffs and lunch in the harbor.

Uniqueness: J.P. Morgan's private library, with a Gutenberg Bible, the original manuscript of A Christmas Carol and a McKim building that feels like a Renaissance study.
Reviews: The East Room and the study are the rooms people remember; the rotating exhibitions pull manuscripts that rarely travel.

Uniqueness: A Charles II style manor with 200 acres of walled garden, allee and pond, built for an heir to the Phipps steel fortune and used as a set for Gatsby and The Age of Innocence.
Reviews: The walled garden peaks in late May; the house tour is short and the grounds are where people spend the afternoon.

Uniqueness: A six and a half acre bluestone sculpture built by one man over 37 years in a quarry he bought for the stone, with ramps and pools that you are allowed to walk on.
Reviews: People call it the best unknown place in the Catskills; the founder fell to his death at the site and is buried under the sculpture.

Uniqueness: An amphitheater in a state park where the New York City Ballet and Philadelphia Orchestra spend the summer and the lawn seats cost less than a city parking garage.
Reviews: The lawn is the experience, with people carrying in full dinners and candles; the sound is better under the shell but the atmosphere is outside.

Company / Access: Village of Sleepy Hollow / Historic Hudson Valley
Uniqueness: The churchyard, bridge and mill pond from Washington Irving's story, plus a lantern-lit cemetery tour and the Great Jack O'Lantern Blaze.
Reviews: The Blaze is the crowd-pleaser; tickets sell out in September. Locals warn that traffic is the real Headless Horseman.

Uniqueness: A 215 foot waterfall that drops into a rock amphitheater, taller than Niagara, with a flat gorge trail that takes you to the plunge pool.
Reviews: The gorge trail is easy and the rim trail is the view; in winter the falls freeze and the trail becomes a ice walk.

Uniqueness: A tiny burlesque and variety club on the Lower East Side with a velvet stage, a live band and acts that range from classic tease to sword swallowing.
Reviews: The room is intimate and the performers are professionals; get a table early and tip well. A reliable weird night out.

Uniqueness: Sixty seven acres of live oaks, a 400 year old oak named after a dueling legend, and a bottle chapel made from thousands of embedded bottles.
Reviews: The Airlie Oak and the bottle house are the icons; spring azaleas are spectacular. A quiet alternative to the beach.

Uniqueness: An 1859 antebellum mansion with a slave quarters building and formal gardens, restored to show both the planter family and the enslaved people who built it.
Reviews: The slave quarters exhibit is the part that stays with people. The guided tour is worth the time.

Uniqueness: A black and white striped lighthouse on the sound side of the Outer Banks, with a climb, a keeper's quarters exhibit and marsh trails around it.
Reviews: Less crowded than Hatteras and just as photogenic, with good birding on the marsh boardwalk.

Uniqueness: A museum in a 1907 courthouse devoted to the banjo player who invented the three finger roll and changed country music, with listening stations and a picking room.
Reviews: Bluegrass people make pilgrimages; the interactive stations are good for kids and the staff let you try a banjo.

Uniqueness: A deep lake backed up behind the tallest dam east of the Rockies, with the Great Smoky Mountains on one side and the Nantahala forest on the other.
Reviews: The drive along the lake is the attraction, with pullouts and swimming holes. The dam tour is seasonal.

Uniqueness: A mountain town at 4,100 feet with waterfalls on the edge of town, a main street of galleries and a summer colony that has been escaping the heat since 1875.
Reviews: The setting is gorgeous and the restaurants are better than a town this size deserves; it is expensive and crowded in July.

Uniqueness: A Carolina bay lake with a white sand shore and tea colored water, ringed by bay forest and a CCC era picnic area, one of the strangest ecosystems in the state.
Reviews: The beach is sandy and the water is warm and dark. The bay forest trail explains why the lake is oval and facing the same way as others.

Uniqueness: A seven-level, 22-room Victorian house with staircases to nowhere, a ballroom on the third floor and a chimney that runs through the middle of the dining room table.
Reviews: People call it the strangest house in the South; guides tell the family tragedy well. Small, cheap and memorable.

Uniqueness: A mountain lake ringed by cliffs and the Hickory Nut Gorge, with a public beach, boat tours and the film locations of Dirty Dancing.
Reviews: The lake is the draw and the beach is small but scenic. Boat tours sell out in summer.

Uniqueness: A 9,000 acre Carolina bay lake with clear water, a white sand bottom and a swimming beach, surrounded by pine and cypress.
Reviews: The water is unusually clear for a bay lake and the beach is shallow. Good for kids and a picnic.

Uniqueness: A 60 foot waterfall right beside the highway, with steps down to the pool and no hike required, which makes it the most accessible big falls in the mountains.
Reviews: You can see it from the car, but walk down for the spray; it is crowded on summer weekends and icy in winter.

Uniqueness: A CCC park on a ancient volcanic ridge above Lake Tillery, with a summit trail, a pool, camping and a museum of the Uwharrie range.
Reviews: The summit view is the payoff and the trails are well built. Less crowded than the Blue Ridge parks.

Uniqueness: A Rafael Viñoly building at Duke with a strong collection of medieval art, African art and contemporary work, plus a cafe in the atrium.
Reviews: The building and the medieval gallery are the draw. Free on some days for students and Durham residents.

Uniqueness: A conservation focused garden of native plants, with a piedmont woodland, a carnivorous plant collection and trails into the surrounding forest.
Reviews: The carnivorous plant house is the kid hit and the trails are quiet. Free, with a small parking fee on weekdays.

Uniqueness: The site of the first documented gold discovery in the United States, where you can walk into hand dug tunnels and pan a creek that still gives up flakes.
Reviews: Rangers are excellent with kids; the underground tour is short and cool. Panning is the reason to stay.

Uniqueness: A park with a replica of the 1585 ship Elizabeth II, a Algonquian village, a settler fort and a museum of the Lost Colony, on the sound at Manteo.
Reviews: Kids can climb the ship and try archery, and the outdoor drama next door tells the Lost Colony story in summer.

Uniqueness: A national forest trail system of red clay and granite ledges, with designated OHV routes, dispersed camping and a lake for rinsing off after.
Reviews: The trails are technical enough to be interesting and close enough to Charlotte for a day trip. Check the forest service closures before driving out.

Uniqueness: A mile and a quarter of boardwalk along the Cape Fear, with riverboats, battleship views, bars and restaurants built into the old warehouse row.
Reviews: Best at sunset, when the river turns pink and the deck bars fill up. The battleship is across the water.

Uniqueness: A national wild and scenic river with class III whitewater, swimming holes, waterfalls and a gorge road, in the Wilson Creek watershed.
Reviews: The tubing and swimming holes are the summer draw, and the gorge drive is scenic. Check water levels before paddling.

Uniqueness: A 144 mile singletrack trail across the badlands connecting the two units of Theodore Roosevelt park, with water crossings and no shade.
Reviews: Mountain bikers rate it among the best in the country and the trail is exposed and remote; carry more water than you think.

Uniqueness: A free encyclopedic museum in Eden Park with a strong collection of Old Masters, Asian art and a wing of Cincinnati artists.
Reviews: The free admission is the local pride and the ancient galleries are quiet; the park around it is a good walk.

Uniqueness: The Beast, still the longest wooden coaster in the world, plus a kids' area and a water park in a wooded park north of Cincinnati.
Reviews: The Beast at night is a genuine rite of passage; lines are manageable midweek. Food is standard park fare.

Uniqueness: The busts of every inducted player in a long gallery, plus a locker room of artifacts and a field where you can run drills.
Reviews: The bust gallery is the emotional stop and the interactive field is the family draw; the August enshrinement is the big week.

Uniqueness: A 1912 market hall with a vaulted ceiling, butcher stalls, pierogi stands and produce vendors under one roof.
Reviews: The building is beautiful and the food is cheap. Go hungry and bring cash.

Uniqueness: A park on the Mountain Fork River below Broken Bow Lake, with trout fishing, a canoe run, pine forest and CCC stonework.
Reviews: The trout stream and the kayak run are the reasons to come and the cabins book months ahead; summer weekends are crowded.

Adventure: Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History
Uniqueness: A museum with a 40 foot Apatosaurus, a gallery of Oklahoma's Native nations and a working paleontology lab, on the Norman campus.
Reviews: The dinosaur hall and the Native galleries are the two routes and the lab is where people linger; it is the best museum in the state for children.

Uniqueness: A 54 mile ridge road along the crest of the Ouachita Mountains from Talihina to Mena, Arkansas, with overlooks and switchbacks.
Reviews: Motorcyclists rate it among the best rides in the region and the fall color is the season; the road is narrow and fog can close the views.

Uniqueness: A museum of the folk singer's life, with his lyrics, drawings, guitars and the archive of his recordings.
Reviews: The archive is serious and the story is moving. Good for anyone interested in American music.

Uniqueness: The largest coastal sand dunes in North America: 500-foot slopes you can sandboard, slide or ride in a dune buggy down to the ocean.
Reviews: Sandboarding is harder than snowboarding and the rental shops give good tips; go early when the sand is firm.

Typical Customer: History families, school groups, road trippers
Uniqueness: A center on the last mountain crossing of the Oregon Trail, with life size wagon displays, a trail you can walk and the ruts still cut into the sagebrush.
Reviews: The wagon and the ruts are the reasons to stop and the ranger talks are good; it is a couple of miles off the interstate and worth the detour.

Uniqueness: A converted gristmill on the Brandywine holding three generations of Wyeth paintings, including the Olson House canvases and N.C. Wyeth's illustrations.
Reviews: The top floor galleries with the Andrew Wyeth rooms are the reason to come; the mill windows look out on the river he painted.

Uniqueness: Eight waterfalls on a privately owned gorge with boardwalks and stairs, the tallest dropping 100 feet, reached by a mile of trail in the Poconos.
Reviews: The red trail covers everything and takes two hours; it is a paid attraction, which people either resent or appreciate for the upkeep.

Typical Customer: Motorcycle people, engineers, families with teens
Uniqueness: The plant where every Harley frame and fuel tank is made and painted, walked on a catwalk above the assembly line with closed toe shoes required.
Reviews: Riders call it a pilgrimage and non riders are surprised by the robots; tours fill weeks out and the plant shuts in some holiday weeks.

Uniqueness: A 1.8 mile curve engineered in 1854 to lift the Pennsylvania Railroad over the Alleghenies, with a funicular up to a viewing park where 100 car freight trains still grind past.
Reviews: Check the train schedule at the visitor center and time your visit; the funicular and the view of the curve from above are the whole experience.

Uniqueness: A Victorian era coal town in a gorge, with a stone main street, a 1883 opera house and the grave of the athlete it renamed itself for.
Reviews: The architecture and the setting between two mountains are the reasons to walk it and the Lehigh Gorge bike trail starts here; the town is busy in fall.

Uniqueness: A 47 mile gorge of Pine Creek with two rim overlooks, a rail trail at the bottom and 800 foot rock walls that turn orange in October.
Reviews: The west rim overlooks are the easy view and the Turkey Path is the steep way down; the canyon is at its best in the first week of October.

Uniqueness: A working rail yard in the old Lackawanna shops with a roundhouse, a turntable you can watch turn a locomotive and short steam excursions through the valley.
Reviews: Train people spend all day and families do the roundhouse and the short ride; check the excursion schedule before going.

Uniqueness: The oldest continuous Fourth of July celebration in the country, a morning parade down Hope Street past colonial houses with the nation's oldest flag still flying.
Reviews: Locals claim their spot the night before; parking is impossible and the walk from the edge of town is part of the ritual.

Typical Customer: House tour people, architecture fans, families
Uniqueness: A Vanderbilt summer cottage of 500,000 cubic feet of marble, with a gold ballroom and a Chinese tea house on the cliff walk.
Reviews: The ballroom and the tea house are the stops and the audio tour explains the suffrage history of the owner; the cliff walk access is the bonus.

Uniqueness: An industrial arts center on a former steel site with blacksmithing, welding, ceramics and jewelry classes, plus public art projects made by members.
Reviews: The teaching is good and the space is honest; intro welding fills fast.

Uniqueness: A short asphalt oval where local teams race late models and street stocks on Saturday nights, with a grandstand you can sit in for ten dollars and a track that produces real contact.
Reviews: Short track racing is the best value in motorsport and this is a friendly little track. Bring a jacket and sit near the first turn.

Uniqueness: A three day downtown arts festival with juried artists, live music, food from local kitchens and demonstrations on the street.
Reviews: One of the better art fairs in the Southeast, and downtown is walkable. Go Friday evening for the crowd.

Company / Access: Free / self guided or carriage tours
Uniqueness: A Lowcountry town of antebellum houses under live oaks, with a waterfront park, a parish church from 1842 and Gullah heritage tours that tell the other half of the story.
Reviews: Less polished and less crowded than Charleston; the carriage tours are good and the shrimp is better. Go in spring.

Uniqueness: A family honey farm with an observation hive you can watch up close, a petting zoo, honey tasting and a keeper who explains how a colony survives the summer.
Reviews: The bee talk is genuinely educational and kids get to see the queen; the honey and pollen are sold on site. Small and sincere.

Uniqueness: Steeplechase racing on a spring Saturday, with tailgating in the infield, hats in the grandstand and a small town that turns out in force.
Reviews: The infield is a party and the racing is real; traffic is slow and the dress code is part of the fun.

Uniqueness: Forty five thousand acres of longleaf pine and sandhill scrub managed for the red cockaded woodpecker, with a driving loop, trails and a wiregrass understory that blooms after fire.
Reviews: The woodpeckers are the prize and the staff will tell you which clusters are active. Bring water, ticks are real, and the auto tour is the easiest way in.

Uniqueness: A theme park built on the state line, with Fury 325, a 325-foot giga coaster that crosses the border twice, plus a water park and a Peanuts kids area.
Reviews: Coaster people rate Fury among the best in the world; the park is clean and the lines are manageable midweek. Food is standard.

Uniqueness: The tabby walls of a 1697 settlement and fort still stand under the oaks above the Ashley River, with a cemetery and archaeology that never got built over.
Reviews: The ruins are atmospheric and the river view is lovely; bring bug spray and read the signs. Free of crowds.

Uniqueness: The pasture where Daniel Morgan's militia broke the British line in 1781, preserved as open ground with a walking loop and a visitor center that explains why it mattered.
Reviews: Rangers give excellent battle walks; the loop is flat and easy. Quiet, free and little visited.

Uniqueness: A boardwalk loop through a cypress swamp in the middle of town, with nesting herons, egrets and ibis a few feet from the rail.
Reviews: Free, flat and easy, and the birds are ridiculously close. Go in spring for chicks, and bring binoculars rather than a flash.

Uniqueness: A working studio carrying on the Edgefield district stoneware tradition, the alkaline glazed pottery made by enslaved potters in the 1800s, including vessels by Dave the Potter.
Reviews: The owner explains the glaze chemistry and the history without a script. Pieces are priced for users, not collectors, and face jugs are the signature.

Uniqueness: A coastal fort that was rebuilt five times from the Revolution to World War II, with gun emplacements, a harbor view and the story of the enslaved and free Black soldiers who served there.
Reviews: The self guided walk through the bunkers is genuinely atmospheric. Combine it with the beach across the street.

Uniqueness: A free museum with a deep collection of Andrew Wyeth paintings and Southern contemporary work, in a building that is easy to miss and hard to forget.
Reviews: The Wyeth collection is the reason art people stop and it is free; the galleries are never crowded.

Uniqueness: A Georgian plantation house with a giant live oak in the yard, reachable by a dirt road through Francis Marion forest, with ranger led tours of the main house.
Reviews: The oak and the quiet are the experience and the house tour is personal; call ahead for hours.

Uniqueness: A 778-acre backcountry plantation with the original 1776 brick house, slave cabins and a working farm, where interpreters demonstrate the divided world of the South Carolina upcountry.
Reviews: The living history days and the battlefield reenactment are excellent; it is quiet, cheap and rarely crowded. The slavery interpretation is honest.

Uniqueness: Four hundred acres of wetland, forest and river floodplain on the Reedy, with boardwalks, gravel trails and more than 200 recorded bird species inside the city.
Reviews: Flat, shady and free, with herons and turtles at every bend. The boardwalk section is stroller friendly.

Uniqueness: A scruffy room across the river from Columbia that books punk, hardcore and indie bands, with a patio, a pool table and a sound system louder than the building suggests.
Reviews: The booking is adventurous and the crowd is there for the music. Cheap cover, no dress code, genuine scene.

Uniqueness: A CCC park on a mountain inside the city, with a swimming lake, four lakes and trails that climb to a fire tower view over Greenville.
Reviews: The lake swim is the summer move and the trails are steep enough to feel like a workout; get there early for parking.

Company / Access: South Carolina Department of Natural Resources
Uniqueness: The highest point in South Carolina at 3,553 feet, with a new observation platform that looks over the Blue Ridge into North Carolina and Georgia.
