Reviews: A short walk from the parking lot with a huge payoff at sunset; the drive up is steep and the road closes in ice.

Uniqueness: A working shrimp boat creek lined with docks and restaurants, where pelicans wait for scraps and dolphins sometimes follow the boats in at sunset.
Reviews: The shrimp is local and the boardwalk is a nice evening walk; parking is tight and the restaurants are busy.

Uniqueness: A 10 mile paved rail trail from Port Royal to Beaufort, over marsh boardwalks and through live oak tunnels, on the old Charleston and Savannah railway grade.
Reviews: Flat, shady in stretches and full of marsh views. Rent a bike in Beaufort and ride to the end.

Uniqueness: A meat and three where the vegetables change daily, the cornbread comes out hot and the line of regulars starts before the doors open.
Reviews: The fried chicken and the squash casserole are the orders; service is fast and the room is loud. A Spartanburg institution.

Uniqueness: Half a million motorcycles take over a town of 7,000 for a week, with concerts, a mile of vendors and the Black Hills as the ride.
Reviews: It is loud, hot and utterly singular; nonriders love the spectacle. Book lodging a year ahead or camp.

Uniqueness: A half million acre forest in the Blue Ridge of east Tennessee, with the Ocoee, Hiwassee and Tellico rivers, trails and remote camping.
Reviews: The forest is huge and the rivers are the draw. Some roads are rough, so check conditions.

Uniqueness: An active fossil site from the Miocene, with a working lab behind glass, a mastodon, a red panda and a tapir, discovered during road construction in 2000.
Reviews: The lab is the interesting part, with paleontologists cleaning bones in view. Good for kids and adults.

Uniqueness: An American art museum on a bluff over the Tennessee River, with a 1904 mansion, a modern wing and a sculpture terrace above the gorge.
Reviews: The view from the terrace is worth the ticket alone, and the collection is stronger than a city this size usually supports.

Adventure: Old Stone Fort State Archaeological Park
Uniqueness: A 2,000 year old Native American ceremonial enclosure on a river bluff, with trails past the stone walls and two waterfalls.
Reviews: The mounds and the waterfalls together make a good half day. The story of the site is still being debated.

Uniqueness: High production escape rooms with practical effects and set design that feels like a film, including a prison break room and a gold rush mine.
Reviews: The rooms are polished and fair, which matters if you have done a few bad ones. Book the whole room for a group and arrive early.

Uniqueness: A full size replica of the Greek Parthenon built for the 1897 Centennial, with a 42 foot statue of Athena inside and a park around it.
Reviews: The scale is absurd in the best way, and the Athena statue surprises everyone. Cheap and quick.

Uniqueness: A paleontology hall with 60 mounted skeletons, a butterfly rainforest, a gem vault and a planetarium, all in a building on the edge of Hermann Park.
Reviews: The paleo hall and the Cockrell butterfly center are the two stops everyone makes; the museum is enormous and the add on exhibits cost extra.

Adventure: San Antonio River Walk and the Alamo
Company / Access: City of San Antonio / Alamo Trust
Uniqueness: A cypress-lined canal below street level, packed with Tex-Mex, mariachi and tour boats, two blocks from the mission where the Texas revolution began.
Reviews: The River Walk is touristy and still lovely at night; the Alamo is smaller than people expect. Eat off the main loop for better food.

Uniqueness: A float through the red rock canyon below Moab with Class II and III rapids, a beach lunch and a view of arches and petroglyphs from the water.
Reviews: The full day Fisher Towers section is the standard and the water is warm in summer; book ahead for holidays and bring sunscreen.

Uniqueness: Three natural stone bridges in a canyon with a loop road and trails underneath, plus a dark sky designation and Ancestral Puebloan ruins on the mesa.
Reviews: The Owachomo bridge at sunset is the photograph and the canyon hike is quiet; the park is remote and the nearest town is 40 minutes away.

Uniqueness: Red and white sandstone formations with lava tubes, petrified sand dunes and a slot canyon, 15 minutes from St. George and often overlooked for Zion.
Reviews: The Petrified Dunes trail and the lava tube are the local favorites; summer heat is brutal and the park is best at sunrise.

Uniqueness: Three connected caves full of helicitites and anthodites at the end of a steep 1.5 mile trail, with a view down the canyon the whole way.
Reviews: The hike is the hard part and the cave tour is the reward; tickets sell out and the trail is hot and exposed.

Typical Customer: Chamber music people, students, summer visitors
Uniqueness: A summer chamber music school where established players and young musicians rehearse together in a barn and perform programs they chose the week before.
Reviews: Audiences say the rehearsals are as good as the concerts and some are open; tickets are cheap for the quality and the barn is unheated.

Uniqueness: The state theater of Virginia, founded during the Depression when actors accepted produce as admission, still producing a full season in a 1930s playhouse.
Reviews: Production values are high for a small town and the history is charming; dinner on Main Street is part of the night.

Uniqueness: A pick your own orchard on a ridge above Charlottesville, with apple cider doughnuts, a bakery and a view of Monticello and the Blue Ridge.
Reviews: The view and the doughnuts are the reason, and picking is a fall ritual. Go early on weekends.

Uniqueness: The Potomac compresses into a quarter mile of Class V rapids twenty minutes from the capital, with cliff-top overlooks and a boulder-strewn gorge.
Reviews: Locals call it the best quick nature fix near DC; the River Trail scramble is the fun part. Parking fills by 10am on weekends.

Uniqueness: A 180 acre drive through safari where bison, zebra and elk stick their heads in your car, plus a walk through village with giraffes and kangaroos.
Reviews: Buy the feed and accept that your car will be licked; the drive through is the fun and the walk through is a bonus. Go early.

Uniqueness: The northwestern tip of the contiguous United States, where a boardwalk leads to sea caves and a view of Tatoosh Island and the open Pacific.
Reviews: The boardwalk and the sea stacks are the photograph and the drive is remote; a Makah recreation permit is required and the trail can be muddy.

Uniqueness: A rain forest lake ringed by the largest trees in the state, with a loop trail through old growth spruce and a 1926 lodge on the shore.
Reviews: The loop drive and the Rain Forest Nature Trail are the easy version and the Enchanted Valley trail is the epic; it rains most of the year.

Uniqueness: A 10,781 foot volcano with the world record for snowfall, a road to Artist Point at 5,100 feet and trails into the Heather Meadows.
Reviews: Artist Point in July and August is the view of Shuksan and the mountain and the snow lingers into summer; the road is closed in winter below the lodge.

Uniqueness: A hot shop near the waterfront where you can blow a float or a tumbler in a class, or watch a demo and buy work from local artists.
Reviews: The make your own class is the draw and the staff are good with nervous beginners; pieces ship if you are traveling.

Uniqueness: A sandstone overlook above the Cheat River gorge with a cliff edge view, plus miles of trails, climbing and a CCC picnic shelter.
Reviews: The overlook is the photograph and the underlook trail is the adventure; the forest is busy in fall and the cliffs are for experienced climbers.

Uniqueness: A vast Gothic Revival asylum built on the Kirkbride plan, with a preserved ECT room, patient art and overnight ghost hunts in the wards.
Reviews: The historical day tour is stronger than the ghost stuff; guides tell unvarnished stories of institutional abuse. The building is enormous.

Uniqueness: The winter quarters of the Ringling brothers, with circus wagons, a big top and daily performances in summer.
Reviews: The wagon collection is enormous and the shows are real. Good for kids and nostalgia.

Uniqueness: The archive of an American icon: prototype engines, a wall of gas tanks, the first serial number bike and a room of custom choppers.
Reviews: Even nonriders enjoy the design story; the factory tour in Menomonee Falls is a separate booking.

Company / Access: US Fish and Wildlife Service and Wisconsin DNR
Uniqueness: The largest freshwater cattail marsh in the country, where Canada geese stage by the hundred thousand in fall and pelicans nest in summer.
Reviews: The auto tour and the visitor center are the easy way in and the fall goose migration is the spectacle; bring bug spray.

Uniqueness: A quarter million acres of roadless Bighorn high country with 13,000 foot peaks, glacial lakes and cutthroat trout, reached by trails from West Tensleep.
Reviews: Backpackers say it is the emptiest big wilderness in the lower 48 and the weather turns fast; the trails are unmarked in places.

Uniqueness: A nightly amateur rodeo in the town Buffalo Bill built, with broncs, bull riding and a crowd that knows the difference between a good ride and a lucky one.
Reviews: It is unpolished and genuine; kids love the mutton busting. Pair with the Buffalo Bill Center of the West.

Uniqueness: A 80 foot stone wheel at 9,600 feet on the Bighorn range, aligned with the summer solstice and considered sacred by several tribes, reached by a 1.5 mile walk.
Reviews: The walk is the pilgrimage and the wheel is roped off for protection; visitors are asked to treat it as a church and the altitude is serious.

Uniqueness: A river that disappears into a limestone cave and reappears a quarter mile down the canyon, with a viewing bridge and trout you can feed at the rise.
Reviews: The disappearing river is the story and the trout at the rise are a hit with children; the canyon trails climb above the road.

Uniqueness: A rusted pig-iron furnace complex preserved as industrial archaeology, now a concert venue and the setting for a thousand ghost stories about men who died in the heat.
Reviews: The self guided walk is eerie and free; locals report unexplained sounds and the place has a genuine reputation. Bring closed shoes.

Uniqueness: A one mile-wide impact crater left by a 150-foot asteroid 50,000 years ago, with an Apollo training site and a guided rim tour.
Reviews: It is more impressive than photos suggest; the museum is good and the wind is constant. A classic Route 66 stop.

Uniqueness: America's oldest continuously operating amusement park, wrapped around a spring fed lake, with Boulder Dash, a wooden coaster cut into a mountainside.
Reviews: Coaster people adore Boulder Dash and say the park is small enough to do in a day without misery. Water park crowds peak in July.

Uniqueness: One of the largest monthly car meets in the country, with supercars, rat rods, vintage race cars and daily drivers filling a mall parking lot before sunrise.
Reviews: Get there by 7am or you will be parking a mile away; the variety is the point and owners are happy to talk. Free.

Typical Customer: Families, kids, gold rush history fans
Uniqueness: Walk 200 feet underground into a real 19th century gold mine with a miner guiding you, then pan a bucket of ore and keep whatever color you find.
Reviews: The underground tour is cool and genuinely interesting; panning is the fun part for kids. The town square is worth an hour after.

Company / Access: Genteel and Bard / local tour companies
Uniqueness: A walking tour through a city built on its own dead, where the stories are half documented history and half performance, told under live oaks and Spanish moss.
Reviews: Pick a small historian led tour over a trolley; the good guides are genuinely funny and know the archives. October is a zoo.

Uniqueness: The actual cornfield and farmhouse from the film, with a maintained diamond where anyone can hit and ghosts of a century of baseball lore.
Reviews: People arrive cynical and leave misty eyed; the movie site is free and the souvenir shop is reasonable. Combine with Dubuque.

Uniqueness: A roadhouse on a swamp pass between two lakes, famous for thin fried catfish and a view of the Manchac swamp from the dining room windows.
Reviews: The thin catfish is the order and the swamp view is the setting; it is a detour people make on purpose. Cash for the tip jar.

Uniqueness: Eight days of cherry pie, pit spitting contests, air shows and a parade in the cherry capital of the world, on a bay that looks like the Mediterranean.
Reviews: The pie and the setting are the draw; traffic is intense. Stay for the sunset over Grand Traverse Bay.

Uniqueness: Barrier islands with white sand and Civil War forts, reachable by ferry, with campgrounds on a spit of land you can walk at low tide.
Reviews: The beaches are emptier than Florida's and the forts are a bonus; the ferry to Ship Island is the best day. Summer heat and storms.

Adventure: Gates of the Mountains Boat Tour
Company / Access: Gates of the Mountains Boat Tours
Uniqueness: A tour boat up the Missouri through limestone cliffs that Lewis and Clark named, with bighorn sheep, eagles and a canyon that still looks unchanged.
Reviews: Relaxed and beautiful; the guides mix geology and expedition history well. Not a thrill ride, and that's the appeal.

Company / Access: Bethel Woods Center for the Arts
Uniqueness: The actual hayfield where Woodstock happened, with a museum on the slope and a modern amphitheater that still books legacy acts.
Reviews: The museum gets credit for honesty about the chaos and the locals; summer concerts are relaxed and picnic-friendly.

Uniqueness: A banked ribbon of track running through the building, pit-crew combines you can try, and every car that matters in stock-car history under one swooping copper roof.
Reviews: The interactive pit stop and the simulator are the hits; nonfans finish in 90 minutes. Good rainy-day pick in Charlotte.

Uniqueness: A one mile dirt oval where NASCAR raced from 1948 to 1968, now a walking trail through the woods with the banked corners still intact.
Reviews: Runners love the flat loop and the eerie feeling of a lost speedway; interpretive signs tell the story. Free and never crowded.

Uniqueness: A historic quarter mile strip known as the Rock, with test and tune nights, bracket racing and a steady stream of cars that range from ten second street machines to purpose built dragsters.
Reviews: The track has history and the pit area is open, so you can watch teams wrench between runs. Night events are the best.

Uniqueness: The colonial capitol of North Carolina, rebuilt on its original foundations with period rooms, formal gardens and costumed interpreters who stay in character.
Reviews: The gardens are as good as the house and the tour is well paced; the downtown waterfront is a short walk.

Typical Customer: Haunted house fans, teens, young adults
Uniqueness: Four attractions on a farm, including a haunted hayride through the woods, a den of darkness and a corn maze, run with a level of set design that has kept it nationally ranked.
Reviews: The hayride is the signature and the actors are relentless; go with a group and buy the combo pass. Lines peak after dark.

Typical Customer: Haunted house fans, teens, young adults
Uniqueness: A haunted attraction inside a real abandoned institution for people with disabilities, with tunnels, wards and a history that is darker than any actor in makeup.
Reviews: The setting does most of the work and the history is worth reading before you go; some visitors find the spectacle uncomfortable given the real suffering.

Uniqueness: A small museum and pottery workshop on the Catawba reservation, where the tribe that gave the river its name still digs clay and shapes it into the same forms their ancestors made.
Reviews: The pottery demonstration is the reason to visit and pieces are for sale; call ahead because hours vary. A living culture, not a diorama.

Company / Access: National Park Service / Fort Sumter Tours
Uniqueness: The island fort where the first shots of the Civil War were fired, reached only by boat, with the original brick walls and a flag that still flies over the harbor.
Reviews: The boat ride and ranger talk are the experience; the fort itself is mostly ruins. Book the early ferry to beat the heat.

Uniqueness: An 1881 opera house with a clock tower, restored to a 400 seat hall that books touring blues, bluegrass and Broadway acts into a town of 10,000.
Reviews: The acoustics and the painted ceiling are lovely; every seat is close. Dinner in town before the show is the routine.

Uniqueness: A beach music club where the Carolina shag is still danced on a big wooden floor, with live bands and a crowd that has been coming for thirty years.
Reviews: If you ask, someone will teach you the basic step. It is a living piece of South Carolina culture and the opposite of a tourist club.

Uniqueness: A CCC-built park of stone cabins and a spring fed swimming lake at 2,000 feet, with the Foothills Trail passing through and a Friday-night mountain music jam.
Reviews: The cabins are cheap and the lake is cold; the old time music on summer weekends is the local secret.

Uniqueness: A CCC park where the coastal plain meets the sandhills, with steep ravines, a mill pond, mountain laurel and a trail network that feels more mountain than lowcountry.
Reviews: People call it the mountains of the midlands, and the ravines are a real climb. The CCC cabins are simple and cheap.

Uniqueness: Thirty thousand acres of former rice plantations turned refuge, with a driving tour along dikes where alligators, herons and eagles are routine.
Reviews: The Laurel Hill drive is the easy wildlife loop and the rice field history is fascinating; stay in the car around gators.

Uniqueness: The brick house where Shoeless Joe Jackson lived and died, moved to a lot beside the minor league ballpark and filled with his bats, shoes and the case for his innocence.
Reviews: The volunteers are passionate and the story of the 1919 Black Sox is told from the local side; open Saturdays and worth planning around.

Uniqueness: The only public park in the country with all eight species of swan, plus a boardwalk through cypress and the largest collection of Japanese iris in the world.
Reviews: The bloom in late May is the reason to come and the swans follow you around; it is free and quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A mountaintop adventure park reached by chondola or rail, with a treetop skywalk, a mountain coaster and a suspension bridge above the Smokies.
Reviews: The views and the tree canopy walk are the draw; it is expensive and the coaster lines are long. Sunset is the best slot.

Uniqueness: The largest commercial caverns in Texas, with a discovery tour through cathedral rooms and an adventure tour that crawls through undeveloped passages.
Reviews: The adventure tour is the one for adults; the main tour is impressive but crowded. Wear shoes with grip.

Uniqueness: A hidden garden of stone carvings by a Mormon bishop, including a sphinx with the face of Joseph Smith, tucked between houses in a residential block.
Reviews: It is free, small and genuinely strange; most locals have never been. A five minute detour.

Adventure: Dog Mountain and the Dog Chapel
Uniqueness: Stephen Huneck's hilltop chapel covered floor to ceiling in photographs and notes to dead dogs, with a pond, meadows and a print shop that doubles as a grief ritual.
Reviews: People arrive skeptical and leave quiet. It is free, uncommercial and genuinely moving; the chapel walls are the whole point.

Uniqueness: A water powered gristmill, sawmill and blacksmith shop on the Blue Ridge Parkway, with a millpond that reflects the whole thing and a weekend craft demonstration.
Reviews: The most photographed spot on the Parkway and it earns it at dawn; the restaurant's buckwheat pancakes are a tradition.

Uniqueness: A 104 foot waterfall in a stone gorge on Lookout Mountain, with a short trail and a swimming area below.
Reviews: The falls are easy to reach and the pool is cold. A good stop on the way to Little River Canyon.

Uniqueness: A museum of Mardi Gras in the city that started it, with elaborate trains, crowns, robes and the story of the mystic societies.
Reviews: The costumes are spectacular and the history explains why Mobile, not New Orleans, claims the first carnival.

Uniqueness: A CCC park on a mountain above Huntsville with trails, a lodge, cabins and overlooks of the Tennessee Valley.
Reviews: The trails are well built and the overlooks are the payoff. Less crowded than the space center.

Uniqueness: A 90 foot waterfall in a city park with a gorge trail, a miniature train, a campground and a statue of the Cherokee woman the falls are named for.
Reviews: The gorge trail gets you behind the falls, which kids love. The park is old fashioned and cheap.

Uniqueness: A courthouse museum in the town that shaped Harper Lee and Truman Capote, with a courtroom modeled on the one in To Kill a Mockingbird.
Reviews: For readers it is a pilgrimage, and the annual play is performed in the courtroom. Check the schedule.

Uniqueness: A gold mining camp at 3,500 feet in Hatcher Pass, with bunkhouses, a mill and tram towers still standing against the alpine tundra.
Reviews: The buildings against the mountains are the photograph and the rangers explain the mining; the road up is steep and the site is only open in summer.

Adventure: Klondike Gold Rush National Historical Park
Uniqueness: The restored gold rush town and the Chilkoot trailhead, with ranger walks through the wooden buildings and a museum on the stampeders who climbed the pass.
Reviews: The ranger walk through town is the best hour in Skagway and the trailhead is a short drive; the town is busy when ships are in.

Uniqueness: The burled arch at the end of the 1,000 mile Iditarod trail, where the mushers arrive after ten days and the town of 3,700 turns out.
Reviews: The finish line in the dark and cold is the experience and the town is welcoming; getting to Nome in March takes planning.

Uniqueness: A family ranch where a herd of reindeer walks with you through the boreal forest, with a tour that explains antlers, lichen and what reindeer actually are.
Reviews: The walk with the herd is the reason people book and the owners are funny and specific; it is a small operation and fills weeks ahead.

Uniqueness: Jump into the Arctic Ocean at the northernmost town in the United States, where the sun does not set and the water is barely above freezing.
Reviews: It is a bucket list bragging right and a genuinely strange place; travel is expensive and logistics are real.

Uniqueness: A canyon in the Huachuca Mountains where 15 species of hummingbird pass through in summer, with a shaded trail along a creek.
Reviews: Hummingbird season from April to September is the reason to come and the feeders at the visitor center are the viewing; reservations are required.

Uniqueness: A 183 foot tall natural travertine bridge with a creek running under it, and trails down to the water through a cave and along the rim.
Reviews: The trail under the bridge is steep and slick and the view from the top is the easy version; the park is small and the parking is limited.

Uniqueness: The adobe ruins of a mission church on the Santa Cruz, with a museum on the O'odham and Yaqui people and a orchard of heirloom fruit trees.
Reviews: The church walls and the quiet are the visit and the rangers explain the mission system honestly; the December fiesta is the local tradition.

Uniqueness: A visitor center and campground on the Buffalo National River, the first national river in the country, with bluffs, gravel bars and floating.
Reviews: The river float is the reason to come and Tyler Bend is the easy access; the water is clear and the crowds are at the outfitters.

Uniqueness: The only public diamond mine in the world where you keep what you find: a plowed volcanic crater you sift by hand in the Arkansas heat.
Reviews: Find rates are low and people still get hooked; rent the sifting kit and go early. Staff identify finds for free.

Uniqueness: A museum of Delta music and life in a former railroad depot, with the King Biscuit Time radio show and the blues trail.
Reviews: The music exhibits are excellent and free, and the town is ground zero for Delta blues radio.

Uniqueness: A street of bars, restaurants and music venues next to the university, with the Walton Arts Center at one end.
Reviews: Busy on weekends and game days, with good local music. Walk it before a show.

Uniqueness: One of only two purse museums in the world, telling the story of American women in the 20th century through the bags they carried and what was inside them.
Reviews: The curated contents of each decade's purse are the clever part; it is small, sharp and unexpectedly moving.

Uniqueness: One of the cleanest lakes in the country, with 200 islands and a state park on a peninsula, near the quartz mines of the Ouachitas.
Reviews: The water clarity is the reason people drive and the islands are the camping; the lake is big and the coves are quiet.

Uniqueness: A historic thoroughbred track with a casino, a grandstand and a racing season that has run for over a century.
Reviews: The cheap seats are close to the rail and the corned beef is a local tradition. Check the racing calendar.

Uniqueness: A lodge and overlook on the second highest peak in the state, at the Arkansas end of the Talimena Scenic Drive, with views into two states.
Reviews: Motorcyclists ride the drive for the curves and the lodge is the stop; the fall color is the season and the ridge is often in cloud.

Typical Customer: Groups, families with teens, adventure seekers
Uniqueness: Class III and IV rapids on the river that flows out of the Sierra south of Sequoia, with a gorge section and a calmer lower run for first timers.
Reviews: Outfitters say May and June are the biggest water and the lower river is the family trip; the water is cold and the canyon is hot.

Adventure: Marshall Gold Discovery State Historic Park
Uniqueness: The sawmill site where gold was found in 1848, with a replica mill, a mine tunnel, a blacksmith and a chance to pan for gold in the American River.
Reviews: Panning is the reason children agree to the history; the park is shaded and the museum explains how the discovery changed the state.

Uniqueness: A 576 foot volcanic plug at the mouth of an estuary where sea otters raft in the channel and a dozen charter boats run fishing trips.
Reviews: The otters in the harbor and the hike around the rock are the two things to do; the estuary is a bird sanctuary and kayak rentals are at the dock.

Adventure: Rosie the Riveter WWII Home Front
Uniqueness: The shipyards where 90,000 workers built 747 ships in four years, with a museum, a preserved child care center and a waterfront walk past the dry docks.
Reviews: The ranger talks and the oral histories are the reason to come; the walk along the bay to the Ford plant is the part most people miss.

Uniqueness: Twenty four acres with a Japanese garden, a tropical conservatory and a Rocky Mountain alpine collection that grows plants from above treeline.
Reviews: The Japanese garden and the conservatory are the winter stops; the summer concert series on the lawn is the local date night.

Uniqueness: A original gold mine cage drops you 1,000 feet underground into tunnels where ore cars, drills and stopes are still in place, guided by miners.
Reviews: The cage ride is the thrill and the guides are retired miners; it is cold underground and the tour is the only way in.

Uniqueness: The high-Victorian Gothic house where Twain wrote Tom Sawyer and Huckleberry Finn, with hand-stenciled walls and a billiard room upstairs.
Reviews: Guides are excellent on the money troubles that forced the family out. The house is the star; the museum is thin by comparison.

Uniqueness: A natural history museum with a brontosaurus mount that helped start the dinosaur craze, a great hall of mammals and an Egyptian collection, reopened after a major renovation.
Reviews: The dinosaur hall is the reason children ask to return; admission is free and the new galleries are brighter than the old ones.

Uniqueness: A hangar of C-5s, C-141s and a C-47 restored as a D-Day aircraft, plus the only B-17 in Delaware, free and walk around open.
Reviews: Volunteers are often retired loadmasters and will open cockpits; the C-5 is the size people cannot get over.

Uniqueness: Sixteen thousand acres of tidal salt marsh and impoundments on the Delaware Bay where hundreds of thousands of shorebirds stop in May and eagles nest within sight of the road.
Reviews: The auto tour loop is the way in and the observation tower at Raymond Pool is where the photographers set up; bring bug spray in summer.

Uniqueness: The brewery that invented continual hopping and put American craft beer on the map, with a tour that includes the original 1995 brewhouse and a tasting.
Reviews: Tours are praised for honesty about failures and for generous pours; book ahead and eat at the brewpub.

Uniqueness: Cedar Hill, the house Douglass bought after the war, with his library, his desk and a view over the Anacostia and the Capitol.
Reviews: The ranger tour is the only way in and the view from the porch is half the story; the site is in a neighborhood most visitors never see.

Uniqueness: The estate of the Post cereal heiress, with a collection of Russian imperial art including Faberge eggs, and a Japanese garden and French parterre.
Reviews: The Faberge collection is the reason art people come and the gardens are the quiet afternoon; it is off the tourist track and never crowded.

Uniqueness: Tradecraft you can touch: a real Enigma, disguise stations, listening devices and the stories of spies who defected, lied and disappeared.
Reviews: The interactive undercover assignment is a hit with teens; adults want more artifacts and less queue. Book a timed slot.

Uniqueness: The only national park devoted to aquatic plants, with ponds of lotus and water lilies on the Anacostia and a boardwalk through a tidal marsh.
Reviews: The lotus bloom in July is the event and photographers arrive at dawn; the park is in a quiet part of the city and feels overlooked.

Uniqueness: A museum of bombs, missiles, guns and aircraft, with a B-52, an SR-71 and a MOAB, on the Eglin base.
Reviews: The hardware is impressive and free. Bring ID for base access.

Adventure: Alfred B. Maclay Gardens State Park
Uniqueness: A 1,200 acre estate with formal camellia and azalea gardens, a brick walk, a lake and a 1920s house.
Reviews: The spring bloom is the reason, and the brick walk is beautiful. Quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A 1920s artist's estate between the beach and the intracoastal, with a shell museum, a courtyard and gardens that survived the condo boom.
Reviews: The house is eccentric and personal, and the grounds are a green surprise in the middle of Fort Lauderdale. Guided tours only.

Uniqueness: A tiny old Florida fishing and clam town on a Gulf island, with a boardwalk, a dock, clam shacks and sunsets over the marsh.
Reviews: The clams and the sunset are the reasons, and the town is small enough to walk. Quiet midweek.

Uniqueness: A 1920s stone house on Biscayne Bay with fossil beds, a hardwood hammock and a canoe trail through the mangroves.
Reviews: The house tour and the nature trail are both good, and the bay is calm for kayaking. Less crowded than Vizcaya.

Uniqueness: A 120 foot deep sinkhole with a boardwalk down to the bottom, fern covered walls and a miniature rainforest at the floor.
Reviews: The boardwalk down is steep and cool, and the sinkhole feels like another world. Quick and cheap.

Uniqueness: Fifty acres of camellias, roses and a tropical rainforest on a lake, with a 1880s house museum and a butterfly garden.
Reviews: Shady and quiet, a good break from the theme parks. The camellia collection is the winter highlight.

Uniqueness: A drive through safari park with lions, rhinos, giraffes and zebras loose around the car, plus a walk through amusement area.
Reviews: The drive is the fun, especially for kids who have never seen a lion outside a cage. Go early when the animals are active.

Uniqueness: A wooden pier on a wide Gulf beach, good for fishing, dolphin watching and the sunset that draws a crowd every night.
Reviews: The sunset is the event and the pier is the viewpoint. Parking is tight, so walk or bike.

Uniqueness: A fruit stand that became a landmark, selling smoothies from fruit you have never heard of, with a petting zoo, live music and a milkshake list that runs to dozens.
Reviews: The smoothies are the reason to stop on the way to the Everglades; the line moves and the exotic fruit tasting is worth it.

Uniqueness: The planned New Urbanist town where The Truman Show was filmed, with pastel cottages, picket fences, a pavilion and a walkable center.
Reviews: The architecture is the attraction and the beach is gorgeous. Busy in summer, quiet in winter.

Company / Access: St. Augustine Lighthouse and Maritime Museum
Uniqueness: A black and white striped lighthouse with a maritime museum and a dark of the moon ghost tour, where staff report footsteps on the tower stairs and a girl in the basement.
Reviews: The climb is worth it for the view alone; the ghost tour is one of the better researched ones in Florida. Book after dark.

Uniqueness: A warehouse of immersive light and sound installations, including a mirrored infinity room and a cloud sculpture you walk through, designed by artists rather than set builders.
Reviews: The mirrored room is the photo everyone wants and the timed entry keeps it calm; it is short for the price. Pair with the Design District.

Uniqueness: A 52 acre museum of Florida history and wildlife with a 1880s farm, a caboose, a zip line and native animals including panthers and bears.
Reviews: The mix of history and animals works for kids, and the zip line is the adrenaline add on.

Uniqueness: An aquarium with a walk through wetland gallery, sharks, otters and a coral reef exhibit, plus a splash pad and a penguin encounter.
Reviews: The wetland walk through is the best part and the splash pad saves a hot afternoon. Book online for a discount.

Uniqueness: A pontoon tour through a chain of lakes and narrow canals, past lakeside mansions and the Rollins College campus, narrated by a local.
Reviews: The canals are the charm and the guides are funny. Cheap, shaded and a good break from the heat.

Uniqueness: Flannery O'Connor's farm, where she wrote her short stories and raised peacocks, with the house, the dairy barn and the birds still on the property.
Reviews: Pilgrimage for readers, and the peacocks are a hit with everyone else. The house tour is small and personal.

Uniqueness: A stacked loop trail system on Corps of Engineers land with flowy berms, rock gardens and a beginner loop, maintained by local riders.
Reviews: The trails are well built and signed, with a skills loop for beginners. Check the trail status after rain.

Uniqueness: One of Georgia's newest and largest state parks, with a bend of the Chattahoochee, riverside campsites, a canoe launch and bluff trails.
Reviews: Quiet and spacious, with real river access. The walk to the bend is the hike to do.

Uniqueness: A nature center on the river with rehab birds of prey, a beaver pond, boardwalks and canoe programs, twenty minutes from midtown.
Reviews: The hawks and owls are the hit and the trails are easy. Check the river programs in summer.

Uniqueness: A zoo and 700 acre park with a splash pad, a nature trail, a train and a collection heavy on African and North American animals.
Reviews: Good value for a family day, with enough shade to survive a Georgia summer. The train is the kid favorite.

Adventure: Chick-fil-A College Football Hall of Fame
Uniqueness: A museum with a field where you run drills, throw passes and kick field goals, plus a wall of every college helmet and the stories of the inductees.
Reviews: The interactive field is the point and adults have as much fun as kids. Allow two hours.

Typical Customer: Band of Brothers readers, veterans, history travellers
Uniqueness: The story of Camp Toccoa, where the paratroopers of Easy Company trained by running up Currahee Mountain, told with a reconstructed barracks, original gear and the horse barn the men lived in.
Reviews: People come because of the series and leave knowing the mountain is real. The barracks reconstruction and the oral histories are the strongest parts.

Uniqueness: A school for freedpeople that became the planning site for the Birmingham campaign, where Martin Luther King Jr and the movement's leaders met in 1963 in a room still standing.
Reviews: The dormitory room where they met is preserved and the guides tell it from memory. A national landmark that gets almost no traffic.

Uniqueness: A listening room above a Decatur storefront where John Mayer and the Indigo Girls played early shows, with tables, a bar and no talking during sets.
Reviews: The sound is excellent and the room is small enough to see hands on strings. Buy tickets ahead for name acts.

Uniqueness: A mountaintop wall of stacked stone almost 900 feet long whose builders nobody can name, with a stone tower and a legend of a moon eyed people, plus a lake and ridge trails above the cloud line.
Reviews: The wall is the reason people come and the debate about who built it has never been settled. The view west from the overlook is the other payoff.

Uniqueness: A heritage farm inside a state park, with a log cabin village, a tobacco barn, farm animals and a boardwalk over the Seventeen Mile River swamp where gopher tortoises dig in the sandhills.
Reviews: The farm is more interesting than the trails and people say so. The Burnham House cottage is the odd overnight option.

Uniqueness: Ten days of pink in a city that claims 300,000 cherry trees, with a parade, concerts, a bed race and pancakes at the Kiwanis tent.
Reviews: The trees are the excuse and the civic energy is the point. Parking downtown is easier than expected on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A fourth generation apple orchard with u-pick apples and berries, a bakery, a hard cider tasting room and a market full of fried pies.
Reviews: The fried pies and cider doughnuts are the reason, and u-pick is a fall ritual. Go early on October weekends.

Season / Dates: Guided walks by arrangement, spring and autumn
Uniqueness: Four thousand acres of old growth longleaf pine and blackwater swamp along the Altamaha, one of the largest remaining old growth longleaf stands left anywhere, with trees older than the county.
Reviews: Access is limited and arranged through the conservancy, which keeps it intact. Red cockaded woodpeckers and the open pine cathedral are what people describe.

Uniqueness: The first museum devoted to Southern art, with landscapes, portraits and contemporary work from the region, on Augusta's riverfront.
Reviews: A serious collection in a small city, and the riverfront location makes a good afternoon. Check for free days.

Uniqueness: A 1,100 acre wetland nature park with boardwalks and dikes through a working water treatment landscape, where herons, alligators and wintering ducks show up close.
Reviews: It sounds industrial and is actually beautiful, with more wildlife than most parks. Bring binoculars and bug spray.

Uniqueness: A peninsula of trails and campsites on Lake Allatoona, with a beach, a marina and a ridge trail through pine and hardwood.
Reviews: The lake views and the easy trails make it a good family day. Summer weekends fill the beach early.

Uniqueness: A honey shop with a tasting bar where you can compare sourwood, tupelo and buckwheat side by side, plus mead flights and a wall explaining how each hive works.
Reviews: The tasting is free and the staff know the difference between varietals; the mead flight is a nice add. Good gifts.

Uniqueness: A preserve with a boardwalk, a visitor center and a summit trail to a rock outcrop with a view over Lake Lanier and the Blue Ridge foothills.
Reviews: The summit trail is short and steep with a big payoff. The Indian Seats rock is the photo.

Uniqueness: A guided walk through the small town that played Alexandria in The Walking Dead, with the storefronts, the wall and the filming stories.
Reviews: Fans love it and non fans still get a good small town walk. Book ahead and wear comfortable shoes.

Uniqueness: A paved rail trail running from Smyrna to the Alabama line, over trestles and through tunnels, built on the old Seaboard Air Line grade.
Reviews: Flat and fast, good for long rides and beginner skaters. Start at the Dallas or Hiram trailhead for parking.

Adventure: Southern Museum of Civil War and Locomotive History
Uniqueness: The home of the General locomotive, stolen by Union spies in the Great Locomotive Chase of 1862, with the engine, the rail car and the spy story in one room.
Reviews: The locomotive is real and the story is better than the movie. Kids love the model train layout.

Typical Customer: Farm families, equipment nerds, curious town people
Uniqueness: North America's largest outdoor farm show spreads over 100 acres of working plots, with combines cutting real corn, a tractor pull and every implement made for the southern row crop trade.
Reviews: It is enormous and free parking, and the demo fields are the part outsiders do not expect. Bring boots, the grounds get deep.

Season / Dates: Runs in seasons, spring and autumn
Uniqueness: Georgia's official folk life play, written each year from interviews with local people and performed by neighbours at the Cotton Hall, with a cast of dozens and a live band.
Reviews: The stories are the county's own and the crowd is the county's own, which is why it works. Book ahead, weekend shows sell out.

Uniqueness: Savannah's beach town, with a working lighthouse you can climb, wide sand, a pier and loggerhead turtles nesting on the dunes in summer.
Reviews: Parking is the main cost and the main hassle. North Beach is quieter, and the turtle patrol runs night walks in season.

Uniqueness: A state park with a lake, a beach, paddleboard rentals, zip lines and trails that connect to Anna Ruby Falls, minutes from the Alpine village of Helen.
Reviews: The lake is the summer draw and the zip line is the surprise. Book cabins early for October.

Uniqueness: The longest covered bridge in Georgia, a 229 foot Town lattice span over the South Fork of the Broad River, with a mill site, shoals and a swimming and tubing hole beneath it.
Reviews: Tubing the shoals in summer is the local tradition. The bridge itself is the photograph, especially in fog.

Uniqueness: A reconstructed 1850s Georgia town with original buildings moved to the site, including a courthouse, a church, a cotton gin and a working print shop.
Reviews: Living history without the theme park gloss. Check the schedule for demonstrations, because weekdays can be quiet.

Uniqueness: A mountaintop winery with a terrace over the Blue Ridge foothills, tastings of estate wines and a Sunday brunch that books out.
Reviews: The view is the reason and the wines are decent. Reserve the terrace table and go for sunset.

Uniqueness: A 442 foot waterfall dropping into a gorge of bamboo and ferns, reached by a loop trail through a rain forest of orchids and ginger.
Reviews: The falls are the photograph and the loop is paved with stairs; it rains often and the trail is slippery, which is why it is green.

Uniqueness: A trail through a volcanic crater and a World War II bunker to a 761 foot summit over Waikiki and the Pacific, with the crater walls around you.
Reviews: The bunker and the view are the payoff and the trail is exposed and crowded; reservations are required and the early slot is cooler.

Uniqueness: A overlook 1,600 feet above the leprosy settlement peninsula where Father Damien worked, with the sea cliffs and the village below.
Reviews: The view is the reason to drive up and the history is the reason to go down; the settlement itself is only accessible by tour, mule or trail.

Uniqueness: A climb up 1,048 railroad ties on an old military tramway to a crater rim view of Hanauma Bay and the southeast coast.
Reviews: The stairs are relentless and the view is the reward; go at sunrise, the trail is exposed and crowded later.

Uniqueness: A short steep climb to two World War II concrete observation posts above Lanikai beach, with a view of the Mokulua islands and the windward coast.
Reviews: Sunrise from the pillboxes is the photograph everyone wants and the trail is short but steep and rooty; parking is in a residential neighborhood.

Uniqueness: One of the deepest lakes in the country, 43 miles long below the Selkirk Mountains, with a town beach, a ski hill and Navy acoustic testing.
Reviews: The lake and the mountains are the reason people move to Sandpoint and the summer water is cold; the winter ski hill is right above town.

Uniqueness: The heart of a park that stretches across four states, with a museum of Nez Perce beadwork, a mission site and the story of the 1877 war.
Reviews: The museum and the ranger talks are the reason to start here before following the trail; the collection is from the tribe and the interpretation is theirs.

Uniqueness: A glacial lake ringed by pine and mountains with a town beach, a winter carnival with snow sculptures and a ski hill above it.
Reviews: The summer lake and the winter carnival are the two seasons; the town is small and the water is cold and clear.

Uniqueness: A 1,500 acre estate with a formal garden, a brick-walled mansion and sculptures in the woods including the Fu Dog Garden.
Reviews: The Fu Dog Garden and the sunken garden are the surprises and it is free; the park is between Champaign and Decatur and easy to miss.

Uniqueness: A university museum designed by I.M. Pei with a broad collection from ancient to contemporary, free and quiet on the Bloomington campus.
Reviews: The building and the ancient galleries are the reasons to stop; it is free and the modern wing rotates often.

Uniqueness: A historic mineral spring resort with a grand hotel, a casino, a spa and the Pluto mineral water that made it famous.
Reviews: The hotel is a step back in time and the grounds are pretty. Worth a walk even if you are not staying.

Uniqueness: A big state fair with livestock shows, a midway, tractor pulls, fried food and the dairy bar.
Reviews: The dairy bar and the livestock barns are the local picks. Go on a weekday.

Uniqueness: A Ohio River town of 1,000 preserved buildings from the steamboat era, stacked on the bluffs, with a main street that runs to the water.
Reviews: The walk up and down the hill is the visit and the river view is the photograph; the town is quiet on weekdays and busy in summer.

Uniqueness: An Amish run livestock auction and a thousand vendor flea market where you can buy a horse, a pie and a hand forged tool in the same morning.
Reviews: The auction is the real show; get there at 8am for the horses. The flea market is enormous and the food is excellent.

Uniqueness: A neighborhood of Czech bakeries, a butcher, a museum and a riverfront, with kolaches and a national Czech and Slovak museum.
Reviews: The kolaches are the reason and the museum is worth an hour. The river walk is a bonus.

Uniqueness: A narrow band of wind deposited hills along the Missouri, with prairie ridges, sharp bluffs and a landscape found in only one other place on earth.
Reviews: The ridges are best at sunrise and the prairie flowers peak in summer. Drive the back roads.

Uniqueness: A five day festival of steam engines, threshing machines and antique tractors on a 200 acre grounds with a narrow gauge railroad and a carousel.
Reviews: The steam engines under load are the spectacle and the tractor parade is the tradition; it is one of the largest old threshing shows in the country.

Uniqueness: A Dutch heritage festival with 300,000 tulips, street scrubbing, costumed dancers and a working windmill in a town of 10,000.
Reviews: The tulips and the parade are the reasons to come and the Dutch bakeries sell out; parking is on the edge of town and the crowds are real.

Uniqueness: A 16 story electric shovel that was the largest in the world, preserved in a strip mine field where you can climb into the cab.
Reviews: The scale is the attraction and children cannot believe the size; it is a pilgrimage for engineers and a good detour for everyone else.

Company / Access: Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks
Uniqueness: A 19,000 acre wetland in the middle of the state where half the shorebirds in North America stop during migration.
Reviews: The migration in spring is the spectacle and the viewing blinds are the way to see it; the roads can flood and the area is remote.

Uniqueness: A university museum with dinosaur fossils, a giant mosasaur, Kansas fossils and a live beehive.
Reviews: Free and genuinely good, especially the mosasaur. A quick stop for kids.

Uniqueness: A copper domed capitol with a mural by John Steuart Curry, a legislative chamber and a dome tour to the top.
Reviews: The Curry mural and the dome climb are the reasons. Free, with tours on the hour.

Company / Access: The Nature Conservancy and Kansas State University
Uniqueness: Eight thousand acres of unplowed tallgrass prairie with bison herds, a trail system and research plots that have run for decades.
Reviews: The bison loop and the spring wildflowers are the reasons to hike and the prairie is hot and exposed; stay on the trails.

Uniqueness: Chalk pyramids and arches left by an ancient sea, rising out of the shortgrass prairie in the middle of nowhere.
Reviews: It is a genuine surprise and completely free; the dirt road is rough after rain. Best at sunset.

Uniqueness: A memorial building over the symbolic birth cabin of Lincoln, with a spring, a museum and the farm site.
Reviews: The memorial is impressive and the story is well told. Free or cheap, and quick.

Uniqueness: A cave tour with a underground river, a suspension bridge over the gorge and a museum of cave science.
Reviews: The bridge and the river are the highlights, and the tour is more physical than a show cave.

Uniqueness: A mountaintop park with sandstone cliffs, a lake and overlooks into the Cumberland Mountains, one of the highest parks in the state.
Reviews: The views are expansive and the trails are short. Quiet and free.

Uniqueness: The Federal style mansion that inspired the state song, with period rooms, outbuildings and the story of the Rowan family and the enslaved people they held.
Reviews: The house tour is honest about slavery and the song's complicated history. The grounds are pretty.

Uniqueness: Every generation of America's sports car, plus the sinkhole that swallowed eight of them in 2014, now preserved as a exhibit with the wrecked cars on display.
Reviews: The sinkhole exhibit is the reason non-car-people come; the motorsports park next door offers laps. Worth the detour off I-65.

Uniqueness: The site of the largest Civil War battle in Kentucky, with earthworks, a museum and a driving tour through the rolling farmland.
Reviews: The museum explains a battle most people have never heard of, and the fields are quiet.

Uniqueness: The tallest state capitol in the country, with an Art Deco interior, a observation deck and the spot where Huey Long was shot.
Reviews: The observation deck view is the reason, and the building is a monument to Long's ambition. Free.

Uniqueness: The warehouse where parade floats are built, with giant figures, props and a tour through the painting and sculpting shops.
Reviews: The scale of the floats is the fun and kids love it. The tour includes a slice of king cake.

Uniqueness: Three hundred thousand lights along a 33-block historic riverfront, with boat parades, fireworks and meat pies, the oldest holiday light display in the South.
Reviews: It is a genuine small town spectacle; parking is the challenge. Eat a Natchitoches meat pie while you walk.

Company / Access: Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands
Uniqueness: A mountain pass with a gorge of potholes and waterfalls, a short trail to Screw Auger Falls and the trailheads for Old Speck and the Mahoosucs.
Reviews: The falls are a five minute walk and the Table Rock trail is the view; the park is quiet compared with Acadia.

Uniqueness: A chain of off grid lodges connected by 80 miles of trail through the Carrabassett valley, with bunk rooms, wood heat and meals cooked by a hutmaster.
Reviews: People ski hut to hut in winter and hike in summer; the huts are comfortable and the booking system fills months ahead.

Uniqueness: A mile and a quarter of paved footpath along the top of the sea wall between Ogunquit beach and Perkins Cove, with granite benches and rose bushes.
Reviews: It is the most walkable mile on the Maine coast and busy on summer mornings; the cove at the south end has the lobster shack.

Company / Access: Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands
Uniqueness: A sand spit that shifts with the tide, with a view of two islands and the remains of Fort Popham at one end, near the site of the 1607 Popham colony.
Reviews: At low tide you can walk to Fox Island and the currents at the river mouth are dangerous; the beach is wide and rarely packed.

Uniqueness: A mile and a half walk through woods to a beach below 30 million year old cliffs where shark teeth and shells wash out of the sand.
Reviews: Children find teeth within minutes and the walk back is uphill; collecting is allowed from the beach but not the cliffs.

Uniqueness: A wooded mountain park built around a CCC camp, with trails to a waterfall and a vista, and Camp David hidden in the next hollow.
Reviews: The Cunningham Falls and the Blue Blazes trail are the walks; the park is quiet on weekdays and the presidential retreat is off limits.

Uniqueness: A 3,900 acre lake in the Allegheny mountains with a swimming beach, boat rentals and a ski area at one end, ringed by state forest.
Reviews: Summer is the lake and winter is Wisp ski area; the state park beach is the cheap way in and the rental houses fill a year ahead.

Uniqueness: A 1891 trolley park and Chautauqua that became an arts center, with a 1921 carousel, a Spanish ballroom with swing dances and a glass studio.
Reviews: The Saturday night swing dance in the ballroom is the local institution; the art studios are open to walk through and the carousel is two dollars.

Uniqueness: The site of Maryland's first capital, with a reconstructed 17th century inn, a tobacco plantation and an ongoing dig that has found the original statehouse.
Reviews: The archaeology is the story and the guides are often students; the living history and the ship reconstruction make it a full half day.

Uniqueness: A network of water trails through a Chesapeake marsh with a beach and campsites reachable only by boat, near the crab houses of Crisfield.
Reviews: The kayak trail and the secluded campsites are the reason to come and the marsh is full of herons; the bugs are intense in summer.

Uniqueness: A four story Atlantic coral reef tank, a rain forest under a glass pyramid and a shark alley you walk beneath, on Baltimore's Inner Harbor.
Reviews: The reef tank and the puffins get consistent praise; it is expensive and crowded on weekends. Timed tickets are mandatory.

Typical Customer: History people, decorative arts fans, families
Uniqueness: A mile long street of 18th century houses from the 1704 raid, furnished with the chairs and textiles of the Connecticut valley, with a working farm and a tavern.
Reviews: The guided house tours are the only way in and the decorative arts collection is serious; the street itself is free to walk.

Typical Customer: Harbor people, sunset chasers, seafood eaters
Uniqueness: A working fishing harbor on Martha's Vineyard where the catch is sold off the boat, the beach faces west and the sunset is a nightly event with people applauding.
Reviews: Buy chowder and lobster from the shack and eat on the bulkhead; parking in the village is tight and the beach lot closes at sunset time.

Adventure: Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame
Company / Access: Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame
Uniqueness: Three floors of basketball history where you can shoot on a court, compare your hand to Shaq's and see the peach basket that started the game in Springfield in 1891.
Reviews: The interactive court is what children remember and the enshrinement gallery is for fans; allow two hours and go on a weekday.

Adventure: Eli and Edythe Broad Art Museum
Uniqueness: Zaha Hadid's pleated stainless steel building on the Michigan State campus, showing contemporary art and free to enter.
Reviews: The building is the reason to stop and the shows are contemporary and changing; it is free and takes an hour.

Uniqueness: Two blocks of abandoned houses covered in polka dots, stuffed animals and painted signs, an outdoor art environment that refuses to be gentrified away.
Reviews: It is free, strange and deeply personal; respect the residents and don't wander into occupied houses. Best with a local guide.

Uniqueness: The Devil's Kettle, where half of the Brule River disappears into a hole in the rock, with a trail along the river and a staircase down to the falls.
Reviews: The disappearing river is the mystery and the trail is 1.5 miles; the staircase is steep and the park is on the North Shore.

Uniqueness: A center on the Mississippi with resident bald and golden eagles, a viewing deck over the river and winter eagle counts that reach hundreds.
Reviews: The resident eagles are close and the staff explain their injuries; the winter viewing deck is the season for wild birds.

Uniqueness: An 1886 festival built to prove winter is survivable, with an ice palace, snow sculpting competition, parades and a Vulcan Krewe that has to be seen.
Reviews: The ice palace is the draw in years it is built; the parade is genuinely fun. Dress for -10 and embrace it.

Uniqueness: The cotton plantation where Charley Patton and Howlin' Wolf worked, called the birthplace of the blues, with the gin and the commissary still standing.
Reviews: Blues pilgrims come from other countries and the site is quiet and unmarked; the fields and the old buildings are the whole visit.

Uniqueness: A state art museum with a strong collection of Mississippi and Southern artists, photography and a sculpture garden.
Reviews: The Southern art is the reason, and the museum is quiet and well organized. Free on some days.

Uniqueness: A 1858 courthouse on a hill with a museum of the siege, Confederate and Union relics, and a view over the Mississippi.
Reviews: The collection is old fashioned and dense, and the view from the hill is the best in town. Pair it with the military park.

Uniqueness: A tour of the historic brewery with the red brick buildings, the Clydesdale stables and a tasting at the end.
Reviews: The Clydesdales are the highlight and the tour is free. Book ahead and bring ID.

Uniqueness: A 1913 soda fountain and sandwich counter in a north city neighborhood, famous for a five pound milkshake challenge and a bacon sandwich that defeats most people.
Reviews: The malts are the real draw and the heart attack burger is a stunt; the line moves and the neighborhood is worth supporting.

Uniqueness: A Missouri River town settled by German immigrants, with a brick main street and a cluster of wineries along the valley.
Reviews: The wines are sweet and the town is charming. Book a designated driver or a shuttle.

Uniqueness: The house where Samuel Clemens grew up, with the whitewashed fence, the museum and the river town that became Tom Sawyer's St. Petersburg.
Reviews: For readers it is a pilgrimage, and the town leans into it. The fence painting is a photo op for kids.

Uniqueness: A limestone capitol above the Missouri River with a mural by Thomas Hart Benton in the lounge and a museum on the first floor.
Reviews: The Benton mural is the reason art people stop and the view from the river steps is the photograph; tours are free.

Uniqueness: A clear Ozark lake with coves, marinas, swimming and bass fishing, next to the Branson strip but a world away.
Reviews: The lake is the quiet alternative to the shows, with good swimming and rental boats.

Uniqueness: A 1914 Beaux Arts train station with a grand hall, a science center, a planetarium and a model train gallery.
Reviews: The grand hall is the photo and the model trains are the kid draw. Free to walk through.

Uniqueness: The largest cave system in the northwest, with a guided tour through limestone passages and a view over the Jefferson River valley from the entrance.
Reviews: The tour is two hours with a lot of stairs and the cave is 48 degrees; the view from the top is the reward before you go in.

Typical Customer: History people, true crime fans, families
Uniqueness: A territorial prison with cell blocks, a dungeon and a walled yard, plus a complex of car museums and a doll museum on the same ticket.
Reviews: The cell blocks and the stories of the 1959 riot are the tour; the car collection next door is the surprise for people who came for the prison.

Uniqueness: A grove of western red cedars up to 12 feet across and 1,000 years old, with a flat loop trail through the trunks in the Cabinet Mountains.
Reviews: The scale of the trees is the surprise and the trail is easy; the road in is gravel and the grove is quiet even in August.

Uniqueness: The base where the smokejumpers train, with a loft of parachutes, a plane you can walk through and a film on jumping into fires.
Reviews: The plane and the gear are the exhibits and the jumpers are often there training; it is free and the tour is short.

Uniqueness: A 9,351 foot peak in the Bitterroot range with a fire lookout on top and a view into Idaho, reached by a steep trail from the valley.
Reviews: Hikers call it the best day hike in the Bitterroots and the lookout volunteer will show you the map; the trail is long and exposed.

Typical Customer: Ghost town hunters, history families, photographers
Uniqueness: A gold rush town of 300 original buildings, including the first newspaper office and a opera house, preserved as a state historic site with board sidewalks.
Reviews: The buildings are unrestored and the town is quiet compared with the Wyoming version; the live theater in summer is the local tradition.

Uniqueness: The farm where J. Sterling Morton started Arbor Day, with a tree adventure course, a orchard and a cider house on 260 acres.
Reviews: The treehouse and the ropes course are the family draw and the history is the reason it exists; the fall apple harvest is the season.

Typical Customer: Oregon Trail people, road trippers, photographers
Uniqueness: The rock spire that guided every wagon train on the Oregon Trail, with a visitor center and a view of the Platte valley that has not changed much.
Reviews: The landmark is smaller up close and that is the story; the center explains the trail and the walk to the base is short.

Uniqueness: An eight story tower over Union Pacific's Bailey Yard, the largest railroad classification yard in the world, where 10,000 cars are sorted every day.
Reviews: Train people call it a pilgrimage and the view of the hump yard is mesmerizing; check the scanner feed and go when the light is good.

Uniqueness: A warehouse district of cobblestone streets, brick buildings, galleries and restaurants, with horse drawn carriages and buskers.
Reviews: The streets are photogenic and the food is good. Busy on weekend evenings.

Adventure: Strategic Air Command and Aerospace Museum
Uniqueness: A hangar of Cold War bombers and missiles, including a B-36 and a SR-71, with a glass wall that lets you watch planes land at Offutt.
Reviews: The B-36 is enormous and the Cold War exhibits are the history; aviation people say it is one of the best collections in the middle of the country.

Uniqueness: A dry lakebed so flat and empty that land speed records and a temporary city are built on it, with hot springs and a canyon at the edges.
Reviews: The playa in summer is brutal and the solitude is the point; check conditions, since rain turns the surface to impassable mud.

Uniqueness: Two hundred cars from the Harrah collection, arranged in streetscapes from 1900s to the 1950s, including the 1907 Thomas Flyer that won the New York to Paris race.
Reviews: The street scenes are what make it different from a parking lot of cars; the Thomas Flyer and the Cadillac V16 are the two people photograph.

Uniqueness: A desert lake with tufa towers and a hot spring, home to the Lahontan cutthroat trout that can reach 20 pounds, on Paiute land.
Reviews: Anglers come for the trout and the tufa formations at sunrise are the photograph; the lake is tribal land and requires a permit.

Uniqueness: A silver boom town on a mountainside with a wooden main street, saloons, a opera house and the mine that produced the Comstock Lode.
Reviews: The board sidewalks and the old bars are the atmosphere; it is touristy in summer and the mine tours are the serious history.

Uniqueness: A 1870s railroad running steam and diesel excursions through Crawford Notch, with a climb up the Frankenstein Trestle and a view of Mount Washington.
Reviews: The Notch train is the scenic one and the valley train is the short one; book the dome car for fall and sit on the left going up.

Uniqueness: A wooden walkway threads a 90-foot granite chasm with waterfalls on both walls, the kind of place that makes geology legible in twenty minutes.
Reviews: Reviewers love the accessibility and hate the queue at opening; go at 9am or after 3pm. The 2-mile loop is steeper than the photos suggest.

Uniqueness: A fall migration bottleneck where thousands of hawks, falcons and eagles funnel past a platform at the tip of the cape, counted daily by volunteers.
Reviews: The counters will show you what is passing and September is the peak; the platform is free and the birds come close.

Uniqueness: A 2,700 acre estate with nine lakes, a 1909 conservatory, a hay barn cafe and miles of paved paths where bicycles are free to borrow.
Reviews: The free bike borrow and the orchid range are the local secret; it is the former Doris Duke estate and the trails are flat.

Adventure: Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge
Uniqueness: Forty seven thousand acres of salt marsh behind Atlantic City where the eight mile wildlife drive passes eagles, ospreys and tens of thousands of snow geese in winter.
Reviews: The drive at dawn is the reason to come and the observation tower is the stop; bring bug spray in summer and a scope for the far marsh.

Uniqueness: The old Central Railroad terminal on the harbor with the Empty Sky memorial, a 30 acre lawn and the ferry dock for the Statue of Liberty.
Reviews: The memorial and the skyline view are the draw; the ferry leaves from here and parking is far cheaper than Manhattan.

Uniqueness: A encyclopedic museum with one of the best Tibetan collections in the west, a Victorian ballroom and a planetarium, in a city most visitors skip.
Reviews: The Tibetan galleries are the reason curators come; the Ballantine House next door is a separate tour and the planetarium is cheap.

Uniqueness: Tea-colored cedar water under a canopy of pitch pine and rare orchids, in a forest so odd it spawned the Jersey Devil and a hundred ghost stories.
Reviews: Outfitters get good marks for shuttles and beginner patience; the water is shallow enough to be forgiving. Bug spray is nonnegotiable.

Uniqueness: The Museum of American Glass with 7,000 pieces, a working glass studio where you can watch a gather and blow, and a folk art center on a wooded campus.
Reviews: Glassblowing demos run all day and the paperweight collection is the surprise; in April the glass festival fills the grounds.

Uniqueness: A forest on the Delaware Water Gap with the Mount Tammany red dot trail, a campground along the river and a view over the gap from the ridge.
Reviews: The Mount Tammany climb is steep and crowded and the reward is the gap from above; the river campground is the quiet alternative.

Uniqueness: A free museum on the Manhattan Project and the lab that grew from it, with a replica of the first atomic bombs, a supercomputer and a defense gallery.
Reviews: The history gallery is frank about the bomb and the science exhibits are hands on; it is the best explanation of Los Alamos anywhere.

Uniqueness: A half mile of adobe houses turned into more than 80 galleries, from cowboy painters to contemporary installations, with sculpture courtyards open to the street.
Reviews: The Friday night openings in summer are the social event and the side streets have the smaller galleries; most places welcome browsers.

Uniqueness: A symmetrical cinder cone with a road spiraling to the rim and a trail around the crater, looking out over a field of older volcanoes and three states.
Reviews: The drive up is the attraction and the rim trail is a mile; the view from the top on a clear day reaches Colorado and Oklahoma.

Uniqueness: A field of volcanic rock columns standing like a city skyline, with campsites tucked between the pillars and a botanical garden of desert plants.
Reviews: The camping between the rocks is the experience and the night sky is dark; the park is exposed and hot in summer.

Uniqueness: A small adobe chapel built around a pit of earth said to heal, visited by hundreds of thousands of pilgrims each year, especially during Holy Week.
Reviews: People describe the room of crutches and the quiet; it is an active church and visitors should be respectful, especially during services.

Uniqueness: A museum owned by the 19 pueblos, with a gallery for each, a courtyard for dances and a restaurant serving pueblo food, on Route 66.
Reviews: The dance schedule on weekends is the reason to check ahead; the restaurant's pueblo oven bread and blue corn enchiladas are the local recommendation.

Uniqueness: The ruins of a 17th century mission church beside the remains of a pueblo that traded with the plains, on the route of the Santa Fe Trail.
Reviews: The church walls and the reconstructed kiva are the walk and the ranger talks explain the Pueblo Revolt; the park is quiet and free.

Uniqueness: More than 21,000 petroglyphs on a ridge of basalt boulders, one of the largest rock art sites in the southwest, with a trail through the middle.
Reviews: The density is what surprises people and the trail is short; the site is exposed and the nearest town is 20 minutes away.

Uniqueness: The largest collection of antique wooden runabouts in the country, in a riverside boatyard where you can row a skiff or ride in a 1930s launch.
Reviews: Boat people call it a pilgrimage; the river cruise in a wooden launch is the add on worth paying for.

Uniqueness: The wooded hill above the Hudson where the Appalachian Trail crosses a zoo of native animals, a 1920s lodge and a stone tower with a view over the river bends.
Reviews: The Perkins Tower drive is the easy win, the Major Welch trail is the real hike, and the lot fills by ten on fall weekends.

Uniqueness: Six working 1920s carousels spread across the city parks, all free to ride, part of a bequest that required them to stay free forever.
Reviews: Collectors come from other states to ride all six in an afternoon; the Recreation Park carousel is the biggest and the oldest.

Uniqueness: An art deco train station abandoned since 1979, with a 225 foot concourse, a tower you can climb and water damage that makes the tile work look like a Roman bath.
Reviews: The volunteer tours are irregular and sell out; photographers call it the best interior in the city and the neighborhood around it is empty.

Uniqueness: A paddle up the Buffalo River between grain elevators the size of cathedrals, through the canal terminus where the Erie Canal met the lake.
Reviews: The scale of the silos from water level is what people talk about; the water is flat and the tour is beginner friendly.

Typical Customer: Food people, couples, parents visiting students
Uniqueness: Four student run restaurants where the people cooking your lunch are weeks away from graduating, on a campus that was a Jesuit seminary above the Hudson.
Reviews: Reservations are essential for the American Bounty and Bocuse rooms; the prix fixe lunch is the bargain and the bread basket is famous.

Uniqueness: A summer opera festival in a barn-like theater on Otsego Lake, with new productions and a young artist program that feeds major houses.
Reviews: Opera people rate the productions with much larger companies and the lake setting is the charm; the season is short and tickets go early.

Uniqueness: A Beaux Arts cathedral of transit with a painted zodiac ceiling, a whispering gallery and a hidden platform once used for presidents.
Reviews: The Oyster Bar and the whispering arch are the easy stops; the official tour gets you into the Vanderbilt room and the catwalks.

Uniqueness: Four hundred acres of hillside where a sculptor planted 250 steel figures among the trees, including a field of giant heads you can walk between.
Reviews: People call it the strangest free art walk in the state; wear boots, since the trails are mown grass and the hills are real.

Typical Customer: History people, students, civil rights pilgrims
Uniqueness: The brick house Tubman bought from William Seward, the home for aged people she ran next door, and the African Methodist Episcopal Zion church where her funeral was held.
Reviews: The ranger tour ties the property to the underground railroad and her later life; the church across town is a separate stop on the same story.

Typical Customer: Jazz fans, history people, design lovers
Uniqueness: The modest Corona house where Armstrong lived for 28 years, kept as he left it, with his reel to reel tapes and the mirrored bathroom he built himself.
Reviews: Visitors are surprised it is a row house on a working block; the guided tour is the only way in and the summer garden concerts are the local secret.

Uniqueness: A five and a half mile road up a 2,030 foot peak with three pull offs, ending in a view of Lake George and the Adirondack high peaks on one side and Vermont on the other.
Reviews: Sunset is the time and the road closes at dusk; the shuttle from the village in summer is easier than parking at the top.

Uniqueness: Theodore Roosevelt's shingle style house full of trophies, books and the rocking chair where he took calls, above a cove on Cold Spring Harbor.
Reviews: The ranger led house tour is the only way inside and sells out; the trail down to the beach is short and usually empty.

Uniqueness: A Victorian mansion with nine formal gardens built for a banker and his wife, including a Japanese garden, a rock garden and a 1903 greenhouse range still in use.
Reviews: The Japanese garden and the greenhouse are the highlights; the mansion is partly unrestored, which regulars prefer.

Uniqueness: The last free big boat ride in the country, passing the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island with a beer and a hot dog cheaper than any museum ticket.
Reviews: Stand on the right going out and the left coming back; if you are short of time, ride over and take the subway back from St George.

Uniqueness: A gorge of three waterfalls and stone stairs cut into the cliff, with a swimming area at the bottom and a trail that climbs beside the falls.
Reviews: The gorge trail is closed in ice season; in summer the creek pools are the swimming and the stairs get slick.

Uniqueness: A walled Persian garden and a rock and water feature built for a Gilded Age lawyer, largely forgotten for decades and now restored above the Hudson in Yonkers.
Reviews: The walled garden is the reveal, and the view down to the Palisades is the second one; volunteers run free weekend tours.

Uniqueness: A free university museum with Asian art, European prints, African textiles and a strong photography collection, on the edge of the UNC campus.
Reviews: Small enough for an hour and free, with a good temporary exhibition program. Parking is the only hassle.

Uniqueness: Dozens of drummers, dancers and hula-hoopers take over a downtown plaza every Friday at dusk, with no organizer, no stage and no permit beyond the city's blessing.
Reviews: It is joyful and completely uncurated; locals either love it or avoid downtown on Fridays. Bring a drum or just watch.

Uniqueness: North Carolina's oldest incorporated town, with a 1751 house, a church, a graveyard and a waterfront on the Pamlico, all within two blocks.
Reviews: Tiny and quiet, with a state historic site that explains the colonial port. A good detour off the highway.

Uniqueness: A small harbor town with a boardwalk, wild horses on the far banks, a maritime museum and streets of 18th century houses.
Reviews: The waterfront is the walk and the ferry to Shackleford is the add on. Good lunch town.

Uniqueness: The farmhouse where Sherman and Johnston negotiated the largest Confederate surrender of the Civil War, with reconstructed buildings and a quiet field.
Reviews: The guided tour explains why the surrender happened here and not at Appomattox. Small, free and well done.

Uniqueness: A cliff edge rock where the wind blows upward hard enough to return a thrown hat, with a view over the John's River gorge and the Blue Ridge.
Reviews: The hat trick is the photo and the view is real. The park is small, so pair it with the town.

Uniqueness: A former Army missile plant and Model T factory turned into a sprawl of food stalls, studios and murals, with the original industrial bones left exposed.
Reviews: The food hall and the free art walks are the draw; it is still filling in, which makes it feel like a discovery rather than a mall.

Uniqueness: A 160,000 acre coastal forest of pine flatwoods, pocosin swamp and salt marsh, with the 21 mile Neusiok Trail and black bear habitat.
Reviews: Flat, quiet and full of birds, with real backcountry camping. Bring bug spray and a map.

Uniqueness: A 380 acre garden with a glass conservatory of orchids, a canal walk and a holiday lights show that sells out, twenty minutes from the airport.
Reviews: The conservatory is the winter move; summer is hot and the cafe is small. Locals buy the annual pass.

Uniqueness: A 300 acre former psychiatric hospital campus turned public park, with rolling fields, old oaks and the best skyline view in Raleigh.
Reviews: The sunflowers in summer and the skyline at sunset are the photo moments. The creek and trails are quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: The State Theatre of North Carolina, founded by touring actors in 1952, still producing Broadway-quality musicals in a converted rock quarry building.
Reviews: Production values are high for a small town; the summer musicals sell out. Dinner in Hendersonville before the show.

Uniqueness: A coastal park where the Tar River meets the Pamlico Sound, with cypress swamp boardwalks, a swimming beach and campsites under live oaks.
Reviews: The boardwalk through the swamp is the walk, and the beach is calm. Bugs are serious in summer.

Uniqueness: An abandoned textile mill village of empty brick houses, used as the Hunger Games district 12 set, with guided walks through the general store and the mill ruins.
Reviews: It is eerie and photogenic and the film connection brings a mixed crowd; check the schedule before driving out.

Uniqueness: A free museum with a strong collection of American art, studio glass and folk art, in a converted post office downtown.
Reviews: Free and surprisingly good for a mill town, with a glass collection that connects to the region's craft schools.
