Uniqueness: A 50,000 acre reservoir on the Roanoke with 800 miles of shoreline, public ramps, swimming areas and some of the best striped bass fishing in the state.
Reviews: The lake is huge and the coves are quiet. Check the access points, because the shoreline is mostly private or Corps land.

Uniqueness: The largest man made lake in the state, with a swim beach, boat rentals and 30 miles of single-track mountain bike trail on the quiet northern shore.
Reviews: Locals come for the beach and the Itusi trail; the lake is busy with powerboats on summer weekends. Go on a weekday morning.

Uniqueness: A working glass studio and gallery where you can stand a few feet from the furnace and watch molten glass become a vase, then buy the one they just made.
Reviews: The demos are free and mesmerizing; the gallery is expensive but worth a browse. A great rainy day stop downtown.

Uniqueness: A blackwater river with sandbars, cypress and tupelo, protected as a state park and a national wild and scenic river, with canoe access and camping.
Reviews: The water is dark and the current is gentle, good for a first overnight paddle. Bring a map and bug spray.

Uniqueness: The site of a 1776 Patriot victory that ended British authority in North Carolina, with earthworks, a bridge reconstruction and a cypress swamp trail.
Reviews: The story is a surprise to most visitors and the trail is easy. Free, with a small museum.

Uniqueness: A resource center and museum at UNC Pembroke with Lumbee history, powwow regalia, pottery and the story of a tribe recognized by the state but not the federal government.
Reviews: Personal and specific, with staff who are part of the community. Free, but check the hours.

Adventure: North Carolina Aquarium at Pine Knoll Shores
Uniqueness: An aquarium built around a sunken shipwreck exhibit, with sharks, otters, sea turtles and a touch tank, on a maritime forest site behind the dunes.
Reviews: The shark tank and the otters are the kid priorities. It is small enough for an afternoon and close to the beach.

Uniqueness: A 90-foot waterfall in a hemlock glen bought by a garden club in 1930 to save it, reached by a quarter mile trail along a trout stream.
Reviews: Small, cheap and lovely; the trail is short and the pool is not for swimming. Combine with downtown Tryon's horse-country feel.

Uniqueness: A riverfront of live oaks, a wooden pier, a lighthouse view and streets of antebellum houses, at the mouth of the Cape Fear.
Reviews: The bench under the oaks is the photo, and the ferry to Bald Head leaves nearby. Quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: Sixteen thousand acres of brackish marsh and cypress swamp on Pamlico Sound, with a boat ramp, a wildlife drive and wintering waterfowl by the thousand.
Reviews: Best in winter for ducks and swans, and the drive is easy. Bring bug spray and a scope.

Uniqueness: One of the largest historic districts in the state, with a 1760 town common, antebellum houses, a courthouse and streets that still follow the colonial plan.
Reviews: The town common is the rare piece, and the houses are beautifully kept. Quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A small downtown bar and venue with a tiny stage, a disco ball and a booking policy that mixes local hip hop, indie rock and drag shows on the same calendar.
Reviews: The room is intimate and the sound is good; shows sell out and the dance floor gets going after the set.

Uniqueness: A quiet barrier island beach at the southern end of Topsail, with a pier, sea turtle nests and a sound side for kayaking.
Reviews: Much calmer than the northern beach towns. Parking is limited, so go early.

Uniqueness: A Wild West theme park built around a narrow gauge steam railroad that climbs a mountain, with staged train robberies, a chairlift and amusement rides.
Reviews: The train robbery show is the reason and kids love it. It is old fashioned in a way that works for young families.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square ringed by barbecue joints, antique shops and a historic theater, in the town that calls itself the barbecue capital of the world.
Reviews: The wood smoked barbecue is the reason, and the square is walkable. Most pits sell out by mid afternoon.

Uniqueness: A barrier island beach town with a wide strand, a pier, surf shops and a sound side for paddleboarding, twenty minutes from downtown Wilmington.
Reviews: Parking is the main cost and the main frustration. The north end is quieter, and the loop is good for running.

Typical Customer: History families, cavalry buffs, school groups
Uniqueness: The reconstructed cavalry post where Custer's 7th Cavalry rode out for the Little Bighorn, with earthworks and a On-A-Slant Mandan village below the bluff.
Reviews: The reconstructed barracks and the Mandan village are the two stops; the living history weekends bring the fort back.

Uniqueness: The largest Amish settlement in the world: draft horses on the road, bulk food stores, furniture workshops and a bakery culture that runs on lard and butter.
Reviews: Go on a weekday, respect the no photos signs, and eat at a family style restaurant. The flea market is enormous on Thursdays.

Uniqueness: A science center on the Scioto with a giant screen theater, a gadget gallery and a working lab where visitors do experiments.
Reviews: The hands on labs and the dinosaur gallery are the family stops; the building and the riverfront park are worth the walk.

Typical Customer: History families, engineering fans, school groups
Uniqueness: A park of moved buildings around a carillon, with the 1905 Wright Flyer III, a 1930s print shop and a working brewery.
Reviews: The Wright Flyer and the carillon concerts are the reasons to come and the park is bigger than it looks; the brewery pours samples.

Uniqueness: A museum with a 70 foot titanosaur, a planetarium and a wildlife gallery, recently renovated around a glass atrium.
Reviews: The dinosaur hall and the planetarium are the family stops; the museum is on the same campus as the art museum and the botanical garden.

Uniqueness: A Tudor revival mansion built by the Goodyear founder, with 65 rooms, a Japanese garden and a conservatory, on 70 acres.
Reviews: The house and the gardens are the two halves and the holiday lights fill the grounds; the tour is long enough to plan two hours.

Uniqueness: The actual house from the 1983 film The Outsiders, restored by a fan with the original paint colors, props and a gift shop full of memorabilia.
Reviews: Fans of the book and film make pilgrimages; the restoration is loving and the guides know the production stories.

Uniqueness: A state park with sea lion colonies on the offshore rocks, a lighthouse and a beach, on a loop road south of Coos Bay.
Reviews: The sea lions at Simpson Reef are the reason to come and the view is close; the loop road connects three state parks.

Uniqueness: A jet boat up the Rogue River through rapids and canyons to a lodge lunch, with black bears, otters and eagles on the banks.
Reviews: The upstream trip is the wildlife one and the fast return is the thrill; the boats are covered and the river is cold.

Uniqueness: A aquarium built around the Oregon coast's own habitats, with a walk through acrylic tunnel under sharks, sea otters and a seabird aviary.
Reviews: The sea otters and the tunnel are the family stops; the aquarium is small enough for three hours and the pass includes the outside exhibits.

Uniqueness: A jet boat through the Hellgate canyon and rapids south of Grants Pass, with stops at a lodge and wildlife on the banks.
Reviews: The Hellgate trip is the half day standard and the fast spins are the fun; bring a jacket, the river spray is cold.

Uniqueness: A viewpoint on the old Columbia River Highway where the road loops over a bluff above the gorge, with wildflowers in spring and a trail along the rim.
Reviews: The loop road is the photograph and the balsamroot in April is the season; the wind is strong and the pullout is small.

Uniqueness: The farm Eisenhower bought as a weekend retreat that became the White House in the summer, with the Angus cattle, the putting green and the house as he left it.
Reviews: The house and the farm are the tour and the shuttle from the battlefield visitor center is the only way in; history people say it is the human side of the general.

Uniqueness: The home port of the Brig Niagara, Perry's reconstructed flagship from the Battle of Lake Erie, with a museum on the 1813 battle and a winter shipyard you can watch.
Reviews: Sailing on the Niagara is the splurge and books out; the museum alone explains why a freshwater lake had a naval war.

Uniqueness: Henry Mercer's concrete house with 44 rooms, 32 stairwells and a ceiling of Moravian tiles, built by hand with no architect and no plan.
Reviews: The guided tour is the only way in and the stairs are steep; visitors say it feels like a medieval house built by a obsessive.

Uniqueness: The 1889 flood that killed 2,200 people when a private dam gave way, told in the old Carnegie library with a relief map, survivor accounts and an Oscar winning film.
Reviews: The film runs on a loop and still lands; visitors say the scale of the disaster is hard to hold until you see the map of the valley.

Uniqueness: A trolley park from 1898 with three wooden coasters, a 1920s Noah's Ark walkthrough and the Thunderbolt, all on a bluff above the Monongahela.
Reviews: Coaster people rank the Phantom's Revenge and the Jack Rabbit; the park is small enough that a day pass covers everything twice.

Uniqueness: A mine car drops you 300 feet into a anthracite seam where a former miner explains the work at a temperature of 53 degrees year round.
Reviews: The guides are retired miners and the stories are the tour; bring a jacket and expect to duck, the seam is low.

Uniqueness: The oldest continuously operating farmers market in the country, in a brick hall where Amish farm stands sell scrapple, chow chow and whoopie pies beside Lebanese and Jamaican counters.
Reviews: Saturday is the crush and Tuesday is the locals; the smoked meats and the pretzels are the standing orders and cash is still normal.

Typical Customer: Architecture people, school groups, statehouse collectors
Uniqueness: A Beaux Arts capitol Roosevelt called the handsomest in the nation, with a 272 foot dome, Moravian tiles and a limestone staircase modeled on the Paris opera.
Reviews: The free tour is the only way into the rotunda and the House chamber; the tile work is what visitors photograph.

Typical Customer: Mosaic people, photographers, South Street wanderers
Uniqueness: Half a block of South Street tiled by Isaiah Zagar with bottles, mirrors, bicycle wheels and folk art, with a basement grotto you crawl through.
Reviews: People come for a photo and stay for the story of the neighborhood; the outdoor lot needs a ticket and the surrounding alleys are free.

Uniqueness: A Victorian glasshouse in Schenley Park with a tropical forest under glass, a butterfly room and a Center for Sustainable Landscapes that is one of the greenest buildings in the world.
Reviews: The winter flower show is the local tradition and the summer butterfly room is the family draw; the glasshouse is hot in July.

Uniqueness: The oldest short line railroad in the country, running a steam locomotive 45 minutes through Amish farm fields from a 1830s depot.
Reviews: Book the open air car and sit on the left; children want the steam engine and the shop sells the wooden version for the ride home.

Uniqueness: America's oldest brewery, dug into a hillside where the cellars are 150 feet of hand cut sandstone and the tour ends with samples in a 19th century bottling house.
Reviews: The cave cellars are the part people remember; tours are free but fill early and the tasting is short.

Uniqueness: A 45 room summer mansion on Narragansett Bay with a 10 acre arboretum, a giant sequoia and a bamboo grove, all on a lawn that runs to the water.
Reviews: Gardeners come for the rare trees and the spring bulb show; the house tour is short and the grounds are the reason to stay.

Typical Customer: Sailors, boat builders, America's Cup fans
Uniqueness: The boatyard where Captain Nat Herreshoff built six America's Cup defenders, with a model room, the catamarans of 1988 and a working waterfront.
Reviews: Sailing people treat it as a shrine and non sailors are converted by the model room; the restored boats are in the water in summer.

Uniqueness: A museum inside the 1880 Newport Casino, with the original grass courts still played on and a gallery of the sport's oddest trophies.
Reviews: The grass courts are the surprise; you can book a hit after the museum. The building alone is worth the ticket.

Uniqueness: A sprawling weekend flea market where you can buy a used tractor tire, a live goat, a sack of boiled peanuts and a 1970s stereo in the same row of tables.
Reviews: Bring cash and a truck; the food stalls are half the reason to come. It is dusty, loud and authentically local.

Uniqueness: A grits mill and general store beside a mill pond in a tiny community, with a restaurant in the old mill and peacocks and goats wandering the grounds.
Reviews: The setting is the draw and the grits are stone ground on site; the restaurant is a Sunday drive destination. Watch for the peacocks.

Uniqueness: A biscuit shop that grew out of a mail order business and now teaches biscuit making, with a counter of ham biscuits and pimento cheese worth the line.
Reviews: The buttermilk biscuits are the benchmark and the classes are short and hands on; go early before the case empties.

Uniqueness: A colonial and Revolutionary War town with a wide main street, antebellum houses and the oldest inland town in the state, plus a horse culture that still runs on the weekends.
Reviews: The architecture and the Revolutionary War sites are the draw. The Carolina Cup in spring is the social event.

Uniqueness: Four blocks of market sheds where Gullah sweetgrass basket makers, spice vendors and artisans sell under one roof, in a building that has been a market since 1841.
Reviews: The sweetgrass baskets are the real craft and the vendors will explain the stitch. Go early before the tour groups.

Uniqueness: The first historically Black college in South Carolina, with a Victorian campus, a historic chapel and a museum of the university's role in Reconstruction education.
Reviews: The campus is beautiful and the history is deep. Check in at the administration building for a visitor pass.

Uniqueness: A slow blackwater river through cypress and sandbars, with rope swings, kingfishers and water the color of strong tea.
Reviews: The current does most of the work, so it suits beginners. Bring a dry bag and bug spray, and check the gauge before a summer trip.

Uniqueness: A minor league ballpark modeled on Fenway, with a Green Monster of its own, cheap tickets and a downtown setting you can walk to from Falls Park.
Reviews: The value is unbeatable and the ballpark is beautiful; Thursday fireworks and dollar hot dogs are the local tradition.

Uniqueness: A laid back beach town at the edge of Charleston with a wide strand, a fishing pier, surf shops and the Washout, the local surf break.
Reviews: Parking is the cost and the hassle. The county park at the west end is quieter, and the pier is good for kids.

Uniqueness: A 250,000 acre coastal forest of pine flatwoods and cypress swamps, with trails, boat ramps and the lonely roads of the old Francis Marion country.
Reviews: The forest is huge and easy to have to yourself. Some roads flood, so check conditions and bring a map.

Uniqueness: A wooden walkway along the Sampit River past shrimp boats, historic warehouses and the steel mill, with the third oldest city in the state behind it.
Reviews: The shrimp boats unloading are the photo, and the walk connects to the front street shops. Best at golden hour.

Uniqueness: A CCC park on a peninsula in Lake Greenwood, with stone picnic shelters, a swimming area, a boat ramp and cabins overlooking the water.
Reviews: The lake is the draw and the CCC stonework is a bonus. Summer weekends are busy, but the campground is quiet on weeknights.

Uniqueness: A 50,000 acre lake with enough wind for real sailing, a fleet of small keelboats and a club culture that will take a beginner out as crew.
Reviews: The Wednesday night races need crew and skippers are happy to teach; the lake is big enough to feel like the coast.

Uniqueness: A 1936 movie house turned art film theater on Main Street, showing independent and foreign films with a small bar and a loyal membership.
Reviews: The programming is ambitious for a Southern city and the room is beautiful; the seats are old but the popcorn is good.

Uniqueness: A protected forest of granite outcrops and old logging roads with a loop of mountain bike trails built by local riders, including a rock garden that humbles visitors.
Reviews: The trails are technical and well built and the climbs pay off with views; bring more water than you think.

Uniqueness: The earthworks of a 28-day siege in 1780, with a reconstructed stockade fort and the original Star Fort still visible in the ground.
Reviews: The ranger tour makes the siege legible; it is small and quiet. Combine with Abbeville's courthouse square.

Uniqueness: The site of the first true canal in the United States, with a museum, a reconstructed lock and boardwalks through cypress swamp where alligators sun on the banks.
Reviews: The canal story is genuinely interesting and the swamp walk is good for kids; it is a quiet alternative to the coast.

Uniqueness: A 30 mile yard sale along Highway 23 through peach country, with hundreds of tables, boiled peanuts, old tools and things nobody can identify.
Reviews: Bring cash, a truck and patience. The early morning is the good stuff and the church barbecue is the lunch stop.

Uniqueness: A 1790 courthouse town with a village green, antebellum houses and a working farm museum, ten minutes from Clemson but two centuries away.
Reviews: The walking tour is short and the farmers market is good; lunch at a local table is the move. Quiet and unpretentious.

Adventure: Rose Hill Plantation State Historic Site
Uniqueness: The Greek Revival home of Governor William Gist, who signed the ordinance of secession, with original outbuildings, a boxwood garden and a slave cemetery in the woods.
Reviews: The house tour is honest about the enslaved people who built and ran the place, which makes it more than a pretty facade. The grounds are free to walk.

Uniqueness: Cabins on piers over Lake Marion, a cypress lake famous for huge catfish and bass, with a nature trail and a swimming area.
Reviews: The over water cabins are the novelty and they book months out. Fishing is the main event, and the lake is shallow and stump filled, so follow the markers.

Uniqueness: 295 acres of Piedmont forest, formal gardens, a duck pond and a natural heritage garden with rare plants, free and open at the edge of campus.
Reviews: Locals use it as a quiet walk; the amphitheater and the art trail are the surprises. Free parking and rarely crowded.

Uniqueness: A museum of cotton from seed to bale, with a gin, a sharecropper cabin, the Lee County veterans room and the story of how one crop shaped the whole Pee Dee.
Reviews: The machinery is the hit with kids and the veteran exhibits surprise adults. Allow ninety minutes.

Uniqueness: A drive in where the call is shouted down the line, the sweet tea comes in a bucket and the chili cheese a plenty is a regional rite of passage.
Reviews: The ordering call is half the experience and the portions are enormous; it is not fine dining and nobody pretends otherwise.

Uniqueness: A steam train that climbs a 4 percent grade through the Black Hills between Hill City and Keystone, with open cars and a view of the granite peaks.
Reviews: The steam engine and the climb are the reason to ride and the open car is the seat to book; the round trip takes two hours.

Company / Access: South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks
Uniqueness: A sacred butte where Lakota and Cheyenne people still come for vision quests, with a trail to the summit and prayer offerings along the way.
Reviews: The climb is steep and the site is sacred, so visitors are asked to stay on the trail and respect the offerings; the view reaches the Black Hills.

Uniqueness: The fossil laboratory and museum behind the commercial diggers, with a T. rex named Sue's original bones and a wall of ammonites.
Reviews: The prep lab is the reason paleontology people stop and the museum is small; the institute also runs digs you can join.

Uniqueness: A mountain being carved into a 563-foot horseman since 1948, with a Native American museum, a sculptor's home and a laser show at night.
Reviews: The scale is staggering and the progress is slow; the museum is excellent and the controversy is worth understanding.

Uniqueness: The surveyor's house and the Ingalls family homes from the Little House books, with a pageant in summer and the prairie around them unchanged.
Reviews: Readers come from other countries and the guides know the books and the family; the summer pageant is the local tradition.

Adventure: American Museum of Science and Energy
Uniqueness: A museum of the secret city that helped build the atomic bomb, with reactors, isotopes and the story of Oak Ridge and the Manhattan Project.
Reviews: The science is accessible and the local history is extraordinary. Good for teenagers and adults.

Uniqueness: A 1920s Sears distribution center turned vertical village with a food hall, a brewery, a school, a radio station and apartments, all under one enormous atrium.
Reviews: The scale of the reuse is the attraction, and the food hall is a good lunch. Free to walk through.

Uniqueness: A main street of antebellum and Victorian buildings, a theater, a bookstore and a square, with the battlefield sites a few blocks away.
Reviews: The street is polished and busy, with good lunch spots and a farmers market. Pair it with the Carter House.

Uniqueness: A museum of mountain life with log cabins, a cantilever barn, Cherokee artifacts and a trail, at the quiet entrance to the Smokies.
Reviews: The outdoor buildings are the fun part for kids, and the Cherokee exhibit is serious. Less crowded than the Sevier side.

Uniqueness: A gentle river between the Cherokee National Forest and the Great Smoky Mountains, with a Class II section, gravel bars and trout water.
Reviews: The float is easy and the scenery is mountain. Outfitters in Reliance run shuttles.

Uniqueness: Tennessee's oldest town, with a main street of 19th century buildings, a courthouse and the International Storytelling Center.
Reviews: The street is handsome and the storytelling center runs shows most weeks. Good small town walk.

Uniqueness: Forty seven acres of gardens on a former family estate, with a stone wall, a bamboo grove, a children's garden and a native plant trail.
Reviews: Free, quiet and full of corners, with a bamboo grove that feels like another country. Good for a picnic.

Uniqueness: The site of a brutal 1862 battle with earthworks, a cemetery and a loop road, in the middle of a fast growing city.
Reviews: The auto tour and the visitor center explain a battle most people have never heard of. Free and quiet.

Uniqueness: A 1891 truss bridge turned pedestrian crossing over the Tennessee River, with a view of the city and the mountains and a park at each end.
Reviews: The walk is short and the view is the point, especially at sunset. It connects downtown to the North Shore.

Uniqueness: Sixty six acres on the shore of White Rock Lake, with a trial garden of 3,000 plants, a prairie and a children's adventure garden.
Reviews: The spring tulips and the fall pumpkin village are the two seasons; the view across the lake to the Dallas skyline is the photograph.

Uniqueness: A wetland and thorn scrub park on the flyway with a boardwalk, a feeding station and a recorded 350 species, including the rare hook billed kite in summer.
Reviews: The feeding station is where the photographers sit and the rangers keep a daily list; it is the easiest birding in the valley for beginners.

Uniqueness: The national wildflower research center with a demonstration meadow, a limestone garden and a tower that looks over the Hill Country.
Reviews: The spring bluebonnets are the peak and the center is quiet the rest of the year; the children's garden and the trails are the family route.

Adventure: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth
Company / Access: Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth
Uniqueness: Five glass pavilions floating on a reflecting pool by Tadao Ando, holding a collection from Warhol to Richter and a film program in the auditorium.
Reviews: The building and the reflection pool are as good as the art; the café overlooks the water and is a destination on its own.

Typical Customer: History families, ranch people, school groups
Uniqueness: A 19 acre outdoor museum of 50 relocated ranch buildings from a 1780s Spanish compound to a 1930s bunkhouse, with longhorn cattle and a windmill collection.
Reviews: The buildings are original and the scale is the surprise; it is free and the signage explains how each structure worked.

Adventure: Perot Museum of Nature and Science
Uniqueness: A cube of concrete and glass with a glass escalator that climbs five floors past a T. rex skeleton, a earthquake simulator and an engineering hall.
Reviews: The paleontology hall and the sports science exhibit are the hits; the museum is best for ages five to fourteen and gets crowded on school holidays.

Uniqueness: A World War II carrier on the bay with a hangar deck of aircraft, a flight simulator and a maze of passages you can climb through.
Reviews: The engine room and the bridge are the tours people remember; the ship is hot in summer and the passages are narrow.

Uniqueness: Pink sand dunes between red cliffs where a slot canyon funnels wind into ripples, with an ATV riding area and a closed preserve for a rare beetle.
Reviews: Sandboarding down the big dune is the family fun and the ATV rental is at the entrance; the sand is hot in summer and the wind is constant.

Uniqueness: One of the largest dinosaur museums in the world, with 60 mounted skeletons, a working paleontology lab and a walk through the eras of life.
Reviews: Children who are serious about dinosaurs will want three hours; the lab where fossils are prepared is the part adults linger at.

Typical Customer: History people, students, civil rights pilgrims
Uniqueness: A museum in Delta telling the story of the 11,000 Japanese Americans imprisoned at Topaz during the war, with barracks, artifacts and an art school that flourished behind barbed wire.
Reviews: Visitors say it is one of the most important small museums in the country; the site itself is 16 miles out of town and marked by a monument.

Uniqueness: The ski jumping and bobsled venue from the 2002 Games, with a museum, a zip line and a summer bobsled ride down the track.
Reviews: The bobsled ride is the thrill and the ski jump elevator is the view; the museum is small but the athletes training are real.

Uniqueness: A Victorian natural history museum with a carved wooden ceiling, a weather station and a planetarium, founded by a scale manufacturer.
Reviews: The hall of animals and the planetarium are the family stops and the building is the setting; it feels like 1890 in the best way.

Uniqueness: Robert Todd Lincoln's 24 room Georgian mansion with the original 1908 Aeolian organ, formal gardens and a working goat dairy on 400 acres.
Reviews: The organ plays on a schedule and the goat dairy is the family draw; the view of the Taconic and Green mountains is the postcard.

Uniqueness: The snowiest ski mountain in the east, close to the Canadian border, with glades, a tram and an indoor waterpark at the base.
Reviews: Skiers come for the snow and the tree runs and the tram is the way up on cold days; the waterpark is the family reason to stay.

Uniqueness: The biggest vertical drop in the east and the longest season, with 155 trails across six peaks and a gondola that runs in summer for leaf peepers.
Reviews: Skiers argue about the crowds but agree on the terrain; midweek in March is the locals' window and the access road is a long drive from anywhere.

Uniqueness: The first state park in Vermont, a 968 foot peak with a road and a trail to a summit view of Lake Champlain and the Adirondacks.
Reviews: The hike is 45 minutes and the view is the best effort to reward ratio in the state; the road is narrow and the lot fills on fall weekends.

Uniqueness: A raptor center with bald eagles, hawks and owls in large flight enclosures, plus a forest canopy walk and a nature playscape.
Reviews: The raptor enclosures are close enough to see feathers and the staff explain the injuries; the canopy walk is the family surprise.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square of 18th and 19th century buildings, brick sidewalks, a brewery and restaurants, in the middle of Virginia wine country.
Reviews: The downtown is walkable and busy on weekends, with good lunch spots and a farmers market.

Uniqueness: A small Shenandoah Valley town with Washington and Lee and VMI, Stonewall Jackson's house, a historic courthouse and brick streets.
Reviews: The colleges and the old houses make a compact walk, and the VMI museum is free.

Uniqueness: A 88 foot neon star on a mountain above Roanoke, with a viewpoint over the valley and the city lights at night.
Reviews: The drive up is easy and the view is the payoff, especially at dusk. Free.

Uniqueness: Sixty machines from the 1950s onward, all playable, in a downtown space where the volunteer mechanics will explain how a flipper works.
Reviews: Everything is on free play and the collection is well maintained; a cheap hour of joy in a city that needed one.

Uniqueness: A three mile oceanfront boardwalk with restaurants, a fishing pier, a statue of Neptune and separate bike and walking lanes.
Reviews: The boardwalk is wide and clean, and the Neptune statue is the photo. Busy in summer, pleasant in the off season.

Uniqueness: The longest natural sand spit in the country, five and a half miles into the Strait of Juan de Fuca, with a lighthouse at the end and a protected estuary behind it.
Reviews: The walk to the lighthouse takes most of a day and most people turn around at the first mile; the estuary is closed in winter for birds.

Uniqueness: A silver wave shaped building above Interstate 5 holding 300 cars from the LeMay collection, including a 1906 Cadillac and a Tucker, with a driving simulator.
Reviews: Car people say the collection is one of the best in the country and the building is the landmark; the rotating exhibits keep it fresh.

Uniqueness: A museum with a working hot shop where you can watch a team gather and blow glass, and a cone of steel and glass on the Thea Foss waterway.
Reviews: The hot shop demonstrations are the reason to come and the Chihuly bridge of glass outside is free; the museum is small enough for two hours.

Uniqueness: More than 120 wineries in a valley that produces some of the state's best syrah, with a walkable downtown of tasting rooms and a sweet onion festival in June.
Reviews: Wine people rate the syrah with the best in the country and the downtown tasting rooms make a car unnecessary; spring and fall are the best weather.

Uniqueness: A warm spring bathhouse in the middle of a small town, used since before the Revolution, with private baths and a Roman bath house.
Reviews: The baths are the reason to come and the town is full of spas and shops; George Washington bathed here and the water is still free at the fountain.

Uniqueness: A island in the Ohio River reached by sternwheeler, with a reconstruction of the mansion Aaron Burr visited and a horse drawn wagon tour.
Reviews: The sternwheeler ride and the mansion are the reasons to go and the island is flat and shaded; the tour runs on a schedule.

Uniqueness: Heritage trains from Elkins into the Monongahela high country, with a dinner train, a wilderness train and a climb to the High Falls of the Cheat.
Reviews: The wilderness train and the fall color are the reasons to book and the dinner train is the date night; seats go early in October.

Uniqueness: A 1928 Moorish Revival movie palace with a ceiling of clouds and castles, restored and used for concerts, films and touring shows.
Reviews: The restoration alone is worth the ticket; sightlines are good from most seats. A grand room in a town people underestimate.

Uniqueness: The clearest lake in the state, with sandstone cliffs rising from the water that are a eastern climbing destination and a beach at the state park.
Reviews: Climbers come for the overhanging sandstone and families come for the swim; the lake is deep and the cliffs are for experienced climbers only.

Uniqueness: A limestone cave with colorful mineral formations, a guided tour and a fossil dig outside.
Reviews: The formations are colorful and the tour is easy. A good rainy day stop with kids.

Uniqueness: An arts center with a major collection of artist built environments, plus galleries and studios, free and in a former Kohler family house.
Reviews: The art environments are the reason curators visit and it is free; the center runs a residency program in the old factory.

Uniqueness: A Lake Michigan beach backed by sand dunes and a boardwalk through a marsh, with a campground in the pines.
Reviews: The beach and the dune boardwalk are the family stops; the water is cold and the dunes are fragile, so stay on the paths.

Typical Customer: History people, families, house tour fans
Uniqueness: A Victorian mansion on a mound above the Mississippi, with original furnishings, a fur trade history and a formal garden.
Reviews: The house and the river setting are the tour and the annual car show on the grounds is the local event; it is one of the best historic houses in the state.

Uniqueness: A granite capitol with the only granite dome in the country and a mural by Edwin Blashfield, on the isthmus between two lakes.
Reviews: The dome and the observation deck are the reasons to go up; tours are free and the Saturday farmers market on the square is the local ritual.

Uniqueness: A state fair famous for cream puffs, cheese, livestock shows and a midway, eleven days in August.
Reviews: The cream puffs are the ritual and the livestock barns are the real fair. Go on a weekday.

Company / Access: National Park Service and Bureau of Reclamation
Uniqueness: A red rock canyon flooded into a 91 mile reservoir with trophy lake trout and a dam you can tour, on the Green River above the Colorado.
Reviews: Anglers come for the big lake trout and the canyon drive on the Sheep Creek loop is the scenery; the water is cold and the wind is strong.

Typical Customer: History families, road trippers, school groups
Uniqueness: A free center where the Oregon, California, Mormon and Pony Express trails all crossed the North Platte, with covered wagons you can climb into and a simulated river crossing.
Reviews: The wagon and the crossing simulation are what children remember; the diaries and the maps are the adult version and the view of Casper Mountain is the setting.

Typical Customer: History families, ghost town hunters, road trippers
Uniqueness: A gold camp of 30 original buildings at the crossing of the Oregon Trail, where Wyoming gave women the vote in 1869 and the first woman justice of the peace was elected.
Reviews: The restored buildings and the Esther Hobart Morris story are the history; the drive over South Pass is half the visit.

Uniqueness: A limestone canyon with hundreds of sport climbing routes on both walls, and a road that switchbacks 2,000 feet up to the Bighorn plateau.
Reviews: Climbers call it one of the best limestone destinations in the country and the drive is the scenic route; the canyon is hot in summer and the rock is sharp.

Uniqueness: A museum with a 106 foot Supersaurus and a dig site on a nearby mesa where visitors can join a real excavation for a day.
Reviews: The dig program is the reason people come from other states and the mounted skeletons are the rainy day version; book the dig weeks ahead.

Typical Customer: History people, families, true crime fans
Uniqueness: A stone territorial prison where Butch Cassidy served time, with cell blocks, a broom factory and a warden's house, on a bluff above Laramie.
Reviews: The cell block and the stories of the inmates are the tour; it is small and the self guided map lets you move at your own pace.

Uniqueness: A beach festival where you watch national acts with your feet in the Gulf sand, between swims and a Ferris wheel on the shore.
Reviews: The setting is the selling point; reviews complain about heat, expensive drinks and the walk between stages. Book a condo early.

Uniqueness: A brick Greek Revival house built on a former gallows site, called the most haunted house in America, with tours through the courtroom, parlor and family bedrooms.
Reviews: It is small and the ghost stories are well documented; evening tours are spookier. Old Town around it is a good half day.

Uniqueness: A 77-room French neoclassical mansion built by Alfred du Pont, with formal gardens modeled on Versailles and a garage full of vintage cars.
Reviews: Less crowded than the du Pont mansions in Pennsylvania; reviews praise the gardens and the car collection.

Uniqueness: A 110-acre alligator park that predates Disney, with a breeding marsh, a boardwalk over thousands of gators and a screaming zipline directly above them.
Reviews: It is old Florida and proud of it; the gator wrestling show is a relic and the swamp walk is genuinely good. Cheaper and less crowded than the theme parks.

Typical Customer: Families, tour buses, Southern food fans
Uniqueness: A family style restaurant that brings every vegetable the garden produced that morning to your table, plus fried chicken, country ham and cobbler, with a mountain view.
Reviews: Come hungry and expect leftovers; it is old fashioned and generous. The porch and the farm animals keep kids happy.

Uniqueness: A drive in with two giant hot dog statues on the roof, carhops on rollerskates and a Chicago style dog with a pickled tomato, unchanged since 1948.
Reviews: The nostalgia is the meal and the dogs are good; eat in the car or at the picnic tables. A classic.

Uniqueness: Sleep in a concrete teepee from 1937, in one of the last surviving motor courts of its kind, with the original metal furniture and a giant teepee office.
Reviews: It is a time capsule and the beds are better than expected; book ahead in summer. Mammoth Cave is twenty minutes away.

Uniqueness: The oldest craft brewery in the South, in a piney town across Lake Pontchartrain, with a tour, a tasting room and a brewpub pouring seasonals you cannot get elsewhere.
Reviews: The tour is casual and generous; the purple haze and the root beer are the local favorites. A good rainy day in New Orleans.

Typical Customer: Young adults, Baltimore locals, racing fans
Uniqueness: The middle jewel of the Triple Crown, with the infield's own lawless culture, a crab-cake picnic and the oldest trophy in American sport.
Reviews: Infield is a party, grandstand is actual racing; reviews warn about traffic and drink prices. Bring sunscreen.

Uniqueness: The actual geography of the 1692 panic, the meeting house site, the jail, Gallows Hill, told by guides who separate the trials from the Halloween economy.
Reviews: Pick a historian led tour, not a ghost gimmick; reviews praise the ones that use court transcripts. October crowds are genuinely unpleasant.

Typical Customer: Food people, Italian American families, curious eaters
Uniqueness: The indoor market where Bronx Italian families still buy pasta by the pound, cigars are rolled in the back room and mozzarella is pulled in front of you.
Reviews: Go on a weekday morning when the butchers are talking; Sunday after church is a crush and half the stalls are shut by three.

Uniqueness: The only museum where you can dub a scene, play a working 1970s arcade and see the actual Muppets, all in a converted Astoria studio.
Reviews: The Henson exhibition is what people come for and the arcade buys another hour; the weekend screenings are quietly excellent.

Uniqueness: A working water powered grist mill with a general store, a mill pond and a fall harvest festival where they grind corn the old way.
Reviews: The mill race and the old store are photogenic; the festival is crowded and fun. Cheap, quiet and real.

Uniqueness: A 1890s textile mill turned food hall with two dozen stalls, a dumpling window, a bao shop and a brewery, in a neighborhood that was a warehouse district a decade ago.
Reviews: The variety is the point and the space is handsome; parking is tight and popular stalls run long at noon. Walk the rail trail after.

Uniqueness: A small natural history museum with a full Catawba village, a hall of taxidermy that borders on art and a planetarium, all for the price of a sandwich.
Reviews: Parents call it the best rainy day value near Charlotte; the stone maze and the outdoor village keep kids busy. Dated in places, loved anyway.

Uniqueness: The largest continuously operating open air crafts market in the country, under a bridge on the Willamette, with food stalls and buskers.
Reviews: The crafts are genuinely handmade; the food row is the lunch move. It is crowded by noon.

Uniqueness: Seventeen thousand acres of teaching forest with gravel roads, single track and lake coves, minutes from campus and open to the public.
Reviews: The trails are quiet and well maintained and the lake views are a surprise; bring a map because the roads all look alike.

Uniqueness: A CCC park where the Edisto River bends into a sand beach and a bluff, with cabins, a ferry landing and a paddling put in.
Reviews: The river is the reason. Tubing and kayaking are easy here, and the cabins overlook the water. Summer weekends fill up.

Uniqueness: A state resort park on a peninsula in Lake Thurmond with a lodge, cabins, a golf course and a marina, the kind of place where you can sleep inside a park without a tent.
Reviews: The lake views are the sell and the lodge is dated but comfortable. Golf and fishing packages are the local secret.

Uniqueness: A quiet park on the shore of Lake Keowee with a natural bridge, a hiking trail to an overlook and a paddle launch into clear water below the Blue Ridge.
Reviews: The natural bridge trail is the easy win and the lake is calm; it is less crowded than the Jocassee parks.

Uniqueness: The site of a 1780 battle where a smaller Patriot force ambushed British regulars, with earthworks, a creek ford and an interpretive trail through the woods.
Reviews: The ranger talk makes the tactics clear and the trail is short; a quiet, free stop that rewards curiosity.

Uniqueness: Fifteen thousand acres of lake, marsh and impoundments on the Santee, with a boardwalk, an observation tower and a Native American mound on the shore.
Reviews: Winter is the season for waterfowl and the drive loop is easy; bring binoculars and bug spray. Free.

Uniqueness: A brewery in a converted 1910s jail and fire station, with the original cell doors, a rooftop bar and a kitchen serving pub food in the old garage.
Reviews: The building is the attraction and the beer is solid; the rooftop is the best seat in the river district.

Uniqueness: A collection of historic instruments including a harpsichord, early pianos and American folk instruments, with listening stations and occasional concerts in the gallery.
Reviews: The collection is broader than expected and the staff let you hear the instruments; a quiet gem downtown.

Uniqueness: An outfitter at the foot of the mountains renting kayaks, bikes and camping gear, with a staff that will tell you which river is running and which trail is muddy.
Reviews: The advice is honest and the rentals are reasonable; the Swamp Rabbit Trail runs past the door.

Uniqueness: A roadside stand that grew into a market with fresh peaches, homemade ice cream, boiled peanuts and a grill, and half of Fort Mill stops there on a summer Saturday.
Reviews: The peach ice cream is the local ritual and the produce is actually local in season; parking is a scrum. Go early.

Uniqueness: The only surviving home of Woodrow Wilson's childhood, restored with an exhibit that confronts the racial history of the era rather than polishing it.
Reviews: The interpretation is unusually honest for a house museum and the guides are good; pair it with the Hampton-Preston house next door.

Uniqueness: A gold-rush gulch town where Wild Bill Hickok was shot, with the actual-saloon rebuilds, a cemetery on the hill and legal casino poker in every other storefront.
Reviews: The history is well presented and the town is fun; the casino carpet is part of the charm. Catch the trial reenactment.

Uniqueness: A longhorn cattle drive twice a day down Exchange Avenue, a rodeo every weekend, and a maze of stockyards, saloons and boot shops.
Reviews: It is touristy and still fun; the rodeo is a real rodeo and the cattle drive takes ninety seconds. Go for the evening rodeo.

Uniqueness: A Tudor manor house built in England in the 1500s, dismantled, shipped across the Atlantic and rebuilt on the James River in 1925, with the original glass and oak.
Reviews: The story of the move is as interesting as the house; the gardens are quiet and the tours are personal.

Uniqueness: A waterfront shop of mummies, shrunken heads and carved totems that has been collecting oddities since 1899, with a real mermaid and a two headed calf.
Reviews: It is free to wander and deeply weird; the mummy is the main attraction. A good stop before the ferry.

Uniqueness: A self guided walk through a huge single chamber with a 45-foot stalagmite called the War Club, plus a wild-cave tour that crawls and gets muddy.
Reviews: The self guided format lets you linger; the wild tour is the adventure. Small, cheap and genuinely impressive.

Uniqueness: A town leans into its own cryptid: a museum, a metal statue, guest speakers, a 5K and vendors selling moth-shaped everything, all in the shadow of the Silver Bridge disaster.
Reviews: It is sincere, cheap and surprisingly wholesome; visitors love the museum and the parade. Parking is easier than you'd think.

Uniqueness: A downtown street of bars, restaurants and live music in historic buildings, with a Mardi Gras parade route running through it.
Reviews: The bars are close together and the crowds are friendly. Busy on weekends and during carnival.

Uniqueness: A hands on science center with a dinosaur hall, an aquarium, an IMAX and a bed of nails, in a former department store.
Reviews: Good for kids of all ages, with enough to fill a rainy afternoon. The aquarium is smaller than it looks.

Uniqueness: A 19 acre linear park built along the railroad tracks downtown, with lawns, a skate park, a playground and a view of the viaducts.
Reviews: The design turned a dead edge into the city's front yard. Good for a walk and a coffee.

Uniqueness: A rehabilitation center with bald eagles, hawks and owls in flight pens, where the staff explain why most of the birds cannot be released.
Reviews: The bald eagles are close enough to see the detail and the flight training is the highlight; it is a working hospital and the birds come first.

Uniqueness: A museum with a two story Tlingit clan house, a Russian era gallery and a room of Alaska Native basketry, plus a mine and fishing exhibit.
Reviews: The clan house and the Russian collection are the two stops; it is a good rainy day in a town that gets a lot of rain.

Uniqueness: The park's working sled dog kennel, where rangers demonstrate a team pulling a cart and explain how dogs still patrol the wilderness in winter.
Reviews: The dogs are the highlight for children and the ranger talk is genuinely interesting; the kennel is at the end of a short road from the visitor center.

Uniqueness: A four and a half mile sand spit into Kachemak Bay lined with charter boats, fish cleaning tables, campgrounds and a view of glaciers across the water.
Reviews: The halibut charters and the fish and chips are the local rituals; the spit is busy in summer and the weather changes fast.

Uniqueness: The site of the 1804 battle between the Tlingit and the Russians, with a trail through totem poles and a Russian bishop's house.
Reviews: The totem trail through the spruce forest is the walk and the visitor center explains the battle; the poles are original and weathered.

Uniqueness: An 11 mile paved path along Cook Inlet from downtown to Kincaid Park, with moose in the woods, beluga whales offshore and a view of Mount Susitna.
Reviews: Locals bike it after work and the moose are a real hazard on the wooded sections; the tide flats at low tide are the birding.

Uniqueness: A clan house and a dozen totem poles in a forest by the sea, carved in the 1930s and 40s as a works project and moved here from abandoned villages.
Reviews: The poles and the clan house are the reason to come and the trail is short; the rain forest setting is half the experience.

Uniqueness: A five story cliff dwelling built into a limestone alcove by the Sinagua, with a path along the creek below and a sycamore grove.
Reviews: The dwelling is viewed from below and the scale is the surprise; it is a one hour stop and the Well nearby is included.

Uniqueness: A 10,720 foot sky island above the desert with a road to the top, a spruce fir forest and an observatory where the Vatican runs a telescope.
Reviews: The drive from desert to alpine forest in an hour is the experience and the observatory tour needs booking; the mountain is closed to the public in some seasons for the red squirrel.

Uniqueness: An 18 room castle built from stone, adobe and salvage by a father for his daughter, with a chapel, a dungeon and furniture made from railroad parts.
Reviews: The story is better than the building and the guides tell it well; it is hidden at the base of South Mountain.

Typical Customer: History people, true crime fans, families
Uniqueness: A territorial prison built into a bluff above the Colorado, with cell blocks, a guard tower and the story of the inmates who built the railroad and died in the heat.
Reviews: The cell block and the dark cell are the tour and the guides tell the stories well; it is a compact site and the river view is the setting.

Uniqueness: A clear lake in the foothills with sandy islands, a swim beach and the Little Red River trout water below the dam.
Reviews: The islands and the clear water are the summer draw; the lake is busy on holidays and the trout fishing below the dam is year round.

Uniqueness: One of the largest springs in the country pours nine million gallons an hour into a river, beside a 1880s railroad depot and a working hydroelectric dam.
Reviews: The spring is startlingly clear and the old depot is a nice surprise; a good half day on the drive to Branson.

Uniqueness: A former oil boom town's downtown turned arts district, with a restored 1920s theater, a speakeasy and a sculpture garden.
Reviews: The restoration is the story and the shows book names bigger than the town; locals say it changed downtown.

Uniqueness: A downtown market hall, food stalls, a farmers market and the riverfront park, connected by a streetcar to the museums.
Reviews: The market is the lunch stop and the river walk is the stroll. Busy on Saturday mornings.

Uniqueness: A Victorian mansion gallery with a bowling alley in the basement, joined to a modern wing holding California art and a strong works on paper collection.
Reviews: The original mansion rooms and the drawing collection are the reason to come; the newer wing hosts the big traveling shows.

Uniqueness: Three coves where decades of dumped glass were polished by the surf into pebbles of green, amber and blue.
Reviews: Take photos, leave the glass, it is illegal to remove and the beach is shrinking. Go at low tide.

Uniqueness: The only state park in California where you can drive on the beach and camp in the dunes, with five miles of sand and a riding area for ATVs.
Reviews: The dune camping is the experience and the wind is relentless; check the closures for snowy plover nesting and air down your tires.

Uniqueness: A working roundhouse and steam shop where the locomotives that appeared in dozens of westerns are still maintained, with weekend steam excursions.
Reviews: The roundhouse is the best part and the train ride runs on weekends; film fans come for the movie train history.

Uniqueness: A free museum in a Shigeru Ban building with a woven wood screen, a rooftop sculpture garden and a glass elevator that opens onto views of Aspen Mountain.
Reviews: The roof deck and the building are worth the stop even if the exhibition is between shows; admission is free and it is a one hour visit.

Uniqueness: A resort built around a pedestrian village and a bird sanctuary, with groomed cruisers, a downhill race course and cookie time at the base each afternoon.
Reviews: Families like the easy layout and the ski school; experts find it tame compared with Vail and the village is quiet at night.

Uniqueness: The highest botanical garden in the country at 8,200 feet, with rock gardens of alpine plants from around the world and a waterfall below the ski slopes.
Reviews: Gardeners call it a miracle of microclimate and it is free; the peak is late June and the paths are steep.

Uniqueness: The highest suspension bridge in the country over the Arkansas River, with a gondola, a zip line and a skycoaster above a 1,000 foot gorge.
Reviews: The bridge walk is the free thrill and the add ons cost extra; the park was rebuilt after a 2013 fire and the views are the point.

Uniqueness: A short climb to a slot where the Zapata Creek drops into a cave behind the rock, with the Great Sand Dunes spread out below the trail.
Reviews: The last stretch is a wade through cold water and the payoff is a waterfall inside a cave; the road is rough for low cars.

Uniqueness: The oldest municipal rose garden in the country, with 15,000 bushes in a formal arbor and a pond, free and open at dawn.
Reviews: Peak bloom is the third week of June and locals come before work; the park is safe and the greenhouses are open in winter.

Uniqueness: The campus where new American plays and musicals are workshopped before Broadway, with a barn theater, a mansion and readings that cost a fraction of a city ticket.
Reviews: Audiences see shows in development and are asked for feedback; the summer season is short and the grounds are open to walk.

Uniqueness: Two miles of beach on Long Island Sound with a boardwalk, a campground in the pines and the Meigs Point nature center at the eastern end.
Reviews: The park is huge and the west beach is the family side; the nature center has live animals and the campground books early.

Uniqueness: A 42 room Roman renaissance mansion on a Long Island Sound point with a formal garden, a pergola and a lawn that runs to the water.
Reviews: The gardens and the mansion terrace are the photo backdrop; the house is only open on tour dates and the beach is rocky.

Uniqueness: The Victorian cottage where Stowe wrote after Uncle Tom's Cabin, kept with her desk, her paintings and a tour that connects the book to the present rather than treating it as a relic.
Reviews: The guides are trained to run a conversation, not a lecture, and visitors say it is the most useful history tour in the city; Mark Twain's house is next door.

Uniqueness: A quarter mile of cascades dropping 250 feet over marble ledges, with a trail alongside and a covered bridge at the bottom.
Reviews: The climb is short and steep and the upper pools are the quiet part; in spring the water is loud and in August it is a trickle.

Uniqueness: A half mile oval that runs Friday night short track racing under lights, with modifieds, late models and a grandstand where you can see the whole track.
Reviews: Friday night races are cheap and loud and the modified division is the local obsession; bring a jacket, the hill is cold after dark.

Uniqueness: The farm where American impressionist J. Alden Weir painted for 40 years, with his studio, a pond and a trail where the park supplies easels and paint.
Reviews: Artists can borrow supplies and paint on the grounds; the studio tour is short and the property is the only national park devoted to painting.

Uniqueness: A mansion with a collection of Stanley steam cars and a one eighth scale steam railroad you can ride through the woods.
Reviews: The steam train ride is the family draw and the cars are a surprise; it is run by volunteers and only open on weekends.

Uniqueness: A WWII coastal defense fort with a concrete observation tower you can climb, plus dunes, bay beach and ocean beach in one park.
Reviews: The tower tour is the reason to come; the beaches are quieter than Rehoboth. Bikes are the best way around.

Uniqueness: A mile concrete oval known as the Monster Mile, with banking that lets you see the whole field from the frontstretch and a campground that becomes a small city.
Reviews: Fans say the concrete makes the racing better and the traffic easier than the big tracks; the September race is the traditional weekend.

Uniqueness: The plantation of the man called the penman of the Revolution, with a Georgian house, outbuildings and the story of the enslaved people who worked the land.
Reviews: The interpretation is honest about slavery and the house is furnished; it is free and quiet and the grounds are flat.

Uniqueness: A Dutch style building that looks like a town hall in Holland, holding the story of the 1631 Dutch settlement and the wreck of the DeBraak.
Reviews: The building is the photograph and the shipwreck artifacts are the surprise; it is free and sits in the middle of Lewes.

Uniqueness: A 1,200 capacity club that has broken more bands than any room its size in the country, with a balcony that puts you almost on the stage.
Reviews: The sound is consistently good and the sightlines from the balcony are the secret; shows sell out and doors are early.

Uniqueness: A subterranean digital art space under the Mall where projectors turn the walls and floor into a moving environment, with a different artist each season.
Reviews: The scale is impressive in a small room; shows change often so check what is running. Good rainy day option.

Uniqueness: A brick market house from 1873 where butchers and a blueberry buckwheat stand still work the hall, with a weekend flea market and a crab cake counter outside.
Reviews: The market hall is best on Saturday morning and the flea is behind it; the blueberry pancakes at Market Lunch are the standing order.

Uniqueness: A cobblestone towpath along the canal from Georgetown to Great Falls, with lock houses, a mule drawn boat and herons in the middle of the city.
Reviews: The first three miles from Georgetown are flat and shaded and the mule boat runs Wednesday to Sunday; the path is gravel and busy on weekends.

Uniqueness: The oldest continuously operating open air fish market in the country, a row of barges on the Washington Channel selling crabs, oysters and fried fish to order.
Reviews: The crabs are sold by the dozen and the fried shrimp box is the cheap lunch; it is outdoors, cash friendly and best at lunchtime.

Uniqueness: Eighteen hundred acres of wooded valley through the middle of the city, with a creek, a mill, a planetarium and a trail network that connects to the Potomac.
Reviews: Locals run the trail on weekday mornings and the Peirce Mill grinding days are the family draw; the parkway closes to cars on weekends in summer.

Company / Access: Supreme Court of the United States
Uniqueness: The marble temple with a courtroom you can sit in, a spiral staircase and exhibits on the cases that shaped the country.
Reviews: The courtroom and the self guided tour are free and quick; oral argument days need a line and the building is across from the Capitol.

Uniqueness: A wooded island in the Potomac reached by a footbridge, with a memorial plaza to Roosevelt in a clearing and trails through swamp and upland forest.
Reviews: The island feels nothing like the city and the memorial is usually empty; the boardwalk on the north end is the birding spot.

Uniqueness: A working marine rescue hospital with dolphins, sea turtles and otters, made famous by the Dolphin Tale films.
Reviews: The rescue stories are the heart of it and kids connect with the animals. Book tickets online.

Uniqueness: A Latvian immigrant single-handedly quarried and moved 1,100 tons of coral rock to build a castle, a rocking chair that weighs tons and a table shaped like Florida, nobody knows how.
Reviews: People come for the mystery and leave talking about the loneliness of it; the audio tour tells the story well. Small and strange.

Uniqueness: A shallow sandbar in the Destin harbor where boats raft up, music plays and people wade in waist deep water, a floating party on the Gulf.
Reviews: Rent a pontoon or take a shuttle, bring a cooler and expect a crowd. Not for quiet seekers.

Uniqueness: A 60 acre botanical garden and wildlife sanctuary with flamingos, a bobcat, otters and a 1930s house, plus a tram through the citrus grove.
Reviews: The flamingos and the tram are the kid draw, and the gardens are shady. Good for a hot day.

Uniqueness: A hands on science center with a giant dinosaur hall, a planetarium, an observatory and a kids zone, in a modern building near downtown.
Reviews: The dinosaur hall and the planetarium are the hits, and it is a good rainy day alternative to the parks.

Uniqueness: An airboat ride into the Everglades with alligators, wading birds and a sawgrass maze, plus a small animal exhibit.
Reviews: The airboat is loud and fast and kids love it. The wildlife show is cheesy but the swamp is real.

Uniqueness: A 2.6 mile paved trail along the Hillsborough River, connecting the aquarium, the history center, parks and the convention center.
Reviews: Flat and scenic, with water taxis and good people watching. Best at sunset.

Typical Customer: Families with teens, history people, couples
Uniqueness: A museum of the dry years with costumed guides, a speakeasy at the end and a replica still, in a city that never really stopped drinking.
Reviews: More fun than a history museum has a right to be, and the speakeasy cocktail is included in some tickets. The tour is the way to do it.

Uniqueness: A 1845 industrial canal with a glass-bottom boat tour, a towpath you can bike and the original mills and locks still standing.
Reviews: The boat tour is calm and informative; the towpath is flat and shaded. A good half day with the Augusta Museum.

Season / Dates: Year round, history center hours vary
Company / Access: Georgia State Parks / Georgia Southern University
Uniqueness: The largest prisoner of war camp of its day, built in 1864 and abandoned within four months, with surviving earthworks and a museum of artifacts recovered by a university dig that began in 2010.
Reviews: The archaeology is the story, a camp that vanished into pine woods and gave up its buttons and coins a century and a half later. The history center explains it well.

Uniqueness: A deep, clear Corps lake in the Blue Ridge foothills with no private development on the shore, plus hiking trails and a beach at Woodring Branch.
Reviews: The lack of houses on the water is the charm. The lake is deep and cold, good for swimming and spotted bass.

Adventure: Center for Wildlife Education at Georgia Southern
Uniqueness: A university raptor center with bald eagles, hawks and owls in open weathering yards and a flight show where a bird passes inches over the crowd, plus a wetland boardwalk.
Reviews: The flight demonstrations are the reason to time your visit. The eagle that flies at football games is the local celebrity.

Uniqueness: The home of Major Ridge, a Cherokee leader who signed the treaty that led to the Trail of Tears, with Cherokee artifacts and the story told from his side.
Reviews: A small museum with a complicated story, told well. The house itself is the exhibit.

Uniqueness: A free museum with American art, decorative arts and a hands on history gallery about the Chattahoochee valley, plus a sculpture garden.
Reviews: Free and quietly good, with a strong regional collection. The children's gallery is a real one, not a corner of toys.

Typical Customer: Short track fans, families, late model teams
Uniqueness: A paved half mile that hosts SpeedFest in January, when Super Late Model teams from across the Southeast shake down new cars in the cold.
Reviews: SpeedFest is the draw, a January race weekend that pulls rigs from four states. The regular season is cheap, loud and easy to walk into.

Uniqueness: A 1916 vaudeville house turned rock room, with a balcony, a painted ceiling and a schedule that runs from indie acts to comedy nights.
Reviews: The room is the draw, small enough that every seat feels close. Check the calendar rather than dropping in.

Uniqueness: A coastal park on a tidal river with a boat ramp, kayak rentals, a nature trail and campsites under live oaks, ten minutes from Cumberland Island.
Reviews: Quiet and shady, with crabs and birds on the marsh boardwalk. Good base for a Cumberland ferry trip.

Uniqueness: A museum in the 1836 courthouse on the square, covering the first American gold rush, the mint that coined it and the Cherokee removal that followed.
Reviews: The gold rush story is the surprise for most visitors, and the building is worth the stop.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square with a bandstand, a farmers market, bookshops and a restaurant row, in a town that feels like a small college city inside the metro.
Reviews: The square is walkable and busy on weekends, with a farmers market on Saturdays. Parking is easier in the deck.

Uniqueness: The newest state park on Lake Lanier, with a sandy beach, rental cabins, paddle craft and trails through hardwood above the lake.
Reviews: Clean, spacious and less developed than the islands. The beach is the summer draw.

Uniqueness: A restored 1935 movie palace on Marietta Square with a neon marquee, showing films, concerts and community theater under a starry ceiling.
Reviews: The room is the attraction and the balcony seats are the pick. Check for classic film nights.

Uniqueness: A nature center with live animals, a discovery room and trails into the Chicopee Woods, one of the largest protected forests in the metro.
Reviews: Good for kids and cheap, with real trails behind the building. Check the weekend programs.

Company / Access: City of Fitzgerald / Fitzgerald-Ben Hill Arts Council
Typical Customer: History people, genealogy visitors, rail fans
Uniqueness: The story of a town founded in 1895 by Union veterans in the middle of the Confederacy, told inside a restored railroad depot, with Grand Army of the Republic and Confederate relics side by side in the same cases.
Reviews: The founding story is the hook and most visitors have never heard it. The depot itself, with the original brick and a caboose outside, is half the visit.

Uniqueness: An aquarium built around a 175,000 gallon blue hole fed by the Flint River, with otters, alligators and a walk through the spring.
Reviews: Small enough for young kids and unusual because the water is real river water. The outdoor aviary is a bonus.

Uniqueness: A state park built as a memorial to Georgia's war dead, with an outdoor museum of tanks and aircraft on the lawn, a Lake Blackshear beach, and a golf course cut through the pines.
Reviews: The military museum on the grounds is the surprise. Locals come for the lake and the camping, and the collection gets a look on the way in.

Uniqueness: A LEED certified center with a 3D theater, a treetop canopy walk and exhibits on water, energy and the Piedmont forest, on a reclaimed site.
Reviews: The canopy walk and the water table are the kid hits. It is a good rainy day option with real content.

Uniqueness: An apple orchard with u-pick, a petting farm, a corn maze, a bakery and hard cider, built for a full family afternoon in the north Georgia hills.
Reviews: It is busy and commercial and kids love it. The apple cider slushie is the local tradition.

Uniqueness: A rice plantation house preserved with its original furniture, live oaks and marsh, telling the story of five generations and the enslaved people who built the rice fields.
Reviews: The house tour is intimate and the grounds are quiet. The marsh boardwalk is a good birding stop.

Uniqueness: A collection of photographs, military records and family histories of Black Thomasville, assembled by a local historian over decades.
Reviews: Personal and specific, with stories you will not find in a state museum. Call ahead for group tours.

Uniqueness: One of the last drive-in theatres running in Georgia, with a double feature on weekends, a gravel lot and a screen you watch from the truck bed.
Reviews: People drive from Savannah and Jacksonville for it. The snack bar is cash and the sound comes over the radio.

Season / Dates: Year round, best spring and autumn
Uniqueness: Thirty seven thousand acres where the Flint and Chattahoochee meet to form the Apalachicola, with standing timber in the shallows and a bass fishery ranked among the best in the country.
Reviews: Anglers rate it top five nationally for largemouth. The standing timber eats lower units, so idle through the stumps the first time out.

Season / Dates: May to September, weekends in spring and autumn
Uniqueness: A 1925 lakeside park with a wooden coaster from 1967, a boat ride that has run since the twenties and a picnic ground where families still bring coolers, minutes from the Tennessee line.
Reviews: Generations of Chattanooga families learned to swim here. The Cannon Ball coaster is short and rough in the way people mean as a compliment.

Adventure: Little Ocmulgee State Park and Lodge
Uniqueness: A 265 acre lake with a sand beach, a nine hole course through the pines and a lodge built by the state in the 1930s, on ground that floods into cypress swamp at the north end.
Reviews: The lake and the lodge make it the only real overnight stop for a wide stretch of south Georgia. Quiet midweek and full in summer.

Uniqueness: A spring that pushes 7 million gallons a day into a blue-green pool, surrounded by boardwalks, cypress and the earthworks of a Confederate prison camp built on the same ground.
Reviews: The spring and the alligator boardwalk are the family draw. The prison history underneath it is what adults talk about after.

Uniqueness: A 19th century courthouse square with a fountain, a theater, independent shops and a food hall, plus a farmers market that fills the streets on weekends.
Reviews: The square is the social center of Cobb and the ghost tour is a local favorite. Parking is free in the deck behind the square.

Season / Dates: Daily in summer, call ahead in cold months
Typical Customer: Potters, families with kids, leaf peepers
Uniqueness: A pottery gallery in a 1930s corn mill over the Soque River, where a balcony hangs above a pool holding rainbow and brown trout so big that visitors feed them from the rail.
Reviews: The trout feeding is the family draw, the pottery is why people come back. The drive up Highway 197 in late October is half the trip.

Uniqueness: One of the best preserved Civil War battlefields in the country, with original earthworks, a ravine and trails where the fighting happened in dense woods.
Reviews: The terrain explains the battle better than any map. Quiet, shaded and rarely crowded.

Uniqueness: Georgia's largest natural spring, pumping 70,000 gallons a minute into a blue pool, the surviving centerpiece of a 1920s resort that once drew celebrities.
Reviews: The water is astonishingly blue and the ruins of the resort give it a melancholy. Free, flat and easy, with turtles on the logs.

Uniqueness: A rail yard museum with locomotives, cabooses and passenger cars you can climb through, plus short train rides on weekends.
Reviews: The train ride is short but the kids do not care. Volunteers are enthusiasts and will explain every engine.

Uniqueness: A Greek Revival house museum with outbuildings, a one room school and a kitchen garden, used as a model for Twelve Oaks in the film.
Reviews: The guided tour covers the plantation economy and the enslaved workers, not just the furniture. Check hours before driving out.

Uniqueness: A 1924 municipal market where Black farmers once sold from the curb, now a hall of soul food counters, butcher stalls and a bakery under one roof.
Reviews: The oxtail and the fried fish are the local picks. It is a working market, not a food hall, and that is the charm.

Typical Customer: Architecture people, couples, travellers stopping between Atlanta and Florida
Uniqueness: An 1892 railroad hotel with a five story atrium, a bridge across the light well and a staircase wide enough for hoop skirts, restored after decades of decline and still taking guests.
Reviews: The atrium stops people in the door. Rooms are period sized, so ask for one of the larger corner ones and eat in the dining room at least once.

Uniqueness: A 186 foot falls at the back of a college campus, taller than Niagara, reached by a short walk up the creek and standing in a bowl of spray at the base.
Reviews: Ten minutes of walking for a waterfall bigger than photos suggest. There is a small gate fee and the campus is quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: One of the most intact of the 55 civilian pilot training fields from the war, with the original barracks, link trainer building and airfield, and about 10,000 pilots who learned to fly here before shipping out.
Reviews: Volunteers who fly and restore the buildings run it, and the link trainer and the barracks rooms are the parts people remember. Small but real.

Season / Dates: Late February to mid March, then closed for the year
Uniqueness: A hardwood slope above a creek that blooms into the largest known stand of trout lilies in the world, millions of them, for about three weeks each February.
Reviews: The bloom window is short and people drive from across the state. Walk the boardwalk, stay off the slope, and check the volunteer hotline before coming.

Uniqueness: A green valley with the Iao Needle rock spire and a stream, where the 1790 battle that united the islands was fought, with a short loop trail.
Reviews: The needle and the stream are the photograph and the trail is short; the parking reservation system catches people out and it rains often.

Uniqueness: A living museum of six Polynesian cultures with villages, canoe pageants and a evening show, run by students from across the Pacific.
Reviews: The evening show is the spectacle and the villages are the learning; it is expensive and the luau package is the full experience.

Uniqueness: A black sand beach of crushed lava where green sea turtles haul out to rest and the palms lean over the water.
Reviews: The turtles are the reason to stop and the sand is genuinely black; give the turtles space and do not touch them.

Uniqueness: A downtown block of Basque restaurants, a market and a cultural center, in the city with the largest Basque community outside Spain.
Reviews: The family style dinners and the market's chorizo are the reasons to come and the July Jaialdi festival fills the city; the block is small.

Uniqueness: A 20 mile lake on the Utah border with turquoise water, a state park beach and raspberry shakes sold in the town of Garden City.
Reviews: The water is clear and the color is the reason people drive; the lake is cold in June and the shakes are the tradition.

Uniqueness: A nonprofit ski area 16 miles from downtown Boise with night skiing, 2,600 acres and a summer mountain bike park.
Reviews: Locals ski after work and the price is the reason; the terrain is gentle and the road up can be snowy.

Company / Access: Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation
Uniqueness: One of the tallest single structure sand dunes in North America at 470 feet, with a lake, a campground and an observatory.
Reviews: Sandboarding down the dune is the family fun and the dark sky is the night reason; the sand is hot in summer and the wind is constant.

Uniqueness: The oldest standing building in Idaho, a church built by Jesuit missionaries and the Coeur d'Alene people with hand hewn timber and painted walls.
Reviews: The church and the story of the mission are the tour; the grounds are quiet and the old cataldo town site is a short walk.

Company / Access: Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation
Uniqueness: A clear lake in the Selkirk Mountains with huckleberry picking, a state park beach and a road that ends at the Canadian border.
Reviews: The lake is quieter than Coeur d'Alene and the water is clear; the drive is long and the nearest town is small.

Uniqueness: A forested peninsula on Lake Coeur d'Alene with a loop trail, granite cliffs and swimming coves, a short walk from downtown.
Reviews: The loop is the local after work walk and the coves are the summer swim; the trail is rocky and the lake is cold.

Uniqueness: A giant state fair with a butter cow, harness racing, a mile long midway and the Illinois Pork Producers' pork chop on a stick.
Reviews: It is the platonic state fair; the butter cow is a genuine attraction. Parking and heat are the usual complaints.

Uniqueness: A gorge of four waterfalls cut into the limestone above the Ohio River, with trails along the creek and a view over the river valley.
Reviews: The falls are best after rain and the trails are steep and slick; the park is quiet compared with the state's northern parks.

Uniqueness: A working dairy and pig farm with a bus tour through the barns, a cheese operation, a restaurant and a giant jumping pillow, all in the middle of Indiana corn.
Reviews: The bus tour is better than expected and the cheese is excellent; it is a long drive from anywhere, which keeps it uncrowded.

Uniqueness: A 40 acre campus of gardens, a museum and historic buildings on the site of the Ball family estate, with a farmers market and a children's garden.
Reviews: The gardens and the farmers market are the local rituals and the museum covers the Ball jar story; the campus is bigger than visitors expect.

Uniqueness: The collection of the wagon maker that became a car company, with the last Studebaker built, a presidential carriage and the Avanti.
Reviews: Car people come for the Avanti and the carriage collection is the surprise; the museum next door covers the same South Bend industrial story.

Uniqueness: A 1886 Queen Anne mansion with 26 acres of grounds, a carriage house and the story of the three families who owned it.
Reviews: The house tour is personal and the gardens are free to walk. Check the event schedule.

Uniqueness: The world's shortest and steepest scenic railway, a 296 foot funicular up the bluff to a view over the Mississippi and three states.
Reviews: The ride is short and the view is the reward. A dollar or two, and a local institution.

Uniqueness: A glass building on the Mississippi by David Chipperfield, holding a collection of American and European art plus a gallery of Haitian painting.
Reviews: The building and the river view are the reasons to go and the Haitian collection is the surprise; it is small enough for 90 minutes.

Uniqueness: A domed conservatory and outdoor gardens on the Des Moines River, with tropical plants, a bonsai collection and a cafe.
Reviews: The dome is the winter escape and the river walk is pretty. Cheap and calm.

Typical Customer: Road trippers, religious pilgrims, art people
Uniqueness: A priest spent forty years building a nine grotto monument out of petrified wood, geodes, agate and malachite, a folk art cathedral in a cornfield.
Reviews: It is free, sincere and stranger than photos suggest; the mineral collection is genuinely impressive.
