Uniqueness: A museum in the old Cotton Belt shops with locomotives, cabooses and a steam engine you can climb on.
Reviews: Volunteers run it and the engines are close enough to touch. Cheap and good for kids.

Uniqueness: A clear reservoir on the White River with 1,000 miles of shoreline, drowned trees and some of the best scuba diving in the mid south.
Reviews: Divers come for the sunken town sites and fishermen for the bass; the lake is deep and cold and the wind comes up in the afternoon.

Uniqueness: A museum in Sam Walton's original five and dime, with the first store, the pickup truck and the story of the retail empire.
Reviews: Free and more interesting than expected, especially for anyone in business. The soda fountain is still there.

Uniqueness: A loop of apple farms in the Sierra foothills where you pick your own, buy cider doughnuts and watch trees turn, 45 minutes from Sacramento.
Reviews: October weekends are a traffic jam and the pie sells out; go on a weekday and start at the top of the loop.

Uniqueness: A coal and sand mining district in the East Bay hills with a cemetery of Welsh miners, a rose garden and a sand mine you can tour underground.
Reviews: The sand mine tour is the reason to book ahead and the hike to the cemetery is short; the park is hot and exposed in summer.

Uniqueness: The only state park in the Napa Valley, with redwood groves, a creek and trails up to a ridge, plus a swimming pool in summer.
Reviews: It is the quiet alternative to the wineries and the campsites book early; the Ritchey Creek trail is the walk.

Uniqueness: Buck Owens' club and museum in Bakersfield, with his red silver sparkle guitar, a restaurant and live country music in the room that kept the Bakersfield sound alive.
Reviews: The museum cases are free to browse and the shows are the draw; the food is better than a club restaurant needs to be.

Uniqueness: A 13th century style Tuscan castle built from scratch on a Napa hillside, with a torture chamber, a chapel and a barrel room painted by Italian fresco artists.
Reviews: People call it Disney for adults; the wine is secondary to the tour and reservations are required on weekends.

Uniqueness: A self guided drive through orchards in bloom, with farm stands selling oranges and almonds and a map that changes with what is flowering.
Reviews: The bloom window is short and weather dependent; locals check the county blossom report before driving and go on a weekday.

Uniqueness: The tenth of the California missions and the only one with twin bell towers, with a cemetery, a lavanderia and a museum of Chumash and mission life.
Reviews: The gardens and the facade are the photograph and the museum is frank about the mission system; the rose garden across the street is free.

Typical Customer: History families, school groups, gold rush fans
Uniqueness: The adobe fort where John Sutter ran a trading post and where the Donner Party survivors were brought, with rooms furnished as workshops and a cannon on the wall.
Reviews: The living history weekends are the time to go and the fort is small; the gold discovery at Coloma is 50 miles away and the story continues there.

Uniqueness: A Victorian mansion with stairs that go nowhere, doors that open onto walls and 160 rooms, built by the heiress to the Winchester rifle fortune to confuse the spirits.
Reviews: The story is better than the house; the tour is scripted and the house is genuinely odd. Go for the lore, not the frights.

Uniqueness: A silver boom town of 2,000 people reduced to a handful of cabins in a meadow at the end of a dirt road, with the hotel and saloon still standing.
Reviews: The setting under Castle Peak is the reason to come and the buildings are unrestored; the road is rough and the site is free.

Uniqueness: Three reservoirs in the Gunnison River gorge, with a 5.5 mile trail to the Morrow Point boat tour and osprey nests on the canyon walls.
Reviews: The Morrow Point boat tour through the gorge is the hidden gem and it runs on a schedule; the lakes are windy in the afternoon.

Uniqueness: A cave system inside Iron Mountain reached by a gondola, with formations lit in color and a cliffside coaster and swing on top.
Reviews: The cave tour is the reason to come and the rides are the surprise; the combo ticket is the way to do both.

Uniqueness: The 1889 Capitol Hill house of the Titanic survivor and suffragist, restored with period rooms and a tour that separates the myth from the life.
Reviews: The guides are good at cutting through the Unsinkable Molly Brown legend; the house is small and the tour runs on the hour.

Uniqueness: A regional museum with Ute baskets, a taxidermy hall and a courtyard of pioneer cabins and farm equipment behind the main building.
Reviews: The Ute collection is the serious part and the outdoor village is good with children; it is small and the staff are local experts.

Uniqueness: A one way road along the crest of a dinosaur fossil ridge, with drops on both sides and a view of the Arkansas valley and the Sangre de Cristo range.
Reviews: Locals take visitors up at sunset and the road is narrow and one way; dinosaur tracks were found along the ridge.

Uniqueness: A high reservoir below the Elk Mountains where the Taylor River runs out and rainbow trout stack up, ringed by forest service campgrounds.
Reviews: Fishermen come for the tailwater below the dam and the jeep roads into the mountains are the local adventure; the water is cold and the wind picks up.

Typical Customer: Art people, families, labor history fans
Uniqueness: The largest indoor collaborative mural in the country, 120 feet long and five stories high, filling a former textile mill with painted tributes to American workers.
Reviews: Visitors are unprepared for the scale; you can walk into parts of the mural and the mill building is part of the exhibit.

Uniqueness: A retired actor built a medieval stone castle on a cliff above the Connecticut River, with hand-carved locks, a secret staircase and a three-mile narrow-gauge railway.
Reviews: People love the eccentricity and the river views; the interior is modest and the tour short. Bring a picnic.

Uniqueness: A three screen drive-in in the woods where you tune the radio, sit on the tailgate and watch two features for the price of one.
Reviews: The snack bar is cash only and the double features are the deal; arrive early for a good spot and bring bug spray.

Uniqueness: A beluga whale habitat, a penguin pavilion and a touch tank of sharks, next to Mystic Seaport so a family can do both in a day.
Reviews: The belugas and the sea lion show are the draw; buy the combined ticket with the seaport and arrive at opening.

Uniqueness: A Gothic revival summer cottage painted bubblegum pink, with original 1850s wallpaper, a boxwood parterre garden and a bowling alley in the carriage house.
Reviews: The color and the bowling alley are the surprises; the tour is short and the garden is free to walk.

Uniqueness: A grocery store built like a theme park, with animatronic farm animals, a bakery conveyor and a dairy that churns its own ice cream while you watch.
Reviews: It is a grocery run that children ask to repeat; the crowds are real on weekends. The fresh mozzarella is the local secret.

Uniqueness: A five eighths mile oval plus a road course on the same property, one of the oldest closed circuit tracks in New England, with open track days for street cars.
Reviews: The road course track days are the way in for drivers; the oval races are cheap and the grandstand is old school.

Uniqueness: The largest collection of Pre-Raphaelite art in the country outside Britain, in a bank building on a wooded park, with a strong Howard Pyle illustration collection.
Reviews: The Pre-Raphaelites are the surprise and the American illustration galleries the local pride; it is a two hour museum and free on Sundays.

Adventure: Delaware Museum of Nature and Science
Company / Access: Delaware Museum of Nature and Science
Uniqueness: A natural history museum with a full dinosaur hall, a shell collection and live animals, in a park north of Wilmington.
Reviews: The dinosaurs and the touch tanks are the family draws; it is small and the outdoor trails are free.

Typical Customer: History people, families, house tour fans
Uniqueness: A campus of moved historic buildings including a 1730s plank house and a Coast Guard station, in the first town in the state.
Reviews: The plank house is the oldest building in Delaware and the guides know it; the complex is small and the town walk is the rest.

Uniqueness: A Swedish Lutheran church built of local stone in 1698, one of the oldest churches in the country still in use, with a churchyard of colonial graves.
Reviews: The stonework and the churchyard are the visit and the guides know the Swedish colonial history; it is quiet and free.

Uniqueness: Ten thousand acres of marsh and forest on Delaware Bay where eagles nest and the spring shorebird migration stops, with a driving loop.
Reviews: The loop and the boardwalk are the easy way in and the refuge is quiet; the mosquitoes are serious in summer.

Uniqueness: A mile of boardwalk with a 1920s merry-go-round, Thrasher's fries in vinegar and a beach town that still shuts its bars early.
Reviews: It is the Mid-Atlantic's cleanest family beach; parking is the eternal complaint. Go in September.

Uniqueness: A Gothic revival mansion with a conservatory, a carriage house and a park of specimen trees, built by a Quaker merchant family.
Reviews: The house is unrestored in the best way and the grounds are free; the Christmas tours are the local tradition.

Uniqueness: A ballpark on the Anacostia with a center field plaza, a presidents race in the fourth inning and a view of the Capitol from the upper deck.
Reviews: The presidents race is the tradition and the standing room areas are good; tickets are cheap on weeknights and the metro stops at the gate.

Company / Access: DC Department of Parks and Recreation
Uniqueness: A paddle boat on the Tidal Basin with the Jefferson Memorial on one side and the cherry trees on the other, from the water.
Reviews: The view from the water is different from the shore and the boats are cheap; the basin is shallow and the queue is long in cherry blossom week.

Uniqueness: A 1931 wholesale market turned food hall with butchers, a tortilleria, a oyster counter and a rotating set of pop ups, north of Capitol Hill.
Reviews: The food stalls change often and the oyster bar and the tacos are the standards; it is busy on weekends and easier on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A 14 acre mound complex built by the Woodland culture 1,500 years ago, with burial mounds, a plaza and a museum on the river.
Reviews: The mounds are subtle but the story is fascinating, and the river setting is pretty. Combine it with a manatee swim.

Uniqueness: A wide Atlantic beach with a pier, surf shops, a boardwalk and a cluster of bars and restaurants, twenty minutes from downtown.
Reviews: The pier is the landmark and the surf is consistent. Parking is easier than most Florida beaches.

Uniqueness: A hilltop lake town with antique shops, a boardwalk, a historic inn and a steam train, in a part of Florida that has hills.
Reviews: The downtown is walkable and the lakefront is pretty, with festivals most weekends in season.

Uniqueness: A professional theater in a converted courthouse square building, with a mainstage season of musicals and plays and a second space for comedians and local acts.
Reviews: Quality is high for a suburban company and the seats are close. The holiday show sells out early.

Season / Dates: Guided visits by arrangement, spring and fall best
Uniqueness: A sandstone outcrop in the middle of flat pine woods with a seasonal waterfall, deep shaded crevices and tropical ferns and orchids growing where they have no business being this far north.
Reviews: Access is limited and arranged in advance, which keeps it wild. People who go call the rock arch and the waterfall the surprise of south Georgia.

Typical Customer: Families, couples, anyone in town for the holidays
Uniqueness: The whole downtown grid is roofed in lights strung tree to tree, so the streets become a lit tunnel that switches on Thanksgiving night and runs into January.
Reviews: People plan their drive home for it. The switch on night fills the square and is the closest this town gets to a crowd scene.

Uniqueness: A 15 mile paved trail along the Chattahoochee, with river access, bridges and a skyline that mixes mills and whitewater.
Reviews: Flat, shaded in stretches and busy at dusk. Rent a bike or walk to the whitewater course and watch the rafts.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square that has played Mystic Falls in The Vampire Diaries and a dozen other shows, with the clock tower, the alley and the storefronts fans recognize.
Reviews: The film map is free at the visitor center and the square is walkable. Weekends bring tour groups.

Typical Customer: Boaters, history walkers, shrimpers at heart
Uniqueness: A shrimp boat waterfront on a bluff above the Altamaha delta, with a 1736 grid of tabby ruins, a small museum and boat trips out to the barrier islands.
Reviews: The waterfront shrimp market is the reason to come in season, and the delta boat tours get you to sandbars nobody else reaches.

Uniqueness: A hilltop grid of antebellum houses above the Chattahoochee, with a reconstructed fort, a cemetery and a view into Alabama.
Reviews: The bluff view is the reason and the town is quiet. Pair it with White Oak Pastures and Providence Canyon.

Adventure: Fort King George State Historic Site
Uniqueness: The reconstructed palisade and blockhouse of the southernmost British fort in North America, built in 1721 to hold the Altamaha, on a bluff over the river marsh.
Reviews: The rebuild is convincing and the story of the garrison dying of disease is told straight. Alligators in the moat ditch are a real feature.

Uniqueness: A log fort built around 1792 by settlers on the Georgia frontier, standing beside a 260 acre reservoir with a swimming beach and a mountain bike trail system that locals rate.
Reviews: The fort is small and easy to walk past, the lake is why people stay. The bike trails are the best kept secret in the park system here.

Uniqueness: A two weekend street festival with hundreds of craft vendors, apple pies, cider, a parade and a car show, in the self proclaimed apple capital of Georgia.
Reviews: Go early for parking and pie. It is crowded, hot and exactly what an apple festival should be.

Uniqueness: A museum of Georgia stock car history in the town that produced NASCAR champions, with cars, trophies and the moonshine running story.
Reviews: Dawsonville's racing pedigree is real and the museum tells it with local pride. Small and cheap.

Uniqueness: One of the largest telephone collections in the country, in a small town exchange building, with switchboards, wooden wall phones, novelty handsets and a wall of colored sets from every decade.
Reviews: Bigger than anyone expects for a town of 400. The switchboard room and the novelty phones are what people photograph.

Uniqueness: The site of Ebenezer, where Lutheran refugees from Salzburg landed in 1734 and built a town, with the 1769 Jerusalem church, a cemetery of original settlers and a living history museum.
Reviews: The church and the cemetery are original and the story of the Salzburgers is one most southern history trips miss. Quiet and free.

Uniqueness: An Alpine-themed village in the Blue Ridge foothills where you float the Chattahoochee in an inner tube with a cooler, then eat schnitzel.
Reviews: It is deeply silly and genuinely fun; the water is cold and the tube chutes are chaotic on weekends. Go on a weekday.

Adventure: Hurricane Shoals Park and Heritage Village
Uniqueness: A shoal on the North Oconee with a covered bridge, a rebuilt grist mill and a village of moved-in log cabins and a chapel, plus a shallow swimming run below the rocks.
Reviews: The mill and village are free to walk and the shoals are the summer swimming spot. The annual Art in the Park weekend fills the place.

Uniqueness: An island resort on Lake Lanier with a water park, a beach, a golf course, zip lines and rental boats, an hour from Atlanta.
Reviews: The water park is the summer draw and the beach is calm. Book parking and rentals ahead on holiday weekends.

Uniqueness: The 1996 Olympic rowing venue, still a working boathouse and regatta course, with a beach, a tower and paddle rentals on the lake.
Reviews: You can rent a kayak and paddle the Olympic course. The tower view is free and the regattas are fun to watch.

Uniqueness: A park on the edge of the Okefenokee with a lake, a golf course, a beach and trails through pine and cypress.
Reviews: The golf course is the local surprise and the lake is quiet. Good base for the swamp.

Uniqueness: A ninety three mile scenic highway along the brow of Lookout Mountain from Gadsden, Alabama to Chattanooga, running through Dade County with overlooks into the valley and pull offs at the canyon rim.
Reviews: The Georgia stretch is short but the views are the best on the route. Motorcycles come up from Chattanooga on weekends.

Uniqueness: A 1754 meeting house rebuilt in 1792, with a slave gallery, a cemetery holding two signers of the Declaration and the graves of Continental officers, in a settlement older than the county.
Reviews: The cemetery is the reason historians stop, with Revolutionary names and a row of Confederate dead. The building is plain and enormous.

Uniqueness: A full antebellum grid of churches, mansions and a Gothic revival asylum, in the town that was Georgia's capital from 1804 to 1868.
Reviews: The architecture is the draw and the town is quiet. Pick up a walking tour map and look up at the windows.

Season / Dates: Year round, outdoor season spring to fall
Typical Customer: Sports families, kids who want to try diving
Uniqueness: A farm pond outside Moultrie that became a national diving center with ten meter towers and eight springboards, and a record of sending divers to the Olympics that a small town should not be able to produce.
Reviews: On a summer morning you can watch college and national team divers train for the price of a spectator fee. The beginner classes are the local kid rite of passage.

Uniqueness: A terraced cemetery on a hill above the confluence of two rivers, with Confederate graves, a monumental arch and a view over Rome.
Reviews: The climb is steep and the view is the reward. Quiet, free and good with the Chieftains museum nearby.

Uniqueness: A craft brewery in a converted cotton warehouse with a taproom, a stage and a patio, serving the lake crowd and the town.
Reviews: The building is the draw and the beer is solid. Check the calendar for live music.

Uniqueness: The original Emory campus, with brick halls, a quad and a cemetery, in a tiny town that still feels like the 19th century.
Reviews: A quiet, pretty walk under old oaks. The cemetery holds early Methodist leaders and Civil War dead.

Uniqueness: A blackwater river backed up into a 375 acre lake with cypress and tupelo standing in the water, plus one of the densest gopher tortoise populations in the state on the sand ridges above.
Reviews: The lake swimming area and the canoe trail get the family traffic. The tortoise burrows along the trail are the thing people did not expect.

Typical Customer: Touring acts, local audiences, theatre people
Uniqueness: A 1921 vaudeville and movie palace that sat dark for forty years and reopened in the 1990s, with a domed ceiling, gilt boxes and a schedule of touring music, theatre and film.
Reviews: The restoration is the story locals tell. Sitting in the balcony for a show is the way to see the ceiling.

Typical Customer: Fruitcake believers, families, food history people
Uniqueness: The bakery that made Claxton the fruitcake capital, selling millions of pounds a year from a storefront on Main Street, where you can watch the mixing and buy a warm slice.
Reviews: People who hate fruitcake change their mind here. Christmas season is a production line running at full speed.

Uniqueness: Four days built around one vegetable, with an onion eating contest, a cooking showdown, a street dance and a Saturday night country concert that draws a real touring act.
Reviews: The onion eating contest is a spectator sport and the concert has outgrown the town. Book lodging early, everything within thirty miles fills.

Uniqueness: A brand museum with the vault, a bottling line and a tasting room of international sodas, next to the aquarium and the civil rights center.
Reviews: It is corporate and cheerful, and the tasting room is the fun part. Skip if you hate crowds, go early if you do not.

Uniqueness: An open air market with 200 vendors selling rambutan, apple bananas, poke and orchid stems, in a town that gets 130 inches of rain a year.
Reviews: Go early for the fruit and the poke; the Wednesday and Saturday markets are the big ones and the prices are the best on the island.

Uniqueness: A aquarium with a walk through tunnel under sharks and rays, a living reef and a Hawaiian green sea turtle hospital, on the Maalaea harbor.
Reviews: The tunnel and the turtles are the family stops; it is a good rainy day and the combo ticket with the harbor cruise is the value.

Company / Access: Idaho Department of Parks and Recreation
Uniqueness: A park on the Snake River at the lower end of Hells Canyon, where Lewis and Clark came through, with a jet boat launch and a beach.
Reviews: The jet boats into Hells Canyon leave from here and the river is the biggest thing in the park; the campground is shaded.

Adventure: Idaho Anne Frank Human Rights Memorial
Uniqueness: An outdoor memorial along the Boise River with a bronze of Anne Frank at her diary, quotations carved in stone and a replica of the attic wall.
Reviews: It is quiet and free and the quotations are the reason people stop; the greenbelt trail runs past it for a longer walk.

Uniqueness: A five mile paved path along the Snake River past a 20 foot waterfall in the middle of town, with a Japanese garden and a museum.
Reviews: The falls in the center of town are the surprise and the path is flat; the greenbelt connects the zoo, the art museum and the river.

Uniqueness: A center on the Lemhi River telling the story of Sacajawea's childhood with the Lemhi Shoshone, with trails along the river and a reconstructed camp.
Reviews: The interpretation is from the tribe and the setting is the valley she grew up in; it is a good stop before the Lemhi Pass drive.

Uniqueness: A trolley ride and a walk into a real silver mine tunnel under Wallace, with a retired miner explaining the drills and the ore cars.
Reviews: The guides are miners and the tunnel is cool; Wallace itself is a silver town with a historic district worth an hour.

Uniqueness: A theme park and water park in the Idaho panhandle with a wooden coaster, a steam train and a 1915 carousel, plus a Boulder Beach water park.
Reviews: The train and the coaster are the family standards; it is smaller than a California park and the lines are shorter in June.

Uniqueness: A visitor center with a 797 mining truck, a simulator and the story of the tractors that changed farming, in the company's hometown.
Reviews: The big machines and the simulator are the family draw and the history of the company is the adult part; it is indoors and cheap.

Uniqueness: A university museum with a strong collection of European painting, African art and contemporary work, free to the public.
Reviews: The permanent collection is better than expected and the shows rotate often; it is free and the café is a campus meeting spot.

Uniqueness: A glass conservatory in downtown with a rainforest, a desert and a seasonally changing garden, warm on a February day.
Reviews: The winter escape is the point and the changing displays bring people back; it is small and cheap and connects to the river walk.

Uniqueness: A small museum with a surprisingly strong collection of American regionalist painting, including Grant Wood and Thomas Hart Benton, free in downtown Terre Haute.
Reviews: Art people call it a hidden collection and it is free; the building is a 1900s library and the galleries are calm.

Uniqueness: A Tibetan temple in the Indiana hills with a prayer hall, a stupa and a garden, founded by a Tibetan lama who settled in Bloomington.
Reviews: Visitors are surprised to find it in Indiana and the gardens are peaceful; the center runs talks and the grounds are free.

Uniqueness: A campus of museums with a natural history hall, a science center and a museum of the Sullivan brothers, the five Waterloo sailors lost together in 1942.
Reviews: The Sullivan brothers gallery is the emotional stop and the science center is for children; the district is bigger than it looks.

Uniqueness: The first capitol of Iowa and later the university's first building, with restored chambers and a spiral staircase, free on the Pentacrest.
Reviews: The chambers and the staircase are the reasons to go in and it is free; the university museum next door is the companion stop.

Company / Access: River City Society for Historic Preservation
Uniqueness: A Frank Lloyd Wright prairie house in a town of 27,000, restored and open for tours, one of the few Wright houses in Iowa.
Reviews: Wright people detour for it and the guides know the restoration; the house is small and the tour is an hour.

Uniqueness: A recreated 1870s cowtown at the edge of the actual Boot Hill cemetery, with a saloon, a jail, a newspaper office and nightly gunfight reenactments.
Reviews: The gunfight show is corny and fun; the museum is better than the show. Combine with the Santa Fe Trail sites.

Uniqueness: A 12 acre farmstead with dairy cows, goats, a one room school and a fishing pond, built to show children where food comes from.
Reviews: Parents say the admission is a few dollars and the animals are gentle; the milk barn and the wagon rides are the hits.

Uniqueness: A hands on science center on the Arkansas River with a design studio, a flight simulator and a dome theater.
Reviews: Good for a rainy day, with enough for kids of different ages. The river setting is nice.

Uniqueness: A museum on the tallgrass prairie with a simulated prairie burn, a bison exhibit and a rooftop prairie garden.
Reviews: The prairie burn exhibit and the kids' area are the family draw; it is the best explanation of the Flint Hills anywhere.

Uniqueness: A Swedish heritage town with a main street of Dala horses, a folk art center, a college and a annual Svensk Hyllningsfest.
Reviews: The Dala horses are everywhere and the town is charming. The Swedish pancakes are the lunch.

Uniqueness: A 8,000 acre lake in the Daniel Boone National Forest with public ramps, camping and muskie fishing.
Reviews: The lake is quiet and the forest setting is pretty. Good for a day on the water.

Uniqueness: A 100 acre public garden with a rose garden, a children's garden, a wetland and trails, on the university campus.
Reviews: Free and well kept, with good shade and a visitor center. A quiet break in horse country.

Uniqueness: The home of the first bottler of Coca-Cola, with the original bottling plant, a museum and formal gardens.
Reviews: The bottling equipment and the family story are the interesting parts. The gardens are a bonus.

Uniqueness: A small park with a 100 foot observation tower, a cypress swamp and a rookery full of egrets and herons.
Reviews: The tower gives a canopy view of the swamp and the birds are close. Free.

Uniqueness: A museum of the Canary Islanders who settled the parish in the 1770s, with a village, a church and the story of the 2005 flood.
Reviews: The Isleno history is unique and the flood exhibit is moving. Free.

Uniqueness: A hands on science center with a planetarium, an IMAX, a space exhibit and a toddler area on the Shreveport riverfront.
Reviews: Good for a rainy day with kids, with enough to fill an afternoon. The planetarium is a bonus.

Uniqueness: A collection of 19th century Acadian houses and barns moved to a site on the St. John River, with guides who speak the French of the upper valley.
Reviews: Visitors from Louisiana and France come for the genealogy; the village is quiet and the river view is the setting.

Uniqueness: A village of moved and restored buildings around a narrow gauge steam railroad, with a Model T ride and a collection of antique automobiles.
Reviews: The steam train ride is short and the village is the charm; good with children under ten and quiet in September.

Uniqueness: The SS Katahdin, a 1914 steamboat still running on Moosehead Lake, with a route past islands and a view of Katahdin from the water.
Reviews: The boat is the attraction and the crew points out moose on the shore; the afternoon trip is the quieter one.

Uniqueness: A lighthouse on a rocky island just offshore, connected to the mainland by nothing, with a keeper's house and a view of Cape Neddick.
Reviews: The classic photo is from Sohier Park at sunset and the island is not open to the public; parking is limited in summer.

Typical Customer: History families, rev war people, school groups
Uniqueness: The oldest surviving wooden fort in New England, a storehouse and garrison on the Kennebec built for the French and Indian War, with the original timbers.
Reviews: The guides are in period dress and the storehouse is the best building; it is small and the river setting is the rest.

Uniqueness: A wooded path of outdoor sculpture in a county park, with a gallery, a children's garden and a program of artist residencies.
Reviews: The sculpture walk is the reason to come and the fairy houses in the woods are the family surprise; it is small and cheap.

Uniqueness: Mile zero of the 184 mile canal towpath, where the canal climbs from Cumberland into the Potomac valley through a lock house and a stone aqueduct.
Reviews: Cyclists ride the whole towpath in two days; the first ten miles from Cumberland are flat and shaded and the Paw Paw tunnel is the highlight.

Uniqueness: A museum with river otters, a fossil hall of Miocene whales and a lighthouse, plus a boatyard where a skipjack is restored.
Reviews: The otters are the family draw and the fossil hall is serious; the drum point lighthouse is the photograph.

Uniqueness: A peninsula between the Elk and Susquehanna rivers with a bay beach, bluffs, a lighthouse and a campground in the woods.
Reviews: The Turkey Point lighthouse trail is the walk and the beach is calm for children; the park is a halfway stop between Baltimore and Philadelphia.

Adventure: National Museum of Civil War Medicine
Company / Access: National Museum of Civil War Medicine
Uniqueness: The story of battlefield medicine in a downtown Frederick building, from amputation tables to the letterman stretcher and the sanitary commission, with a second site at Antietam.
Reviews: Nurses and doctors find it fascinating and children find it grim; the guides do not sanitize the surgery.

Uniqueness: A bay beach under the Chesapeake Bay Bridge with calm water, a fishing pier and a view of the bridge towers from the sand.
Reviews: The beach is the easy swim for children and the bridge view at sunset is the photograph; the lot fills early on summer weekends.

Uniqueness: A cluster of log cabins and a church beside a covered bridge where working artisans demonstrate pottery, weaving and woodwork.
Reviews: The artisans are the reason to stop and the covered bridge is the photograph; it is small and the drive through the Casselman valley is beautiful.

Typical Customer: Gardeners, history people, house tour fans
Uniqueness: A Georgian mansion with a two acre pleasure garden restored to its 1765 plan, hidden behind a Annapolis street.
Reviews: The garden is the surprise and the guided tour explains the signer's life; the house is small and the tour runs on the hour.

Adventure: Dr. Seuss National Memorial Sculpture Garden
Uniqueness: Bronze Lorax, Horton and Cat in the Hat statues in a courtyard in Theodor Geisel's hometown, with a seated Geisel at his drawing board.
Reviews: A free 20 minute stop that photographs well; the museum next door has the original drawings and is the paid companion.

Uniqueness: A quarter mile granite chasm with walls 70 feet high that you scramble through on boulders, formed by glacial meltwater and a popular local rite of passage.
Reviews: The chasm floor is a boulder hop and not for sandals; the rim trail is the easy version and the park is free.

Uniqueness: The brewery that helped start the Michigan craft beer scene, with a beer garden, a pub and a tour that explains Two Hearted and the state's hop history.
Reviews: Beer people make the pilgrimage and the garden is the summer spot; the tour books out and the pub is family friendly until evening.

Uniqueness: Twelve hundred acres of forest, prairie and marsh with a interpretive center, live owls and trails along the Kalamazoo River.
Reviews: The trails and the birds of prey are the reasons to come and the center is good with children; the spring migration is the season.

Uniqueness: Three hundred acres of gardens and trails along the Huron River, with a conservatory of arid and tropical plants and a bonsai collection.
Reviews: The conservatory is the winter stop and the trails are free; the bonsai and the children's garden are the local favorites.

Uniqueness: A post Civil War capitol with a dome covered in copper and a rotunda of Michigan stone, restored to its 1879 appearance.
Reviews: The rotunda and the glass floor are the details people remember; tours are free and run on the hour.

Uniqueness: A deli that became a food institution, with a case of cheeses, a wall of olive oil and a sandwich list that people argue about.
Reviews: The line is part of the experience and the reuben is the standard; the bread and the cheese counter are worth the detour alone.

Uniqueness: Abandoned granite quarries filled with clear water, with swimming holes, cliffs and trails through the stone piles.
Reviews: The quarry swimming is the local summer ritual and the water is cold and deep; the county limits access and the cliffs are dangerous.

Uniqueness: A Gulf coast town of restored cottages and live oaks on the bay, with a beach, a small arts district and a rebuilt main street after Katrina.
Reviews: The town is quieter than the casinos and the beach is free; the old town walk and the seafood are the reasons to stop.

Uniqueness: A 1848 lighthouse standing in the middle of a highway, with a climb to the top and a view of the beach and the bay.
Reviews: The setting in the median is strange and the climb is short. A quick photo stop.

Uniqueness: The only cave in the country you tour by jeep drawn tram, riding through a underground river passage without leaving your seat.
Reviews: The ride is the reason children love it and the cave is accessible for people who cannot walk far; the tour is about an hour.

Typical Customer: House tour people, history fans, families
Uniqueness: A 30 room mansion on a bluff above the Mississippi, with original furnishings and a view over Hannibal, left empty for decades and restored.
Reviews: The house and the river view are the tour and the story of its abandonment is the interest; it pairs with the Mark Twain sites.

Typical Customer: House tour people, gardeners, history fans
Uniqueness: A 50 room Georgian revival mansion built by a copper king, with original furnishings, a carriage house and 46 acres of lawns and gardens.
Reviews: The house is enormous and the family story is the tour; the grounds are free and the summer concerts are the local event.

Uniqueness: A museum of Plains Indian beadwork, quillwork and clothing from the Blackfeet, Crow and Sioux, with a diorama hall built in the 1940s.
Reviews: The beadwork is museum grade and the collection is unexpected for a small town; the annual Indian Days powwow in July fills Browning.

Uniqueness: Three rock shelters with painted figures up to 2,000 years old, excavated in the 1930s, on a rim above the Yellowstone valley.
Reviews: The pictographs are faint and the story is the archaeology; the loop trail is short and the view of Billings is the bonus.

Uniqueness: A roadless area that starts at the edge of Missoula, with a creek trail into alpine lakes and enough climb to feel remote in an hour.
Reviews: Locals run it after work and the lake is a half day; the trail is shared with mountain bikes on some sections.

Uniqueness: A ski hill above a historic coal town with long groomers, tree skiing and a view of the Beartooth range, at half the price of the destination resorts.
Reviews: Locals like the price and the lack of lines; the mountain is modest and the town is the reason to stay overnight.

Uniqueness: Buffalo Bill Cody's 1886 ranch house and barn, where the showman came home between tours, with longhorn cattle and a view of the Platte valley.
Reviews: The barn and the house are the visit and the story of the Wild West show is the context; it is cheap and quiet.

Typical Customer: History families, trail people, school groups
Uniqueness: A frontier fort on the Platte that supplied every wagon train heading west, with rebuilt stockade and blacksmith shop and the trail ruts nearby.
Reviews: The stockade and the demonstrations are the visit and the ruts are a short drive; it is quiet and cheap.

Uniqueness: A small city museum with a planetarium, a giant screen theater and the Kool-Aid exhibit, since the drink was invented here in 1927.
Reviews: The Kool-Aid room is the quirky reason people stop and the planetarium is genuinely good; it is cheap and good with children.

Uniqueness: Adobe ruins of a Civil War era army post on the Carson River, built to protect the emigrant road, with a cemetery and a cottonwood campground.
Reviews: The adobe walls and the river walk are the visit and the campground is green and quiet; it is a good stop between Reno and Las Vegas.

Typical Customer: Ghost town hunters, photographers, road trippers
Uniqueness: A silver camp of 30 surviving buildings kept up by a handful of residents, with a saloon and a general store you can walk into.
Reviews: The caretakers live on site and will talk about the town; the road in is gravel and the nearest gas is 30 miles away.

Uniqueness: A museum with a roof deck of giant letters spelling out a landscape essay, plus a strong collection on the Great Basin and the environment.
Reviews: The rooftop sculpture and the view of the Sierra are the reason to go up; the galleries are small and the building is the surprise.

Uniqueness: A museum in the old Carson City mint building, with a working coin press, a Nevada history hall and a full skeleton of an ichthyosaur found in the state.
Reviews: The mint press and the ichthyosaur are the two things people remember; the building itself is the oldest mint still standing west of the Mississippi.

Uniqueness: A hillside cemetery where the graves outnumber the living town several times over, with wooden markers and the story of a silver camp that killed its men faster than it buried them.
Reviews: The handwritten grave markers and the view over town are the reason to climb; the town below has a restored opera house and a mile long main street.

Uniqueness: A desert lake below the Wassuk Range where the water has receded for decades and the shoreline is a study in alkali and abandoned piers.
Reviews: Photographers come for the emptiness and the mountains; the lake is too salty for most fish now and the shore is stark.

Uniqueness: A hillside of stone chambers, walls and astronomically aligned rocks whose origin nobody agrees on, with a herd of alpacas and a woodland trail.
Reviews: Archaeologists argue about it and visitors love the mystery; the alpacas are a bonus. Wear shoes for the rocks.

Uniqueness: A 1928 family park with a steam train that climbs a trestle, a water blaster boat ride and trained bears performing in a ring, run by the same family for four generations.
Reviews: The train and the bear show are the tradition and both feel like 1965 in a good way; teenagers may be bored and small children are not.

Uniqueness: A series of ledge pools and small waterfalls on Lucy Brook where the water has cut potholes into the granite, a half mile walk from the road.
Reviews: The lower falls are crowded and the upper pools are quieter; the rocks are slippery and the water is cold even in August.

Uniqueness: A ski hill with a view of Lake Winnipesaukee from every run, plus a summer adventure park with a mountain coaster and an aerial treetop course.
Reviews: Families like the smaller scale and the lake view; the terrain is not steep and the lodge is old but the snowmaking is serious.

Uniqueness: A 1859 brick tower with 199 steps and a view over the Cape May point where two bays meet, inside a state park that is a major migration stop.
Reviews: The climb is worth the view and the fall hawk watch at the park is a separate draw; the beach below is free.

Adventure: Delaware and Raritan Canal State Park
Uniqueness: Seventy miles of towpath along an 1830s canal, flat and gravel, with a mule drawn boat at Griggstown and herons the whole way.
Reviews: The Princeton to Kingston stretch is the standard ride; the path is flat and shaded and the canal is stocked with fish.

Uniqueness: A 1907 ferry and rail terminal with a copper clad waiting room, stained glass and a clock tower, still handling commuters from the Hudson waterfront.
Reviews: The waiting room is the room to see and it is free to walk in; the ferry dock outside is where the skyline view is best.

Uniqueness: A chain of sinkhole lakes in the desert, formed when groundwater dissolved the limestone, with a swimming beach and a dive training area.
Reviews: The water is clear and cold and the diving platforms are the local training spot; the lakes are small and the park is quiet outside summer.

Uniqueness: A plaza ringed by 900 historic buildings from the Santa Fe Trail boom, including a hotel where Doc Holliday and Billy the Kid drank, largely unrestored.
Reviews: Architecture people call it the best preserved Victorian town in the southwest and it is nearly empty; some buildings are fragile.

Uniqueness: The adobe plaza that was briefly the Confederate capital of Arizona, with the Basilica of San Albino, a double eagle on the wall and a cantina where Billy the Kid was jailed.
Reviews: The plaza is small and the history is dense; the restaurants around it serve some of the best New Mexican food in the state.

Uniqueness: An open air amphitheater on the Canandaigua lakefront where the lawn slopes toward the stage and the sunset happens behind the audience.
Reviews: The lawn is the value and the wine from the region is allowed in; the covered seats are for rain and the parking lot takes an hour to clear.

Company / Access: Catskill Fly Fishing Center and Museum
Uniqueness: A museum on the Willowemoc with a collection of bamboo rods and flies, casting lessons on the pond and the history of American dry fly fishing.
Reviews: Anglers call the Catskills the birthplace of American fly fishing and the center explains why; lessons are cheap and the river is across the road.

Typical Customer: Aviation people, families, rainy day crowds
Uniqueness: Hangars of Grumman fighters, a Lunar Module and the radar dome from Mitchell Field, telling how Long Island plants built the planes that won the Pacific.
Reviews: Aviation people call it underrated; the cockpit exhibits and planetarium make it the reliable rainy day backup for families.

Uniqueness: A one street village of bars and gear shops below a ski hill that runs 750 vertical feet, with a summer jazz festival and mountain coaster.
Reviews: Buffalo and Toronto both claim it in winter; the bars on Washington Street are the apres scene and the mountain is beginner friendly.

Uniqueness: A museum inside the 1850 weighlock building where canal boats were weighed, with a full canal boat cabin, the original locks and a room on the engineering that made New York the Empire State.
Reviews: The building is the exhibit and the weighlock is the only one left; the upstairs gallery on the canal's labor history is what surprises people.

Uniqueness: A fourth generation family brewery in a brick complex where you walk past open fermentation tanks and end in the 1888 tavern for samples of Saranac and Utica Club.
Reviews: The tour is short but the tasting room and the old brewery architecture carry it; book ahead for Saturdays.

Uniqueness: Ten thousand acres of marsh and hardwood between Lake Ontario and the Niagara escarpment, with an eagle nest, a driving loop and spring migration that fills the trees.
Reviews: Birders time it for the first week of May; the observation deck at Cayuga Pool is where the photographers set up at dawn.

Uniqueness: The octagonal study where Twain wrote most of Huckleberry Finn, moved from his sister in law's hilltop farm to the Elmira College campus and kept as he left it.
Reviews: It is a small wooden room and the visit is short, which is the point; the campus also has his grave in Woodlawn Cemetery nearby.

Uniqueness: The oldest continuously operating tavern in the city, with sawdust on the floor, two beers on offer and a room that has not changed since the last century.
Reviews: Order the ale and skip the menu; it is crowded and cash only and the history is the point.

Uniqueness: The country's hang glider and sailplane archive on Harris Hill, with 50 gliders overhead and a workshop where you can watch a wooden wing being rebuilt.
Reviews: Small but serious; combine it with a glider ride next door and the day makes sense.

Typical Customer: Food crawlers, Flushing regulars, translators in training
Uniqueness: A basement food court in downtown Flushing with thirty stalls of Sichuan, Xi'an and northern Chinese cooking, most plates under twelve dollars and almost nothing translated.
Reviews: Hand pulled noodles and cumin lamb skewers are the standards; go hungry, carry cash and a translation app, and avoid Saturday noon.

Company / Access: New York State Office of General Services
Typical Customer: Architecture people, school groups, statehouse collectors
Uniqueness: A capitol built over 32 years without a dome, with a carved stone staircase that climbs four floors without support and a hall of governors that looks like a cathedral.
Reviews: The Million Dollar Staircase is the thing to see; tours are free and run on the hour, and the observation deck is open in summer.

Uniqueness: Herzog and de Meuron's long barn of a building on the Water Mill fields, showing the painters who worked the light of the South Fork from Chase to today.
Reviews: The building and the studio visits carry it; locals go Friday nights when admission is free and the galleries are quiet.

Uniqueness: The only city beach where surfing is legal, with a forgiving summer beach break and a subway station two blocks from the sand.
Reviews: Beginners say the whitewater is gentler than expected and the lesson plus board package is the cheapest way into the water from New York.

Typical Customer: History people, house tour fans, students
Uniqueness: The Auburn home of Lincoln's secretary of state, with the desk where he wrote the Alaska purchase, a hidden staircase and a collection of Civil War flags.
Reviews: The guided tour is the only way through and the guides know the Alaska story cold; the garden and the carriage house are included.

Uniqueness: A small museum in the Adirondack woods with a reconstructed longhouse, dugout canoes, beadwork and a collection put together by a Mohawk family over three generations.
Reviews: Visitors are surprised by the quality of the collection and the personal tour; it is off the main road and worth the detour.

Adventure: Ska nonh Great Law of Peace Center
Uniqueness: A center on the shore of Onondaga Lake interpreting the Haudenosaunee confederacy and the Great Law, on the site of a French mission and a salt works.
Reviews: The lake itself is the point, since it was sacred ground and later the most polluted lake in the country; the exhibits are small and the guides carry it.

Uniqueness: Eighteen miles of books in a 1930s building at Broadway and 12th, with a rare book room on the third floor and dollar carts on the sidewalk.
Reviews: Book people call the rare room a museum and the crowds are part of the experience; go on a weekday morning.

Uniqueness: A year round Saturday market under a brick riverside canopy where upstate farms sell cheese, cider and mushrooms and the knife sharpener works the crowd.
Reviews: Locals say it is the best market in the capital region; get there by nine for the bread and stay for lunch from a stand.

Typical Customer: History walkers, architecture people, jazz fans
Uniqueness: 400 acres of marble and granite where Duke Ellington, Herman Melville and Miles Davis lie under mausoleums designed by McKim, Mead and White.
Reviews: The weekend trolley tour is the easy way in; the gate map is good enough to walk to Ellington and Melville yourself.

Uniqueness: A 1922 cotton mill bridge turned pedestrian crossing over the Haw River, with graffiti, rope swings and a swimming hole below.
Reviews: The bridge is a local hangout with a view of the river and the old mill ruins. Park at the Bynum lot.

Uniqueness: A 500 acre equestrian competition venue with cross country courses, arenas and a calendar of horse trials, polo and clinics.
Reviews: Even non riders enjoy the cross country phase, where horses gallop past on grass. Check the calendar before driving out.

Uniqueness: A new state park around a 1930s Rockefeller estate, with longleaf pine restoration, a millpond and trails past the old farm buildings.
Reviews: Quiet and flat, with good birding and a sense of an old estate. Free and rarely crowded.

Uniqueness: A hands on science museum with a freshwater aquarium, a planetarium and a saltwater touch tank, in the old Hickory post office.
Reviews: Good for kids under twelve, with enough live animals to hold attention. The planetarium is a bonus.

Uniqueness: A TVA reservoir on the Hiwassee with wooded coves, a swimming beach and a view of the mountains on both sides, at the far western tip of the state.
Reviews: Warm water and quiet coves, good for swimming and bass. Rentals are limited, so bring a boat or a kayak.

Uniqueness: A 1760s plantation house on a bluff over the Cape Fear, with original outbuildings and a view of the river that carried the rice and naval stores trade.
Reviews: The house is small and the setting is the star. Check the hours, which are limited.

Uniqueness: A coffee shop and gallery in a converted warehouse with a stage in the corner, open mic nights and a crowd that is half art school, half neighborhood.
Reviews: The coffee is good and the room is welcoming; the gallery shows are hit or miss. A reliable third place.

Uniqueness: A 1790s plantation house with original outbuildings, a boxwood garden and the story of the Kenan family, in a small town named for them.
Reviews: The house tour is personal and the grounds are quiet. Check hours before driving out.

Uniqueness: The original 1883 general store in a mountain valley, with wooden floors, a potbelly stove, barrels of candy and overalls hanging from the ceiling.
Reviews: It is a store, but the building and the setting are the attraction. The candy counter is the kid bribe.

Uniqueness: A regional museum of mountain life with a log cabin, farm tools, a moonshine still and the story of the railroad climb up the Blue Ridge.
Reviews: Free and genuinely interesting, especially the railroad and moonshine rooms. A good rainy day stop.

Uniqueness: A hangar museum with restored military and civilian aircraft, engines and memorabilia, on a small town airfield.
Reviews: The planes are close enough to touch and the volunteers flew some of them. Check flying days.

Uniqueness: A fenced pasture on Ocracoke where the descendants of the island's wild Banker ponies live, with an observation platform and a short trail.
Reviews: The ponies are smaller and shaggier than expected, and the story of how they got here is the fun part. Free and quick.

Uniqueness: A grid of antebellum and Victorian houses around a courthouse square, with a farmers market and a growing arts scene.
Reviews: The houses are the draw and the town is quiet. The farmers market on Saturdays is a good reason to stop.

Uniqueness: A 1911 wooden covered bridge over the Uwharrie River, one of only two left in the state, in a small park with a trail.
Reviews: A five minute photo stop that is prettier than expected, especially in fall. Free.

Uniqueness: A winery with two rentable treehouses in the oaks and a tasting room built around them, plus muscadine and fruit wines made on the property.
Reviews: The treehouses are the gimmick and the tasting is friendly. Book the treehouse months ahead for a weekend.

Uniqueness: A revived downtown of bars, restaurants, a theater and a Sunday farmers market, a few blocks from the East Carolina campus.
Reviews: Busy on weekend nights and calm on Sunday mornings. The farmers market is the local ritual.

Uniqueness: A huge closed basin lake in the middle of the prairie that has risen for decades and swallowed farmland, with excellent fishing and pelican colonies.
Reviews: Fishermen come for the walleye and the white pelicans are the surprise; the lake level has changed the shoreline and some roads end in water.

Uniqueness: A 1926 atmospheric movie palace with a marquee on Broadway, restored and showing films, concerts and the Fargo Film Festival.
Reviews: The organ and the ceiling are the reasons to look up and the festival in March is the local event; the seats are original.

Uniqueness: North America's largest Scandinavian festival, with Viking reenactors, lutefisk, wood carving and headline entertainment in a town of 48,000.
Reviews: It is warm, weird and deeply sincere; the food is an adventure and the craft demos are excellent.

Company / Access: State Historical Society of North Dakota
Uniqueness: A reconstructed Mandan earth lodge village on the Missouri, with a interpreter in the lodge and a museum on the trade and the smallpox epidemic.
Reviews: The earth lodge and the interpreter are the reason to come and the tour is short; it is included with Fort Lincoln.

Uniqueness: A park with a full size replica stave church, a Danish windmill, a Finnish sauna and a Swedish Dala horse, celebrating the immigrants who settled the prairie.
Reviews: The stave church is the photograph and the park is free; the Norsk Hostfest in the fall fills the city.

Uniqueness: A museum on a bluff above the Great Miami with a collection from ancient to American, in a building modeled on the Villa d'Este.
Reviews: The building and the American galleries are the reasons to stop; admission is free on some days and the collection is broader than expected.

Uniqueness: A warehouse district of brick buildings, restaurants, a canal with water taxis and a ballpark, next to downtown.
Reviews: The canal walk is the thing to do and the food is decent. Busy on weekends.

Uniqueness: A clear reservoir in the Ouachita Mountains with 180 miles of shoreline, pine covered islands and water deep enough for skiing.
Reviews: The lake is the summer destination for Oklahoma and Texas and the rentals fill early; the water is clear by Oklahoma standards.

Uniqueness: A museum in the old Union Agency building on Agency Hill, with art by Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek and Seminole artists and a collection of historic baskets.
Reviews: The art collection is the reason to come and the building is a landmark; the museum is small and the staff are knowledgeable.

Uniqueness: A downtown festival where they cook the world's largest onion fried burger on a giant griddle and the town's burger stands sell them all day.
Reviews: The burger history is real and the line for the giant one is the event; El Reno is where the onion burger was invented during the Depression.

Uniqueness: A town of bronze foundries where you can watch a sculpture being cast and see finished pieces on the main street, in a valley below the Wallowas.
Reviews: The foundry tours are the reason art people stop and the main street galleries are free; check hours, the foundries run on production schedules.

Uniqueness: A working fishing bayfront where you can buy crab off the boat, watch sea lions on the docks and eat chowder in a shack over the water.
Reviews: The sea lions are loud and the crab is the order; the bayfront is touristy and the working boats are still there.

Uniqueness: A steam train along Tillamook Bay and the coast, with open cars and a view of the water most of the way.
Reviews: The open car is the seat to book and the ride is 90 minutes; the dinner train and the fall pumpkin train are the local events.

Uniqueness: A restored narrow gauge logging railroad with a steam Heisler locomotive, running through the gold dredge country of the Blue Mountains.
Reviews: The steam engine and the open cars are the fun and the dredge is a short drive away; the ride is short and the volunteers run it.

Uniqueness: A dairy cooperative visitor center with a viewing gallery over the cheese making floor, a scoop counter and a cafeteria of grilled cheese.
Reviews: The ice cream line is the longest and worth it and the factory view is self guided; go early, the parking lot fills by noon in summer.

Uniqueness: A woolen mill and four pioneer houses on the mill race, with working looms and the story of the Methodists who founded Salem.
Reviews: The mill machinery runs on weekends and the houses are furnished; it is small and the walk along the race is pleasant.

Company / Access: General Church of the New Jerusalem
Typical Customer: Architecture people, stained glass fans, quiet seekers
Uniqueness: A Gothic cathedral built by hand in the 1910s by craftsmen who worked without straight lines, with glass made on the grounds and a hilltop view over the Pennypack valley.
Reviews: Architects call the craftsmanship a century ahead of its time; the cathedral is free and the neighboring Glencairn Museum is the paid tour.

Uniqueness: A 1878 trolley park in the Laurel Highlands with Storybook Forest, a 1930s walk through nursery rhymes, and a wooden coaster in the woods.
Reviews: Parents say Storybook Forest is the reason to come before children turn eight; the water park and the coaster extend the day.

Uniqueness: Nine blocks of 9th Street where cheesemakers, butchers and tortilla factories still work behind open counters, with the Philadelphia side of the market running since the 1880s.
Reviews: Go on a weekday morning and start at the top; the weekend crowd is a wall and the produce prices are the best in the city.

Uniqueness: The steepest vehicular inclined plane in the world at 70 percent grade, built as an escape route after the flood and still carrying cars and people up the hill.
Reviews: The ride is short and the view from the top over the Conemaugh valley is the point; the operator will explain the counterweight.

Uniqueness: A university art museum with American painting, Japanese prints and a sculpture garden, free on the Penn State campus.
Reviews: The collection is broader than expected and it is free; the new building is a short walk from the student union.

Uniqueness: A narrow gauge mine train that carries you 1,800 feet into a working anthracite vein, then a steam locomotive ride on the surface along the old colliery.
Reviews: The guides are former miners and the mine is cold; children like the train and adults like the stories about breaker boys.

Typical Customer: Train people, families, labor history fans
Uniqueness: The old PRR master mechanics building holding a K4 steam locomotive, a cab you can climb into and the story of the Altoona shops that built and repaired the railroad.
Reviews: The simulator and the cab are for children and the labor history galleries are for adults; combine it with Horseshoe Curve on one ticket.

Typical Customer: Families, road trippers, model train fans
Uniqueness: A 6,000 square foot miniature village of tiny houses, farms and a working railroad, built by one man over decades and lit by a day to night show.
Reviews: It is a time capsule of a roadside attraction and children are hypnotized; the night show is kitsch perfection.

Uniqueness: A creek that has drilled a series of round pools into the bedrock at the foot of a mountain, with a trail through the glen.
Reviews: The tubs are the photograph and the trail is short and steep; it is free and cool in summer and the water is dangerous after rain.

Uniqueness: A trolley era park with a 1908 carousel, a wooden coaster and a water park, free to enter so you can walk the midway without buying a ride wristband.
Reviews: Locals love that admission is free and parking is cheap; the Ravine Flyer II is the coaster enthusiasts come for.

Uniqueness: The factory museum where the lighter that became a soldier's talisman is displayed with the case knives, including the prototypes and the lifetime guarantee repair bench.
Reviews: Collectors come from overseas and the staff still repair any Zippo for free; the museum is free and takes an hour.

Uniqueness: A 464 acre shore park on Narragansett Bay with a bike loop, formal gardens, a beach and a view of the Providence skyline.
Reviews: The bike loop and the shore road are the local ritual and the park is free; the breeze keeps it cool in summer.

Company / Access: IYRS School of Technology and Trades
Uniqueness: A boatbuilding school on Newport harbor where you can watch students restore wooden yachts and a 1885 schooner in the water.
Reviews: The workshop is open to visitors and the smell of varnish is the attraction; it is free and the students will explain what they are doing.

Uniqueness: A wide barrier beach with real surf, a boardwalk of food stands and the Atlantic on one side and a salt pond on the other.
Reviews: It is the busiest beach in the state and the surf is the draw; arrive before nine or park in the private lots across the road.

Uniqueness: A museum in a former textile mill telling the story of the French Canadian workers who came to the mills, with a mill floor and a company store.
Reviews: The mill floor and the immigration story are the reasons to come; it is specific and local and the guides know the families.

Uniqueness: The rocky point where Narragansett Bay meets Block Island Sound, with a lighthouse, a surf beach and a row of clam shacks.
Reviews: The clam cakes and the view of the lighthouse are the stop and the surf is consistent; the point is windy and the rocks are slippery.

Uniqueness: A flying horse carousel built in 1879 hanging from chains rather than mounted on a frame, still turning beside a Rhode Island beach.
Reviews: Collectors say it is one of the oldest in the country; the ride is two dollars and the beach and lighthouse are a short walk.

Uniqueness: A museum in Banksia, a 1930s winter colony mansion, with rooms on the Aiken Institute, the Savannah River Site and the horse culture that made the town.
Reviews: The house is the exhibit and the local history is well told. Free or nearly so.

Uniqueness: A reptile park at Barefoot Landing with giant alligators, crocodiles, snakes and a live feeding show, built around a cypress swamp.
Reviews: The feeding show is the draw and the gators are genuinely huge. Good for kids who like reptiles, less so for anyone who does not.

Uniqueness: A new county park on the Ashley River with a kayak launch, river overlooks, trails and a playground, built on a former plantation site.
Reviews: The river access is the draw and the trails are easy. Bring a boat or a picnic.

Uniqueness: A broad, wooded river with shoals and sandbars, flowing past Revolutionary War crossings and pine forest, with put ins at Chester and Fish Dam Ford.
Reviews: The current is gentle and the shoals are easy. Check the gauge and bring water.

Uniqueness: The collection of Dalton Stevens, the Button King, who covered a car, a coffin and a suit in buttons, with the car parked outside and thousands of buttons inside.
Reviews: It is exactly as strange as it sounds and the family is proud of it. Call ahead, because hours depend on the family.

Uniqueness: An island campground on Lake Murray with coves for swimming, a fishing pier and rental cabins, reachable by a causeway and full of herons.
Reviews: The lake swimming and the sunsets are the draw; book a cabin months ahead for summer.

Uniqueness: Fifty acres of roses, azaleas and cypress along the Edisto River, with a boardwalk over the water and a festival that draws gardeners from across the state.
Reviews: The rose garden peaks in May and costs nothing; the river walk is shady and the playground makes it a family stop.

Uniqueness: A small town festival named for the swamp where bootleggers once ran liquor, with a parade, gospel singing, a snake show and the kind of food stalls that only exist one weekend a year.
Reviews: It is deliberately unpolished and that is the appeal. Parking is in fields, bring cash, and stay for the gospel program.

Uniqueness: A nonprofit bookshop in a restored Masonic temple, run by a writers' collective that publishes local authors and hosts readings in a room with the original tin ceiling.
Reviews: The curated Southern shelf is excellent and the staff picks are honest; events are frequent and free.

Uniqueness: The quiet western shore of a 50,000 acre lake, with public ramps, fishing coves and sunsets that pull people off the road.
Reviews: The lake is the local summer. Rentals and ramps are on the Saluda side, and the striper fishing is the quiet draw.

Uniqueness: A Corps lake on the Savannah River with wooded shorelines, a swimming beach, boat ramps and campgrounds, less developed than the big reservoirs.
Reviews: Quiet and cheap, with good bass and crappie fishing. The beach is small but calm.

Uniqueness: A year round farmers market on the highway with produce sheds, a restaurant and a garden center, where growers from the Pee Dee sell what they picked that morning.
Reviews: The tomatoes and peaches in summer are the reason, and the restaurant serves a proper vegetable plate. Go early on Saturday.

Uniqueness: A revived main street with a fountain, a theater, a brewery and a market, plus a textile mill history that built the town.
Reviews: The old town is walkable and busy on weekends. The velodrome and the river park are minutes away.

Uniqueness: A festival built around the iris beds at Swan Lake, with a parade, arts and crafts, a car show and food stalls under the cypress.
Reviews: Parking is the challenge and the morning is the time to go. The iris display is the reason, and the car show draws a crowd.

Uniqueness: A working national forest of pine and hardwood with trails, old mill sites and dirt roads that connect the Piedmont to the mountains.
Reviews: The forest is quiet and free, with good spring wildflowers and hunting in season. Some roads are rough, so check conditions.

Uniqueness: A historically Black college campus with Victorian brick buildings, a registered historic district and the story of Elizabeth Evelyn Wright, who founded it.
Reviews: The campus is quiet and the history is remarkable. Check in at the administration building.

Uniqueness: A walk up ice cream stand that has been selling soft serve and chili dogs since 1944, with a neon sign and a line of cars on a summer night.
Reviews: The soft serve is the order and the prices are stuck in another decade; cash moves faster.

Uniqueness: A reservoir on the Missouri below Gavins Point Dam with 90 miles of shoreline, sandy beaches and some of the best walleye fishing in the state.
Reviews: The lake is the summer water for the region and the dam is the history; the wind makes afternoon boating rough.

Uniqueness: A thousand year old village of earth lodges under a protective dome, with an active dig and a lab where students process what they find.
Reviews: The dig under the dome is the reason to come and the site is active in summer; it pairs with the Corn Palace down the road.

Uniqueness: The state fair on the prairie with livestock shows, a draft horse pull, a carnival and grandstand concerts.
Reviews: The livestock barns and the horse pull are the real fair and the concerts draw the region; it is hot and the parking is in fields.

Uniqueness: A hands on children's museum and nature center on a spring fed wetland, with a water table, a tree house and trails.
Reviews: Good for kids under ten, with enough live animals and water play to fill an afternoon.

Uniqueness: A main street where the state line runs down the middle of the road, with Tennessee on one side and Virginia on the other, and brass markers in the sidewalk.
Reviews: The photo is standing in two states at once, and the storefronts are a pleasant walk. The birthplace of country music sign is the local claim.

Uniqueness: Ten Cadillacs buried nose-first in a wheat field, spray-painted by every visitor since 1974, in the middle of a Panhandle nothing.
Reviews: Bring your own spray paint; it is free, fast and exactly as good as you make it. Combine with the Big Texan steak challenge.

Uniqueness: Two thousand acres of beach and salt marsh on the west end of the island, with a kayak trail through the bay side and a beach that is never crowded.
Reviews: The bay side is calm and good for beginners and the beach side has real surf; the park is quiet compared with the seawall.

Uniqueness: A Market Square institution open around the clock since 1941, with a bakery counter, a mariachi trio and a ceiling of painted panels and Christmas lights.
Reviews: The pan dulce and the breakfast plates are the orders; it is loud, brightly lit and the wait at midnight is part of the experience.

Uniqueness: A 1884 brewery turned museum holding Latin American art, Greek vases and Asian ceramics, with a river walk extension along the back.
Reviews: The Latin American collection is the reason curators visit; the building's brew house bones are visible and the river terrace is free.

Company / Access: Animal World and Snake Farm Zoo
Uniqueness: A roadside reptile zoo with hundreds of snakes, alligators and a venom lab, running since 1967 on the highway between Austin and San Antonio.
Reviews: It is old school and proud of it; the venom demonstration is the highlight and kids leave thrilled.

Uniqueness: A Gulf of Mexico aquarium with a dolphin bay, a shark exhibit and a splash park, on the ship channel next to the Lexington.
Reviews: The dolphins and the touch tanks are the family draw; the splash park is the summer reason to stay and the combo ticket with the ship saves money.

Uniqueness: The 1931 movie palace where Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested, now a repertory cinema with a bar and a programming mix of cult films and new releases.
Reviews: The balcony and the art deco lobby are the atmosphere; the November 22 programming is the local history lesson.

Uniqueness: A 607 foot double cataract at the mouth of Provo Canyon, with a paved trail to the base and a pool that freezes into a blue cone in winter.
Reviews: The walk is short and paved and the falls are visible from the road; the ice climb in winter is a local spectacle.

Uniqueness: A heritage railroad along Deer Creek Reservoir into Provo Canyon, with a steam engine on some weekends and a murder mystery train at night.
Reviews: The canyon view from the open car is the reason to ride; the themed trains sell out and the ride is 90 minutes.

Uniqueness: A distillery on a historic ranch with a saloon and a barrel room, making rye whiskey at altitude in a state that used to ban the stuff.
Reviews: The tasting is generous and the food is better than a distillery needs; the original Park City location is smaller and harder to park at.

Typical Customer: Rock art people, road trippers, photographers
Uniqueness: A wind cut gap in the rock covered with hundreds of petroglyphs, including a calendar spiral that marks the solstice.
Reviews: Archaeologists argue about the meanings and the site is free and unguarded; the drive is a short detour off Interstate 15.

Adventure: Utah Field House of Natural History
Uniqueness: A museum with a garden of full size dinosaur sculptures, a walk through time hall and a fossil prep lab, next to the road into the monument.
Reviews: The outdoor dinosaur garden is the photograph and the inside is a good rainy day stop; it takes 90 minutes.

Uniqueness: A 24 acre corn maze cut with a different design each year, plus a smaller maze for children and a cow train, on a working Vermont farm.
Reviews: Adults get lost for two hours and children do the small maze; wear closed shoes and go early, the field is hot in September.

Uniqueness: A roadside pull off at 2,400 feet on Route 9 with a long view into the Green Mountains and a trail along the ridge.
Reviews: The first week of October is the reason to come; the pull off is small and the trail is a gentle walk along the top.

Uniqueness: A flat loop across the islands of Lake Champlain on quiet roads, with orchards, a ferry crossing and water on both sides most of the way.
Reviews: The islands are flat and the traffic is light; the apple orchards in September and the ferry back to New York are the local route.

Uniqueness: A delta of marsh and river on Lake Champlain where ospreys and black terns nest and a canoe trail winds through the cattails.
Reviews: The canoe trail and the spring migration are the reasons to come and the refuge is quiet; the bugs are serious in June.

Uniqueness: The stone house where Frost wrote Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening, with the orchard and the poem's landscape around it.
Reviews: Poetry people come for the room where he wrote and the grounds are free; the museum is small and the docents know the poems.

Uniqueness: A family ski mountain in a notch where boulders pinch the road and the trails run through birch and hemlock, with a summer water park and zip line.
Reviews: Parents like the ski school and the slope side lodging; the notch road is closed in winter and the drive around is long.

Typical Customer: Statehouse collectors, school groups, history people
Uniqueness: A granite capitol with a gold leaf dome and a cedar statue of Ceres on top, in a town of 8,000 that is the smallest state capital in the country.
Reviews: Tours are free and the Representatives Hall is the room to see; the farmers market on the lawn in summer is the local ritual.

Uniqueness: A brewery built in the middle of a hop field that the family has farmed for four generations, with a taproom that looks out over the bines.
Reviews: The fresh hop beers in September are the reason beer people make the drive and the outdoor seating is the setting; the taproom is closed early on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A man made island of sand and dune grass in Puget Sound, reached by a free ferry, with shallow warm water and a long empty beach.
Reviews: The shallow water is warm by Puget Sound standards and the ferry is free; the island is only open in summer and the wind is constant.

Uniqueness: Ninety acres with a formal Duncan garden, a Japanese garden, a rose hill and a greenhouse conservatory, all free in the middle of the city.
Reviews: The Japanese garden and the Duncan garden are the two stops and the park is free; the greenhouse is the winter visit.

Uniqueness: A zoo and aquarium in a 760 acre park on Puget Sound, with polar bears, walruses and a Pacific seas aquarium, plus a ferry to the park.
Reviews: The walruses and the aquarium are the family draw and the park around it has trails and a beach; the hill is steep and the zoo is compact.

Uniqueness: More than 70 murals painted on downtown walls telling the history of the Yakama Nation and the railroad town, best seen by horse drawn wagon.
Reviews: The wagon tour in summer is the way to see them and the murals are genuinely good; the town is small and the drive from Yakima is 30 minutes.

Uniqueness: The site of the 1847 mission where the Whitmans were killed, with the foundation of the mission house, a wagon ruts trail and a museum on the Cayuse War.
Reviews: The ranger talks tell the story from both sides and the wagon ruts are the real thing; it is free and the walk is flat.

Uniqueness: Six thousand acres on Cacapon Mountain with a lodge, a lake, horseback trails and a ridge trail to a view of three states.
Reviews: The ridge trail and the lake are the reasons to come and the lodge is a good base; the park is quiet compared with the gorge.

Uniqueness: A reconstructed palisade fort and cabins on the Monongahela, with interpreters in period dress and a 1770s job of work going on.
Reviews: The fort and the demonstrations are the family draw and the site is on the river; the living history weekends bring it alive.

Company / Access: West Virginia Division of Culture and History
Uniqueness: The custom house where the Restored Government of Virginia met and the debate over West Virginia statehood happened, with the original courtroom and chambers.
Reviews: The room where statehood was argued is the reason to come and it is free; the building is a cast iron fronted landmark in downtown Wheeling.

Typical Customer: Art people, gardeners, house tour fans
Uniqueness: A Tudor revival mansion with a formal garden, showing art in the family rooms and hosting a holiday lights event that fills the grounds.
Reviews: The house and garden are the visit and the holiday show is the local tradition; it is small and the art rotates.

Uniqueness: One of the highest points in the state with a 60 foot observation tower and ski runs on the same hill, above the Wisconsin River.
Reviews: The tower view in fall is the reason to climb and the ski hill is a local winter spot; the trails are steep and rocky.

Uniqueness: Twenty acres of themed gardens on a former dairy farm, with a Japanese garden, a children's garden and a holiday light show.
Reviews: The Japanese garden and the winter lights are the two seasons; it is small and cheap and the paths are flat.

Uniqueness: A WWII amphibious vehicle drives straight from the street into the Wisconsin River and up a sandstone gorge, with a driver who tells terrible jokes.
Reviews: It is exactly as silly as it sounds and kids love it; the Dells is a waterpark town with a strange natural core.

Uniqueness: A spring that flows heavily for several minutes and then stops, probably because of a natural siphon in the mountain, reached by a mile and a half trail.
Reviews: The timing is unpredictable and that is the fun; scientists have studied it and locals take visitors up in summer.

Uniqueness: A drugstore owner's collection of frontier weapons, saddles and Lakota artifacts, with a room on the Johnson County War and the cattle barons' invasion.
Reviews: The Johnson County War exhibit is the reason history people stop and the collection is bigger than the building suggests; it takes 90 minutes.

Uniqueness: The Super Bowl of duck calling, held in a rice-and-mallard town during the Wings Over the Prairie festival, with a duck gumbo cookoff and a queen.
Reviews: It is exactly as niche and sincere as it sounds; visitors love the cookoff and the calling finals are surprisingly dramatic.

Typical Customer: Ghost hunters, true crime fans, teens
Uniqueness: An unsolved 1912 family murder house preserved almost as it was, with bullet holes in the walls and overnight investigations if you want to stay.
Reviews: The tour is matter of fact about a real tragedy; it is eerie rather than theatrical. Not for young kids.

Uniqueness: A five story cavern lit in neon, billed on barn roofs for a hundred miles, with a sound and light show and a Jesse James outlaw legend.
