Reviews: It is unabashedly old school roadside Americana; the formations are impressive and the show is kitsch. Kids love it.

Uniqueness: A 24 hour French bakery in NoDa with mismatched furniture, a salted caramel brownie worth the trip and a dining room that gets stranger after midnight.
Reviews: The late night crowd is the charm; service is slow and the pastry case empties. Locals order the brownie and a latte at 1am.

Uniqueness: A gallery of the deliberately bizarre, with alien autopsies, a giant bigfoot and a room of cursed objects, made by local artists with a sense of humor.
Reviews: It is silly and handmade, and kids over ten love it; the ice cream counter is a nice palate cleanser.

Uniqueness: A county museum with a reconstructed main street, a cotton mill exhibit and a room on the electric car that once ran through town.
Reviews: The main street recreation is charming and the mill history is well told; free and air conditioned.

Uniqueness: A campus holding the county museum, a science center, a theater and artists' studios, where you can watch a glass blower or a potter at work for free.
Reviews: The open studios are the best part; the museum is small but well done. A good rainy afternoon that does not feel like a chain.

Uniqueness: A river town of antebellum houses, a 19th century market hall and a theater where jazz bands played on the chitlin circuit, all within a few blocks.
Reviews: Pick up a walking tour map at the chamber and look for the Dizzy Gillespie marker; he was born here. The town is quiet, so the architecture is the show.

Uniqueness: A small museum in a historic Rosenwald school telling the story of the Black families, farms and schools that predate the university, with oral histories recorded by the people who lived them.
Reviews: Visitors call it a necessary counterweight to the campus story; the oral history room is the heart of it. Free and quiet.

Uniqueness: A short asphalt oval on the coastal plain where late models and street stocks race under the lights, with a grandstand close enough to feel the exhaust.
Reviews: Cheap, loud and friendly, with a crowd that has been coming for decades; check the schedule before the drive.

Uniqueness: A counter downtown that has been frying burgers and chicken since 1907, with a griddle that has never been replaced and a menu that fits on one board.
Reviews: The burgers are the order and the place is a time capsule; lunch rush is fast and loud.

Uniqueness: A peninsula of campground and boat ramps on one of the largest man made lakes in the Southeast, with fishing piers and a swimming area under the pines.
Reviews: The lake is huge and the park is a good base for boating; the swimming area is basic but cheap. Book campsites early in summer.

Uniqueness: A peninsula of campsites and fishing piers on a 13,000 acre lake, with a nature trail through hardwood and a reputation for crappie and catfish.
Reviews: The lake is the point and the park is simple. Sunsets over the water from the pier are the postcard, and the campground is quiet midweek.

Uniqueness: A dairy tour with a glass viewing walkway over the bottling line and an ice cream shop at the end, in a Tennessee company town that has been churning since 1910.
Reviews: It is a cheap, air conditioned hour with kids and the ice cream is the reward. The yellow jugs are a Southern grocery memory.

Uniqueness: A 145-foot underground waterfall at the end of a cave walk 1,120 feet inside Lookout Mountain, lit in colored light with a soundtrack.
Reviews: It is deeply touristy and kids love it; the falls are genuinely impressive. Combine with Rock City and the Incline.

Adventure: Jule Collins Smith Museum of Fine Art
Uniqueness: A university museum with American and European art, a sculpture garden and a cafe, free to the public.
Reviews: Small and free, with good temporary shows. A quiet break from campus.

Uniqueness: A 19th century drugstore counter that sells lemonade so tart it makes people flinch, across from campus, where the trees were poisoned by a rival fan and the town replanted.
Reviews: The lemonade is a rite of passage and the line moves fast; the football lore is worth asking about.

Uniqueness: A museum of the gold rush, the serum run and Iñupiat life on the Seward Peninsula, with photos and objects from the 1898 stampede.
Reviews: The serum run and gold rush exhibits are the reason to stop and the staff are local; it is small and warms you up on a cold day.

Uniqueness: A World War II coastal defense post on a spruce covered point, with gun emplacements, a lake and a trail along the cliffs.
Reviews: The bunkers in the moss are strange and photogenic and the tidepools are good; the weather is usually wet.

Uniqueness: The quartermaster depot and the siphon that diverted the Colorado to irrigate the desert, in a park on the river levee.
Reviews: The engineering story of the canal is the reason to stop and the buildings are restored; it is small and pairs with the prison.

Uniqueness: A lake in the White Mountains with a campground under ponderosa pines, a swim beach and a trail around the shore, at 6,300 feet.
Reviews: It is the cool summer escape for Phoenix and the campground is the draw; the lake is small and the trout fishing is stocked.

Adventure: Gila Box Riparian National Conservation Area
Uniqueness: Twenty three miles of the Gila and San Simon rivers with cottonwood galleries, beaver and 200 bird species, in a desert canyon.
Reviews: The float in spring is the reason to come and the creek trails are quiet; the water is seasonal and the roads are rough.

Uniqueness: Ancestral Puebloan village sites on the Little Colorado, with pottery sherds on the surface and a campground with a view of the Painted Desert.
Reviews: The ruins are unexcavated and the rangers ask you not to pick up the pottery; the park is quiet and the sunset over the mesa is the reason to camp.

Uniqueness: The 1831 London Bridge, bought, dismantled stone by stone and rebuilt over a Colorado River canal in the desert, with an English village around it.
Reviews: The story is better than the bridge and the boat tour under it is the fun; the lake is the real attraction for most visitors.

Uniqueness: A viewpoint over one of the largest open pit copper mines in North America, where the pit is miles wide and the haul trucks look like toys.
Reviews: The scale is the attraction and the overlook is free; the mine is active so check access and do not enter closed roads.

Uniqueness: The reservoir formed by the Theodore Roosevelt Dam, the first big federal reclamation project, with a bridge named after the dam and desert mountains all around.
Reviews: The lake is the fishing and the dam is the history; the water level varies and the summer heat is brutal.

Uniqueness: A nature center on the Arkansas River with a swamp boardwalk, live alligators and a aquarium of river fish, free to the public.
Reviews: The alligators and the boardwalk are the family stops and the center is free; it is a good break on the drive through the Delta.

Uniqueness: The largest natural lake in the state, an oxbow of the Mississippi, with cypress trees, a campground and a boardwalk through a swamp.
Reviews: The cypress and the birding are the reasons to camp and the lake is warm and shallow; the mosquitoes are serious in summer.

Uniqueness: A Ozark reservoir with 550 miles of shoreline, clear water and a trout fishery below the dam, ringed by forest.
Reviews: The lake is quieter than Bull Shoals and the trout water below the dam is famous; the town of Mountain Home is the base.

Uniqueness: A market hall on the Napa River with a oyster bar, a spice shop, a butcher and a taco counter, where locals eat between wine appointments.
Reviews: The oysters and the ice cream are the standard stops; it is smaller than the Ferry Building and easier to park.

Uniqueness: The oldest working wooden wharf in California, with a sea center, fish and chips stands and a view back at the mountains and the red tile roofs.
Reviews: The sea center touch tanks are good with children and the sunset from the end is the local ritual; parking on the pier is expensive.

Uniqueness: A preserve where a herd of tule elk survives on the valley floor, with a viewing platform and a fence line you can drive along.
Reviews: The elk are visible most mornings and the reserve is a short detour from Interstate 5; bring binoculars and go early.

Uniqueness: A walk through the tea factory past the mint room, where the smell is so strong visitors are warned, ending in a tasting room of every blend.
Reviews: The mint room is the story everyone tells and the tasting is generous; the tour is free and requires a reservation.

Uniqueness: A tilapia farm that became an alligator rescue in the San Luis Valley, with 200 gators in geothermal water and a chance to hold a small one.
Reviews: People cannot believe alligators live in Colorado; the staff are rescuing animals and the feeding shows are the reason to check times.

Typical Customer: Families, history kids, gold rush fans
Uniqueness: A real gold mine tunnel you walk into with a hard hat, and a hillside of ore chutes and buildings above Breckenridge, with gold panning at the end.
Reviews: The underground tour is short and cool and the panning keeps children busy; it is the best rainy day activity in town.

Uniqueness: One of the largest planetariums in the country, with a dome 60 feet across and student led shows that include live tours of the current sky.
Reviews: The live star talks are better than the recorded shows and the laser nights are the student tradition; check the schedule before driving.

Uniqueness: A short trail through the remains of a hydraulic gold mining operation, with sluice cuts, a miner's cabin and a view over the town.
Reviews: Locals use it as an easy evening walk and the signs explain what the ditches were for; it is free and takes an hour.

Uniqueness: A small ski hill on the Grand Mesa with a view into the Colorado National Monument, lift tickets half the price of the destination resorts and no lift lines.
Reviews: Locals call it the best value in the state and the terrain is modest; the drive up the mesa can be snowy and the lodge is basic.

Uniqueness: A 50 mile gravel rail trail on the old Air Line route, crossing stone arch bridges and a gorge on the Natchaug River.
Reviews: The Thompson to Putnam section and the Willimantic bridge are the highlights; the surface is gravel and better on a hybrid than a road bike.

Uniqueness: A 1914 Stein and Goldstein carousel with 48 hand carved horses and a Wurlitzer organ, still turning in a glass pavilion in the middle of downtown.
Reviews: A two dollar ride that adults take without children; the park around it is the oldest public park in the country.

Typical Customer: Boat people, history families, river walkers
Uniqueness: A museum in a 1878 steamboat warehouse on the river, with a working shipyard, a 1906 schooner and the story of the Connecticut's shipbuilding trade.
Reviews: The schooner sails in summer and the museum is small; combine it with the Essex steam train across town.

Uniqueness: Eighty foot Chapman Falls drops into a pothole marked gorge on the Eightmile River, with trails through hemlock and a legend about the devil that the park does not endorse.
Reviews: The falls are a five minute walk and the orange trail climbs above them; it is small and popular on summer weekends.

Uniqueness: A traprock ridge with a carriage road to a soldiers' monument and a cliff view over New Haven harbor, plus a trail down to the Mill River.
Reviews: The summit is a 20 minute walk and the view of the city and Long Island Sound is the payoff; the road is closed to cars in winter.

Typical Customer: History walkers, architecture fans, Yale visitors
Uniqueness: The first chartered cemetery in the country, laid out in family plots on a grid with an Egyptian revival gate, holding Eli Whitney, Noah Webster and Lyman Beecher.
Reviews: The gate and the Whitney monument are the landmarks; it is a quiet walk between Yale and the Hill and free maps are at the entrance.

Uniqueness: A aquarium built in a 19th century ironworks on the Norwalk River, with a shark tank, seals and a research vessel that takes people out on Long Island Sound.
Reviews: The touch tanks and the seal feeding are the hits; the harbor cruise is the add on and the building itself is a nice piece of industrial reuse.

Uniqueness: The Hale family farmhouse where the 21 year old schoolteacher who said he had only one life to give grew up, with period rooms and a heritage breed farm.
Reviews: The house tour ties the famous last words to a real family; the grounds and the farmers market in summer are free.

Uniqueness: A half mile of beach with a 1940s boardwalk, a carousel, a bandshell and a bathhouse that still looks like a seaside postcard.
Reviews: The boardwalk and the ice cream stand are the tradition; parking is the cost and the beach is calm and shallow.

Uniqueness: The first state park in Connecticut, 238 acres of beach and salt marsh on Long Island Sound with a nature center and a September 11 memorial garden.
Reviews: The beach is wide and the parking is the only cost; the marsh boardwalk is quiet and good for birds at low tide.

Uniqueness: Four thousand acres of woods, ponds and boardwalks around a small nature museum with live owls and a working weather station.
Reviews: The boardwalk and the owls are good with children; the trails are flat and the museum is small enough for an hour.

Uniqueness: A nature center in the Red Clay valley with trails through meadow and woods, a hawk watch and a stream for children to explore.
Reviews: The hawk watch in fall is the local birding event and the trails are easy; it is quiet on weekdays.

Uniqueness: A quiet half mile boardwalk with a bandstand, a totem pole and a beach that is calmer than Rehoboth's, in a town that bans alcohol on the sand.
Reviews: Families choose it for the calm water and the quiet; the boardwalk is a walk, not a carnival, and parking is free but tight.

Typical Customer: Art people, decorative arts fans, families
Uniqueness: A collection of Delaware valley furniture and silver from the 18th and 19th centuries, in a row of historic houses on the Dover green.
Reviews: Furniture people call it a serious collection and it is free or nearly so; it is small and the period rooms are the charm.

Uniqueness: A 14 mile sea level canal across the Delmarva peninsula with a bike trail along the towpath and ships passing close enough to see the crew.
Reviews: The ship watching is the reason to stop and the trail is flat; the canal is one of the busiest in the country.

Uniqueness: A barrier beach between the ocean and Rehoboth Bay, with a surfing beach on the inlet side, a fishing pier and a campground under the bridge.
Reviews: The inlet is where the surf is consistent and the bay side is flat for kayaks; the bridge traffic in summer is the local joke.

Uniqueness: A quiet barrier beach at the southern end of the state, between the ocean and Little Assawoman Bay, with a surf beach and a fishing area.
Reviews: The beach is less crowded than Rehoboth and the bay side is calm; parking is the only cost and the state line is a short walk.

Uniqueness: A state park without land, a walking trail through Dover's colonial and state buildings including the old state house and the green.
Reviews: The guided walks are the way to see inside the buildings and they run on weekends; the trail is flat and free.

Typical Customer: House tour people, history fans, families
Uniqueness: A Federal mansion in the old colonial capital, with original wallpaper, a riverside garden and a collection of silver and furniture.
Reviews: The house is the tour and the town of New Castle is the walk; the guides connect it to the state's colonial history.

Uniqueness: A Victorian camp of mediums and healers in the pine scrub, with a bookstore, a hotel and readings you can book like a haircut.
Reviews: Skeptics and believers both enjoy the earnest weirdness; readings vary wildly in quality. Walk the lake at dusk.

Uniqueness: A 800 foot pier over the Atlantic with restaurants, a surf shop and a view back at the space center launches.
Reviews: Good for a walk and a drink, and the surf below is beginner friendly. Parking costs.

Uniqueness: A rehabilitation center for injured birds and small wildlife, with pelicans, owls, eagles and a turtle pond, run by volunteers.
Reviews: Small and free, with staff who explain each animal's story. Good for kids.

Uniqueness: A coastal spring and salt marsh park with a deep spring, paddling trails and a boardwalk, hidden behind the commercial strip.
Reviews: The spring is a surprise and the paddle is quiet. Bring bug spray.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square with a fountain, a theater, coffee shops and a music venue, next to a university campus in west Georgia.
Reviews: The square is the town's living room, busy on weekday mornings and cool on summer nights.

Uniqueness: A 150 acre farmers market with sheds of peaches, greens and tomatoes sold by the growers, plus a garden center and a meat market.
Reviews: Go early in summer for peaches and boiled peanuts. It is a working market, not a boutique, which is the appeal.

Uniqueness: Nearly fifty years of a festival built on the eastern diamondback, with captive snakes, a milking demonstration, wildlife exhibits and a parade, run with the state DNR on handling and conservation.
Reviews: The snake handling demonstration is the draw and it is genuinely educational, not a stunt show. Busy on Saturday.

Uniqueness: A driving and walking route through rice plantations, Liberty ships, a Civil War fort and the remains of Henry Ford's experimental southern town, with markers at each stop.
Reviews: Ford built a whole village here in the 1920s and almost nobody outside the county knows. The trail signposts it well enough to do on your own.

Uniqueness: An 1891 covered bridge over a shoal on Coheelee Creek, the southernmost surviving covered bridge in the United States and one of the few in Georgia still standing on its original site.
Reviews: Nine miles off the highway and almost always empty. The falls below the bridge are the reason people stay longer than they planned.

Uniqueness: The story of Crawford Long, the Georgia doctor who used ether to remove a tumour in 1842 and did not publish for seven years, losing the credit to a Boston dentist.
Reviews: A small museum that tells a genuinely important and slightly tragic story well. Medical visitors leave annoyed on his behalf.

Season / Dates: Year round, flowers April to June
Uniqueness: Six hundred acres of longleaf pine and seepage bog where thousands of white-topped pitcher plants stand in the open, holding rainwater and whatever insects fell in.
Reviews: The boardwalk makes it easy and the pitcher plants are dense enough to photograph without hunting. Best in spring when they flower, and the frogs are deafening.

Uniqueness: A village storefront packed with original uniforms, a drum carried by a boy soldier, and Mary Surratt's bonnet, one of the few personal effects of a Lincoln conspirator on display anywhere.
Reviews: Visitors call it a cabinet of real things rather than a storyboard museum. The Surratt bonnet is what they mention on the way out.

Uniqueness: Ashburn decided its worst pest was its best brand and built a whole festival on it, with a parade, a carnival, a 5K and a pageant named for the fire ant.
Reviews: Thirty years in, it is the county's biggest weekend and the T shirts are the souvenir. Free to walk in, rides cost extra.

Uniqueness: A wetland preserve with boardwalks and a paved path, connected to the city's 100 mile golf cart trail system.
Reviews: Flat, shady and full of turtles and herons. Rent a golf cart and use the paths, which is the local way.

Uniqueness: Canoe and kayak rentals on the Flint from a riverside campground, with a shuttle and a long run that starts at the Radium Springs landing and takes you past limestone bluffs and sandbars.
Reviews: The eight mile run is the standard and takes about three hours at a drift. Bring water, there is almost no shade on the gravel bars in July.

Uniqueness: A marina and campground on Lake Eufaula with a fishing pier, boat rentals and a boardwalk, in the far west corner of the state.
Reviews: The lake is huge and the park is quiet midweek. Good bass fishing and a decent restaurant at the marina.

Uniqueness: A state park on Lake Eufaula with a lodge, a golf course, a marina and a beach, at the end of a peninsula in southwest Georgia.
Reviews: The lodge is dated but the lake setting is excellent, and the golf course is a bargain.

Uniqueness: Fifty years of a festival in Georgia's blueberry capital, with fresh berries, a pie contest, a parade and a 5K at Goldwasser Park.
Reviews: The berries sold at the park are picked that week and priced like a farm stand, not a festival. Go early before the flats run out.

Uniqueness: Sylvester calls itself the Peanut Capital of the World and closes the middle of town for two days of boiled peanuts, a parade and a recipe contest in Jeffords Park.
Reviews: Boiled peanuts by the bucket and a hometown parade that fills the route. It is the county's homecoming more than a tourist event.

Uniqueness: An Art Deco house on the brick main street with one of three theatre organs still in its original building in Georgia, a 1926 Barton that gets played before films.
Reviews: First run movies at small town prices in a room with a real balcony. The organ nights are the ones to catch.

Uniqueness: A courthouse square with antebellum houses, a 19th century jail and a main street that has kept its brick storefronts, near Lake Oconee.
Reviews: Quiet and well kept, with a good coffee stop on the square. The old jail is the curiosity.

Uniqueness: A 1921 grist mill still standing at the edge of a 225 acre lake, with the original machinery inside, a campground under the pines and a boat ramp onto the mill pond.
Reviews: The mill is open for tours on weekends and still looks ready to run. Small park, big cypress, and quiet except in deer season.

Uniqueness: A peninsula of pines on Lake Hartwell with a beach, a boat ramp and campsites close to the water, fifteen minutes from the dam that made the lake.
Reviews: The swimming beach and the lakeside sites are why people book. Bass and striper fishing is the other reason.

Adventure: Hudgens Center for Art and Learning
Uniqueness: A community art center with galleries, studios and classes, showing regional artists and teaching pottery and painting to anyone who signs up.
Reviews: Free or cheap, with changing shows and a real studio program. Check the class schedule if you want to make something.

Season / Dates: Year round, warmest April to October
Uniqueness: A flooded Flint River valley where dead cypress stand in open water, so you can idle a boat between gray trunks that died when the dam went in and never rotted.
Reviews: The cypress water is the picture everyone takes. Fishing for crappie is the reason a lot of people keep a boat here.

Uniqueness: A roadside farm market on Highway 82 that has sold melons, preserves, casseroles and boiled peanuts for thirty years, with a pumpkin patch and corn maze in autumn.
Reviews: The casseroles and the fried pies are what people drive for. It gets shoulder to shoulder on October weekends.

Uniqueness: A preserved battlefield and farm where the last major cavalry battle of the Atlanta campaign was fought, with earthworks, a museum and a walking trail.
Reviews: Quiet and free, with a small museum that explains the cavalry fight. Good for a history hour off the interstate.

Uniqueness: A square of antebellum and Victorian buildings with a gold dome courthouse, independent shops and a restaurant row, in a town that calls itself the City of Homes.
Reviews: The architecture is the draw and the square is walkable. Look for the old theater and the court square fountain.

Uniqueness: A Victorian main street with a train depot, a theater, antique shops and a restaurant row, plus a concert series on the depot lawn.
Reviews: The train still comes through downtown, which delights kids. The antique shops are the browse.

Uniqueness: A nature center on a bend of the Chattahoochee with live reptiles, a pollinator garden and trails through bottomland forest, run by the university.
Reviews: Cheap, hands on and good with kids. The snake room is the highlight and the trails are flat.

Uniqueness: A complete cotton mill village with brick worker houses, a company store and the mill buildings along the Yellow River, much of it still standing.
Reviews: The scale of the village is the story, and the old store is being reused. Quiet and photogenic.

Uniqueness: Preserved earthworks and a walking trail across the ground where the first big battle of the Atlanta Campaign was fought in May 1864, with the Union and Confederate lines still visible in the woods.
Reviews: Recently preserved and lightly visited, with good interpretive signs and a loop that follows the trenches. Free and open at daylight.

Uniqueness: A campground on the bank of Lake Seminole under big hardwoods, with a swimming beach and a boat ramp a hundred yards from the tent pads, and alligators in the shallows.
Reviews: People camp here to fish at daylight, and the lakeside sites are the ones to ask for. Quiet, cheap and full of birds.

Uniqueness: The original Six Flags park, with a wooden coaster from 1967, a hypercoaster and a water park next door, forty minutes from downtown.
Reviews: Go on a weekday and buy the flash pass if you care about coasters. The food is what it is, and the parking lot is enormous.

Uniqueness: A museum of the southern pine forest with a walk through a simulated swamp, logging equipment and the story of the turpentine and pulp industries.
Reviews: Small and old fashioned, with a great snake exhibit. A good rainy day stop with kids.

Uniqueness: A grid of 19th century houses and oak shade on the St. Marys River, the oldest town in Georgia and the ferry landing for Cumberland Island.
Reviews: The waterfront and the old houses make an easy hour, and the ferry runs from the park downtown.

Uniqueness: The world's largest exposed granite monolith, carved with a Confederate memorial the size of a football field, surrounded by a theme park and a laser show.
Reviews: The hike up is a genuine workout with a great view; the carving is historically fraught and the park is unapologetically kitschy.

Season / Dates: Every Tuesday and Saturday, year round
Uniqueness: An open air flea market on the highway that has run twice a week since 1976, with produce, tools, chickens, cast iron and whatever came out of somebody's barn that week.
Reviews: Get there before seven for the good tools. It is a genuine country trade day, not a curated antique fair.

Uniqueness: An outdoor amphitheater on the square with a summer concert series, lawn seats and a lineup of regional rock, country and soul acts.
Reviews: Bring a chair and arrive early for a good spot. The sound is solid and the crowd is local.

Uniqueness: A dive bar in the basement of a shuttered hotel where the dancers are over forty, the drinks are cheap and the walls are covered in decades of stickers and bras.
Reviews: It is not for everyone and it knows it. People either love the lack of polish or leave in ten minutes. Cash only.

Uniqueness: The world's largest drive in, open since 1928, where the counter staff shout What'll ya have and the chili dogs and frosted oranges have not changed.
Reviews: It is an institution, not a quiet meal. Order the chili dog and a frosted orange, and do not ask for a menu at the counter.

Uniqueness: An outdoor amphitheater on the square with a summer concert series, lawn seating and a small town crowd.
Reviews: Bring a blanket and a cooler. The shows are affordable and the sound is good for an outdoor room.

Uniqueness: A 1935 Art Deco movie house on Main Street, restored and running again as a performing arts venue with a neon marquee that lights up the block.
Reviews: The room is small enough that a touring country or tribute act feels close. Sightlines from the balcony are good and tickets stay cheap.

Typical Customer: House museum people, stagecoach history readers
Uniqueness: A stagecoach inn and tavern on the old road to the gold country, with the original detached kitchen, slave quarters and a dining room set for travellers who arrived by coach.
Reviews: Guided tours only and worth timing your day around. The detached kitchen and the dependencies explain more than the big house does.

Uniqueness: The career of the Georgia Peach in his own hometown, with his 1907 batting champion medal, bats, uniforms and a frank account of a man remembered as much for his temper as his .366 average.
Reviews: Small rooms, real artifacts, and the museum does not sand off the difficult parts. Baseball people say it is better than they expected.

Uniqueness: A narrow gauge train through a working plantation where you feed the pigs and pick fruit, ending at a 1930s plantation house.
Reviews: Children love the animals and the ride and the rum tasting at the manor is for the adults; the train is short and the grounds are pretty.

Uniqueness: A working farm with a tram tour through tropical crops, a duck pond and a restaurant that cooks what grows on the grounds.
Reviews: The tram is good with children and the farm-to-table restaurant is the reason adults come back; the zip line is the add on.

Uniqueness: A museum in Julia Davis Park with a strong collection of American art and a sculpture garden, next to the zoo and the state historical museum.
Reviews: The sculpture garden and the rotating contemporary shows are the draw; it is small enough for an hour and the park is the rest of the afternoon.

Uniqueness: A museum with a giant short faced bear, a saber tooth cat and the fossils of the Snake River plain, on the Pocatello campus.
Reviews: The Ice Age mammals are the family draw and the collection is serious; it is small and cheap.

Uniqueness: A sandstone capitol with a marble dome covered in native copper, and a law library in the basement that looks like a Victorian club.
Reviews: The dome and the original chambers are the tour and it is free; the basement library is the room people photograph.

Uniqueness: A regional museum with a walk through Idaho history, a children's discovery area and traveling exhibits, in a converted warehouse downtown.
Reviews: The history walk is good with children and the traveling shows are the reason locals return; it is small and cheap.

Uniqueness: A natural history museum with Jane, a juvenile T. rex, and a working paleontology lab, on the Rock River.
Reviews: Jane is the reason children ask to come and the lab is where visitors can watch preparation; the museum is small and cheap.

Uniqueness: A Japanese house and tea garden on the university campus, used for tea ceremonies and open to walk through.
Reviews: The garden is the quiet corner of campus and the tea ceremonies need booking; it is free and small.

Uniqueness: A combined art, history and science museum on the Illinois River with a giant screen theater and a dome planetarium.
Reviews: The riverfront view and the planetarium are the reasons to go and the galleries are small; the museum is good with children on a rainy day.

Uniqueness: A Moorish revival villa on the bluffs above the Mississippi, built by a wealthy traveler who never lived in it, with a courtyard and a view of the river.
Reviews: The house is strange and photogenic and the river view is the reason to climb the hill; the tour is short and the restoration is ongoing.

Uniqueness: The museum and baking store of the baking powder company, with the history of the product, a soda fountain and a test kitchen.
Reviews: The soda fountain and the free museum are the stops and the baking aisle is a bargain; it is a quick detour in downtown Terre Haute.

Uniqueness: A museum with a strong print and glass collection, in a modern building on Main Street, with a studio space for visitors.
Reviews: The print collection and the contemporary glass are the highlights; it is small enough for an hour and the café is a local stop.

Uniqueness: The largest lake in Indiana, with arms running into wooded hills, a beach and a state forest around it.
Reviews: The lake is the summer water for Bloomington and the coves are quiet on weekdays; the wind comes up and the water gets rough.

Typical Customer: History families, road trippers, western fans
Uniqueness: A museum in Buffalo Bill Cody's birthplace town with his saddle, letters and a paddlewheel steamboat exhibit, on the Mississippi.
Reviews: The steamboat and the Cody memorabilia are the two rooms and the town is a good stop; it is small and cheap.

Typical Customer: Theater people, families, Meredith Willson fans
Uniqueness: A recreation of the River City main street from The Music Man, with a boyhood home and a museum on Meredith Willson, in his hometown.
Reviews: The set and the story are the draw and the summer musical is the local event; it is small and specific.

Uniqueness: A brick street that climbs a hill in five switchbacks, built in 1894 and called the crookedest street in the world, in a Mississippi river town.
Reviews: The drive up or walk down is the fun and the comparison with Lombard Street is the joke; it takes ten minutes and the neighborhood is historic.

Uniqueness: A frontier post on the Smoky Hill with four original stone buildings and the story of the Buffalo Soldiers stationed here.
Reviews: The stone buildings are original and the guides tell the Black troop history; it is small and cheap.

Uniqueness: A zoo in a 100 acre park with elephants, big cats and a walk through aviary, free or nearly free in a town of 26,000.
Reviews: The price and the shade make it a good stop on Highway 50; the zoo is small but the animals are well kept.

Uniqueness: Three hundred acres of prairie, woodland and formal gardens with a children's discovery garden and a sculpture walk.
Reviews: The prairie and the children's garden are the reasons to come and the trails are easy; the spring wildflowers are the peak.

Adventure: Prairie Museum of Art and History
Uniqueness: A museum with a 1930s sod house, a barn and a main street of pioneer buildings, plus a gallery of western art.
Reviews: The sod house and the buildings are good with children and the art is a surprise; it is a good break on Interstate 70.

Uniqueness: A zoo on the prairie with a walk through rainforest building, giraffes and a museum of wildlife art in the same complex.
Reviews: The rainforest building is the winter stop and the giraffe feeding is the family hit; it is bigger than expected for a town of 47,000.

Uniqueness: A brick fort on the Mississippi below New Orleans, used in the Civil War and later as a prison, with a moat and a river view.
Reviews: The fort is weathered and quiet, and the river is right there. A good stop on the way to the delta.

Adventure: Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul
Uniqueness: A granite French Gothic church with a 160 foot tower and rose windows, built by French Canadian mill workers in a mill town.
Reviews: The scale is a surprise in a small city and it is free to look; it is an active parish, so avoid Mass times.

Uniqueness: A working waterfront with a footbridge, a farmers market, a boatyard and a rail trail along the bay, in a town that rebuilt itself around its harbor.
Reviews: The coop and the harbor walk are the local ritual; the town is quieter than Camden and the sailing school takes beginners.

Uniqueness: A hangar of Maine snowplows, logging trucks, fire engines and a 1920s bus, put together by a truck dealer who bought back the state's working vehicles.
Reviews: The snowplow and logging equipment are the local history; the military hall next door is separate and free.

Uniqueness: A university anthropology museum with a strong Wabanaki collection, birchbark canoes and baskets, free and open to the public.
Reviews: The Wabanaki baskets and the Penobscot canoe are the highlights; it is small and the staff are helpful.

Uniqueness: A paved trail along the Kennebec from Gardiner to Augusta, past shipyards, a paper mill and the river where the state's shipbuilding began.
Reviews: The Bath waterfront and the river views are the reason to ride; the trail is flat and connects to downtown Bath.

Typical Customer: History walkers, Stephen King readers, photographers
Uniqueness: A Victorian garden cemetery on a hill above Bangor where Hannibal Hamlin is buried and the gates and stone chapels appear in Stephen King's fiction.
Reviews: King readers come for the locations and historians come for the Civil War generals; the self guided map is at the gate.

Typical Customer: Labor history people, local families, students
Uniqueness: A museum in a former shoe shop telling the story of the mills that drew French Canadian, Greek and Somali workers to Lewiston, with the machines still threaded.
Reviews: The oral histories are the exhibit and the volunteers are often former mill workers; it is small and personal.

Uniqueness: A canal town split by the Chesapeake and Delaware Canal, with a high bridge over the cut, a waterfront of 19th century houses and ships passing at eye level.
Reviews: People stop to watch the ships from the bridge and stay for lunch; the town is small, the canal museum is free and the walk is flat.

Uniqueness: Five thousand acres of rolling fields and woods on the Delaware line, with horse trails, a steeplechase course and fox hunting country.
Reviews: The spring and fall race meets are the local event and the trails are quiet; the fields are open and the ticks are real.

Adventure: Harriet Tubman Museum and Educational Center
Uniqueness: A community museum in downtown Cambridge with Tubman's story, local African American history and the murals that led to the larger state park.
Reviews: The volunteers are descendants and local historians and the museum is small; it pairs with the Tubman visitor center 15 miles away.

Uniqueness: The oldest privately operated ferry in the country, a small boat that carries cars and bicycles across the Tred Avon between two colonial towns.
Reviews: The crossing is ten minutes and the point is the ride; cyclists use it to loop the Talbot county back roads.

Uniqueness: A point where the Potomac meets the Chesapeake, with a Civil War prison camp cemetery, a lighthouse and a beach on the bay.
Reviews: The prison history is grim and the markers are quiet; the fishing pier and campground are why locals come back.

Uniqueness: A lake in a gap of the Allegheny Mountains with a sandy beach, a lodge and trails up to rocky overlooks, just off Interstate 68.
Reviews: The lake swim is the summer draw and the canyon trail is the hike; the lodge and casino make it a weekend base.

Adventure: Washington County Museum of Fine Arts
Company / Access: Washington County Museum of Fine Arts
Uniqueness: A small museum in a city park with American and European painting, including a Singer Sargent, free or nearly free.
Reviews: The collection is better than a town this size suggests and the park setting is pleasant; it is quiet and the staff are welcoming.

Uniqueness: A brewery, winery and distillery in a gray shingled barn outside town, with picnic tables, oyster shucking and live music on summer afternoons.
Reviews: The outdoor scene is the point and the island prices are real; go early, the tasting room fills after three.

Typical Customer: Families with small children, train people
Uniqueness: A narrow gauge railroad built to run through cranberry bogs, with a steam engine, a holiday lights season and rides scaled for children under ten.
Reviews: The Christmas lights train is the tradition and the summer crowd is thin; parents say one visit a year is enough for older children.

Typical Customer: True crime people, history fans, ghost hunters
Uniqueness: The 1892 house where the Borden murders happened, now a bed and breakfast, with a tour that walks the rooms and lays out the evidence.
Reviews: Guides present the case without pretending to solve it; overnight guests report things and the tour is more history than haunt.

Uniqueness: A three mile sand spit that looks back at Plymouth's waterfront and out to the Gurnet lighthouse, with warm shallow water on the bay side.
Reviews: Locals park at the town lot and walk on; the tip at the Gurnet is the walk and the beach is quieter than the Cape.

Uniqueness: A college museum with a Degas, a Mondrian and a room of African textiles, free to the public and small enough to see before lunch.
Reviews: Locals treat it as a free hour; the contemporary galleries rotate often and the print room is open by appointment.

Typical Customer: Families with young children, school groups
Uniqueness: A science center in a 1907 firehouse with water play, a maker space and a physics floor, scaled for children under ten.
Reviews: Parents like that everything can be touched and the water room is the hit; it is small and easiest on weekday mornings.

Uniqueness: The only freshwater aquarium in the country, with a walk through tunnel under Lake Superior fish, otters and a river otter slide.
Reviews: The otters and the tunnel are the family stops and the freshwater focus makes it different from a coastal aquarium; it is on the Duluth harbor.

Uniqueness: An indoor amusement park with a log flume and roller coasters in the middle of a shopping mall, plus an aquarium and a LEGO store.
Reviews: The park is better than it has any right to be; it is a suburban temple of consumerism and kids love it. Weekdays are calmer.

Uniqueness: A dinner train along the St. Croix valley in restored 1940s cars, leaving from a Stillwater depot.
Reviews: The dome car and the river view are the reason to ride and the brunch run is the family one; book ahead for the fall color weekends.

Uniqueness: A nature center built into a limestone quarry with trails through oak woods, a cave and a pond, free and open to the public.
Reviews: The cave and the trails are good with children and it is free; the center has live animals and a bird viewing room.

Uniqueness: A neighborhood of restored mill cottages, bars and restaurants next to the Mississippi State campus, rebuilt after a tornado.
Reviews: The district is walkable and busy on game weekends. Good for a casual dinner.

Uniqueness: The boyhood home of the playwright, with family furniture, photographs and the bedroom where he wrote his first stories.
Reviews: Small and personal, best for theater people. The Columbus historic district around it is worth a walk.

Uniqueness: A river museum and boardwalk on the Mississippi with aquariums of river fish, a replica of a 19th century riverboat and a nature trail.
Reviews: The riverboat and the boardwalk are the family stops and the river is right there; the casinos across the road are the other Tunica.

Uniqueness: A university museum with ancient Greek pottery, a mummy and American painting, free in a building on the Columbia campus.
Reviews: The ancient collection is the surprise and the museum is free; it is small and the campus is a pleasant walk.

Uniqueness: A reservoir on the Beaverhead where Lewis and Clark camped, with trophy rainbow trout and a campground on the shore below the Tendoy Mountains.
Reviews: Fishermen come for the big rainbows below the dam and the lake is quiet; the wind makes afternoon boating a chore.

Uniqueness: A concrete dam 422 feet high on the Kootenai with a visitor center, a tour inside the powerhouse and a reservoir that runs 90 miles into Canada.
Reviews: The tour into the dam is the reason to stop and the lake is beautiful; it is free and the guides explain the flood control.

Typical Customer: House tour people, history fans, families
Uniqueness: A 1903 sandstone mansion built by a cattle and banking family, with original furnishings, a ballroom and a staircase that curves three stories.
Reviews: The woodwork and the family story are the tour; the October ghost tours are the local tradition.

Uniqueness: Thirty eight vintage cars buried nose down in a circle to replicate Stonehenge, built by a farmer as a family reunion joke and now a beloved landmark.
Reviews: It is exactly as good as the premise; free and quick. The visitor center explains the replica's solstice alignments.

Uniqueness: Pine covered buttes and a canyon in the Pine Ridge, the oldest state park in Nebraska, with trails to a lookout and a swimming pool in summer.
Reviews: The ponderosa forest feels like the Black Hills and the park is quiet; the trails are steep and the pool is a summer bonus.

Uniqueness: A state park on the Platte with a lodge, a water park, horseback trails and a theater, built as a flagship park between Omaha and Lincoln.
Reviews: The activity center and the pool are the family draw and the trails are easy; it is busy on summer weekends.

Uniqueness: A building that spans Interstate 80, with a museum on the overland trails that crossed here, from the Oregon Trail to the Lincoln Highway.
Reviews: The architecture is the novelty and the exhibits are better than a roadside attraction needs to be; the view over the interstate is strange and fun.

Uniqueness: A museum of dryland farming on the high plains with a collection of tractors, a windmill yard and a restored 1900s farmstead.
Reviews: The machinery and the farmstead are good with children and the volunteers know the history; it pairs with Scotts Bluff.

Uniqueness: A silver boom town climbing a canyon wall on the Loneliest Road, with a church, a castle and brick ruins stacked above the highway.
Reviews: The drive through town is the attraction and the grid of streets is steep; it is a good leg stretch on Highway 50.

Typical Customer: History people, music fans, road trippers
Uniqueness: A restored 1880 opera house in a silver mining town of 500 people, with painted scenery, a horseshoe balcony and a season of concerts and plays.
Reviews: The room is the attraction and the acoustics are good; call ahead, it is not open every day.

Uniqueness: A four story 1876 schoolhouse with original desks and chalkboards, built for 1,000 students when Virginia City was one of the richest towns in America.
Reviews: The building is the exhibit and the classrooms are intact; the top floor view of the town and the mountains is the bonus.

Typical Customer: Military history people, road trippers, families
Uniqueness: A museum of artillery, bombs and ammunition from the naval depot that stored munitions here for decades, with rows of shells and a atomic cannon shell.
Reviews: The scale of the collection is what people remember and the volunteers are veterans; it is free and takes an hour.

Company / Access: Carson City Convention and Visitors Bureau
Uniqueness: A walking tour of the state capital's Victorian houses and the governor's mansion, with a audio guide and a cemetery where the city's founders are buried.
Reviews: The self guided map is free at the visitors center and the October ghost walk is the local tradition; most of the trail is flat.

Uniqueness: A desert reservoir on the Carson River with sandy beaches, cottonwood groves and good fishing for walleye and catfish.
Reviews: The beaches are the summer swim and the river inlet is the fishing spot; the water level varies a lot year to year.

Uniqueness: A diner and motel on the Extraterrestrial Highway at the edge of Area 51, with alien murals, a gift shop and a burger named after the nearby base.
Reviews: The owner tells the stories and the walls are covered in visitor tags; it is a long empty drive and the diner is the only thing for 50 miles.

Uniqueness: A three story stone tower built by a silver baron as a summer home, abandoned after a few months and now standing over the Reese River valley.
Reviews: The story is better than the ruin and the view down the valley is the reason to climb the short hill; it is a ten minute stop.

Typical Customer: History families, rev war people, school groups
Uniqueness: A reconstructed palisade fort and village on the Connecticut River where settlers held out during King George's War, with period gardens and livestock.
Reviews: The reenactment weekends are the time to go; on ordinary days the fort is quiet and the guides have time to talk.

Uniqueness: A old fashioned seaside strip of fried dough, arcades, a bandshell and a wide sand beach, with the state's biggest free summer fireworks on Wednesdays.
Reviews: It is loud and crowded and that is the point; parking is the hassle and the north beach is quieter.

Company / Access: Society for the Protection of New Hampshire Forests
Uniqueness: The stone staircase and foundations of a costume designer's castle in the woods, with a trail to a swimming pond and an old quarry.
Reviews: The staircase is the photograph everyone takes; the trail is short and the pond is a local swimming hole in summer.

Uniqueness: A planetarium and science center named for the teacher who died on Challenger and the first American in space, with a Mercury capsule and a full dome theater.
Reviews: The planetarium shows are the draw and the exhibits are best for ages six to twelve; the building is next to the state technical college.

Uniqueness: A two screen drive-in in the woods north of Nashua, with a playground under the screen and double features that run past midnight.
Reviews: Cash only at the snack bar and the early show fills; bring a battery radio if your car stereo is not great.

Uniqueness: A ski mountain inside a state park with a view of Lake Sunapee from the summit and a beginner area that is genuinely separate from the expert runs.
Reviews: Families like the layout and the lodge; the summit chair is the scenic ride in fall and the state beach is across the road.

Uniqueness: A 1950s Christmas theme park in the White Mountains with a reindeer herd, a train through the woods and a bakery that sells gingerbread all summer.
Reviews: Parents call it the cleanest small park they have visited; children under eight are the right age and the reindeer are real.

Uniqueness: A nursery rhyme theme park in the White Mountains with a wooden coaster, a pirate ship and a pumpkin coach, scaled for small children and shaded by real trees.
Reviews: Parents say it is the right size for a first park and the lines are short before noon; teenagers will be bored by two.

Uniqueness: A shark tunnel you walk under, a hippo exhibit with underwater viewing and a touch tank of stingrays, on the Camden waterfront across from Philadelphia.
Reviews: The hippos and the shark tunnel are the hits; tickets are cheaper online and the garage is the easiest parking.

Uniqueness: A brick 1849 lighthouse at the mouth of the Maurice River, surrounded by marsh and one of the best shorebird staging areas on the Delaware Bay.
Reviews: In May the horseshoe crabs and red knots draw birders from other countries; the lighthouse opens on select weekends and the road is gravel.

Uniqueness: The bluff where Washington's army built a fort to block the Hudson, with reconstructed huts and a cliff edge view of the George Washington Bridge.
Reviews: The view is the reason to stop and the history is the bonus; the cliff trail below is a separate walk with real exposure.

Uniqueness: An 1890s harbor defense fort on the Delaware with concrete batteries you can walk through, a ferry to a island fort and a river beach.
Reviews: The batteries are open and dark and children love them; the ferry to Pea Patch Island and Fort Delaware runs in summer.

Uniqueness: The ironworks village where Samuel Morse demonstrated the telegraph in 1838, with the original factory building, a wheelwright shop and a working letterpress.
Reviews: The telegraph story is the hook and the volunteers demonstrate it; the site is small and best combined with Jockey Hollow.

Uniqueness: Twin canal towns facing each other across the Delaware, with antique shops, a 1830s mule drawn canal boat and a footbridge over the river.
Reviews: The walk across the bridge and the canal towpath are the easy pleasure; weekends are busy and the shops close early.

Uniqueness: A rock garden built into a wooded ravine with a stream, ponds and paths that switchback through alpine plants, hidden behind a suburban office park.
Reviews: Gardeners call it the best small garden in the state; spring is the peak and the paths are steep and narrow.

Uniqueness: A tidal river through the Pine Barrens with a marked water trail past osprey nests, a lighthouse and the old glassmaking town of Millville.
Reviews: The water is flat and the birds are the draw; check the tide, since the river runs both ways and low tide exposes mud.

Uniqueness: The bluff above the Delaware where a 1777 fort held off a Hessian attack, with earthworks, the Whitall House and a view across to Philadelphia International.
Reviews: The archaeology dig that found soldiers' remains made news; the park is free and the river path is a good evening walk.

Typical Customer: House tour people, history fans, gardeners
Uniqueness: A 51 room ironmaster's mansion in the Ramapo hills with period rooms, a walled garden and the forges and mines that armed the Revolution nearby.
Reviews: The house tour is the only way in and the guides know the families; the state park trails behind it are free and quiet.

Uniqueness: A colonial house with a Gothic revival addition where Aaron Burr married, with original wallpaper and a story that runs from the Revolution to the Gilded Age.
Reviews: The guides know the family scandals and the house is small; it is a quiet hour and the garden is free to walk.

Adventure: Thomas Edison Center at Menlo Park
Company / Access: Thomas Alva Edison Memorial Tower Corporation
Typical Customer: Science people, families, local history fans
Uniqueness: A 131 foot Art Deco tower of Edison's light bulb on the site of his Menlo Park lab, with a small museum of phonographs and early bulbs.
Reviews: The tower is visible from the highway and the museum is one room; locals bring visiting engineers and the ranger talk is good.

Uniqueness: The modest Camden row house where Whitman spent his last eight years, with his bedroom as it was and the printing press that kept him solvent.
Reviews: The guides read the poems in the rooms and the house is small; it is the most personal literary site in the state.

Uniqueness: Two thousand acres of forest with a lake, a nature center and the Deserted Village of Feltville, an 1840s mill town abandoned and still standing in the woods.
Reviews: The deserted village is the strange draw and the lake trail is the easy walk; the nature center has live animals for children.

Uniqueness: A natural stone bowl above the road where the echo comes back clearly, with a short trail to the base of the cliff.
Reviews: It is a ten minute stop on the drive to Ghost Ranch and people shout into it; the picnic tables and the red rock are the rest.

Uniqueness: The adobe plaza founded in 1706, with the San Felipe de Neri church, a row of shops under portales and a bandstand where mariachi plays on weekends.
Reviews: It is touristy and small and the church and the plaza are worth the walk; the rattlesnake museum and the candy shop are the family stops.

Uniqueness: A ranch house and campground at the mouth of Dog Canyon on the west face of the Sacramento Mountains, with a trail into a cool canyon and desert views.
Reviews: The canyon trail is the hike and the campground has shade; it is a quiet base for White Sands 30 minutes away.

Uniqueness: Red sandstone cliffs and a box canyon just outside Gallup, with trails to petroglyphs and an amphitheater that hosts the intertribal ceremonial in August.
Reviews: The August ceremonial is the reason to time a visit and the trails are quiet otherwise; the park is a short drive off Interstate 40.

Company / Access: International UFO Museum and Research Center
Uniqueness: A former movie theater filled with affidavits, newspaper clippings, dioramas and a very serious research library about the 1947 crash that the government says was a weather balloon.
Reviews: It is cheesy and sincere and the gift shop is excellent; the alien-themed town is half the fun.

Uniqueness: A copper mining town in a canyon with a brick downtown, the Big Ditch that carries the creek under the street and a museum of the mining wars.
Reviews: The town is the base for the Gila wilderness and the historic district is a good hour; the university and the bike trail keep it alive.

Uniqueness: A visitor center at the entrance to Jemez Pueblo with a small museum of pueblo history and access to Red Rock canyon, where the pueblo's story is told by its own people.
Reviews: The center is the only way to learn about the pueblo without intruding; photography rules are strict and the red rock formations are the draw.

Uniqueness: A half mile harness track where the horses come straight at you down the stretch and a two dollar bet lasts a whole evening.
Reviews: Locals bring folding chairs to the apron and explain the betting to newcomers; the casino inside is louder than the track.

Uniqueness: A clear glacial lake below the Bristol Hills with a city beach at one end and a shoreline of docks, cottages and a few protected coves.
Reviews: Morning is flat and empty and the lake gets choppy by afternoon; rentals are at the north end and the state park launch is quieter.

Typical Customer: Seafood people, boat watchers, city escapees
Uniqueness: A Long Island Sound fishing village inside the city limits: one avenue of clam shacks, boatyards and a small nautical museum, reached by a city bus.
Reviews: Locals argue over which fried clam wins; the point is to walk the length of City Island Avenue and eat at two or three counters.

Uniqueness: A cheese shop in the town that supplied New York's cheese market for a century, with a cut to order counter, cheese curds and a viewing window into the plant.
Reviews: The curds are the reason people detour and they sell out by afternoon; the shop is small and the sandwich counter is the local lunch.

Uniqueness: The original Syracuse barbecue joint, started as a motorcycle gang's fundraiser and now a brick riverside hall with a blues stage and brisket that people drive from Albany for.
Reviews: Expect a wait on weekends and order the ribs and the salt potatoes; the live music is loud and the room is louder.

Uniqueness: The clapboard house where Hopper was born and painted the light he spent his life chasing, with his easel and a garden that faces the same south light.
Reviews: Small and personal, and the reason to come is seeing the rooms that appear in the paintings; the upstairs gallery shows young artists.

Typical Customer: History families, rev war people, school groups
Uniqueness: A rebuilt timber fort in the middle of downtown Rome where the 1777 siege turned back the British and where the treaty that opened the west was signed.
Reviews: The rangers fire the cannon in summer and the earthworks walk is short; the museum does a good job on the Oneida alliance.

Typical Customer: Families, school groups, local history people
Uniqueness: Thirty original buildings around the old county seat, with trade shops where a tinsmith and a carpenter work in front of you on weekends.
Reviews: Living history weekends are the time to go; on a quiet weekday half the buildings are locked and the visit is over in an hour.

Uniqueness: A waterfront museum with a 1890s wooden tug, a working boat shop and the story of the ice harvest and brick barges that built the river economy.
Reviews: Small and well made, and the lighthouse cruise and the tug are the reasons to check the schedule before driving over.

Adventure: Jacques Marchais Museum of Tibetan Art
Uniqueness: A stone temple built into a Staten Island hillside by a self taught collector, with a terrace pond that looks lifted out of Ladakh.
Reviews: Small, strange and peaceful; the terrace view is what people remember and several of the bronzes are genuinely old.

Uniqueness: A river otter and penguin operation on the Peconic with a shark tank you can snorkel and a butterfly room, small enough to finish before the children wear out.
Reviews: The ray touch tank and penguin encounter are the hits; the shark snorkel is the splurge and books weeks ahead in summer.

Uniqueness: A 110 foot waterfall inside the city where the Genesee cuts a gorge through 400 million year old rock, reached by a path from Maplewood Park.
Reviews: Locals treat it as a secret and warn about the unofficial trails; the official overlook is a five minute walk from the lot.

Typical Customer: TV people, families, I Love Lucy fans
Uniqueness: Lucille Ball's hometown museum with the actual Ricardo living room set, her costumes and a recreation of the chocolate factory wrapping line.
Reviews: Fans love the costumes and the set; non fans are done in an hour, and the comedy center next door is the better value.

Uniqueness: A professional musical theater in a 1930s carousel building in a state park, where Broadway actors do summer stock beside a lake.
Reviews: Locals say the productions are better than a small city deserves; bring a picnic and arrive early for the park.

Uniqueness: The worker owned vegetarian restaurant that produced the best selling cookbook of its kind, still in a converted downtown Ithaca building with a menu that changes daily.
Reviews: People arrive expecting a legend and get a busy casual room; the soups and the daily specials are the order, and the cookbook shelf is by the door.

Uniqueness: A Victorian rural cemetery on a bluff above the Hudson holding Samuel Wilson, the meat packer behind Uncle Sam, along with Civil War generals and Tiffany windows in the chapel.
Reviews: The Uncle Sam grave is the photo everyone takes; the self guided map at the gate points to the Earl Chapel, which is the real monument.

Uniqueness: The naval base that kept the American fleet on Lake Ontario during the War of 1812, with earthworks, a navy yard and a view across the harbor to the Canadian shore.
Reviews: The hilltop earthworks are the walk; the reconstructed barracks and the summer reenactment are the reason to check the calendar.

Typical Customer: Science people, history walkers, TB families
Uniqueness: The first laboratory in the country built for tuberculosis research, where the cure was studied and where the village of cure cottages outside grew up around it.
Reviews: The docents tell the story of the patients who came for the air; the lab is small and the walking tour of the cure cottages is the better half.

Uniqueness: A Spanish revival mansion on a Centerport bluff holding William Vanderbilt's natural history trophies and marine collection, plus a planetarium in the old garage court.
Reviews: The house is odd and personal in a way that sticks; planetarium shows are cheap and sunset over Northport Bay is why people linger.

Uniqueness: An 1808 Federal house museum with period rooms and a gallery of regional art, on the edge of Tarboro's colonial town common.
Reviews: The house and the common together make the visit. Small, cheap and well kept.

Uniqueness: One of the last two remaining covered bridges in North Carolina, with a rare lattice truss designed by a bridge engineer, standing in a quiet meadow.
Reviews: A five minute stop that rewards anyone who likes old structures. The truss is the interesting part.

Uniqueness: A 75 acre park with a 1911 carousel, a miniature train, a lake and a stadium, in the middle of a textile town.
Reviews: The carousel and train are a dollar or two and still run. A good cheap afternoon with small kids.

Uniqueness: A driving trail of painted quilt squares on barns and buildings across the county, part of a national folk art project.
Reviews: Pick up a map and drive the back roads. It is a good excuse to see the county, and the squares are photogenic.

Uniqueness: A county park around a 350 acre lake with a beach, boat rentals, trails and campsites, south of Charlotte.
Reviews: The beach and paddle boats are the summer draw. Quiet on weekdays and cheap.

Uniqueness: A gentle piedmont river with shoals and wooded banks, popular for tubing and canoeing below Hanging Rock.
Reviews: The float is easy and the water is warm in summer. Check the gauge and arrange a shuttle.

Uniqueness: An 1832 market house on the site of the 1789 ratification convention, where North Carolina joined the Union, now a landmark in the middle of downtown.
Reviews: The building is the photo and the history plaque is the story. A quick stop on the downtown walk.

Uniqueness: A free museum in a 1920s building with a collection of North Carolina art, American painting and a sculpture garden.
Reviews: Small, free and quietly good, with a strong regional collection. A good rainy day stop.

Adventure: Imagination Station Science and History Museum
Uniqueness: A hands on museum in a former train station with a tornado simulator, a fossil dig and a history gallery, small enough to do in an afternoon.
Reviews: Good for kids under ten, with enough to fill two hours. The train station building is part of the charm.

Uniqueness: An arts center in a converted tobacco warehouse with galleries, a theater, a children's museum and studios, beside the old mill district.
Reviews: More going on than expected for the size of the town, with cheap tickets and changing shows.

Uniqueness: A riverside park around the stone foundations of an 1840s iron furnace, with a swimming hole, a picnic area and the Dan River running through.
Reviews: The furnace ruins are the surprise and the river is the swim. Good after a Hanging Rock hike.

Uniqueness: A main street of 1920s storefronts, a granite quarry history and the Mayberry nostalgia industry, in the town that inspired the show.
Reviews: The downtown is walkable and busy with visitors. The squad car tour is the cheesy fun.

Uniqueness: A city nature park on the Tar River with a nature center, trails, a fishing lake and canoe rentals.
Reviews: The nature center has live animals and the trails are flat. Cheap and good for kids.

Uniqueness: A county museum in the 1854 courthouse, with Civil War rooms, Native American artifacts and the story of Salisbury's Confederate prison.
Reviews: The prison history is the heavy part and the exhibits do not soften it. Small and cheap.

Uniqueness: A national cemetery holding Union soldiers who died in the Salisbury prison, with rows of markers and a monument, beside the historic district.
Reviews: Quiet and sobering, with the scale of the prison deaths made visible. A short, respectful stop.

Uniqueness: A Corps recreation area on Kerr Lake with a sandy swimming beach, picnic shelters, a boat ramp and a fishing pier.
Reviews: The beach is shallow and shady, good for kids. Get there early on summer weekends.

Uniqueness: A park on a free flowing stretch of the Missouri with cottonwood forest, a canoe launch and trails through native prairie.
Reviews: The river and the big cottonwoods are the reason to camp and the birding is good; it is quiet and the nearest town is small.

Typical Customer: Families, fossil hunters, local history fans
Uniqueness: A museum with a badlands dinosaur hall, a pioneer wing and a collection of Depression glass, on the edge of the oil country.
Reviews: The dinosaur exhibits are better than a town this size deserves and the staff are local; it takes 90 minutes.

Company / Access: State Historical Society of North Dakota
Uniqueness: The frontier post where Sitting Bull surrendered in 1881, with the surviving commanding officer's quarters and the confluence of the Missouri and Yellowstone nearby.
Reviews: The one standing building and the story are the visit; the site is remote and the confluence overlook is a short drive.

Uniqueness: A wooded island campground surrounded by Devils Lake, with a boat ramp, a swim beach and some of the best walleye water in the state.
Reviews: The fishing is the draw and the campground is the base; the lake level rise has taken some of the shoreline.

Company / Access: State Historical Society of North Dakota
Uniqueness: An interpretive center where the two great rivers meet, the camp site Lewis and Clark described, with a trail to the confluence and a gallery on the fur trade.
Reviews: The view of the two rivers running side by side is the reason to come; it is free and the birding on the flats is good.

Uniqueness: A university art museum in a former student union with a sculpture court, free and showing contemporary work that rarely reaches the state.
Reviews: The sculpture court and the visiting shows are the reason to stop; it is free and the coffee bar is a local meeting spot.

Uniqueness: A 19 story art deco skyscraper capitol on the prairie, the tallest building in the state, with an observation deck and a museum in the basement.
Reviews: The observation deck and the art deco lobby are the reasons to go in; it is free and the grounds have a buffalo herd.

Uniqueness: The state fair in Minot with livestock barns, a midway, a rodeo and grandstand concerts, in the oil boom town of the north.
Reviews: The barns and the horse pulls are the real fair and the concerts draw the region; parking is a walk and the heat is real.

Uniqueness: A 63 mile drive through the wooded Sheyenne valley with a 19th century mill, a scenic overlook and one of the few forested river corridors in the state.
Reviews: The fall color is the season and the valley is a surprise after the flat prairie; the road is two lane and the towns are small.

Uniqueness: A CCC built picnic shelter and a river winding through wooded coulees, with trails and a campground 20 minutes from Grand Forks.
Reviews: The CCC shelter is the architecture and the trails are easy; it is a good half day and the fall color is the best in the region.

Uniqueness: A medieval style castle built by hand from river stones by a scoutmaster and his troop, with a dungeon, a great hall and a sword in a stone.
Reviews: It is homemade and earnest and kids love it; the story of the builder is the best part. Cheap and quick.

Uniqueness: The ruins of a pre Civil War fort on the Washita, with stone buildings, a cemetery and the story of the Chickasaw and Choctaw who settled around it.
Reviews: The ruins are evocative and the site is quiet; the reconstruction is limited and the history is the reason to stop.

Uniqueness: A hilltop park with 40 acres of azaleas, a duck pond, a miniature train and a view over Muskogee, free and open every day.
Reviews: The April azalea festival is the local event and the train is the family draw; the rest of the year it is a quiet picnic park.

Uniqueness: A museum of American wrestling with the honors court, Olympic medals and a gallery on the sport's place in Oklahoma, the state that produces champions.
Reviews: Wrestling families plan trips around it and the staff are often coaches; it is small and specific and the sport's history is deeper than outsiders expect.

Uniqueness: A museum of Southern Plains beadwork, regalia and paintings by Native artists, in the town that hosts the American Indian Exposition each August.
Reviews: The beadwork and the annual exposition are the reasons to visit; it is small and free and the artists are often there.

Uniqueness: A museum on the gorge's geology, ice age floods and the Lewis and Clark route, with live raptors and a trail into the oak woods.
Reviews: The raptor center and the flood geology are the reasons to stop; it is a good rainy day alternative to the waterfalls.

Uniqueness: A stripped classical capitol with a gold pioneer on top and a rotunda of marble, plus a tower you can climb in summer for a view of the valley.
Reviews: The tower climb and the murals in the rotunda are the two reasons to go in; it is free and the weekday sessions are open to the public.

Typical Customer: Car and truck people, families, dads
Uniqueness: A transportation museum on the Lehigh River with a Mack truck gallery, a 1950s gas station and a rotating exhibit of cars you can walk around and under.
Reviews: The truck room is what makes it different from every car museum; it is small and the admission is cheap enough for a rainy hour.

Typical Customer: Families, first time visitors, school groups
Uniqueness: A 1805 farmhouse and working farm where a guide explains Amish schooling, barn raising and plain dress, with a bus tour into the back roads.
Reviews: The house tour is better than the bus for understanding the religion; visitors say the guides answer the awkward questions honestly.

Typical Customer: House tour people, railroad history fans, families
Uniqueness: A Greek revival mansion built by the ironmaster who supplied the railroad, with period rooms and a collection on the Horseshoe Curve.
Reviews: The house and the railroad family story are the tour; the volunteers connect it to the curve and the shops.

Uniqueness: Two brick market houses from the Civil War era, one of the oldest continuously operating markets in the country, with Pennsylvania Dutch stands and a growing row of Syrian and Vietnamese counters.
Reviews: The stone building is the food hall and the brick building is the produce; go hungry and expect a line at the sandwich stands.

Uniqueness: A town mostly erased by an underground coal fire that has burned since 1962, with a few streets, a cemetery and graffiti on the closed highway, watched over by a handful of residents.
Reviews: It is eerie and quiet and you should stay on the road; the fire is still burning and the ground is unstable. A sobering detour, not a playground.

Uniqueness: A 1884 trolley park with a 1920s carousel, a steel hypercoaster and a water park on the same ticket, in the hills above Allentown.
Reviews: The water park is the summer value and the coasters are the reason enthusiasts come; weekdays in June are empty enough to loop everything.

Uniqueness: A volunteer museum in a small town with a room for each theater of the war, mannequins in original uniforms and a collection of home front ration books and letters.
Reviews: Visitors say the personal donations make it better than the big museums; it is free will donation and the volunteers are often veterans.

Uniqueness: A former revolutionary war hospital and spa village with stone buildings, an art school and a trail along the creek.
Reviews: The village is quiet and the art school studios are open to walk through; the history goes back to Washington's army.

Uniqueness: A CCC built lake and beach in the Laurel Highlands with a hemlock gorge trail and a spillway that freezes into ice climbs in winter.
Reviews: The beach is the summer draw and the gorge trail is the walk; the ice climbing at the spillway is a local winter secret.

Uniqueness: A 1,600 acre lake in the Allegheny plateau with a beach, a marina and one of the largest campgrounds in the state.
Reviews: The lake is the summer draw and the campground is the base; the park is quiet in the shoulder seasons.

Uniqueness: A town of 6,000 hosts tens of thousands at 3am on a frozen hill to watch a groundhog named Phil be consulted about spring by men in top hats.
Reviews: People describe it as the most American thing they've ever done; the cold is brutal and the actual prognostication lasts seconds.

Uniqueness: A seven story Japanese pagoda built on a Pennsylvania mountain in 1908 by a manufacturer who never saw Japan, now a landmark above the city with a view of five counties.
Reviews: It is a free oddity with a real view; the tower interior is closed most of the time and the hillside garden is where people sit.

Uniqueness: A 2,600 acre park with a paved trail along Ridley Creek and a stone mansion, in the suburbs west of Philadelphia.
Reviews: The paved trail is the easy ride and the creek is good for children; it is quiet on weekdays and busy on summer weekends.

Uniqueness: A two story brick market house with a balcony of lunch counters, where York's German farm stands became Pennsylvania Dutch lunch stands over 130 years.
Reviews: The pretzel and the chicken corn soup are the orders; it is smaller than Lancaster's and easier to actually shop.

Uniqueness: A former naval airfield turned refuge of salt ponds and grassland where ospreys and herons nest and a bike path runs to the beach.
Reviews: The trails and the salt pond are quiet and the bike path connects to the beach; the ticks are bad in summer.

Uniqueness: A small park around the reported birthplace of Andrew Jackson, with a museum, a one room schoolhouse, a lake and an equestrian statue of the young Jackson.
Reviews: The museum is better than expected and the lake is good for kids; the history is complicated and the exhibits do not hide it.

Adventure: Artesian Wells at Lee State Park
Uniqueness: Four flowing artesian wells drilled by the CCC, still running, where people fill jugs with cold mineral water in the middle of a state park.
Reviews: Locals swear by the water and bring jugs. It is a five minute stop that pairs with the park trails and the CCC stonework.

Uniqueness: A small town park with azalea beds, a duck pond, a gazebo and a sculpture garden, at its best in late March.
Reviews: The spring bloom is the reason and the park is free. Pair it with the Flowertown Festival if you are in town.

Uniqueness: A wooded park on the South Carolina side of Lake Strom Thurmond with a swimming beach, a fishing pier and trails that look over the water.
Reviews: The lake is huge and the park is quiet, especially in spring; the drive through McCormick is part of the trip.

Uniqueness: A metal sculptor's gallery and yard full of welded animals, suns and figures, where the artist works in back and sells from the front.
Reviews: The yard sculptures are the fun part and the artist is often there to talk. A good browse.

Uniqueness: A small liberal arts campus with brick buildings, a lake and the Kalmia Gardens ravine at its edge, founded by the Coker family.
Reviews: The campus is pretty and the gardens next door are the real draw. Park and walk.

Uniqueness: A one day festival in a watermelon town with a parade, a seed spitting contest, free slices and a street dance.
Reviews: It is small, hot and exactly what a town festival should be. Bring cash for the vendors and sunscreen.

Uniqueness: A week long civic festival with topiary displays, a flower show, a street dance and a concert series in the uptown square.
Reviews: The topiaries are the photo op and the street dance is the local party. Check the schedule because events are spread across the week.

Uniqueness: One of the oldest continuously running community theaters in the state, in a converted church with a small stage and a loyal company.
Reviews: The productions are ambitious for a volunteer company and the room is intimate. Check the season.

Uniqueness: A county museum with Native American pottery, a railroad room and changing art exhibits, in a converted post office downtown.
Reviews: Small but well done, and free or nearly so. The railroad and Native American rooms are the strongest.

Uniqueness: A county museum in a former school with Gullah Geechee baskets, rice culture tools and the story of the Port Royal experiment, where freed people first bought the land they farmed.
Reviews: The Gullah history is the heart of it, and the volunteers speak from family memory. Call for hours.

Typical Customer: Teens, young adults, families with older kids
Uniqueness: A woods walk haunted trail on a farm outside Bishopville, built and performed by local volunteers, with a hayride and a midway of food stalls.
Reviews: Community theater with chainsaws, and people say the trail is longer than expected. Check the weather and wear closed shoes.
